#3259. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3258. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang set to be fired, with Johny Srouji among possible replacements [U]

Following reports of a potential second affair – this time with a subordinate – Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang looks certain to be fired by the company’s board, probably later today (though he may be allowed to ‘resign’). Apple’s chief hardware officer Johny Srouji has been listed among the potential replacements, though this seems unlikely.

Update: As we predicted, he’s gone today and Kress was indeed named interim CEO …

For anyone who’s been away from the planet for the past fortnight, Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy has been the main headline news in the tech press since it came to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days.

Things got even worse yesterday when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

It was already looking inevitable that he would be fired, and the latest revelation adds to the urgency. The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was meeting last night to discuss the CEO’s future. That future at Nvidia is likely to be measured in hours rather than days.

The board now needs to find a replacement, and Bloomberg provides a rundown on some of the potential candidates. CFO Colette Kress looks likely to head the list for at least an interim appointment. The paper names a number of other possibilities, including Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji.

Srouji has led one of the most successful in-house silicon programs in the industry, overseeing the custom chips that power the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. His track record gives him deep credibility on chip design, product integration and long-term technology roadmaps. But much of his experience has been built inside Apple’s tightly controlled ecosystem, and he hasn’t been tested in the kind of high-profile salesmanship which Huang is famous for.

Given the urgency, my money is on Nvidia announcing Kress as at least interim CEO, if not a permanent replacement. It seems exceedingly unlikely that Srouji would be appointed at this time, given the in-depth negotiations and discussions that would need to take place.

As to whether he’s a potential candidate following an interim appointment, it still seems unlikely. There was an earlier report of his claimed dissatisfaction at the company, but it seems a stretch to imagine him jumping ship so soon after his promotion to chief hardware officer.

#3256. 30% of iPhone Duo buyers may have returned it, but I don’t think Apple should worry

A poll of 9to5Mac readers who were lucky enough to take delivery of their iPhone Duo in the first few days shows that 30% of them have returned it for a refund.

While that could be considered bad news for the future of the device, I don’t personally consider it either surprising or worrying …

Following a report by The Verge on iPhone Duo buyers who opted to return the device for a refund within Apple’s 14-day “no questions asked” period, we thought it would be interesting to get a sense of how many people may have done this.

9to5Mac readers were always likely to have had their fingers hovering over the pre-order button for the best shot at taking early delivery, with the first of these having hit the end of the 14-day window. We ask those of you who fall into this category to tell us whether you kept or returned the device.

With close to 6,000 total votes, the results showed that close to a third of you returned your Duo.

For any other device, that would be a disastrous return rate. For the Duo, however, I don’t think it’s terribly surprising.

I voted to say I returned it just so I could see the results. I’ve never ordered nor returned an iPhone Duo.

Not providing a way to see the results without voting will have massively skewed the results. Even if the poll were better, this is a wild claim to draw from one specific, poorly assembled assembled poll.

As we noted yesterday, Apple described the iPhone Duo as “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original.” The size of that change shows up in a whole range of ways, from the weight of the device through the changed aspect ratio of the front display to a completely new way of using an iPhone.

Throw in the extremely high price tag, and I’ve always suspected that a significant number of iPhone Duo buyers would be viewing it as an experiment rather than a committed purchase. Our own Ryan Christoffel is an example of that “try it and see” attitude. One week in, he’s reached an interim conclusion that it’s probably not for him.

For those who’ve decided to return it, a number of readers shared their reasons.

“Returned it – I can’t go back to Touch ID.”

“I want to like it, but I just can’t get there. It’s awkward, and the outside screen is way too small.”

“Returned it. Not for me. I do not want to open the phone every time I want a larger screen and Apple made the outer display much less usable than it should be with that silly permanent dock. I also use my phones left-handed.”

“During a vacation in Morocco, we spent a night camping in the Sahara Desert. I was extremely careful with the phone and tried to avoid using it in the sand altogether. However, on the second day, when I opened it inside the tent, I heard a crunching sound coming from the hinge. Sand had somehow gotten inside. I tried everything I could to clean it, but nothing worked. The inner display was still functioning perfectly, but the phone would no longer open all the way. Even worse, when I tried to close it, I had to force it shut.”

For me personally, it couldn’t be my only phone, given the priority I place on the device as a camera, but I am still lusting after it. Given the continued extended delivery times – with random checks showing shipping in late January – I don’t think Apple has much to worry about here.

#3255. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

Google and Samsung's "intelligent eyewear" AI glasses are finally launching today (Nov. 12) with designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. The Meta Ray-Ban rivals utilize Google's Gemini AI platform to bring "real-time assistance" throughout your day.

Starting at $395, intelligent eyewear costs much less than the Ray-Ban Meta (gen 3) glasses, but Meta still sells the Gen 1 and Gen 2 versions, plus a variety of styles with varying prices.

Read on to see what Google and Samsung are offering and how to pre-order a pair.

Google and Samsung partnered with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker to produce frames that are meant to look more stylish and like a normal pair of glasses.

Gentle Monster's collection includes six designs in multiple colors, including pink, dark red, gray and yellow, which can be paired with tinted, clear, blue or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster frames are more premium, with a starting price of $449.

Warby Parker's designs come in three styles — Alden, Reid and Wren — which are inspired by existing Warby Parker frames. You can choose optical or sun styles in "Pine, Saddles or Jet Black" colorways.

Prescription lenses are available for both Gentle Monster and Warby Parker options.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Google says that the frames weigh around 41 grams. For comparison, the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer design weighs 51.5 grams and the newer Aviators weigh 54.5 grams.

The glasses feature open ear speakers that can provide the Gemini voice as well as music from YouTube or audiobooks.

They do feature a 12MP ultra-wide camera for capturing photos and videos by pressing a button or asking Gemini.

Meta has faced increasing backlash over what have been deemed "pervert glasses," including increased scrutiny from international governments.

According to Google, camera visuals are not saved in your Gemini history or used for AI training or ad targeting. The company says that your data is encrypted even if it leaves the glasses for processing on your phone or in the cloud.

You have control over what apps can access the camera, as they need to ask permission, which you can revoke. Gemini history can be reviewed and deleted as needed. Though, one aspect is that you may need to go into settings and tell Gemini if your chats can be used in generative AI models.

Like Meta's glasses, an LED light turns on to indicate when the camera is recording. Similarly, the light is designed to detect tampering and prevent photos or videos.

Google claims the glasses are designed to redact faces before sending images to Gemini.

Google is bringing its Gemini AI platform to intelligent eyewear glasses. It's similar to how you would expect AI to work on smart glasses.

You can access Google apps and services hands-free by saying "Hey Gemini" or tapping the frames to ask for recommendations or learn about what the cameras can see. Examples provided by Google include adding items to your grocery list or checking your Uber status while keeping your eyes up.

During Google I/O back in May, we didn't get a chance to test out the official intelligent eyewear glasses. Google only had prototypes available, but we did try the software.

"Gemini Live is the key to making these true Ray-Ban Meta beaters, and it frankly makes Meta AI seem feeble in comparison," my colleague Jason England said at the time. "Rather than having to follow rudimentary vocal steps to do certain things, a press and hold on the stem turns it on and I’m having a full conversational interaction with the AI about the world around me."

He was able to get turn-by-turn directions using Google Maps and AI image generation using Nano Banana.

Pre-orders are now open on both the Gentle Monster and Warby Parker websites and in their retail stores. You can also pre-order directly from Google here.

If you want to wait, Intelligent eyewear will hit store shelves on December 10, where you can purchase both in-person and online.

The glasses work with Pixel and Samsung phones and even Apple's iPhones.

#3251. All Microsoft Services Are Currently Down

If you're having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you're not alone. As of early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service currently has hundreds of thousands of user reports, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports have "slowed" since their peak earlier this afternoon, but Downdetector is still showing over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes.

When I first published this article, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) The page now says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender XDR.

At the moment, the root cause isn't clear. Microsoft has been posting to its Microsoft 365 Status account on X since 12:54 p.m. ET. The company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks.

As of 3:19 p.m., the company thinks a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. As of 4:40 p.m., the company is actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service. We'll have to see if these mitigations fix the issue swiftly.

Microsoft isn't the only company with connection issues today. Downdetector is showing user reports with Google services like Gmail, Amazon Web Services, and Cloudflare. While we could be looking at something more widespread, those reports pale in comparison to users complaining of Microsoft issues, so, for the time being, it seems more likely to be a Microsoft-specific issue. I'll keep this article updated with the latest news.

#3249. Microsoft Outlook Still Down In 365 Outage: Company Sees Sporadic Improvements, Though No Sustained Recovery

UPDATED with latest company comments: Earlier this evening Microsoft posted an update on the outages to its 365 platform noting “positive results with our efforts to restart affected infrastructure and recover server availability.” The optimism was short lived.

About an hour later, the company announced that their efforts were “not taking as expected.”

The company subsequently said it was “adjusting traffic protocols, redistributing traffic, and applying strategic traffic blocking measures,” and “observing partial recovery across regions in which we’ve applied these adjustments.” The bad news was, it reported, “these actions aren’t resulting in sustained recovery.” Related Stories News Microsoft Offers Buyouts To 60,000, A Quarter Of Its Workforce News Eyeing More 'Minecrafts' And 'Fallouts', Microsoft Xbox Launches XP Unit To Take Properties Beyond Video Games

The widespread outages began around 1 p.m. ET, and impacted users in the United States and elsewhere. Watch on Deadline

The tech giant issued a string of social media posts throughout the day on Thursday acknowledging that users had been reporting issues with access, throwing a major wrench into business communications across sectors. Enterprise and business customers of Microsoft 365 were experiencing problems connecting to email via the Exchange server as well as accessing other services. The U.S. is one of the main regions affected, but Microsoft says it potentially poses a problem across the world.

As the outage dragged into the end of the work day, the tech giant put out a less-than-encouraging status report. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the company wrote. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.”

Workers are “fully isolating a portion of our service infrastructure, restarting the affected components, and gradually reintroducing traffic to confirm our services remain stable,” the company went on to say. “We’re also analyzing traffic patterns across our entire service infrastructure and evaluating whether isolating traffic within each region may allow affected regions to recover independently.”

After the initial issues with email, word surfaced about users unable to connect with Teams, Azure, OneDrive, Copilot and other offerings. The home page of outage detection site DownDetector was filled almost entirely by Microsoft alerts.

“We’re investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas,” the company posted at around noon ET on Thursday. “While we’re working to mitigate impact, we’ve confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region.”

Microsoft later clarified, “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”

A status hub designed to provide service updates cited “an unexpected increase in a specific type of service traffic to determine whether it’s contributing to the elevated load. In parallel, we’re evaluating options to redirect traffic to alternate infrastructure to expedite relief.”

Media companies were among those across all business sectors whose activities slowed to a crawl due to the tech glitch. Employees at Amazon Prime Video, Skydance and NBCUniversal and other companies confirmed to Deadline they were in the dark.

There were no immediate indications of a possible cause, though online speculation touched on factors like digital downloads of Grand Theft Auto VI pre-orders or hackers looking to make a statement. Still other theories sought to connect the outage to the day’s other momentous tech news: the ouster of Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia. Huang was forced to resign after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and amid reports of affairs with executives at his own company.

The origins of Microsoft 365 date to the early 2010s, when the company was ramping up its efforts to transition its Office programs Word, Excel and PowerPoint to the cloud. After a meteoric rise as a software maker in the 1980s and 1990s, Microsoft weathered some lean years after a federal antitrust lawsuit and a sluggish initial response to the advent of the internet. Under CEO Satya Nadella, Microsoft has successfully pivoted into cloud computing and, more recently, AI en route to a multi-trillion-dollar market valuation.

Shares in Microsoft have thus far not been affected by the outage, finishing Thursday’s trading day up a fraction to $523. The company’s stock, along with those of a dozen or more large companies placing heavy bets on AI, will come under increasing scrutiny on Wall Street in light of the Nvidia news.

#3248. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3245. Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of Nvidia

Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO of Nvidia following recent reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman suspected of spying for China. Here are the details.

In late October, The New York Times reported on Jensen Huang’s “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former managing director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset suspected of passing information to Beijing.

According to subsequent reports, Chinese intelligence allegedly recruited her to gather information about Jensen Huang and influence his position on selling advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. China disputes the espionage allegations, dismissing them as groundless speculation intended to smear the country.

That said, while Nvidia previously denied any impropriety in their relationship, Huang admitted last weekend to having an extramarital affair in a message to employees, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” He did not mention Alice Huang directly.

In the following days, concerns grew over the potential national security implications of the relationship, in addition to Nvidia seeing its stock plummet.

And while Huang remained CEO as Nvidia’s board commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations, The New York Times reported on Wednesday that he had a second extramarital affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him.

In the hours that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board was preparing to meet to decide Huang’s future. Soon after, Semafor reported that some board members favored Nvidia CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, while other reports suggested that Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, could eventually succeed him. Madison Huang works at Nvidia as senior director of product marketing.

Semafor also named Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji, as a potential successor, while Bloomberg reported that Nvidia had hired an outside firm to identify candidates.

Now, Nvidia has officially announced that Huang “has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.”

The company confirmed that Kress has been appointed interim CEO, while retaining her current responsibilities, until a permanent successor is named. The company is considering both internal and external candidates.

Nvidia also announced that Harvey C. Jones, a longtime technology executive and venture investor, has been appointed the company’s first-ever board chair.

In a statement, Jones said the board has “full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” adding that Nvidia expects its operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

The shareholder lawsuits over the broad-spectrum mismanagement are going to be incredible.

No succession plan. Lying to investors to cover up the CEO’s unethical and foolish behavior. Having a super-weak board of directors absent anyone with high-level relevant experience.

Nvidia did not directly address the allegations surrounding Huang in its announcement, instead thanking him for his contributions to the company over the past 33 years.

Following the Times’ Wednesday report, Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading, erasing the day’s 2.9% gain after two consecutive sessions of losses.

The stock continued to fall following today’s announcement, dropping more than 10% at the time of writing from Wednesday’s closing price of $173.73, bringing its total decline to approximately 35% from its October 6 record close.

How Nvidia’s stock will behave when the market opens today and in the days that follow is anyone’s guess, especially with the company scheduled to report its quarterly earnings next Tuesday, November 17.

#3243. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3242. Mount Thor raises $45 million to build Mac data centers for AI agents

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional-grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage & protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Mount Thor, a Bay Area startup building cloud infrastructure on Apple silicon, announced today that it has raised $45 million across Seed and Series A rounds. The pitch to its investors was simple: AI agents are incredible on Apple silicon, and nobody is renting them at data-center scale.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers managed an enterprise IT network from 2009 to 2021. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade Wi-Fi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

CRV and Conviction co-led the Series A. Chad Byers and Offline Ventures co-led the Seed. CSC Leasing, Enea Capital, Long Journey Ventures, and Upper90 participated, along with angel investors from OpenAI, Meta, Cognition, Together AI, and Vercel. The company also raised separate non-dilutive financing for new hardware as well.

Mount Thor runs macOS on Apple silicon as elastic compute instances, just as a cloud provider rents Linux VMs. Customers get on-demand fleets of Macs for work that only happens on macOS: training computer-use models in reinforcement learning environments, running secure macOS sandboxes for agents, long-running instances that let an agent work across a user’s devices under one Apple ID, and build and test farms for Apple software.

There are two ways to use its solution. With managed compute, customers pick a machine class and image, and get either a full bare-metal Mac or an isolated macOS VM with administrator access, provisioned through a web portal, a command-line tool, Kubernetes, or the API, and billed per Mac on a 24-hour basis. With customer-managed compute, an organization runs its own Macs at a Mount Thor site using its own MDM, while Mount Thor operates the facility and provides inventory by serial number, problem reporting, and event notifications.

The argument is that agents are becoming macOS users, and the demand for Apple’s platform now scales with the number of agents rather than the number of people.

“Making Apple’s operating system and silicon available at datacenter-scale is a massive untapped opportunity in AI infrastructure,” said Peter Voell, Founder and CEO of Mount Thor. “Decades of investment in accessibility and human-computer interaction make macOS the best place for agents to work and for humans to hold them accountable. And with chips like the M5 Ultra, Apple silicon is becoming a high performance, more power- and cost- efficient platform for production inference.”

The other half of its pitch is inference. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio shipped in August with up to 512GB of unified memory, which puts large open-weight models within reach of a single machine at a fraction of the power draw of a traditional GPU-based server. Mount Thor says a focus of the new funding is building what it calls the best inference lab for open-source models on Apple silicon.

“Mount Thor sits at the intersection of two important shifts: the rapidly expanding capabilities of autonomous agents and the increasing demand for compute that can support both local and cloud workloads,” said Brittany Walker, General Partner at CRV. “We’re thrilled to back Peter and the team as they make it easier to use Apple’s platforms at scale for agentic AI.”

The team comes from Cerebras, CoreWeave, Fluidstack, Nebius, OpenAI, and xAI. The company was founded this year and deployed its first data center in under six months.

Macs in the cloud are not new as AWS has rented Mac instances for a few years, and MacStadium has been doing so longer than AWS. Mount Thor’s pitch is that the larger customer is an AI agent that needs a Mac to do its job, and that demand grows with the number of agents rather than the number of developers.

The company says the funding will go toward expanding its compute footprint and building out the team, and that it plans to add capacity quickly to keep up with customer demand.

The Apple HomeView is built well, but as a smart display, it can't do as much as rivals from Amazon, and Siri isn't as capable as other AI assistants.

No physical button to turn off camera or mic

Fewer streaming apps than other smart displays

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

After years of waiting, Apple has finally come out with a smart display, but is it already too late? The Apple HomeView is a sleek device with a nice-looking interface, but scratch deeper than the surface, and you’ll find that it quickly comes up short against the best smart displays. Yes, Amazon’s are the only other game in town, but that company’s much longer history when designing a smart home device — and AI — shows just how far Apple needs to go.

Yes, there are some redeeming qualities of the HomeView — it’s great at music, and integrates well with your iPhone — but when testing it alongside an Amazon smart display, I was left wanting for features time and again.

A post shared by Tom's Guide (@tomsguide)

The HomeView goes on sale November 13, 2026, for $299. It comes in two versions, a freestanding model, and a wall-mounted version. The freestanding HomeView is offered in four colors (silver, starlight, rose pink, space gray) while the wall version comes in just silver or space gray.

If you opt for the wall-mounted version, you’ll have to pay an additional amount for either the USB-C wall connector ($59) or the hardwired mount ($79); if you choose the latter of these two, you’ll probably want to call an electrician to install it.

The base of the HomeView is a small aluminum cylinder that’s rounded at the top, where it connects to the display. The bottom of the base has several rows of perforated holes for the display's speaker.

In an era where most smart home speakers (Apple’s included) are using more fabric-covered finishes, the HomeView reminded me, more than anything, of the love child of a first-generation Amazon Echo and the iMac G4.

The HomeView’s screen is smaller than I would have imagined from the early videos and hands-ons. It definitely won’t take up a ton of room on your counter, which is a nice thing if you have limited space.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Apple’s specs say the display is 7 inches on the diagonal, but owing to the bezels, the usable space is about 6.4 inches. Measuring vertically and horizontally, the screen is 4 7/8 inches in each direction.

It’s very nice to look at; its 1088-by-1088-pixel resolution (220 pixels per inch) made all of my photos look excellent, and the display can automatically adjust its brightness from 0.3 to 500 nits.

For a device that’s smaller than the HomePod mini, the HomeView does a pretty impressive job with music. Apple says that the HomeView has two custom full-range drivers and a custom down-firing woofer, which delivered stronger bass than I would have expected for a device this size.

I was able to blast the “Hamilton” soundtrack throughout my kitchen, and it was loud enough that I had to turn down the volume. In order to do so, though, I had to either yell at Siri, or tap the screen; there’s no dedicated volume controls.

A 12MP camera with Center Stage sits at the very top center bezel; it was perfectly adequate when making FaceTime calls, and the Center Stage feature was welcome, as it let me move around my kitchen while chatting.

You can set up the HomeView with any number of faces. As a Peanuts fan, one of my favorites was an animated clock with Snoopy and Woodstock doing a bunch of shenanigans — and easily swipe between them. However, due to its size — or because of Apple’s design decisions — the HomeView’s homescreen feels more limited than Amazon’s.

Here’s an example. Like the Echo Show devices, the HomeView has a face, called Home Modular, that lets you control smart home devices, and even get a live look from any cameras connected to Apple Home. However, if you want to see pictures of your kids, know what the weather is, and see what’s happening at your front door, good luck. You can create a custom Modular face that incorporates some of these elements, but you can't fit them all.

By contrast, the Echo Show 8, which admittedly has a larger 8.7-inch screen, lets you pack more on there, so you get a much more holistic look at everything going on both in and outside of your home.

In order to simplify things for developers, the HomeView uses the same widgets that you can install on an iPhone. But what works for a smartphone doesn’t necessarily work for a smart display.

You can add Widgets to the HomeView, but surprisingly — and somewhat aggravatingly — some of them don’t work, or aren’t optimized for the device. For example, I added the Disney+ widget, but when I tapped on it, it displayed a message saying “The Disney+ app is only available on iPhone.” Same with the Anker Eufy app and YouTube. The only widget that lets you play videos natively is Apple TV.

Even more frustrating for me was the Photos widget. After setting it up — which requires you to use your iPhone to select the photos you want — the widget then displays a picture from your collection. However, if you tap on the widget to change the image, you get a message saying “App unavailable. The Photos app is only available on iPhone.” I felt a bit like Charlie Brown right after Lucy swiped the football away.

Those widgets do serve a purpose — you can start playing a video on your iPhone, and then cast it to the HomeView, but it’s an extra step that you don’t need to take with any other smart display.

What’s odd is that the HomeView lists dozens of widgets, but few are optimized for the HomeView. Perhaps this will change once the product goes on sale. And, what Widgets are available aren’t that many. While there’s a Stocks widget, there’s none for News or Sports, so you’ll have to ask Siri for updates on the game.

Forget using the HomeView as a smart TV; while you can watch Apple TV content, there aren’t any other widgets for most popular streaming services, such as Hulu, Peacock, or Netflix. One of the main reasons I like smart displays is that they can act as mini TVs, so I can cook Sunday dinner in the kitchen, but still be able to watch football games without running into the living room.

So, for example, if I walk up to the HomeView, I’ll see my photos and calendar appointments, but if my wife were to approach the device, she would see her content, provided she were a registered user. In either instance, our iPhones would also have to be on the same Wi-Fi network for any personal content to appear.

One of the reasons that the HomeView was delayed was that Apple was waiting for Siri to get smarter. So, I put it to the test versus Alexa+ on an Echo Show 15. Tl;dr — Apple needs to do a bit more work.

The first challenge was asking for the weather. The first time I asked Siri, I received a very terse “Expect partly cloudy skies today,” and the HomeView’s screen changed to show me the current temperature. The next time I asked, I got a slightly more detailed response: “Expect clear skies today with a high of 59 degrees and a low of 47 degrees.”

By contrast, Alexa+ was much more conversant. “Right now it’s cloudy and 56 degrees, feeling 53. Today’s high is 61 with a low of 45, and it’ll stay breezy with decreasing clouds and no rain expected.”

Next, I asked both Alexa+ and Siri to look up local pizza places. Again, Siri gave me a list, but Alexa+ was more effusive, telling me how late some of the more popular restaurants were open.

I then asked both AIs to order me a pizza from one particular restaurant. Siri couldn’t, but offered to place a call, but Alexa+ linked to Uber Eats, and walked me through ordering a large pie.

Another key function for the HomeView is that it can act as a central control panel for all of your smart home devices. Not only can you tap widgets on the screen to turn your lights on and off, but you can also use your voice to control things. For example, I said “Hey Siri, show me my video doorbell” and the HomeView brought up a live view of my front door nearly instantly.

I also liked that you can add a widget to show a live view of your security cameras. I have a Eufy camera, which worked well with the HomeView, but this is one area where Apple needs to incentivize its partners a bit more; there are far fewer security cameras compatible with Apple Home than there are for Amazon and Google.

How well can a home assistant get you where you need to go? I asked both Siri and Alexa+ to get me directions to Newark airport. Siri gave its usual brief response: “It will take about 13 minutes to drive to Newark Liberty International Airport in light traffic.” I then asked Siri to send the directions to my phone, which it did as a text message with a link to Apple Maps to my phone.

Alexa+ was more chatty, but less helpful. “Navigation isn’t supported on this device, but I can give you the route info. It’s about 12 minutes and 5 miles to Newark Liberty International Airport, with light traffic on I-78.” I then asked Alexa to send the directions to my phone, but the best it could do was send a copy of the conversation to the Alexa app.

When I asked Alexa+ to book me an Uber ride, it went so far as to ask me if I wanted to start from my work or home location, and went through all the rest of the steps. The best Siri could do was offer to open the Uber app.

One thing I did like is that Siri can scan through your calendar and messages to surface things you might have missed, or forgot about. For example, I asked “what time are my neighbors having people over today?”

It then dug through all of my messages and replied “Your neighbors are having people over for a fire today at 4:30 p.m.” On the screen, it added further detail: “There will be drinks for the adults and marshmallows to roast for kids.”

Historically, Apple has generally not been first to any particular category, but when it enters a market — MP3 players, phones, tablets, etc. — it’s generally learned from the mistakes of the competition, and delivered a device that outshines everything else on the market.

The HomeView is not that. While the physical design of the device is lovely, its software does not live up to the same standard. It can do far less than rival smart displays from Amazon, and Siri is still a less capable home assistant AI than Alexa+ or Gemini.

I think Apple probably had to release it; there have been reports that the HomeView was languishing in a warehouse for the better part of a year, which makes sense considering it’s using the A18, rather than the A19 chip — but maybe it should have stayed there.

Michael A. Prospero is the U.S. Editor-in-Chief for Tom’s Guide. In his spare time, he also tests out the latest drones, electric scooters, and smart home gadgets, such as video doorbells. Before his tenure at Tom's Guide, he was the Reviews Editor for Laptop Magazine, a reporter at Fast Company, the Times of Trenton, and, many eons back, an intern at George magazine. He received his undergraduate degree from Boston College, where he worked on the campus newspaper The Heights, and then attended the Columbia University school of Journalism. When he’s not testing out the latest running watch, electric scooter, or skiing or training for a marathon, he’s probably using the latest sous vide machine, smoker, or pizza oven, to the delight — or chagrin — of his family.

#3240. Apple TV 4K review: The best streamer comes at a cost

It’s been four years since Apple last updated the Apple TV 4K, but a new version is here. There’s Siri AI support, a faster chip, an improved remote, and more.

Here’s everything that’s changed, what’s better, and whether the new Apple TV 4K justifies its new $299 price.

The Apple TV 4K’s overall design is largely unchanged. It’s still the same familiar black box that sits underneath your television. The only visual change is that the front status light has moved from the right side to the center.

Inside, Apple has upgraded the A15 Bionic to the A19 chip, touting 50% faster CPU performance and twice the GPU performance.

Those are great improvements on paper. In practice, I’m not doing anything on my Apple TV that really stresses the performance. Compared to my third-generation Apple TV 4K, I’ve occasionally noticed slightly smoother animations and faster performance in apps that handle more processing locally, like Infuse.

I think the biggest advantage of the A19 chip is future-proofing. People tend to buy and keep these devices for years. In fact, I’m still using a first-generation Apple TV 4K from 2017 in my bedroom, and it still works just fine nearly a decade later. The A19 gives the new Apple TV plenty of performance headroom for future tvOS updates and more demanding apps, even if those advantages aren’t particularly noticeable today.

The Siri Remote looks the same as before, but it now supports Precision Finding in the Find My app, making it easier to track down when misplaced. You can also play a sound on the remote to help locate it. I lose my Siri Remote all the time, so this honestly might be the change I’ve noticed and appreciated most in my 10 days testing the new Apple TV.

It’s worth noting Apple also sells the new Siri Remote separately for $59, and it’s compatible with every previous Apple TV 4K generation. You do, however, need a newer iPhone model to use Precision Finding.

One of the more interesting new features is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room. Apple TV automatically calibrates the speakers based on their positions in the room.

For context, I typically use my Apple TV with a stereo pair of full-size HomePod (2nd generation) speakers. I’ve spent some time testing the new four-speaker surround sound setup by adding a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers.

My house’s layout isn’t particularly well-suited for a traditional surround sound setup, but to my admittedly untrained ears, this sounds great. I can’t speak to how it compares to a dedicated surround sound system, but I appreciate Apple continuing to expand what’s possible with HomePods and Apple TV.

One of the biggest changes with the new Apple TV 4K is the addition of three far-field microphones. This means you can now interact with Siri without picking up the Siri Remote. In conjunction with this, Siri AI is also coming to Apple TV.

Siri AI brings the same broad world knowledge and personal-context capabilities you’ve experienced on iPhone and HomeView, but adapts them to finding and watching content on your television. Siri AI on Apple TV requires the owner of your Apple Home setup to have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

Personal context requests also require a paired compatible device connected to the same Wi-Fi network as Apple TV.

What was that TV show Lily recommended a few weeks ago?

What are some baseball movies I might like?

What did the vet say after Blake’s vet appointment?

For each example, tvOS responded with a dedicated interface on Apple TV, showing the answer along with poster art, cast information, and more. It also offers built-in contextual suggestions when you ask for recommendations, so you can refine the results further.

You can also ask Siri contextual questions about the show or movie you’re watching. This includes things like “where was this show filmed?” and “when is the next season coming out?”

I’ve found Siri AI’s responses to those contextual questions less accurate. It struggles to accurately identify the show or movie that’s playing, leading to completely inaccurate responses to those types of questions.

It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021 and the third-generation model from 2022. The far-field microphones are what’s exclusive to the new hardware. This lets you shout Siri commands into the air without talking directly into the Siri Remote.

In my testing, hands-free Siri works relatively well, and it’s convenient to control Apple TV without reaching for the remote. It does a good job at picking up commands

I can’t go any further in this review without talking about the price. The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) costs $299. That’s a huge increase over previous Apple TV models. Here’s a brief history of Apple TV 4K pricing over the years to set the stage:

After Apple introduced the $129 Apple TV model in October 2022, I started to notice a change. More and more people had Apple TVs when I would visit. Friends and family who had previously bought an Amazon or Roku box, or just used their TV’s built-in software, had purchased an Apple TV.

At $299, I worry that type of adoption is going to come to a screeching halt. And it’s unfortunate because the Apple TV is so much better than anything else out there. tvOS is fast, clean, and relatively free of the clutter and advertisements you find on competing platforms. The Siri Remote is excellent, and the integration with the rest of Apple’s ecosystem is hard to beat.

I could justify the $299 price for the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) if it were just one option available in a broader lineup. If there were lower-priced options for people who don’t need all the bells and whistles. That’s not the case, though. In fact, this is the first Apple TV 4K generation to be sold in just one configuration. There’s no cheaper version with less storage or fewer features.

To Apple’s credit, these are devices that can last for years. The fact that I’m still using an Apple TV 4K from 2017 makes the $299 price a tiny bit easier to swallow, but it doesn’t really change my frustration.

Apple seems serious about its new smart home strategy. There’s the HomeView smart display, a new HomePod mini, and the Apple Home Collection family of smart home accessories launching later this year. One of the best ways to get deeper into people’s homes is by controlling how they watch TV. I can’t help but think pricing the Apple TV 4K out of reach for so many people will hinder those ambitions.

Don’t get me wrong, I love the Apple TV. I have three of them in my house. If one of them broke, I would reluctantly pay $299 for a new one. Whether you fall into that category is for you to decide. All I can say is that the new Apple TV 4K is the best streamer on the market.
