#3239. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3238. Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

Apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-new software experience that actually feels really familiar.

I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

HomeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

HomeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

In terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-issue. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

Sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

In practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

HomeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could quickly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone users.

You can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple says that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

The faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly draw your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

Swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center (which annoyingly isn’t customizable). Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

There is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:

I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now. HomeView also needs a dedicated Photos app.

I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

However, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

One of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

HomeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

This is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

The feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

There are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

HomeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

The facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

In practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

In addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

HomeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple says that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:

In terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

Siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

HomeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

There is one limitation: you currently can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software update coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for quickly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

HomeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

When you get a new iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

HomeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

At first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

It’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

In fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

I think that’s the best example of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

#3237. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3236. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#3234. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3232. OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly hits $10bn as its losses grow

Its adjusted operating margin improved to -109%, according to the WSJ. But OpenAI revenue is still below Anthropic’s $17bn for the quarter, and Anthropic lists on Nasdaq next week.

OpenAI’s revenue reached $10bn in the third quarter, up almost 50% from the second, The Information reported. OpenAI shared the figures with investors on Tuesday. Demand for its newer models and enterprise products had picked up, Valida Pau and Jemima McEvoy wrote, citing a person familiar with the matter.

It is the first quarter in which OpenAI’s revenue has reached $10bn, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Revenue was almost three times its level a year earlier, they said. OpenAI declined to comment to Bloomberg.

The Wall Street Journal’s Berber Jin saw documents on the results. They show OpenAI’s adjusted operating margin improved to -109% in the third quarter, from -150% in the second. Its adjusted operating loss still rose, to $10.9bn from $10.1bn.

In the second quarter, OpenAI’s revenue grew 18% to $6.7bn, the Journal reported at the time. That left it behind Anthropic on quarterly revenue for the first time.

Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, spoke on the investor call. So did Sarah Friar, its chief financial officer, and product leader Thibault Sottiaux, Bloomberg’s Rachel Metz and Rebecca Torrence reported.

OpenAI revenue has regained momentum thanks to new models, aggressive price cuts and a bigger push into AI agents, according to Bloomberg. The company told investors it ended September with roughly $50bn in annualised revenue. That matches the $50bn run rate reported in October.

Anthropic reported $16.96bn in revenue for the same quarter. It first disclosed it in its IPO filing on 2 November. Its operating loss was $567m, and its adjusted operating margin was 15%.

Anthropic’s growth has slowed. Its revenue rose about 47% from the second quarter to the third. It had jumped 144% the quarter before, its filing shows.

The two companies count revenue differently. Anthropic includes sales made through its cloud partners, while OpenAI counts only its share of some partner sales, TechCrunch noted.

#3231. Cardinal Infra (CDNL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Margin pressure and a CFO exit followed a sharp profit drop at the contractor.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cardinal Infrastructure Group Inc. (CDNL -62.38%) reported a significant decline in quarterly profitability despite high revenue growth, leading management to withdraw its full-year 2026 financial guidance. The company experienced material margin compression driven by cost estimate revisions on a small number of residential projects in the Carolinas alongside rising fuel and transportation expenses. Management is responding with a leadership transition in the finance department, the postponement of a planned acquisition to focus on internal execution, and the implementation of more rigorous project selection and review standards.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Cardinal Infrastructure Group Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Tiffany Gidley, Cardinal's General Counsel. Please go ahead.

Tiffany Gidley: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Cardinal's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Jeremy Spivey, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; Benji Wood, our Chief Operating Officer; and Mike Rowe, our Chief Financial Officer. Please refer to the earnings release and presentation issued this morning and available on the Investor Relations section of our website. Today's call will include certain non-GAAP financial measures. Please refer to our earnings release for definitions and reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measures. Today's call will also include forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Additional information regarding these risks is available in our SEC filings.

Cardinal undertakes no obligation to publicly update or revise any forward-looking statements, except as required by law. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jeremy.

Jeremy Spivey: Thanks, Tiffany, and good morning, everyone. Revenue grew 65% this quarter to $202 million, but our third-quarter adjusted EBITDA margin totaled 4.2%, well below our expectations. The decline primarily reflected project estimate revisions, residential pricing pressure, lower initial bid margins on certain commercial and industrial work, and higher fuel and transportation costs. Mike will provide the detailed financial bridge, but I want to be direct. These results are not acceptable, and they make clear that we need to strengthen how we estimate, manage, and execute projects across Cardinal. As a second-generation operator with more than 30 years of experience in this industry, I know what strong project execution requires, and I recognize when we need to raise our standard.

We are taking several actions to do just that. Benji Wood, our Chief Operating Officer, is a fourth-generation operator with more than 30 years of experience and a demonstrated record of success leading ALGC. Benji will now take a more direct role in establishing and implementing consistent operating standards across the Cardinal platform, focusing on project selection, estimating, project reviews, and accountability. We will also engage an experienced independent third-party adviser to support implementation of these operational changes and assess our estimating and project review processes. Separately, in collaboration with Hughes Brothers, we decided to postpone the proposed acquisition.

We continue to view Hughes Brothers as a strong strategic fit, and our near-term priority is strengthening our existing platform, and we will revisit Hughes when appropriate. We believe the right priority today is strengthening execution across our existing operations and realizing the benefits of the businesses we've already acquired. We also remain focused on capital allocation. Given the strength of the balance sheet, our Board of Directors has authorized a share repurchase program up to $50 million of our Class A common stock over the next 12 months. Although our third-quarter performance exposed areas where our execution and operating processes must improve, we have made meaningful progress this year in building a more diversified, vertically integrated platform.

We expanded our self-performance capabilities, added complementary services in Atlanta, and brought an asphalt plant online in the Carolinas. Our strategy remains intact. Our immediate priority is strengthening execution and building the operating discipline and supporting infrastructure necessary to translate growth into more consistent profitability. With that, I'll turn over the call to Benji to discuss the operational changes we're making.

Benjamin Wood: Thanks, Jeremy. My immediate focus is applying the operating practices that have worked well at ALGC to the broader Cardinal platform. Our operating priorities are improving project selection, project execution, and accountability. We have identified several actions that are already underway. First, we are tightening project selection and estimating through more consistent bid review standards, greater management oversight, and increased selectivity around project risk and expected returns. Second, we are strengthening project management and field execution through more frequent and rigorous project reviews, standardized estimates to complete, and earlier identification and escalation of changes in productivity, schedule, scope, and expected profitability. Third, we are strengthening operating accountability through consistent estimating, reporting, and financial control standards across the platform.

These changes are intended to provide earlier visibility into project performance and allow us to act sooner when a project deviates from plan. We will implement them while continuing to invest in our employees and safety programs, bringing greater discipline and consistency across the Cardinal platform. With that, I'll turn the call over to Mike.

Mike Rowe: Thanks, Benji. I'll briefly review the financial results, balance sheet, and the outlook. Revenue grew 65% to $202 million in the third quarter, an increase of $80 million, of which $24 million was organic growth. Backlog reached $816 million. Revenue growth and backlog demonstrated continued demand across the platform. However, that growth did not translate into acceptable levels of profitability during the quarter, as adjusted EBITDA was $9 million compared to $21 million last year, while adjusted EBITDA margin declined to 4.2% from 17.5%. Gross profit for the third quarter was $11 million, resulting in a gross margin of 5.4% compared to 15.9% last year.

As Jeremy referenced, on an adjusted EBITDA margin basis, project estimate revisions accounted for approximately 6.5 percentage points of the decline. Residential pricing pressure and lower initial bid margins on certain commercial and industrial work accounted for approximately 3.6 points, and higher fuel and transportation costs accounted for approximately 3.5 points. These impacts were partially offset by approximately 0.3 points from other factors, resulting in a 13.3 percentage point decline in adjusted EBITDA margin. G&A increased to $15 million for the third quarter. This increase reflected acquired businesses, stock-based compensation, acquisition-related costs, and investment in personnel, systems, and infrastructure to support the growth and increased complexity of the organization.

Net loss for the quarter was $11 million compared to $10 million of net income in the same period in 2025. For the year-to-date results, revenue for the first 9 months of 2026 increased 92%, from $286 million to $596 million. Organic growth contributed $144 million, or about half of the increase, with the balance attributable to acquired businesses. Gross margin was 11.5% compared to 15.4% in the prior year period, primarily reflecting higher fuel and transportation costs, residential pricing pressure, and lower initial bid margins on certain commercial and industrial projects, as well as project estimate revisions recorded in the third quarter.

Net income for the first 9 months was $12 million compared with $46 million in the prior year period. Adjusted EBITDA increased to $63 million compared to $56 million last year, while adjusted EBITDA margin declined to 10.6% from 17.9%. We ended the quarter with $335 million in cash and cash equivalents and approximately $136 million of net cash, along with substantial additional borrowing capacity. Net cash provided by the operating activities was $30 million for the first 9 months of 2026, and capital expenditures were $42 million. Turning to our outlook.

Given the magnitude of the project estimate revisions recorded in this quarter and the work underway to strengthen our project-level forecasting, we are withdrawing our previously issued full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA margin guidance. While we currently expect fourth quarter adjusted EBITDA to improve from third quarter, we are not providing a specific revenue or margin outlook. Our priority is to complete the necessary project reviews, strengthen our forecasting processes, and establish greater confidence in our timing and profitability of the work in our portfolio. With that, I'll turn the call back to Jeremy.

Jeremy Spivey: Thanks, Mike. I also want to share a leadership update. Mike Rowe will be stepping down as Chief Financial Officer and will remain with Cardinal to support an orderly transition. We have engaged Spencer Stuart to conduct a comprehensive search for his successor. I want to thank Mike for his contributions to Cardinal and for his commitment to supporting the transition. I'll close with this. Our long-term strategy continues to center on vertical integration, end market diversification, and acquisitions, supported by disciplined capital allocation. Right now, our focus is clear: strengthen execution, improve project visibility, and translate our growth into more consistent profitability. We understand that credibility will be built through execution and demonstrated results.

Our management team is focused on delivering those results. With that, Operator, let's open the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question is going to come from Keith Hughes with Truist.

Keith Hughes: On the project estimate hit, which is the biggest hit to the margins here, could you talk about which regions were affected or what regions were affected more by that negative in the quarter?

Jeremy Spivey: Keith, this is Jeremy. The revisions were primarily driven by a handful of projects in the Carolinas. And more specifically, we had $13.2 million revision in our cost estimates, which accounts for about 6.5 points of the gross margin decline. There's some stuff tied to those revisions with elevated fuel and transportation costs versus third quarter 2025. Of that, 10 projects account for 61% of the estimate revision, and simplifying that even further, 3 projects accounted for 50% of the estimate revision. So it's a select few projects, and it's isolated in the Carolinas.

Keith Hughes: And are those residential projects or more commercial? Or how would you care, particularly the 3 that seem to be the most problematic here?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes, the 3 were residential projects.

Keith Hughes: Final question for me. We talked about some changes with Benz getting involved. Can you talk about how that works structurally? Do you set a faster review on cost versus revenue? What are the individual steps to make that?

Jeremy Spivey: I'll tell you, we're focused on 3 areas: project selection and estimating, project-level oversight and accountability. We're timing the bid reviews to better evaluate expected profitability, resource requirements, and execution risk before committing to new projects. We're increasing the frequency and rigor of the project reviews so we can identify the overruns or changes in estimated profitability earlier than we have in the past. Our new ERP and visibility help with that. And we're realigning leadership there at the same time to support the resources so that we have clear ownership of project performance moving forward.

Operator: And our next question is going to come from Brian Brophy with Stifel.

Brian Brophy: Yes. Just following up on the projects with estimate revisions discussion. Can you provide, I guess, a little bit more color on the expected completion dates or the cadence of expected completion dates for these projects?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes. So most of these projects on the revision are over 75% complete. So they will be completed either this fiscal year or early Q1.

Brian Brophy: And then just maybe touching on the backlog. It was down sequentially. Book-to-bill was sub-1. It looks like it's the first time in a while. I guess, just what are the drivers there? Is it primarily res or anything else? And any thoughts on when we could see a pickup in backlog?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes. So thanks, Brian. So Q3 is historically slow for new awards for us in our business because most project owners don't want to start new projects in the winter months. Our backlog did increase 26% year-over-year to $815.5 million. And we are also becoming more selective in pursuing new work, particularly here in the Carolinas where pricing competition has intensified. If we follow an annual cadence historically, Q3 is slow for us, and we tend to see things pick up late Q4, starting in Q1.

Operator: And our next question is going to come from Louie DiPalma with William Blair.

Louie Dipalma: For Jeremy and Benji, you both have been in the industry for several decades. Is the issue that took place in the third quarter related to execution? Or did something abruptly take place over the spring and summer that changed the industry's economic structure? And is it something with a higher cost of labor or materials? Or are Pulte, Lennar and D.R. Horton are they and other customers pricing contracts differently? Or is it a function of, like, there are certain just isolated projects that are now carrying a negative gross margin, and things will improve after these troublesome projects end?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes. Thank you, Louie. I'll answer some of that, and if Benji needs to step in, he can. The execution certainly is not all of it. But any execution impact is not acceptable to us. And especially in soft markets where there's margin compression in residential and others, we have to execute at a top level. So when we speak to that, that's the only thing that we know we have control over and that we're focused on making right and improving on. So there is a substantial amount of impact in fuel and transportation. Our visibility in Q2 and moving into Q3 was not where it is now. We were moving ERP systems.

We have a lot of tools now that allow us to see things that we previously could not see: where the impacts are coming from, how they were arriving, where they were, and we now have that. So we are getting a tremendous amount. A lot of these estimate adjustments are related to fuel and transportation moving forward. And it was impacted prior to, so we have to account for that. And then moving forward on the remaining cost to complete, we have to account for that. The residential market is soft.

There is a significant amount of margin compression in the Carolinas, and I'll let Benji speak to Atlanta, but we're going to continue to see that throughout 2027 unless things change with rates and there's some geopolitical resolution. And I'll let Benji talk.

Benjamin Wood: Yes. Louie, really, just going to echo what Jeremy said, it's a little bit of all of it. There's macro shifting out there on the market that's continued throughout the year. The fuel has been a steady pressure increase that has not alleviated. And as everyone knows, fuel really permeates throughout the system. So the visibility is going to help manage it going forward, and then just focusing on project selection and setting ourselves up for winning jobs and then executing on the job as well is going to put us on a better path.

Louie Dipalma: Okay. And for the soft residential market, does that encompass the residential projects in the Atlanta region in addition to the Carolinas? Or is that the weakness at least right now?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes. I think you're seeing a softer resi market in the broader Southeast region. I don't think it's unique to Carolina or Atlanta. I think it's a broader macro shift. And it's not the worst market. It's just a softening market.

Mike Rowe: Yes. Louie, I'll say that tacking onto that is that when interest rates hit in Q3, we saw expedited softness. It was teetering for most of Q2, with the hope of a rebound if fuel prices and some other things fell in our favor, and they didn't, and rates rose. And so we just had accelerated softness that we feel is stabilized for now, but if rates continue, who knows what happens. Great.

Louie Dipalma: And so when you're bidding on these new projects, and your costs are higher, is it just that the margins are compressed? Or are you able to still, in your estimation, generate positive EBITDA for these projects in the residential market under, like, these new conditions?

Mike Rowe: We are, Louie, and part of what we've done is we have to get back to basics and establish the projects that we bid on and the margin that we expect from those projects. There is a little bit of loss of sight there, and we have part of the processes that we're doing with oversight of project estimating and operating processes to create some better consistency and visibility on the projects that we are getting awarded and make sure we have a floor on the projects that we agreed to execute for our clients.

Operator: And our next question will come from Brent Thielman with Oppenheimer.

Brent Thielman: I guess I recognize it's a low bar with the third-quarter results. But over the short term, what backs the belief that adjusted EBITDA should get better quarter-over-quarter? I guess the question is really what headwinds alleviate for you in the current quarter?

Mike Rowe: We feel that the revision has already addressed what we know to be true. We expect adjusted EBITDA to improve sequentially in Q4 compared to Q3. Our efforts on the operation and execution side should do nothing but support that. And we stand firm behind that.

Brent Thielman: And I guess a follow-up, Jeremy or Benji, I guess, with respect to the new business booked in the quarter, how do we get comfortable and recognize you're working through, or pretty much through some of these, we'll call it, legacy work? How do we get comfortable with the bid margins associated with what you picked up in the current quarter?

Jeremy Spivey: Sure, Brent. I think the big issue for us was visibility and being able to get real-time data that allows us to make decisions on active projects that we can efficiently move through and mitigate any downside risk as we move through it. That lack of visibility for a period was an impact, and we feel that we have the tools now with our new system to be able to head off and get real-time feedback on the projects that we do have ongoing. There's been no change of the way that we conduct business.

I mean, we have to get back to the basics, and we have to rely on more structured data now that we have available to us to be able to make decisions and mitigate any potential downside.

Brent Thielman: Okay. If I could sneak one more in. Just ALGC, could you talk about the performance relative to the mid-20s EBITDA margins that the business delivered when it was acquired? Did it meet those thresholds or not?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes. I mean, listen, ALGC has performed the way that we expected. They have been affected by the impacts of rising fuel and transportation costs. They do have impacts from a softening market on both residential and C&I, but they are executing at a high level. And in fact, we're extending from ALGC certain aspects of its approach to estimating and project reviews and accountability. And we're going to work with a third-party adviser to refine those processes further and standardize them and implement them across all of Cardinal. And we will also plan to use them as a framework when integrating future acquisitions. So there's a lot of good things that we're getting out of AOGC.

They're subject to transitory headwinds. And when that goes away, they're back to operating as they have in the past and hopefully exceeding that with the integration model that we provide.

Operator: And the next question is going to come from Kevin Gainey with Thompson, Davidson Company.

Kevin Gainey: I was going to ask about -- given everything and the changes that you're making, how are you guys dealing with acquiring Allied Paving in the quarter? And how has that gone so far? How that integration is going?

Benjamin Wood: Kevin, this is Benji. The Allied integration is going really well in Atlanta at the moment. We worked with Allied for years as a partner, and a lot of the familiarity and synergies are already being realized from that. So, from a high level, it's proceeding as planned.

Kevin Gainey: And then I wanted to ask about the backlog. How much of that do you guys expect to go through over the next 12 months? And how are you guys thinking about the percentage of that work that is still kind of at this low-margin piece and the percentage of the new work that would be better?

Mike Rowe: So the backlog we show in September is $815 million; $640 million of it was signed, and $175 million was letter intent with issued contracts pending execution. The 12-month conversion estimate for the current project is scheduled, but we are not giving any '27 guidance on how we think that the backlog will fall into '27.

Kevin Gainey: Okay. And just finally, just if you guys have any other details on the Hughes Brothers, whatever costs may be associated with that in Q4?

Jeremy Spivey: We don't expect any cost impact in Q4 from Hughes. The acquisition has been postponed. We continue to talk to Hughes on a daily, if not weekly basis. They're a priority for us. But obviously, there are some things we have to get organized on our end before we can bring them into the fold.

Operator: And the next question is going to come from Noah Levitz with William Blair.

Noah Levitz: I wanted to ask, since you're experiencing the softness in the residential market and it sounds like it could persist, you came in with a pretty healthy mix towards residential after IPO. Does that at all change your opinion as it relates to resi versus C&I mix over the long term, pursuing more C&I?

Jeremy Spivey: Our priority is to continue to focus on diversification. And we are prioritizing the work that we feel is going to provide the best opportunity for us with the best clients. So as we look to '27 and even into finishing Q4, we're focusing on the diversification process. We are establishing new relationships with a lot of the general contractors that carry these C&I projects. And naturally, due to the state of the market right now, C&I is more abundant. And so I would expect, and we've seen it here in Q2 and Q3 and in Q4 and probably into next year that our end market mix leans more towards the C&I space for the foreseeable future.

Noah Levitz: And then just given that this was your first full quarter of having the asphalt plant online, I just wanted to check and see was everything going according to expectations in terms of in-sourcing and cost savings there?

Jeremy Spivey: Yes. I think in future quarters, we'll be able to speak more to it because we're just getting it on plan this quarter, but it has been an exceptional addition to our operation here, specifically for Aviator. I mean they've put down some incredible volume of asphalt out of that plant. Our models that we're running are make us very excited about what it's going to offer to us and the payback and the long-term accretion to our operations. So yes, we're excited more to come on that, but it is running on full plan right now.

Noah Levitz: And then just a quick last one. Back in April, you won the big data center award. You haven't talked about it in a bit, but I want to check in and see how that's going. And how is the pipeline of those or other kind of mission-critical type opportunities looking for you guys?

Jeremy Spivey: Obviously, that transitory end market we're focused on. It offers a good opportunity for us, and we're not only in Atlanta, but in the Carolinas and some other states that we're looking to opportunities. But the one that we currently have, we're still on Phase 1. There was a substantial revision to the Phase 1 plan, and we had a change order that is either pended or executed at this time, but represents a 50% increase in the original contract. The anticipated Phase 2, as I understand it, is to be awarded and to begin March, April, so late Q1, early Q2 of next year. We're doing great. The customer is happy.

We've made some good relationships, not only with that customer with some other trades to help support the work that we do there. So hopefully, we have opportunities with them on future projects in other markets.

Operator: That concludes the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the call back over to Jeremy for closing remarks.

Jeremy Spivey: Thank you. Thank you all for your time today. I want to take a quick moment to thank our employees for their continued hard work and dedication. We know we have some work to do, and I'm confident we have the team to focus on and implement the necessary changes. We have and we will continue to deliver the quality complex infrastructure projects for our clients across the Southeast. Thank you, and I hope you all have a great day.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, this does conclude today's conference call. We thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect, and have a great day.

#3229. Apple Notes adds a powerful new advantage in iOS 27.3

There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a new advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI.

Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a big upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week, iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many new capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

The one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole new set of powers with the new update.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. One common example is that I’ve been able to have Siri save a link to the webpage I’m currently viewing inside a note, and even specify exactly where in the note I want it to go.

In theory, third-party notes apps may be able to offer similar controls sometime next year when app skills officially launch. For now though, anyone who wants to control their notes app by voice—or via Spotlight, as I tend to do on my iPad Pro—have another reason to use Apple Notes.

Have you tried Siri AI’s new Notes features in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.
