#3228. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

#3227. SpaceXSI’s Grok Build left 35,000 apps open, security firm Claroc says

Grok Build proposes ‘Anyone with the link’ when users publish an app, and app addresses land in public DNS records. SpaceXSI says apps stay private until their creator shares them.

Anyone who found the address of a Grok Build app could open more than 35,000 of them, security firm Claroc found in research published on 10 November. Two dozen belonged to staff at SpaceXSI, the company that makes Grok. They held a confidential onboarding plan, a sales territory map and advertising proposals.

SpaceXSI took its own 24 apps offline after the report, Claroc said. It left the apps of other Grok users open. Ars Technica’s Dan Goodin reported that SpaceXSI started removing them within hours of his email asking about the findings.

Grok Build turns a description typed into a chat into a working app. The user can then publish it at its own address on grok.me. Claroc tried more than 43,500 of those addresses. Of the 37,571 still online, 35,578, or 94.7%, opened without any sign-in.

Most were games, landing pages and calculators. About one in ten held internal business or personal data. Claroc estimates that 650 to 800 apps held private data.

Claroc confirmed some cases by hand. They included one intensive care patient’s lab results, a hospital group’s roster of more than 3,500 staff, and a fire department’s shift board. One contractor’s timesheet app carried 18 accounts with their passwords in plain text, in code that every visitor’s browser downloads.

Besides SpaceXSI and X, Claroc identified 30 organisations, six of them in the Fortune 500. It named none. Ars Technica listed more. They include a Tesla service-centre scorecard naming 22 technicians and a roster for a US Navy logistics contract.

SpaceXSI’s own open apps included a map of 594 strategic sales accounts and eight X advertising proposals. Claroc said one proposal, to a US federal agency, carried a confidential label.

Grok gives every published app its own hostname of random words, such as name.grok.me. Nobody needs to guess one. When a visitor opens an app, its name reaches passive DNS services. These commercial databases log internet lookups, and anyone with an account can search them.

Shared chats from Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini keep the secret part of the link in the path, Claroc said. DNS never sees it. Last month, the same method exposed Meta’s Muse links.

In the paid account Claroc used, the publish screen proposed “Anyone with the link” as the access setting. It also offered “Invited users” and “Only you”.

“AI app builders turned publishing into a few clicks, and the default answer to who can see it is everyone,” Asaf Aprozper, Claroc’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said in the firm’s report.

Claroc also built two test apps of its own. In a team customer list, Grok’s code added anyone who signed in with Google to the team before checking membership. An outside account could then read, edit and delete records, the firm said.

A representative for Cursor, the coding company SpaceX bought in August, responded in an email to Ars Technica.

“Apps are private by default and nothing goes public unless the creator chooses to share it,” the representative said, according to Ars Technica.

SpaceXSI also told a reporter that publishing takes several steps, including a legal notice, and that employee accounts start on “Only you”, Claroc said. Claroc’s answer is that the people who published the 35,578 open apps went through every one of those steps.

The representative said ChatGPT, Lovable and Bolt also make shareable links. Aprozper agreed that apps on Lovable, Bolt and Replit have the same exposure.

“However, Grok is where we found by far the most sensitive company data,” Aprozper told Ars Technica.

Claroc sells security tools for AI-built apps. It asked SpaceXSI to make “Only you” the default, move shared apps onto hard-to-guess paths, and warn builders when an app has a database but no sign-in. It is now notifying the affected organisations itself.

It is not the first data problem for Grok Build. In July, the tool sent entire Git repositories to xAI’s servers. In October, Musk said the merged company would be renamed SpaceXSI.

#3224. Allot Ltd. (ALLT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Recurring security revenue is becoming a growing share of Allot's business.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Allot Ltd. (ALLT -13.27%) reported a return to sustainable profitability driven by double-digit growth in its core security and network intelligence business lines. Management highlighted the transition toward a recurring revenue model, with Security-as-a-Service (SECaaS) now contributing one-third of total revenue. The company raised its full-year revenue outlook and emphasized its strong cash position and lack of debt as foundations for both organic growth and potential acquisitions. Management stated that the growing sophistication of cyber threats, particularly those utilizing artificial intelligence, is increasing demand among communication service providers for network-native security solutions.

Kenny Green: Good day to all of you, and welcome to Allot's conference call to discuss its financial results for the quarter. I would like to thank Allot's management for hosting this conference call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. If you have not received the company's press release, please check the company's website at www.allot.com. With me today on the line are Mr. Eyal Harari, CEO; and Ms. Liat Nahum, CFO. Following Eyal's prepared remarks, we will open the call for the question-and-answer session. Both Eyal and Liat will be available to answer those questions.

You can all find the highlights of the quarter, including the financial highlights and metrics, including those we typically discuss on the conference call in today's earnings press release. Before we start, I'd like to point out the following safe harbor statement. This conference call may contain projections or other forward-looking statements regarding future events or the future performance of the company. Those statements are early predictions and Allot cannot guarantee that they will, in fact, occur. Allot does not assume any obligation to update that information.

Actual events or results may differ materially from those projected, including as a result of changing market trends, delays in the launch of services by Allot customers, reduced demand and the competitive nature of the security services industry as well as other risks identified in the documents filed by the company with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Also, the financial results in this call will be presented mainly on a non-GAAP basis. Allot believes that these non-GAAP financial measures provide more consistent and comparable measures to help investors understand Allot's operating performance in the quarter.

For all the data, please refer to the financial tables published in the results press release issued earlier today, which also includes the GAAP to non-GAAP reconciliation tables. And with that, I would now like to hand the call over to Eyal Harari, CEO of Allot. Eyal, please go ahead.

Eyal Harari: Thank you, Kenny. This quarter demonstrated continued excellent execution and showed the strengths of our business model. Allot is now a sustainably profitable company, and we continue to expand our profitability as we deliver growth. We reported a strong third quarter, combining double-digit revenue growth across both our business lines, SECaaS and SMART, with improved profitability and solid cash generation. Revenues increased 16% year-over-year to $30.6 million, our fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth.

Beyond the growth, we delivered solid profitability with 13% non-GAAP operating margin, a good improvement over the first two quarters of this year, and we had another quarter of strong cash flow generation of $7.4 million, bringing our cash position to $112 million, our highest level in over 4 years. We are progressing well against the key objectives we established for 2026. Our results demonstrate continued execution of our strategy, profitable growth led by SECaaS, supported by a solid contribution from our SMART business. SECaaS ARR reached $39 million at the end of September, an increase of more than 40% year-over-year. This growth continues to expand our recurring revenue base and enhances our visibility into future revenue.

And while we are very pleased with the performance of SECaaS, the SMART business has also been performing well. During the quarter, we won a number of key expansion orders from existing SMART customers. These orders demonstrated continued customers' engagement and confidence in our product and services. Satisfied and returning customers are one of the most efficient ways for us to grow. They know us, they trust our technology, and they come back to us as their network and their needs grow. This type of growth is also good for our business mix. Expansion orders carry a higher proportion of software and services, which is supportive of gross margins. SECaaS continued to perform well and in line with our expectations.

It is a win for the telco, a win for us, which shares the revenues for this protection, and of course, a win for the customers, which gain peace of mind for only a small increase in their monthly bill. We believe this trend will only grow in the coming months, and we believe expected increased demand for our SECaaS solution as the threat environment continue to grow exponentially. We recently announced new capabilities for securing SIM-enabled IoT devices with Allot NetworkSecure, giving telcos a network-based way to protect connected devices across 4G and 5G networks of their business customers. As businesses connect cameras, sensors, meters, trackers, industrial equipment, and other IoT devices, securing those devices present a particular challenge.

Our IoT security technology is designed to help prevent cyberattacks from compromising IoT services. With Allot NetworkSecure, telcos can provide network firewall security services for business IoT communications without depending on security software installed on each protected device. Another development for us during the quarter relates to the emerging quantum compute threats. During the third quarter, we announced that Allot is a founding member and Chair of a new Post-Quantum Communications Consortium supported by the Israel Innovation Authority. The consortium brings together leading technology companies, including NVIDIA, along with leading academic institutes, to develop technologies that will secure communication networks and protect data and users against future quantum computing threats.

While the threats in the future, quantum computers are one day expected to render many of today's encryption methods vulnerability, and quantum-safe security is fast becoming a critical priority for governments, enterprises, and communication providers. We are proud to be helping leading this effort to protect networks and users in the quantum era. In summary, the company is executing very well, having turned the business around to a sustainably profitable company that is increasing its profitability as we continue with our growth. The third quarter was another strong quarter for Allot, with continued double-digit revenue growth in both of our SECaaS and SMART business lines.

Overall, our strategy is working, and Allot is well-positioned to continue its profitable, cash-generating, recurring revenue-led growth into 2027 and beyond. And now, I would like to hand it over to our CFO, Liat Nahum, for the financial summary. Liat, please go ahead.

Liat Nahum: Thanks, Eyal. We reported revenue of $30.6 million in the quarter, up 16% year-over-year. Revenue from our growth engine, Security as a Service, were $9.9 million in the quarter, up 37% year-over-year, comprising 33% of our total revenue. Growth was led by Asia Pacific, where revenue nearly doubled year-over-year, together with 13% growth in product and professional services. Our SECaaS annual recurring revenue as of September 30, 2026, were $38.8 million, up 41% year-over-year. 64% of our overall revenue this quarter was recurring in nature. I will now discuss the non-GAAP financial measures. For all our financial results, including the GAAP financial measures and other various breakdowns of our revenue, please refer to the table in our results press release.

Our non-GAAP gross margin in the quarter was 71.9%, compared with 72.2% in the third quarter of last year and 71.8% last quarter. This was above our general expectations of around 70% gross margin for 2026, supported by the software and services part of our revenues, including the expansion orders that Eyal mentioned. Non-GAAP operating expenses for the quarter were $18 million, compared with $15.4 million in the third quarter of last year. The increase primarily reflects planned investment in research and development to support our product roadmap, as well as increased sales and marketing expenses as we continue to invest in building our pipeline to support our future growth.

In addition, we had higher general and administrative expenses, reflecting non-recurring professional fee and tax-related items relating to prior periods. Despite this increase, operating expenses declined to 59% of revenue compared with 62% in the prior quarter, reflecting the operating leverage inherent in our business model. We reported non-GAAP operating income of $3.9 million with an operating margin of 12.9%. Compared with the non-GAAP operating income of $3.7 million, or an operating margin of 14% in the third quarter of last year. Allot had 498 full-time employees as of September 30, 2026.

In terms of non-GAAP net profit, we reported $4.7 million in the quarter, or a profit of $0.09 per diluted share, compared with a non-GAAP net profit of $4.6 million, or a profit of $0.10 per diluted share in the third quarter of last year. We again generated strong operating cash flow of $7.4 million in the third quarter, compared with $4 million in the third quarter of last year. For the first 9 months of 2026, operating cash flow totaled $26.4 million. During the quarter, we began executing on our $40 million share repurchase program and purchased 213,000 Allot shares, totaled $1.6 million. Allot has a robust balance sheet with no debt.

Cash and cash equivalent, bank deposit, restricted deposit, and investment as of September 30, 2026, totaled $112 million, as compared with $88 million as of December 31, 2025. Our strong balance sheet positions us well to pursue both organic and non-organic growth to execute our long-term strategy. Looking ahead to the remainder of 2026, we are narrowing our full year 2026 revenue guidance to between $116 million to $118 million, representing the upper end of our previously announced range and increasing its midpoint. This implies a Q4 revenue of continued double-digit year-over-year growth. We also expect SECaaS revenue growth for 2026 to be above 40%.

We expect our gross margin to remain at around its current levels in the coming quarters, with the specific gross margin in any given quarter dependent on our product mix. Overall, we continue to expect profitability improvement over the coming quarters. That ends my summary. Eyal and I are now happy to take your questions.

Some of them are coming from existing customers that are adding more capabilities, some of our new cyber engines, like the identity and off-net services that we launched in the recent year. Some are growing the, what we call the organic growth of the service by adding more customers.

Overall, we see that the SECaaS is continue to grow, and we are looking to continue and invest in our both on the sales and marketing in order to hunt into new partnerships and new CSPs, as well as continue innovate with our R&D to provide more value to our customers, as demonstrated with our recent announcement about IoT security services. So far, we are comfortable with the growth, and we expect this growth to continue in the next quarters.

Jonathan Ho: Got it. Just as my follow-up, you mentioned IoT security a number of times inside of the call. Can you talk about what that broader opportunity looks like, especially with some of your commentary around the increased breach activity? As Allot unique value proposition is about providing network-enabled security. This allow you to protect mass amount of devices without the need to install any specific software on the endpoint. Now, this is definitely valuable when you look to protect a mobile phone, but when you look to protect a device that could be a meter or a sensor, you don't really have a choice.

And this is why we decided to add this capability to our product, which is making sure those devices are not interrupted. Now, while the IoT devices are relatively, might be simple and not necessarily have a large amount of volume in terms of network bandwidth, it might be very critical if they are not performing well.

So, by adding ability to avoid denial of service and by adding the ability to do firewall protection to SIM-based devices [Audio Gap] choosing and helping our said supermarkets and there are more stories like that as [indiscernible] becoming wider and we believe this is a need that will come and, we are going to promote solutions with our install base and, with new potential customers.

Matthew Calitri: Understood. And then Liat, are there any guardrails you can provide as we look out to SECaaS growth and to calendar year '27, and particularly thinking about where penetration levels are with existing vendors?

This is starting to materialize into revenue. If you look on our RPO as shared in our mid-year financials, this was growing quite significantly, and we start '27 with a very strong visibility and a very strong backlog.

Therefore, we are definitely looking to continue to grow. We are now finalizing the plan, and once we next quarter, we will be able to share more in terms of guidance and other KPIs to provide more color of the growth rates.

#3223. Axle raises $9M to bring AI agents to Wall Street’s meeting-makers

The startup replaces spreadsheets that banks use to set up investor meetings with company bosses.

Axle has raised $9M led by Eniac and Bonfire Ventures. It makes software that helps investment banks arrange meetings between investors and company management, and will add more AI agents. It says some of North America’s biggest banks use it.

Axle, a startup that makes software for investment banks, has raised $9M in a round led by Eniac and Bonfire Ventures, it announced on Thursday. Teamworthy Ventures also joined.

Axle works on what banks call corporate access. Banks arrange meetings between big investors and company bosses, analysts and industry experts. Those meetings help investors decide where to put money, and they shape which banks get their trading business.

CEO Sam Shapiro says much of this work still runs on old software, spreadsheets and manual scheduling. He worked in corporate access at Goldman Sachs before starting Axle, according to the company’s 2024 pre-seed announcement.

Axle puts conferences, investor meetings, roadshows and expert calls into one system. Clients can request meetings and see schedules through portals that need no login.

The company says it works with some of North America’s largest investment banks but did not name them. One bank started using Axle earlier this year and, within months, dropped three other providers.

The new money will go into AI agents that help bank staff understand clients and spot opportunities. Axle is also building tools to show how much the meetings are worth to clients.

AI startups are moving fast into banking. Berlin’s Taktile raised $110M from Goldman Sachs to automate bank decisions, and Anthropic has launched ready-made finance agents for Claude, while OpenAI sells a ChatGPT for finance.

#3222. Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This naming scheme is not the most intuitive.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

#3221. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3218. Apple is closing its Support Community forum after 28 years

Users can still browse the Apple Support Community, but can no longer ask or answer. Apple told AppleInsider it will take the forums completely offline, old answers included.

Apple has stopped taking new posts on the Apple Support Community and will close the forum on 20 November. The site has been read-only since 10 November, according to a notice on its homepage.

“You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site,” the notice says.

9to5Mac’s Marcus Mendes first reported the notice on the evening of 10 November. The last post appears to have gone up at 5:49pm Pacific time that day, Joe Rossignol reported for MacRumors.

Apple told MacRumors it made the decision after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs.

The forum launched in 1998 as Apple Tech Exchange, according to MacRumors. It became Apple Discussions in 2000, Apple Support Communities in 2011 and Apple Support Community in 2022.

The notice does not say what happens to the old posts. Apple told AppleInsider it will take the forums completely offline, William Gallagher reported on 11 November.

Apple has not read the forums in at least five years, according to AppleInsider’s sources. The sign-in button now leads to an internal portal for Apple’s corporate employees, MacRumors reported.

MacRumors pointed users to Apple Support, its own forums and Reddit. Reddit is moving to login-only viewing, and it now uses AI to summarise product threads.

Customers can still contact Apple Support directly, MacRumors noted. Last month, Apple Support took on Apple’s offer to replace iPhone Duos with failing inner screens.

#3217. New Era Energy (NUAI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Power sidesteps the ERCOT queue, with service eyed for late 2027.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

New Era Energy & Digital, Inc. (NUAI +16.74%) reported progress on its flagship Texas Critical Data Centers project, transitioning to a self-execution model for Phase 1 delivery. Management stated that the company has secured power outside the standard ERCOT Batch Zero process, providing a path to service by late 2027. The company entered into a nonbinding letter of intent with a global technology firm for both Phase 1 and Phase 2, while concurrently strengthening its balance sheet through a private placement. The development strategy emphasizes modular construction to reduce capital outlays and an islanded power solution for future phases to mitigate grid-related constraints.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the NUAI's Third Quarter 2026 Business Update Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Lincoln Tan, Investor Relations at New Era. Please go ahead.

Lincoln Tan: Thank you, operator, and good morning. My name is Lincoln Tan, Investor Relations for New Era. Thank you for joining our third quarter fiscal 2026 business update call. Joining me today are Charlie Nelson, Chairman and CEO; Ted Warner, President and CFO; Jose Rodriguez, Chief Operating Officer; and Evan Pierce, Chief Development Officer. Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that today's call is being recorded and will be available on the investor relations section of our website. [Operator Instructions] Certain statements made on this call that are not historical facts, including those related to our future plans, objectives, and expected performance, are forward-looking statements.

These forward-looking statements represent our outlook only as of the date of this conference call. While we believe any forward-looking statements made on this call are reasonable, actual results may differ materially because these statements are based on our current expectations and subject to risks and uncertainties. These risks and uncertainties are discussed in our filings with the SEC, including our most recent annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly report on Form 10-Q. You should refer to and consider these factors when relying on such forward-looking information.

Any forward-looking statement made speaks only as of the date on which it is made, and we do not undertake and expressly disclaim any obligation to update or alter our forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events, or otherwise, except as required by applicable law. So with that, I'll now turn the call over to Charlie Nelson.

Charles Nelson: And thank you, Lincoln. And again, thanks everyone for making the time here. So we're going to go over everything to date at TCDC and where we are as a company during this call. We've made a lot of important progress at TCDC during Q3 and into Q4. We've secured the power in our own name, we're rapidly progressing lease negotiations, and strengthening the team and balance sheet really needed to move this project towards final delivery. That progress comes against a challenging backdrop. We've had multiple black swan events, the capital markets have been volatile, and investors are asking harder and harder questions about how data center projects will be funded and delivered.

And communities want to understand what these developments mean for their electricity supply, the water resources, local infrastructure, and essentially a social license to operate in these different communities that we're in. And we believe that environment makes the quality of our power position and our development approach and contracting approach increasingly important. And so since our last update, we've signed a 20-year PPA for up to 207 megawatts. In conjunction with that, we posted a $118 million cash collateralized letter of credit to be able to hold that power, which we have already completed. The power availability is expected in Q3 of '27.

And this power, again, just to remind everyone, is through an existing grandfathered private use network, which is not subject to Batch Zero constraints within Texas, and it allows us to have this ready-for-service date in Q4 of '27. And we believe that we have one of the more valuable power positions at a time when customers have kind of limited alternatives on that time line. Additionally, there are many of those in the Batch Zero process who are facing uncertainty around the magnitude and the timing of their power.

And so we're just looking at the rest of the market adding and compounding risk with these countless data center projects that are up for permitting, and we're sitting here relatively insulated here. And so with our permits pertaining to Phase 1 in hand, an adjacent generation plant and Phase 1 power as part of an existing and seasoned private use network outside of the batch process, we believe the timing and certainty of our project have made TCDC an even more attractive asset going forward. And so the task now is to translate our position into a definitive lease, and we can go through what we're doing there.

Look, but this is a financial development plan, and ultimately we want to communicate what this means in terms of earnings to our shareholders. So shortly after the PPA announcement that we made in September, we signed a non-binding LOI that covers both TCDC's Phase 1 and Phase 2 with the same prospective tenants. We are now in advanced negotiations with the Phase 1 lease, and the Phase 2 lease documentation is being worked on concurrently but separately. And it's important to note that Phase 1 can proceed without Phase 2 documentation being fully complete. So they are not -- those are mutually exclusive; they're not reliant on each other.

And so for Phase 1, we believe that the proposed modular approach will have -- that we've referenced in our business updates, historically speaking will offer a substantially lower build cost as well as an accelerated timeframe. And we've added -- since then, we've added experienced development and construction professionals that will go over the whole new team to what we believe is already a best-in-class team to support our work on both phases. We also strengthened our balance sheet. Recently, we did a $64 million PIPE, and that was used to pay down debt and support leasing and development activities.

So now we sit here with a clean balance sheet and a project that we believe is arguably one of the most favorable in the country in the current market and beyond. And we believe that what we have done has given us a strategic advantage heading into the next phase of the company. So today, we want to connect all these pieces for everyone because a lot has been going on. And the power that we've secured, how we plan to deliver the project, our partnership model, how we intend to fund it.

And our immediate priority is completing the lease, obviously, and putting the financing and delivery arrangements around it, giving shareholders a clearer view of the capital required and ultimately what the potential returns are. And so before going into this project detail, I'm going to hand it over to Evan right now to address directly our approach to responsible development and how we're approaching power, the water stewardship, and giving the local community a seat at the table, which is really what's the world that we've been planning and living in, and we're excited to just talk through this. So with that, I'll hand it over to Evan real quick. And Evan, go ahead.

Evan Pierce: Thanks, Charlie. I was born in Texas, I was raised in Texas, and my family lives in Texas. So these issues are important to me. Our team has deep experience in both data center development and sustainability. That experience has reinforced how critical it is to strategically address power, water and community needs at all stages of development, including site selection, land development, design, construction, and operations. New Era's approach to TCDC is aligned with Governor Abbott and Governor-elect Hinojosa's priorities and concerns for utility ratepayers, water, and local communities. This is not reactionary; this is how we approach TCDC from the outset.

Stewardship was core to our development philosophy well before these issues became a prominent part of the data center debate. Regarding power, our strategy is designed to avoid increasing transmission costs for Texas ratepayers. Phase 1 uses an existing utility connection via behind-the-meter private use network. For Phase 2, we plan to bring new islanded on-site generation to power the rest of the site. Addressing water, we simply plan on deploying closed-loop cooling to limit consumption at TCDC. That being said, I want to highlight a unique and underappreciated feature of the Permian Basin.

This region generates a significant amount of produced water from the oil and gas industry, and we're partnering with Texas regulators and the University of Texas to evaluate how that water can be treated and reused for industrial cooling. With the aim of reducing demand on local freshwater supplies while also lowering the volume sent to disposal wells. Finally, we agree that Texans should have a seat at the table. New Era continues to engage directly with Ector County, the City of Odessa, as well as local businesses and community organizations. We're aiming for maximum transparency, want residents to understand the development, and provide opportunities to raise questions as our plans take shape.

Our project is supporting local jobs, and we want to continue to work with local suppliers and contractors whenever that makes sense. These principles will continue to guide us as we develop TCDC. Now, let me explain Phase 1 power in more detail. Phase 1 will be served via an executed PPA for up to 207 megawatts. This power is part of an existing registered private use network supplied by Vistra's adjacent Odessa-Ector Generating Station. It's essentially a behind-the-meter arrangement with front-of-the-meter reliability, and Phase 1 power is not contingent on progressing through ERCOT's Batch Zero process.

During Texas Senate Bill 6 implementation, the Texas Public Utility Regulatory Act, or PURA, was amended and exempts net metering arrangements registered with ERCOT prior to 2025 from the batch process. This is why we feel that TCDC is both unique and valuable. Our recent commercial discussions continue to reinforce the value of near-term power. Across the United States, new data center capacity in '27 is extremely constrained due to power. We believe the combination of contracted supply, scale, and expected Q3 2027 availability makes TCDC particularly relevant to those customers. Additionally, our partnership with Vistra supports future power development, and there's an alignment of interest here.

Vistra has been a great partner, and once power delivery begins, they will receive a 5% non-voting stake in Phase 1 power. Our goals are aligned, and they have a direct interest in the long-term success of development. Customers understand this, and it is a relevant consideration for how they could expand their footprint at the campus over time. And of course, delivering on that opportunity takes an experienced team. Charlie, over to you.

Charles Nelson: Thanks, Evan. At our Q2 update, we introduced several of the new senior leaders who had joined the team here at New Era. Since then, we've continued to add technical depth around them. The roles span everything from development, engineering, construction, power, operations, et cetera. These are people who understand firsthand what needs to happen between just securing a site and bringing a facility into full service, and these are obviously giant projects. So just to highlight a few examples, we brought on Erin Henderson, she's our Senior Vice President of Energy and Policy, who joins us from Microsoft, where she was the Director of Data Center Flexibility and Energy Infrastructure.

We've got Marlon Millington, our new Vice President of Engineering and Operations, who joins us from Meta, where he was a Critical Operations Manager. We have Morgan O'Connor, our new VP of Construction, who joins us from AWS, where she was Senior Manager of Construction, running a lot along their critical Eastern Seaboard. We have Doug Hofmockel and Maria Rodriguez, our Mechanical and Electrical Engineering leads bringing experience from Meta, ByteDance, Amazon, and Microsoft; and Dana Herrick, our Director of Physical Security, who previously led Global Security Operations at CyrusOne, who's obviously a fantastic legacy operator.

And finally, just this week, we're excited to announce Ashlie Alaman, our new General Counsel, who joins our executive leadership team from CleanArc Data Centers, who has also had previous roles at CyrusOne and Vistra. So just a whole ton of relevant experience here. And look, we need this collective experience as a company throughout project planning, site preparation, construction and commissioning. And our team needs to fully understand the detail and nuance around delivery obligations that we are taking on. And really, for the intent, this is to test whether the proposed schedule is achievable and to coordinate with many of the other parties that are involved to aid in this seamless execution.

And we're building these capabilities obviously for TCDC, but it's not exclusively for TCDC. We're building this platform, and I know we've talked about it before, but we're building a platform that enables us to continue to execute confidently with our counterparties and tenants that will not require us to rebuild the team every single process. And so just to talk through some of the Phase 1 delivery approach, I'm going to hand this over to Jose, and then he can cover some of that.

Jose Rodriguez: Thanks, Charlie. The team you just introduced brings direct experience building and operating large data center campuses. Let me explain how we're applying that experience to our own delivery approach. We are in advanced negotiations on a definitive Phase 1 lease around our proposed modular approach, which we think makes sense for a number of reasons. From a physical construction perspective, modular means completing more work offsite while site preparation progresses in parallel. That gives us better visibility of our production schedules and can shorten the path to commissioning. It also reduces our reliance on large on-site construction crews, helping us manage the risk of labor shortages as competition for skilled data center workers remains elevated.

We're working with multiple vendors across various parts of the supply chain and designing for flexibility as customer hardware requirements evolve. We're also working through long lead equipment requirements, including transformers and other enabling electrical infrastructure. The networking and physical security specialists we have onboarded are also involved in the design, and we're planning for testing and commissioning from the outset. The aim is to identify and manage dependencies early on to reduce the risk of late changes impacting delivery time lines. Ted, over to you on the economics and capital requirements.

Ted Warner: Thanks, Jose. Based on our initial estimates, we expect Phase 1 build costs to be less than half that of a comparable traditional development. At the same time, we're negotiating what we believe are attractive lease economics that reflect the value of our near-term power and the current state of the market from a cost of capital perspective, focusing on maximizing our return on equity dollars. Alongside the build cost and lease economics, we're also seeking to negotiate favorable timing for capital outlays, leveraging tenant relationships for design and supply chain, all with the aim of limiting the funding New Era needs to provide, even in the near term post-signing of a Phase 1 lease.

Ultimately, the overall funding requirement will depend on our agreed scope, payment timetable, and allocation of delivery responsibilities. Once the agreements are finalized, we'll be able to explain these commitments and the economics in far more detail. What we can say now is we are working tirelessly to get all the details finalized for Phase 1 lease execution. Evan, over to you for an update on the site itself.

Evan Pierce: Thanks, Ted. Alongside the commercial work, we're making tangible progress on site and continue to de-risk the asset. We own 493 acres and are under contract with Grow Odessa to acquire another 99 acres. We have an executed PSA, we've paid the deposit, and expect to close in the coming weeks. That acquisition is expected to reduce easement constraints and increase the site's capacity potential. We've secured key site approvals, and site preparation is already underway, including clearing and grading. The team has also carried out significant cleanup remediation and removed thousands of feet of pipeline. The photographs on this page show some of that progress.

Our next major commercial milestone remains the definitive Phase 1 lease, and we are in advanced negotiations on that documentation alongside the financing and delivery work streams. Our timing remains unchanged. Power availability is expected in Q3 2027 with initial ready-for-service targeted for Q4 2027. That brings us to the expansion opportunity alongside Phase 1. Turning to Phase 2, we're planning for approximately 550 megawatts of new on-site generation with Thunderhead Energy Solutions. The intention is to create an islanded solution supplying power directly to the campus that is not subject to the risk associated with the ERCOT batch process. Together with Phase 1, that would take planned capacity across the first two phases to approximately 757 megawatts gross.

A Thunderhead subsidiary has filed the standard air permit application with the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, and we still believe that permit will be approved. From a timing perspective, we expect turbine deliveries in Q4 2027 and Q1 2028. Commercial negotiations continue to progress with the same prospective tenant as Phase 1, and we're working through separate lease documentation for Phase 2. We anticipate a similar build cost for Phase 2, which, as Charlie mentioned, would be substantially lower compared to a traditional development. Beyond the first two phases, we're evaluating the campus layout as a whole to maximize the capacity the site could support.

Phase 3 remains in design, and its ultimate capacity will depend on the layout and the density we can achieve. Our immediate focus remains on Phases 1 and 2. Now I'll hand it back to Ted to discuss our financial position and approach to funding development.

Ted Warner: Thanks, Evan. How we fund TCDC will have a direct bearing on the value we create for shareholders. In a volatile market, we have to balance the capital needed to move the project forward with the cost and risk of raising it. A couple of weeks ago, we closed a $64 million PIPE to repay Macquarie borrowings that helped fund the credit support for our Vistra PPA, preserve cash for the next stage of development, and ultimately support our leasing work streams. Turning to the balance sheet, we believe we're in a strong cash position post capital raise, giving us ample flexibility as we work toward lease execution and arrange project financing.

As of October 31, we had a total of $187 million in cash, comprising $49 million of unrestricted cash and $138 million of restricted cash, including collateral supporting the PPA letter of credit. We also have $20 million outstanding debt on our Macquarie facility, which is fully cash-collateralized. After lease execution, we believe we will have various options to restructure the LC arrangements with the aim of releasing some of our restricted cash while maintaining the required credit support, allowing us to put more of our existing cash to work on development. On project funding, we retain the option for up to $200 million of financing under the Macquarie facility following lease execution, subject to the applicable conditions.

We are also in discussions with other potential lenders on larger pre- and post-lease debt funding partnerships with the aim of getting credit instruments in place that fit the agreed development scope and timing of both Phase 1 and Phase 2. Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Mike Grondahl with Northland.

Mike Grondahl: It was highlighted that you expect Phase 1 build cost to be about 50% below traditional builds, and that the timing of capital outlays was kind of limited up front. With that, this color kind of alludes to a similar structure that Riot and Anthropic had with a powered land lease we saw 1 week or 2 ago. Can you just walk us through how we should think about that commentary for Phase 1. And if this is a structure we should expect to be replicated across Phase 2 and potentially Phase 3?

Ted Warner: Yes. Mike, thanks for the question. Yes, I mean, the short answer is yes, it's a similar -- seems to be a similar-looking structure, right?
