With the capital markets where they are, they're getting more creative.

And yes, we feel that the returns that we're going to get off of a project like this are great given what's happening in the credit markets. And as for Phase 1 versus Phase 2, yes, we're still trying to figure out what we'd like Phase 2 to look like. We're working closely with the client, but I think as Evan alluded to earlier, yes, there's a good chance that Phase 2 looks remarkably similar to Phase 1, but that hasn't been completely ironed out yet. We're far more focused, as Charlie said, on just finalizing Phase 1.

Mike Grondahl: Got it. And then one more with Phase 1. Can you just clarify, are there any remaining approvals, permits, regulatory issues? And then can you give us a little bit of insight into any Phase 2 approvals or how TCEQ air permitting is progressing?

Ted Warner: Yes. I'll let Evan to answer that.

Charles Nelson: And actually, I might chime in here real quick, and then Evan. But one thing to kind of state, when our team sort of took over development a few months ago, we really just started knocking down every single outstanding item and really taking all of the risk off the table in terms of the development and constructability of this, that was reflected in the permits that we talked about in the last call, as well as securing the power in the manner that we did secure it as well, and the quality of that power. And so -- but yes, I'll let Evan kind of chime in a little more on detail.

Evan Pierce: Thanks, Charlie. No, great question. We're fully permitted. We have been for a while. I mean, we included the pictures. We've already started site work. For Phase 1, there's nothing in between us and delivering the project at this point. As far as the question about standard air permits, as I stated in the last call, we still anticipate that's going to be approved by end of year. It does appear like TCEQ is open for business again. They are accepting new permits. And so we did file that permit rather early. I wish I had filed maybe a week earlier, we would not be having this discussion, but we don't anticipate that's going to impact our project at all.

Mike Grondahl: Okay. And then just lastly, it looks like you picked up an incremental 99 acres. Where are those 99 acres? And what was the reason for the acquisition?

Charles Nelson: Yes. I mean, it was just one of these little pieces of land that's contiguous to the property that we have. We've done this once before, picked up an extra 50-some acres just to -- it essentially creates an ease of utility build-out. And so, we worked with the City of Odessa on this, which was who we bought the original acreage from to begin with. And so basically, it's some connective tissue. It's usable, and so it just bolsters the position and makes all the execution of getting powered A to B even easier.

Operator: Our next question comes from Nick Giles with B. Riley Securities.

Nick Giles: Just was curious, you mentioned you're in advanced negotiations on Phase 1 at this stage. And so what would you say is really still being worked through? Is this more of a technical or design nature? Is it economics? Just curious on anything more you might be able to say on kind of where things stand?

Ted Warner: Yes. I think we've got a full agreement on what the economics are going to look like, so we're really excited about that. And these modular builds are fairly simple from an SLA perspective. But yes, you're right, I mean, there are a few more technical things to work out. And yes, I mean, we feel really good about where we are at the moment.

Nick Giles: Ted, I guess it sounds like you've already made a lot of progress in de-risking the supply chain. I just -- I struggled to catch it all. Can you just walk us through kind of what remaining long-lead time items still need to be secured for Phase 1, and what kind of -- if there's any deposits you might need to make on that? And then how are you thinking about reserving capacity for Phase 2?

Ted Warner: Yes, maybe I'll let either Evan or Jose touch on the long-lead time items, but what I can say is, the tenant has been -- the prospective tenant has been extremely helpful, as it relates to procurement of any long-lead time items that we may not have on hand. Leveraging their supply chain has been something that we've really wanted to do. But Evan, Jose, I'll let one of you go.

Jose Rodriguez: Yes, Nick. And as we're working to finalize the design of what it looks like, which not to put the cart before the horse, we have to finish the lease in order to understand that technical specifications completely. We are talking in parallel to various equipment providers to understand the supply chain to make reservations. We know the electrical equipment that is going to enable the delivery. We're working on that to secure that. And there are no blockers for us to be able to execute once our final design is complete.

Charles Nelson: Yes. I think it's important just to note, how the -- like the voltages that we operate under, what the power is being delivered under, and frankly, the scope of the type of modules that are going in. A lot of that is being handled externally that we aren't exposed to. So a vast majority of -- because these are long-lead time items, a lot of that's 345 kV step-down transformers, stuff like that, that's traditionally taking from, like transmission-level voltages down into usable voltages. We are already down in that usable voltage range.

So it is a little bit different, easier, and we're not exposed to the same kind of constraints that you would typically see in that type of execution.

Nick Giles: I appreciate all that color. And then just last one for me. You mentioned some of the new hires. It's impressive to see you guys add this amount of talent. I guess, given that Phase 1 is already in late stages, Phase 2 a little further down the road, what is the team really working on here and now? Are you looking at new sites? What are some of the key criteria in the pipeline? Just any more color on kind of that ongoing work.

Charles Nelson: Yes. I mean, I'll say this, our ability to take on this development ourselves is largely attributed to the team that we have. When we talked to the tenant, they looked at our team and said, "Wow, you've got world-class execution capability here, and you're solely focused on executing this one project." That actually became an attractant that led us into what we're doing right now, which is self-execution. So I mean, look, every member of the team is busy doing different aspects, preparing for execution for this project. And so really, building the team the way that we did was largely a function that allowed us to get to this self-execution model.

And so going forward, look, right now I think it's best for our shareholders and everyone that we execute on our deal, we get to RFS, and there's a whole lot that can be done afterwards. Like everyone else, I mean, look, we see a ton of projects. We also look at the markets and say, "Well, what makes sense right now?" Like, there's a whole series of evolutions that we can do as a company once we get to execute on this Phase 1 properly, and even into Phase 2. And so, yes, I mean, like, of course we have a whole bunch of pipeline. It's just where do we allocate resources right now?

And I think the best thing for ourselves, our shareholders, et cetera, is to get this one done finally and then evaluate the world after that.

Operator: Our next question comes from Bryan Baratian with ROTH Capital Partners.

Bryan Baratian: Great news on all the progress in the quarter. I have a couple of quick questions. Last week or 2 weeks ago, Cipher was -- you guys were mentioned on Cipher's earnings call, and what they mentioned was that they see monetization value in the Odessa site, pointing to speed of site access and scarce long-lead equipment. Can you guys provide any color on the source of that claim? And does that have anything to do with you guys and how you're structured now, whether it's getting equipment delivered to the site or whether it's doing a potential JV? My read is that's not the case.

I mean, you guys have your whole -- you've built a really strong team and you can do this yourselves. Can you provide any color on that?

Ted Warner: Yes. Sure. I mean, I can't comment as to what they mean from a monetization standpoint there. I can only say what we said in the presentation, which is, what we're looking at right now in our current Phase 1 plan is delivery in the September time frame for this first modular deployment on the 207 on our acreage. What that will require is spending a little bit of money to get that power over to our site versus where it's going to right now, which is theirs. And that's simple.

And then the existing PPA between them and Vistra has a clause in it where the substation they have right there and all the electrical equipment needs to be bought back by Vistra or, in this case, us. What we've agreed to in our PPA is to execute this PSA, which says, we will pay for a new line run from their plant to our acreage, and we'll also take on that obligation to purchase their substation and all the electrical equipment, which, like you said, that helps as far as long-lead time items go, right? Just an existing substation -- everything we need is right there.

And the mechanism for the pricing there is just that they've already got a baseball appraisal mechanism that's built into their documentation, which I think is publicly filed. So that's -- I mean, that would be definitely the one thing that we would be purchasing from them ultimately or purchasing from Vistra. I'm not really sure exactly how that mechanic will work, but that is a part of the transfer of the power from them to us. And purchasing all that equipment, which is, we find that to be really convenient.

Bryan Baratian: Ted, my next question is, with the elections now done and Governor Hinojosa taking office in January, there was a New York Times report that happened a couple of days ago, where she mentioned we're looking to stop projects that have already begun construction but still need certain permits. What I found interesting about that was originally my take was, if you were under construction and a lot of capacity was being delivered and there were large sums of capital being invested, especially to grow these areas. I thought it was interesting that it was the whole thing on permits. Can you give -- and I may have missed this on the call back, I'm sorry.

But can you give a little bit more color on -- I saw the TCEQ website is now up and running. They're accepting new permits. Can you give a little bit more color on why you guys feel de-risked in achieving that air permit and some color on timing on that?

Charles Nelson: Yes. And I'll chime in here real quick. Look, the objective here that they're trying to do is make sure that -- yes, and she's been very clear about this, to make sure that projects that are being permitted now, or filing permits post-election are -- or ones that are in the batch process, follow a certain set of criteria that take care of the local communities and a whole bunch of social license to operate types of things. Given the fact that we already have the permits, I think we're insulated from that. And so, the objective isn't to pull back permits that are already issued. That is not something that they want to do.

But I mean, furthermore, we looked at how we intend to operate, like from a thesis-wise, and there's actually a fair bit of alignment between what everyone's been asking for and what we've just been electively doing as a company. And it's built into the ethos of what we do. So talking about our risks on Phase 1, I mean, that's one thing, we've kind of already covered that. On Phase 2, as it relates to the air permits, this is a standard air permit. It's not like we're going to stop like country or Texas or anyone's going to stop allowing air permits to be issued.

I think just as it relates to the specific application of this industry, they just want to see a few things checked off, making sure that there is a -- the social license to operate aspect of these developments that are considered, which, again, has been built into our operating thesis before anyone ever asked for it. So to the extent that these permits are now kind of dislodged and the processes are moving, they're going to get issued when they get issued, but I don't think the intention of the new government whatsoever is to stop these developments. I think it's just to make sure that communities are taken care of.

And we've spoken pretty aggressively about making sure that community engagement is a core tenet of what we do. And so as far as Phase 2, beyond even additional projects, I think the way that we operate our company is pretty well suited for kind of the new world that everyone found themselves in last Tuesday. So yes.

Bryan Baratian: Great. Last one for me is, as we think about the language in the release and in the presentation about deliberately using the word tenant. I don't know if I'm reading too much into it, because previous things -- previous releases were using the word hyperscaler. Can you talk a little bit about, I know that you're in conversations with this one tenant under a non-binding LOI for both phases, Phase 1 is moving ahead. Can you talk about demand for the site? Like, are you still speaking with other prospective parties? Are you seeing the same strong inbound demand from a range of both hyperscaler and other tenants? Could you give color on that?

Ted Warner: I can say that we are under that LOI that Charlie referenced. It's with a leading global technology company is what I would use as the description here, and they are under exclusivity. So our other conversations that we were having with a wide range of high-quality potential tenants, those have all ceased as we are trying to get to the finish line.

Bryan Baratian: Perfect. But the main thing I'm getting at is there is still like -- I guess that means that there is a lot of demand from a series of diverse counterparties for power like this that's available before.

Ted Warner: Absolutely. I mean, just pointing back to the reason why it was so hard for us to begin conversations with a lot of these entities is they were also trying to get a hold of that power once it became available back in July, right? So they were first our competitors, and then they became our prospective tenants once we were able to secure the power. So tough to fight against some trillion-dollar companies out there, but we were able to do that executing that DFA framework that we've laid out, where Vistra has -- they're aligned with us. They've got that 5% ownership stake in anything they supply power to and a ROFR on that entire Phase 3.

And that to them, being utilities, is a very valuable thing. So that was how we ended up with it. And then immediately once that question was settled of who's getting this power, we were able to have conversations with numerous tenants, and over the last 3 months with what's happening with the uncertainty in the Batch Zero process, has our power become more valuable commodity? Absolutely. There was a ton of interest, and we chose to work with the party that we felt was going to give us the best chance for success and a really high-quality lease in the current market.

Operator: Our next question comes from Kevin Pimental with Alliance Global Partners.

Kevin Pimental: Just one for me. Could you help us bridge the timing between power availability in Q3 '27 and initial ready-for-service in Q4 '27? What needs to happen kind of during that period before the first tenant can begin operations?

Ted Warner: I think I'll let Evan speak to this. I know that the timing that we're talking about for trying to start lighting up some of this modular compute is September. But I'll let Evan talk about what we actually have to do between now and then.

Evan Pierce: Thanks, Ted. I mean, generally, the way I look at it, there's really 2 kind of barriers to landing capacity for customers. The first one is getting to the point where you can start construction, and the second is data center commissioning, which requires power. And so we're clear for construction right now. So that's -- the question really is about when is power availability. And so if you go to Google Earth, you look at the location of where the substation is now and our site, you can see it's a relatively short run for distribution lines from that substation to our site.

So basically what needs to happen is, once the current PPA owner is no longer has the PPA, in the interim is the build-out with Vistra of the distribution infrastructure from their site to our site, which is a pretty simple matter. And then bringing it to our switching station on our site. And due to the nature of how we're building this site out with the modular solution, it's not like a standard stick-built in the sense that the -- that's going to take a long time to do.

And so really, there's just some final site work preparing the site for delivery of those modules, and then that rather short distribution run from their site to our site, and then our on-site switching station, which will include metal-clad switchgear, and then the delivery of the assets from the customer, and then commissioning. That's kind of it. It's not super complicated. Did that answer your question, Kevin?

Kevin Pimental: Yes, yes. That was great.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn it back to Charlie Nelson for closing remarks.

Charles Nelson: Yes. And look, thanks everyone. And honestly, thanks for the questions. And just to reiterate, our focus now is squarely on completing this lease and putting the financing and delivery arrangements around it. Our non-binding LOI covers Phases 1 and 2 at TCDC with the same tenants, which is, as Ted mentioned, a leading global technology company. Just to summarize what we've been doing. I mean, we've contracted this very valuable Phase 1 power. We've posted our initial credit support, so we're safe there. We've made really good strides on this leasing since we've taken the reins here. We've strengthened our balance sheet. We continue to add the technical depth to be able to execute.

And look, I believe it's important to address the evolution of our partnership strategy in these closing remarks as this asset has been developed. We've made the election. And again, this is not at the request of the tenant to proceed with executing and delivering this project by ourselves. And there were several factors that played into this decision, but it's important to note that only until recently, when we controlled the PPA that we were we able to take control of this leasing processes ourselves and not rely on other parties. And since then, the contracting phase has significantly accelerated to the place it is today.

And look, we're only able to do that because of the strength of the team, the position of the power contract. Moving away from our potential JV was not a function of contention. We love those folks, but it was merely a decision that controlling our own destiny was deemed the lower-risk path forward by both us and the prospective tenant. And in today's market, when a tenant sees a team of our caliber who is not being pulled in numerous directions by numerous, like, large-scale projects, they see something rare that points to lower execution risk, which is how we ended up here.

And so in summary, that was not a decision that was taken lightly, but we believe that it will provide significantly higher value to our shareholders long term. And so we believe owning all of the current Phase 1 and whatnot is -- put us -- and leaves us in a similar CapEx position, and I think that the outcome of this whole process and the evolution that got us here is really going to produce the best value for all of our shareholders. And with that, I'll just say we appreciate your time, we appreciate your support, and our team is always available if you'd like to follow up. So thank you very much.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3214. J.Crew launches an AI stylist built on Anthropic’s Claude

Style Advisor suggests full outfits from J.Crew's own photo shoots instead of single items.

J.Crew built its new Style Advisor with several of Anthropic’s Claude models.

J.Crew has launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on its US website built with Anthropic’s Claude. Shoppers describe an occasion and get complete outfits from looks J.Crew’s stylists put together. Personal recommendations based on past purchases will come later.

J.Crew has launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on its website built with Anthropic’s Claude, Anthropic announced on Thursday. It is available in the US for women’s and men’s clothing.

Instead of searching for a sweater, then trousers, then shoes, shoppers can describe what they need, such as an outfit for a beach wedding or a first job interview. Style Advisor replies with complete looks, and shoppers can keep refining them. They can also start from one item and ask what goes with it.

Every suggestion comes from outfits J.Crew’s own stylists put together for the brand’s catalogue shoots. The AI picks and shows those looks rather than inventing new ones, which keeps it in line with the brand’s style.

“We see an opportunity to fundamentally rethink the shopping experience,” said Libby Wadle, CEO of J.Crew Group.

J.Crew built the tool using several Claude models. In each conversation, the mid-sized Sonnet 5.5 acts as the stylist, while the smaller Haiku 5.5 handles quick tasks so answers come fast. For now, it does not tailor suggestions to each shopper’s past purchases, but J.Crew plans to add that and expand to more countries.

Retailers are racing to add AI stylists. Ralph Lauren launched its Ask Ralph assistant late last year, and Kate Spade uses Amazon’s shopping AI, while Zalando’s agent will shop other retailers from 2027. On Prime Day, shoppers sent by AI assistants were more likely to buy than those from search.

Everybody’s working for the weekend, but Microsoft Outlook clocked out early. The mission-critical email service is facing a widespread outage.

The outage appears to have started about an hour ago. Based on status checks with the service, the issue is widespread and ongoing.

Downdetector reports over a hundred thousand Outlook outage reports today.

If you’re having trouble with Microsoft Outage, err.. Outlook, you’re not alone.

Usually you can check the latest Outlook outage status here, although it appears to maybe be down as well.

We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. As a precaution, we’ve paused all deployments and configuration changes while we review recent changes for any correlation to this event. We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure. We’re investigating what’s causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service.

#3211. iOS 27’s Find My app adds convenient feature I’ve long wished for

iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app. One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

That’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple:

users [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with new options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

#3210. Anthropic lets companies run Claude’s agent service on their own servers

Agent data and credentials can stay in-house, but conversations still go to a model provider.

Anthropic now lets companies run Claude Managed Agents in their own cloud or data centre. Agent histories and credentials stay on their systems, but each model call still goes to an outside provider such as Anthropic or AWS.

Anthropic now lets companies run its Claude Managed Agents service on their own servers, Help Net Security reported. The self-hosted version launched on Thursday, and customers must request access through their Anthropic account team, the company said in its release notes.

Managed Agents is Anthropic’s service for running AI agents that use tools and remember past sessions. Customers could already run the agents’ tools on their own machines, but Anthropic ran the rest, including the stored history and credentials.

Now customers can run the whole service in their own cloud account or data centre. Agents, session histories and credentials stay on their systems, and every tool call can be logged.

There is a catch. Each time the agent asks Claude a question, the conversation still goes to a model provider, such as Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry. Customers choose which one, but Claude itself does not run inside their network.

Customers also take on the work Anthropic used to do, such as securing and updating the server. Nothing moves over from Anthropic’s hosted service, so agents and saved data must be rebuilt, and some features, such as webhooks and scheduled runs, are missing.

The move gives cautious companies more control over where agent data lives. That matters in Europe, where ECB president Christine Lagarde has warned of the risk of relying on foreign AI. Rivals such as Mistral have long pitched sovereign AI as the answer.

OpenAI took a different route in September, letting companies run its agents inside Amazon’s cloud. Nvidia, meanwhile, has built hardware for safer agents.
