#3209. Figure Tech (FIGR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fee revenue more than tripled as the marketplace model pulled margins higher.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Figure Technology Solutions, Inc. (FIGR +6.12%) reported a significant expansion in its capital-light marketplace model during the third quarter, with fee-based volume reaching record levels and adjusted EBITDA margins expanding to 58%. The company integrated its acquisition of Kiavi, which introduced residential transition loans and debt service coverage ratio loans to its blockchain-native platform. Management announced an expanded $400 million share repurchase program and provided fourth-quarter guidance that accounts for seasonal slowdowns in the broader mortgage market. The company also reported operational improvements from its new AI-driven loan officer assistant and continued growth in its small business lending segment through over 150 active partners.

Operator: Welcome to the Figure Technology Solutions Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Lastly, today's call is being recorded. I would now like to turn the call over to Bryan Michaleski, Head of Investor Relations.

Bryan Michaleski: Good morning, and welcome to Figure's third quarter 2026 earnings call. I'm Bryan Michaleski, Head of Investor Relations for Figure. Joining me today are Mike Cagney, our Executive Chairman and Co-founder; Michael Tannenbaum, our Chief Executive Officer; and Macrina Kgil, our Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that today's discussion will include forward-looking statements within the meaning of federal securities laws. These statements are based on management's current expectations and involve risks and uncertainties, many of which are beyond our control, that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied.

For a discussion of these risks, please refer to the risk factors in our most recent 10-K, 10-Q, and other SEC filings. These statements reflect our views as of today and we undertake no obligation to update them, except as required by law. During the call, we will also refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures. These measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for GAAP results. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in the earnings release we issued earlier today and an appendix to our supplemental slide presentation, both of which are available in the Investor Relations section of our website.

A replay of the call will be available shortly after it ends, and following our prepared remarks, we'll open the line for questions. With that, I'll turn the call over to Michael.

Michael Tannenbaum: Good morning and thank you all for joining. Our third quarter was big for Figure, financially and strategically. Our top and bottom line results again outperformed, demonstrating the durability and resilience of our model. Our Figure Connect platform continues to gain momentum, and the acquisition of Kiavi takes us another big step closer to our vision of bringing the capital markets on-chain. I'll cover each of these topics in my remarks, as well as provide more color on our margins and capital allocation as we build on the growth we've generated year-to-date.

In Q3, we grew volume of 107% year-over-year at 58% EBITDA margin with over 70% Figure Connect mix and maintained a 3.7% net stand-alone take rate, exceeding everything I said we'd do on our last call. First on volume, in another record for Figure, our consumer loan marketplace processed $5.1 billion on an organic basis. Kiavi closed on September 1, so the reported $5.8 billion volume reflects that one-month contribution. Our ecosystem now produces approximately $30 billion annualized run rate volume, making us the largest credit tokenizer by over 2x, achieving the scale in only eight years. As projected last quarter, we saw 72% of our stand-alone volume on Figure Connect, reflecting the increasingly balance sheet-light nature of our business.

This quarter saw another record number of partner additions, ending at 612 stand-alone and 894, including Kiavi's broker partners. In addition to all of the net new growth I just described, we're also seeing expansion from existing origination partners. Those that were with us a year ago in Q3 '25 are now doing over 40% more volume this Q3 '26, a testament to the value we drive for partners. Growth vectors we have been highlighting in the past are strengthening. We now have over 20 active depository partners and over 150 partners in our fast-growing SMB business, which crossed $500 million in run rate volume in Q3. And there's more growth to come.

Our pipeline is robust, including some of the largest mortgage companies and banks in the country, larger than any we work with today. As we expand our marketplace, we're also making important improvements to the platform itself. Most notably, our new Agentic Loan Officer Assistant has shown a 29% increase in funded dollars per loan approval. Figure stands out here, having trained it on outcomes only possible via our standardized data and marketplace with tangible immediate payoff. We jointly developed this with Sierra. In just the first few months since launch, we funded roughly $260 million in loans when Sierra is involved. The agent is now live with our wholesale lending partners and will complete full partner rollout shortly.

Prospects are noticing it's among the highest priority buying criteria they raise in meetings with us. Now turning to the Kiavi acquisition. I'll touch on 3 primary levers and what they mean for our business: new asset classes, the integration and the impact on our product road map. With Kiavi, we have added residential transition loans, RTL, and debt service coverage ratio loans, DSCR, diversifying our platform beyond HELOC into a $200 billion-plus addressable market. RTL loans are made to professional investors who improve properties and sell them or rent them out. Kiavi's loan origination software estimates the home value post renovation by underwriting the property, the contractor and the scope of work.

They do this quickly and with strong accuracy with only roughly 50 basis points of annual losses over their 13-year history. Kiavi's other large product, DSCR loans, are also investor loans made to rental property owners. Kiavi's technology and capital markets are the closest thing to standardization for these products. The Kiavi RTL business was roughly $600 million volume in September. In RTL, we leapfrogged into our marketplace structure through a capital-efficient transaction with Sixth Street. Sixth Street bought the balance sheet and is now an originator of the assets, and Figure provides the rails.

Once we open up the RTL technology to Figure's existing partners and net new partners, Sixth Street will then be only one of many originators using the Kiavi technology. Sixth Street committed to a forward flow post transaction and to using Figure's loan marketplace, securitization shelf and prime platform in connection with the loans. With DSCR, which was a roughly $60 million volume in September business, we are marrying Kiavi's lending technology stack with our existing distribution rails to scale across our partners. Our existing loan investors were already buying this product, so we don't have the same Sixth Street involvement. Our DSCR plans are among some of the most meaningful for this quarter and beyond.

In short, this quarter, we will launch a DSCR product that was built entirely agentically. Arvind Mohan, Kiavi's CEO and now Figure's Chief Business Officer, brings a technical background and business domain expertise to orchestrating where AI can accelerate Figure's build. This is our first product built with AI at every level, from writing the code to reimagining the workflow itself, allowing us to move faster and scale throughput dramatically. We are closing loans within 2 to 3 weeks. And when we add Figure's approach to property verification, we think this can be reduced further. Later this quarter, we'll offer DSCR on a broker basis to our existing customers.

Next quarter, we will offer the full white label Figure Connect option for our partners. Kiavi closed ahead of schedule. The loans have been tokenized and we've actioned over $30 million of initial cost synergies. We are now focused on upselling existing partners, of which we've already onboarded 12 and have over 30 in the pipeline. Kiavi also brought on a number of new full loan and securitized investors. Macrina will cover more here, but moving forward, all of our metrics and our IR will reflect Kiavi volume. In addition to the technology and revenue synergies, Kiavi also adds purchase market expertise to grow our product road map.

In fact, Kiavi does primarily purchase mortgage volume and its platform represents about 50 basis points of the national purchase mortgage market. In summary, we expect Kiavi to be materially accretive to Figure. We added around $8 billion of volume to our marketplace, important new asset classes and acquired market-leading technology we can offer to our partners, originators and investors alike. All this for an under 4-year unlevered payback period. Transitioning from Kiavi to discuss our growth resilience, I'll start with the interest rate environment. Being the most efficient provider in the marketplace has benefits when the broader mortgage industry is navigating higher interest rates.

For many of our partners, rate increases harm their funnel as marginal consumers are less likely to borrow at higher rates. We certainly feel some of that. However, what's more notable for us is that since we're 80% plus B2B, the environment is actually improving our sales motion. Prospects want to add HELOCs, which are popular as borrowers don't want to refinance their low existing rate loans. Right now, we're aggressively getting in front of all of our prospective B2B partners with what I refer to as polite persistence. This polite persistence is paying off. This recent quarter, we saw record volumes, continued 100% volume growth and record partner additions, all as rates rose rapidly.

The fact that we are now 70% Figure Connect further insulates Figure's P&L from volatility tied to rates. Our extremely high product velocity, a median of 10 days, including the government-mandated 3-day loan decision period allows our partners to adjust pricing rapidly as interest rates change. This quarter's results capture very clearly why we have been so focused on a fee-driven marketplace model. As rates rose, the investor side of the marketplace also showed strong resilience. In Q3, we processed $2.7 billion of loan sales and executed 8 securitizations. We added marquee AAA buyers, including New York Life and Nationwide Insurance.

In rockier markets, our loan investors value the differentiated aspects of our marketplace, the liquidity, the credit ratings, the years of history and the transparency of the servicing data we put on chain. As we grow more, we attract larger loan buyers who bring lower cost of capital, leading to more growth. Lastly, in terms of the capital markets milestones we saw this quarter, our stablecoin YLDS is reducing the cost and increasing the speed of settlement, and we now have 28 participants in our marketplace doing so. Our capital market strength gives our partners the confidence to grow with us in all market environments.

As shared similarly last quarter, we've seen greater than 40% of our growth this year from existing customers. If 2026 was the year of the first lien, which was significantly bolstered with Kiavi, 2027 will be the year of the upsell. Two primary reasons here. We've expanded products significantly with Kiavi, and we have organic product expansion as well. Per Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data, our partner base today had greater than $500 billion in originations in 2025. Moving on to growth. As we talked about last quarter, we plan to provide updated disclosures on our margin trends as Figure Connect rapidly expands and as Kiavi comes into the fold.

First, our Q3 3.7% net take rate, excluding Kiavi, exceeded the guidance we gave last quarter. This was despite the aggressive increase in interest rates during the latter part of the quarter, again, a reflection of our increasingly balance sheet-light business model. As we've shared, the decline in take rate over the past year has been the output of the faster-than-expected success of Figure Connect, which is lower take rate but capital-light and drive strong margins. The Figure Connect only take rate has been steady in recent quarters. As we have stated before, Connect take rates are an output of relatively consistent volume-based tier ecosystem fees.

As partners scale their volume, ecosystem fees and therefore, take rates drop as a percentage of volume, but take rates are not meaningfully influenced by negotiated partner rates. The take rate forecast range we are now sharing accounts for both the introduction of new large whale partners likely to hit lower tier pricing and also for the increased role of banks who may not use Figure's Capital Market for all of their originations as they see some production on -- as they keep some production on balance sheet. As we said before, growing the platform as fast as possible is how we win. It extends our first-mover advantage and makes our marketplace more robust.

And as we add asset classes like Kiavi's loans, we further widen our moat. It's a trade we make any day of the week. And that trade gets even easier when we consider contribution margin, which was reflected in our march higher towards 60% EBITDA margins. As I've shared before, we price our partnerships to contribution margin as we grow the marketplace to new products and become the place that lenders and increasingly agents search for new yield, take rate will move. Judge us by our volume growth, our platform traction, our ecosystem and our bottom line. We earn our business on the value we deliver to customers, originators and loan investors alike.

And our products and marketplace, therefore, command strong margins. Before I close it out, I want to briefly cover capital allocation. Figure is in a great position with access to the equity, debt and securitization markets, a robust balance sheet, strong liquidity and meaningful cash flow generation. Our stock is attractive at these current levels, and we will be actively pursuing buybacks. We have been trading below our IPO price recently despite over 100% annual volume growth since IPO, and that's before the full benefit of a highly accretive Kiavi acquisition. While we had approved a $200 million share buyback plan earlier, we hadn't implemented that plan in the open market.

Today, we're announcing an expanded $400 million share buyback plan that will start tomorrow. Given our profitability, cash levels, balance sheet liquidity and access to the capital markets, we will be opportunistic about share repurchases on an ongoing basis, including beyond this initial $400 million program. That said, we see huge organic growth and look at inorganic opportunities as well, especially those that can accelerate our marketplace reach. We will remain disciplined, and we will allocate capital accordingly. Our business continues to fire on all cylinders and the durability of our model gives me the confidence to share that we're going to continue to deliver rapid growth in Q4 at attractive economics.

As the buyback indicates, we're in the early stages of value creation. I'm now going to turn it over to Macrina, who will review financials. After her section, as Bryan noted at the start, our Exec Chairman, Mike Cagney will speak. He'll share more about why the company he co-founded, Navra, matters for Figure but doesn't change what we're building today. Knowing Mike as I do, he's thinking expansively about the future while continuing to work as hard as ever to grow Figure. We get the best of both worlds. I'll also stay for the Q&A period. But first things first. Macrina, the floor is yours.

Minchung Kgil: Thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. This was a great quarter. Growth continued across every part of the business. Loan marketplace volume was $5.8 billion, including Kiavi, up 135% year-over-year as reported and 107% on a figure stand-alone basis. On last quarter's call, we guided Q3 stand-alone volume to a range of $4.8 billion to $5.2 billion. We came in at $5.1 billion towards the upper half of that range. The Kiavi acquisition, which closed September 1, contributed approximately $670 million of volume for the 1 month in our results this quarter. Figure Connect volume, including Kiavi, grew to 74% of overall volume, up from 65% last quarter and from 46% a year ago.

Ecosystem and technology fees are now roughly 40% of our revenue. These more than tripled since a year ago this quarter after becoming the single largest contributor to our P&L last quarter, and we expect that share to continue climbing as the business shifts further towards fee-based capital-light volume. Prime, which was previously known as Democratized Prime, ended the quarter with lender supply of $825 million and matched offers balance at $588 million, including third-party borrow of approximately $200 million. As with Figure Connect, every dollar of third-party demand on Prime is a dollar choosing our infrastructure over a traditional warehouse line, and we expect that to keep building. Net income was $89 million, flat year-over-year.

As a reminder, last year, primarily from a recent merger with Figure Markets, we recognized a onetime $31 million tax benefit, which increased net income to $90 million. Adjusted EBITDA was $164 million, up 91% year-over-year, with margin expanding to 58% from 55% a year ago, continuing progress toward our medium-term 60% target. With the acquisition of Kiavi in September, we expect near-term EBITDA margin to decline below Figure stand-alone year-over-year margin growth as Kiavi pre-Figure was running at or below 40% adjusted EBITDA margin. As we head into 2027, we expect revenue synergies and operating leverage to kick in and normalize back up to overall medium-term target.

Take rate is an output of our channel and product mix, not a target we manage to, as Michael has discussed. We assess our marketplace partnerships and product diversification to contribution margin and to the benefit each brings to adjusted EBITDA. This quarter, I want to provide additional color on gross take rate, especially for Connect as we have shorter duration products such as residential transition loans starting in September. As a reminder, Connect volume carries no customer acquisition cost. That's why we're shifting our focus to gross take rate going forward rather than net take rate.

We expect gross take rate from shorter duration RTLs to be in the 1.5% to 2% range, whereas for longer duration Connect HELOC, we expect to be in the 2.9% to 3.4% range over the next 6 to 12 months. Figure Connect may carry a lower gross take rate than our other channels, but have strong contribution margins and the lowest capital intensity. With higher volume year-over-year, adjusted EBITDA margin continues to expand even as take rate decreased on Connect. Contribution margin is profit that each dollar of incremental revenue generates, taking into account operating leverage and efficiency. In future earnings calls, we plan to discuss contribution margin upfront with color on gross take rate.

To share with you net take rate, what we have been reporting previously for one final time, net take rate was 3.5%, including 1 month of Kiavi results and 3.7% stand-alone figure within the range we've discussed previously. In terms of additional expense from the Kiavi acquisition, onetime M&A and restructuring costs were $22 million in total that were incurred in Q2 and Q3. Of the $35 million run rate cost synergy target we set at announcement, we've actioned $30 million at close, with the remainder to be actioned over the next 12 months. I'll keep you posted in future quarters with progress on cost synergy.

Our cash position remains strong post acquisition of Kiavi with $1.59 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We have been deliberate in building our capital toolkit, starting with our IPO over a year ago. And in Q3, we raised -- rated unsecured debt of $600 million. We are also closing on a $465 million revolving credit facility this month. This is in addition to our ability to generate cash flow each quarter from strong adjusted EBITDA. We approximate 50% or so of adjusted EBITDA converting to cash inflow, taking into account income tax payments and interest expense on unsecured debt. Turning to other parts of our balance sheet.

Our loan receivables of $644 million include approximately $395 million of loans Figure has placed as collateral on prime from the beginning of the year as well as approximately $16 million of DSCR loans that we acquired from Kiavi. Typically, loans held by Figure stay on the balance sheet for a few weeks before being sold or securitized and fluctuates as a percentage of volume during that month. On share repurchase and returning capital to our shareholders, we've continued our routine practice of retiring shares withheld for employee tax obligations on vested equity. $35 million this year, which is approximately 1.1 million shares. That is ordinary course and not part of the announced share repurchase program.

As Michael outlined, we are beginning to execute on share repurchases, including our entry into a 10b5-1 plan to begin executing the up to $400 million authorization with cash flow we have generated this year and expect to in the future. Credit quality has remained stable across the first 3 quarters of the year. Underwriting discipline and portfolio performance held consistent quarter-over-quarter even as volumes scaled at triple-digit rates. Our underwriting and pricing platform that we offer to our partners is nimble with HELOCs, our largest product funding in a median of 10 days, we can reprice the loans as overall macro markets move faster than other lenders that funds on average in 45 days.

We also have been hedging rates for the loans that stay on our balance sheet for a few weeks before they are sold as whole loan sales into Connect or securitized. These actions have allowed us to continue to execute consistently through rate volatility for loan sales directly on Connect or via our securitization shelf. Looking ahead for the fourth quarter, we are establishing our Q4 loan marketplace volume guidance in the range of $6.2 billion to $6.7 billion and combined gross take rate guidance of 3.1% to 3.4%. I want to briefly touch on the overall Q4 outlook in terms of seasonality and ongoing expenses coming from the Kiavi acquisition.

As a reminder, our HELOC, RTL and DSCR products experienced seasonality similar to the broader mortgage industry, and we have historically seen the winter months from November through February be slower than Q2 and Q3 volume levels as much as 10% to 15% from Q3 to Q4 sequentially. Last Q4 was an exception as Figure experienced an increase in volume sequentially from Q3. This was due to IPO tailwinds that helped us originate more Figure direct-to-consumer volume as well as the addition of more Connect partners, including a few whales earlier in the year that helped offset the natural seasonal decline.

Returning to seasonal norms in this year's Q4 suggests lower sequential volumes from Figure and Kiavi, which would also result in lower adjusted EBITDA margin. Q4 will also be the first full quarter post acquisition as one company. We expect to see incremental $18 million to $23 million of adjusted expenses in Q4 from the acquisition as compared to Q3 with 1 month of expenses from legacy Kiavi overhead. As a reminder, Kiavi prior to Figure acquisition was at or below 40% adjusted EBITDA margin.

Moving forward, as seasonal pressures abate and as we execute on planned revenue synergies in '27, we expect adjusted EBITDA margin to improve meaningfully, reflecting the full benefits of the Kiavi acquisition alongside continued rapid growth in our HELOC business. Before I go, I want to close with the same note I opened on. This was a genuinely strong quarter across volume, revenue and margin and consistent credit quality. Kiavi is integrating ahead of plan. Prime continues to build real third-party demand, and our balance sheet is stronger and more diversified than it's ever been.

With that, I'll hand it over to our Executive Chairman, Mike Cagney, who will share more on the longer-term vision before we open the line for questions.

Michael Cagney: Thanks, Macrina. Last month, most of you likely saw that I launched a new company called Navra. I know we periodically get questions about how I prioritize my exec Chair role at Figure and my entrepreneurial initiatives. As Michael said earlier, I'm full time at Figure and leading our 0 to 1 efforts across blockchain. They're not mutually exclusive roles. Figure is on the leading edge of bringing the capital markets on chain and the time I spend adjacent to Figure is focused on that objective over the long term. So with that, I want to spend a couple of minutes on Navra and specifically on why it exists and what it does for Figure.

Figure uses blockchain in 3 ways. We use the immutability of the ledger to take out transactional expenses. We use bilateral marketplaces that self-settle and self-clear as the foundation of our capital markets, and we use DeFi to reduce financing expenses. These 3 things underpin our ability to rapidly grow our lending volumes in our Figure Connect marketplace. They enable our flywheel and our competitive advantage. The DeFi piece has always had a simple thesis. We take out the middleman and both sides do better. Take our warehouses as an example. We pay SOFR plus 250 to the Street and the Street finances those warehouses in the asset-backed commercial paper market at roughly SOFR plus 15.

That 235 basis point spread pays the warehouse provider to manage risk and liquidity. On blockchain, the protocol does both. You can't double pledge an asset on chain and the collateral has a referenceable liquid market. The spread gets split between borrower and lender instead. This has become more than theory. We have roughly $600 million financing HELOCs on chain today at SOFR plus 120. And this month, we plan to launch a AAA ABS issuance on chain where the buyers can finance the bond at better terms than through traditional prime brokerage. The model works. The constraint is the size of the market, not the economics.

We estimate from public data roughly $6.5 billion of stablecoin available to borrow across the top 5 DeFi protocols against upwards of $2.5 billion a month of assets Figure is putting on chain. If we financed our flow through DeFi, we consume available capital in months. To be clear, we don't rely on DeFi for growth on margins today. It's an interest expense advantage. But over time, it bears on something bigger. Cheaper bond leverage means better securitization execution, and that shows up as both margin and defensive moat. So the question is how to make the market bigger given the obvious institutional investor aversion to the wallet choices today. Wallet UX is unfamiliar at best.

Nobody has solved self-custody with qualified custody and wallet lack enterprise controls, who can do what with an audit trail that connects to core systems. These are product problems. Michael and I discussed this, and we agreed on 2 things. The problems we're solving because solving it widens the capital market for everything Figure puts on chain and the solution has to live outside of figure. A wallet owned by one issuer caps out that issuer's assets because no other issuer will adopt it. That's Navra. The Figure ABS deals are the first proof point.

Real yield on real assets is what pulls TradFi dollars on chain and every dollar that comes over is a dollar that can finance figure collateral. Figure is aligned with Navra in 2 ways: directly via 10% ownership stake and more importantly, indirectly is Navra's success bring on chain capital for Figure loans. The second company wasn't on their bingo card after the IPO, but Navra widens the market for what Figure builds, and that's why I'm spending the extra time to put the solution into the marketplace. With that, we're now ready for questions. Operator, please open the queue.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our first question from Ryan Tomasello with KBW.

Unknown Analyst: This is [indiscernible] on for Ryan. Congrats on the stellar results. Just on supporting the third-party assets that aren't originated through Figure's LOS, particularly for those depositories you called out, remind us again what sort of economics you're expecting from this? And how do you expect to build out the investor demand for these third-party assets?

Michael Tannenbaum: Thanks for the question, and thank you for the compliment. With third-party assets on Figure, what we're doing is starting with Prime. So you've seen us take originators on HELOC and home equity as well as in the SMB space and as well as in auto. Those are all the categories that we announced. And we've shared already that the economics of Prime are roughly around 50 basis points. We also expect to do securitizations in those asset classes, which will bring additional ecosystem fees. And then we have banks and other nonbank originators that will use Figure Connect as a way to do whole loan sales and we will extract ecosystem fees from those transactions as well.

So that's the rough economic model. And the reason why we started with those asset classes is we have some lighthouse originators that are participating. We bring on the investors, we bring on the securitization and then we start to flow lots of volume through. And I think in the coming quarters, you'll see us talk more about that as we have more proof points and share more about what it means for economics long term. But as Macrina shared in her prepared remarks, most of that benefit is going to flow through that ecosystem and marketplace fee line item, which has been the priority for Figure and again, reflects that balance sheet-light business model.

Unknown Analyst: Okay. That's helpful. Just on this HELOC Connect and near-term gross take rate outlook, guiding to roughly 2.9% to 3.4%. That seems to be a decline from recent trends. I know you called out that as being driven by these large whales. So could you give us some context around what large kind of whale pricing looks like and what that pipeline in the near term looks like as well?

Michael Tannenbaum: Yes. As we shared in the prepared remarks, our pricing doesn't reflect negotiated partner rates. So when we talk about whales and pricing, what we're talking about is an expectation that we hit high volume tiers or lower pricing quickly. And you've seen some of that variability in our take rates over the past couple of quarters. And we give ourselves that flexibility, one, for those large whales that come on, right? We don't expect those to come on at worse economics than other large whales.

But two, we also give -- which relates to your first question, we also give us some room for banks which may want to use our origination technology, but keep some of the loans on balance sheet. When they do that, they're not going to pay the same pricing. They're not necessarily going to securitize the loans and they may, in fact, sometimes service their own loans. So because of that, we wanted to give that flexibility. But at the end of the day, as you've seen in recent quarters, Figure Connect take rate has been relatively steady, and we're feeling really good about where we stand economically in the coming months.

Operator: We will take our next question from Patrick Moley with Piper Sandler.

Patrick Moley: So I just had one on the 4Q volume guide. The range looks consistent with a normal 10% to 15% seasonal decline that you described. But Michael, I think you also said that rates moved up sharply and you're feeling some of that in the consumer funnel. So is there any cushion in the 4Q guide for rates beyond seasonality? And then if you could give us any update on what you're seeing beyond that in the fourth quarter, it would be helpful as well.

Michael Tannenbaum: Thank you. I'll turn it over to Macrina, but just to quickly address that comment. What we do see is when there are rate movements and there's been continued rate movements through this quarter, certainly at a greater velocity than it has been in prior quarters. We're repricing loans all the time. That's a benefit of our platform. And most of our partners look to us to help on pricing, and that's a service we provide. And so when there is volatility in pricing, there's always going to be some near-term impact in the funnel, and that's what I meant in the prepared remarks. But in terms of volume guidance and seasonality, I'll turn it over to you, Macrina.

Minchung Kgil: Patrick, I did mention in my prepared remarks that we do expect to see seasonality of 10% to 15%, as you mentioned. This quarter is the first time we have Kiavi volume coming through, and we wanted to be able to give a range that we felt comfortable with. I expect us to be somewhere down the middle in terms of guidance. As always, that's how we're thinking about it. This is a new quarter with Kiavi coming through with their RTL and DSCR loans, but we're very confident with the pipeline that we're seeing.

Patrick Moley: Okay. That's helpful. And then just as a follow-up, Macrina, you mentioned that you're shifting the disclosure from net take rate to contribution margin going forward. So since that's kind of how you price these partnerships, could you give us a sense today for what the contribution margin looks like on Connect, HELOC versus non-connect versus RTL? And then -- I guess I'll just leave it there. I think that would help us get a little bit more comfortable with a 3% Connect dollar looking as good as a 6% balance sheet dollar.

Minchung Kgil: Sure. Two parts really. So going forward, we want to talk about gross take rate instead of net take rate. And that is because our Connect volume is the majority of what we do, and that's what you're seeing in our loan marketplace volume. In terms of contribution margin, I will -- we will talk more about the details of how contribution margin comes together in our next earnings call. We want to be able to see how Kiavi continues to season with those loans coming through and then be coming out with more information in the next quarter earnings call.

But just to give you a little bit of a flavor, as Michael mentioned, contribution margin is something that we look at when we price for our partners and when we look at each of the different products. And at the end of the day, our contribution margin does need to be higher than our adjusted EBITDA margin in the medium term. So it's something that we look at as part of our platform and discussions with our partners.

Operator: We will take our next question from Craig Siegenthaler with Bank of America.

Craig Siegenthaler: I wanted to start with the long-term growth one. How are you sizing your unique TAM for Figure Connect given that most of your partners are not in the bank channel and are not traditional HELOC originators?

Michael Tannenbaum: Craig, thank you. So for us, we've often shared that we have 10 of the top 20 independent mortgage banks. And one of the reasons we share that stat candidly is because we don't have a large number of the top 10. And we do see, as I shared in my prepared remarks, meaningful traction with some of the largest nonbank originators as well as some of the largest depositories in the country. So for us, we see meaningful growth ahead there. I'll also point to a few other levers of growth that we've been sharing. One has been in our SMB business, where we see a huge amount of white space.

We actually have not yet brought an SMB originator on the Figure Connect. And what we've shown over the past 2 years is that when Figure Connect is involved, there's significant incentives for partners to do more volume with us. So we think there's significant upside there. We also have been building a lot in the home improvement space. And with the addition of Kiavi and the purchase technology I mentioned, we see a big amount of opportunity to combine our product set there. And then lastly, I mentioned a few numbers in the call that I'd point you to. One is the $200 billion addressable market just for DSCR and RTL.

We think Kiavi is the market-leading technology in that business in both of those businesses. So we expect significant upsell opportunity. Again, we've proven our ability to do that. And then lastly, I shared $500 billion in origination per HMDA data for our existing partners. That would include a significant amount of business that's addressable today, in particular, first lien and in particular, purchase, which we've shared already a few calls ago now bolstered with Kiavi technology is a product we're launching in the near term.

Craig Siegenthaler: And just for my follow-up, I'm curious if you could provide an update on your ability to expand into other consumer loan segments post Kiavi. And I'm specifically thinking about auto after the Agora partnership and non-prime auto. And I'm not that familiar with auto, but I think a lot of the relationships are with big banks, top of the house across auto brands. So how do you sort of break into auto and gain meaningful share if you don't sign up the big banks?

Michael Tannenbaum: Yes, in 2 ways. One, we have a partnership, I called it a lighthouse partnership in the previous answer with Agora. And their role is to actually interface with a number of dealers. And they have a significant amount of volume growing through their platform. And what we're doing in the coming months is a securitization with them. And we also have a significant amount of our existing whole loan investors that buy mortgages but also buy auto. So we already have the pieces of that marketplace.

And what Agora will do is start to originate more volume, again, because they're tactical on their capital markets and their ability to grow until that's why they came to Figure, that's why they see the opportunity in our capital market, again, very similar to the people that came to us for HELOC because there was no and is no Fannie Mae for home equity. People want liquidity. And so as we bring those investors, both in securitized and whole loan form, Agora can grow its business, working with getting more volume from their existing dealers, and that's a big factor in auto. And we're going to bring that standardization to the space.

Because ultimately, it's very difficult, especially outside of the banks, to your point, to build a nonbank capital markets business, but a huge amount of auto origination is nonbank, and we feel really good about our position there. Similarly, in SMB, I know you didn't ask about that, but it's a very similar market where we now have 150 different originators. Yes, they're doing our HELOC today, but they all have other whole loan products that they're looking for capital markets outtake for, and we can again provide that standardization layer through Figure Connect, whole loan sales securitization, and we have a lot of momentum there. So look for more from us in the coming quarters.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our next question from Dan Dolev with Mizuho.

Dan Dolev: Michael, Macrina, really, really strong results here. Congrats, well-deserved stock reaction. I wanted to ask about the partners and the year of the upsell. Maybe can you help us understand like what you need to unlock within your partners to be successful in the year of the upsell? And how did you size the opportunity in your partner set? And congrats again.

Michael Tannenbaum: Thank you, Dan. For upselling the existing partner base, one, I'll just remind you, it's a motion that we are very familiar with. It's been a huge part of our success. I think last quarter, we talked about a few originators that had been with us for years, like Mutual of Omaha; NAF, New American Funding, those are originators that have been with us for many months, and we unlocked them via Figure Connect and other upsell efforts in Q2. So we've proven our ability to take what will -- could look like -- I know our data is very transparent, relatively small originators and find bigger shares of wallet. So we've done that in HELOC.

There's a lot more room in HELOC, and I shared that in my prepared remarks. But we also now have the 2 very high-quality products from Kiavi that are the closest things to standardization and liquidity in both RTL and DSCR. Our partners do a lot of those. We have a waiting list. There's a lot of demand for those products. And at the same time, just as we've unlocked smaller balance refinance and cash out refinance with our home equity alternative, we're going to do something similar in the purchase space. And purchase volume has been resilient in this rate environment on a relative basis. So we see significant opportunity there.

And that is why we're comfortable talking about 2027 as the year of the upsell.

Operator: We will take our next question from James Yaro with Goldman Sachs.

James Yaro: I was hoping you might be able to talk to the buyer base growth trends more recently as well as the reactions from that cohort to the Kiavi product? Do they exhibit the same demand for the Kiavi loans as for the core Figure HELOCs?

Michael Tannenbaum: Yes, happy to. Well, as you know, we worked on the transaction with Sixth Street, which had been a key player in our guarantor vehicle and was also a key buyer for Kiavi. So there is some overlap, and there's overlap among other existing investors. And I also shared in my prepared remarks that with Kiavi, we brought on new investors into our marketplace. And one of the benefits of the Figure Connect flywheel is that investors want to buy more when they work with us.

And so we're confident that some of -- I think there's been at least a couple of hedge funds that are now on Connect that weren't previously that are now excited to buy more loans and securitized products from us. So what we've seen in the past quarter is and also all year has been really strong securitizations. I think we shared a little bit more in our new supplemental financial materials out this morning, but we've had really robust both securitization activity and whole loan activity. We feel strong about that activity continuing through the end of the year. And we've also seen even more foreign demand recently.

So we continue to look for us to have more capital markets milestones in the coming months. And we're feeling really good about our position, the liquidity that we bring to the marketplace that stands to be true even more so in more rockier environments.

James Yaro: That's great. I wanted to touch maybe a little bit on Sierra, which I thought was an interesting product rollout. Could you just maybe expand a little bit on exactly how this works across the platform and what allowed it to drive the 29% increase in the funded dollars per loan approval?

Michael Tannenbaum: Thank you for giving me that opportunity, James. We're really excited about this. It's only rolled out in a small portion of our business and partners have been clamoring for this. It's very special for a couple of reasons. One, as I shared -- look, ultimately, and you saw this in the SaaS era, right, there's lots of mortgage SaaS that hasn't lowered the cost to originate. There's tons of SaaS out there. And at the same time, cost to originate a mortgage has gone to $12,000. We've obviously taken a very different approach with a very different cost profile. And the Agentic era is going to bring the same problems.

Just because you throw agents at the problem, that's not going to lower the cost. And what we've done is something a bit different, right? We have trained this Sierra agent on our specific business model, our marketplace, which is much simpler and the outcomes, therefore, are much more dramatic. And another thing that we did is we specifically trained it on conversion, right? Lots of people will train things on volume. They want the bot to make as many calls as possible. We trained it on conversion to optimize for that 29% that I shared.

And as a result, we've done something really meaningfully different, and we are now hearing in many of our sales conversations, as I shared, that people want this. This is part of the buying criteria, and it's a real differentiated mode for Figure. So we're really excited about it.

Operator: We will take our next question from Kyle Peterson with Needham.

Kyle Peterson: Nice results. I wanted to start out a little bit and ask on the growth, particularly with the different mix of assets now with Kiavi in the fold here. I guess, like is there anything we should be mindful of on either the RTL or DSCR growth rates or interest rate sensitivity. Obviously, they're smaller businesses. So kind of log numbers makes it so it should be easier to grow, but the momentum you guys have had in HELOC is so strong. So I guess just how should we think about the different kind of push-pull dynamics and the mix of the volume, at least in the near term?

Michael Tannenbaum: I'll start and Macrina, feel free to add. When we bought Kiavi, we assumed that we were in a very, almost record low housing inventory environment. So that was baked into the assumptions and that 4-year payback. So any increase or improvement in the market will just be upside to that 4-year payback that we've shared, that unlevered payback. So this is definitely a dynamic that we understood. At the same time, Kiavi has had, at least prior to Figure, its business model and approach was a direct-to-investor originated model. So they were really focused on taking their secret sauce, which is meaningful, their technology and using it only for their own distribution and brand.

We think the growth is going to come by taking that secret sauce and unlocking it for our very large and increasingly growing partner base that's eager to originate those assets. So this is all part of our expectation and also is reflected in the guidance that we've shared. But Macrina, I'll let you add anything.

Minchung Kgil: Just one item to add. Historically, and we've mentioned this before, Kiavi has been growing at about 25% to 35% in terms of volume. That does not include the revenue synergies that Michael had mentioned. So we're optimistic about what's to come in 2027.

Kyle Peterson: Great. That's really helpful. And then I guess for my follow-up, I want to switch over to funding. There's been an area you guys really shined. But I guess, how are you guys thinking about whether it's whole loan sales or securitization, especially given there has been a little more volatility in the debt capital markets in the last few weeks. So I guess does this make whole loan sales potentially a little more attractive? Or how are you guys thinking about kind of matching execution with investor demand for these assets?

Michael Tannenbaum: Liquidity and flexibility for both Figure as well as for the Figure Connect marketplace is our superpower. So what we're ultimately offering is permanent takeout to our partners. And they're looking for us to standardize a capital market that has previously not been so. And as a result, there's -- we're always going to look at and our partners are going to look at best execution across securitization and loan sales. That's a very natural thing.

And I think what you see both in the additional disclosure that we shared, what you saw in particular in Q3 and what you're hearing from both the tone of our voice as well as the information we've shared in the prepared remarks is we feel that this is a huge competitive advantage for Figure. There is a lot of investor demand for what we do. We've been doing it for years with great ratings, strong credit performance and a lot of work by our capital markets team to engage with investors and ensure that they're excited about the high-quality collateral that our marketplace partners produce.

And so we're always going to have that flexibility, and it's a huge advantage of the marketplace that someone can look to the securitization market, they can look to the whole loan market. We have increasing conversations, as I've shared with depositories coming on to the marketplace that are liking the volume that we see. And one of the things that we even show is how many of our customers are their customers, right? A lot of the nonbanks are originating customer transactions from consumers that are ultimately depository customers. And so when people see that, when depositories see that, it makes them interested in the assets and it makes them interested in engaging with us.

And that's been a big shift we've seen as we started to scale and it's driven depository interest, which is just another lever that we have in the coming months as well as insurance, right? And we shared 2 insurance names in our prepared remarks, we see more opportunity ahead pension funds as well. Thank you.

Minchung Kgil: I would just add that the securitization or whole loans or prefunded deals, it really depends on where the demand is and where the buyer market is. And the other part I would also add is that the players that are contributing to the securitization are either our origination partners who can make that decision themselves depending on what is more attractive to them in addition to the whole loan buyers who bought in the past and then can contribute to these securitizations.

Operator: We will now take our next question from Randy Binner with Texas Capital.

Randy Binner: That's actually well timed. I'd like to follow up on the capital markets question. So I think it looks like you're back in the market with the securitization in the last few days. And so the question and kind of building off your comments on confidence in whole loan sales and securitization, and there's a good slide that's been included on that. When credit markets got wider over the past month or so, were you kind of able to pivot to whole loan sales?

And if so, can you speak a little bit to kind of that process and how -- like what the frictions are or how easy it is to pivot if that's the way you kind of can handle markets when they get a little bit wider?

Michael Tannenbaum: Yes. Well, to start, we are in the market, and we do see some recent strong AAA prints. So expect that despite the interest rate volatility and just the overall amount of noise in the capital market, Figure has done about 20 securitizations to date, and we expect many more in the coming months. We also do not see, just to address your question, any friction between moving from a whole loan sale to a securitization. At the end of the day, Figure Connect is a marketplace. And what you see is auctions that people are running and they're always getting feedback on where the market is.

And at the same time, there's going to be times where whole loan sales and investor demand there is going to be stronger. It's a dynamic market. And especially as new investors come on the platform, there -- that will change those dynamics at any one time. And I think it's really important to share 2 things. One is Macrina just talked about those prefunded securitizations. And what that shows you is there is so much investor demand for the standardized product. And we're really one of the -- I think we're the only nongovernment agency that's been ever able to pull something like that off, and we have more capital markets milestones coming.

And we also ultimately have really significant permanent capital demand, right? That's -- at the end of the day, whether the loans are going whole or whether they're going to securitized form. At the end of the day, there's been this huge rise of insurance companies and asset management, nonbank financial institutions seeking yield, there's retirement, all sort of the tailwinds that are -- have been growing that business. We see none of that changing. And if anything, the -- and this is something we've shared previously, the diversification that we bring with high-quality consumers at high FICO with lots of home equity behind them is increasingly attractive in any market.

Randy Binner: All right. Great. If I could just squeeze one other one in. The G&A expense line just continues to outperform at least in my model. And I know you have a very scalable platform there that's been built over time. I guess the question is, as we think about G&A expense, as your largest expense line in the income statement relative to revenue, I mean, does it get a lot better than this? Just how do you think about that kind of expense control margin which has been really good kind of going into '27. I'd just be kind of interested in thoughts on that.

Minchung Kgil: Sure. Just a few items on the G&A expense line item. We do have the Kiavi-related M&A costs flowing through there for the most part. There's a lot of legal and accounting fees that went through. I mentioned on the call, it was about $22 million in Q2 and Q3. So you're seeing a large number there coming across. The other part is that there are some stock compensation expenses for a lot of the executives are going through the G&A line item as well. And so you're seeing that pretty much stable across 2026. We expect that to continue as a percentage of revenue, stock compensation expense is going down because the absolute dollar value is pretty stable.

I would highlight those 2 items. At the end of the day, this is our second year as our public company that we will continue to look at optimization. But this year, I would say, we also have SOX controls going in, so we have some additional professional fees coming through.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Fannon with Jefferies.

Daniel Fannon: Michael, I wanted to follow up on your comments around the pipeline for new origination partners and how that maybe compares to a year ago in terms of the type of partners that you're talking to now versus previous periods?

Michael Tannenbaum: As I shared in the prepared remarks, there is conversations today at a level of partner that we have not yet been able to work with, not due to lack of trying, but as we've scaled, as we've gone public and as I shared, I think, a few quarters ago, as frankly, the growth of the non-QM and home equity space has materialized, you just have more people that are looking for standardized capital markets. And so what we're offering is increasingly attractive to larger partners. And so you absolutely have a level of partnership and size of partner that we have not previously engaged with.

But at the same time, I'm very close to the sales process, and we feel significant runway across smaller partners. We feel that in the SMB space. We feel that in kind of the broad nonbank space as well. And we're also starting to see, as I mentioned, significantly more activity with depositories. So expect more to come there. Flagstar was very much a light -- I keep using this word, lighthouse. I'm always doing ocean analyses, the New England heritage. So anyway, it's a strong -- that was an example for many other depositories that someone that is publicly traded and well known is working with us, and that's unlocked a lot.

Sales cycles are slower there, but pipeline is very robust. And we had -- prior to our IPO, starting to do some in the fintech space, which has just been crowded out with some of the other success we've had. But there are absolutely a large number of housing and home improvement-related fintechs that are looking to grow their businesses, and we can provide really interesting point-of-sale financing. Again, there's $35 trillion of home equity out there. And in any interest rate environment, our product is going to be the lowest cost and also the longest. So the combination of those 2 things means it's going to be the lowest payment, and there's always interest in low payments.

Daniel Fannon: Great. That's helpful. And then as a follow-up on Kiavi, could you give us the latest run rate EBITDA? I think the last one we had was $100 million maybe for 2025. And then also the $30 million of expense synergies, what's a reasonable time period you think you will execute upon that?

Minchung Kgil: I'll start and Michael, feel free if you want to add anything. As you mentioned, we have said Kiavi had $100 million of adjusted EBITDA before joining Figure. We haven't given guidance or indication on what Kiavi's EBITDA will be in the future. This is the first month that we've done the integration. We'll come back to you with more information in the next earnings call as we move forward is really how we think about it. And in terms of the $30 million synergy, we've actioned the $30 million at close in September. The majority of that has gone through when we onboarded the company. Some costs have gone to the JV. Some have come to us, Figure.

And then we are continuing to work through the rest of the synergies. The other part I would mention is this is expense synergies, and we've talked about revenue synergies and being able to onboard partners to use these products. And so that will continue to improve the operating efficiency and the leverage that we expect to see in '27.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's Figure Technology Solutions Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Please disconnect your line at this time, and have a wonderful day.

Since the Twitter days, X has limited media-per-post to four items. As of today, you can share five times more photos and videos per post.

X now lets you post up to 20 photos and videos per post, dramatically increasing the number of attachments.

The change is already live on the web. If you’re not seeing support for the vastly expanded media sharing feature on mobile, update to the latest version of X for iOS and Android.

Today’s update comes after the service added over a dozen new app icons to the mobile app last week.

X has also pushed a new financial service this year with X Money. Meanwhile, XChat, which launched this year as a standalone app, was discontinued in favor of building out chat inside the X app.

Thriller fans won’t want to skip these recently added Netflix movies

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Looking for thriller movies to watch on Netflix this week? Then you’ve come to the right place. Every week I comb through the new arrivals on the world’s most popular streaming service to find the recently added thriller movies to bring some excitement to your watchlist.

This week, I’ve not been short on options. For starters, we’ve got a “Bonnie and Clyde” style crime drama that mixes a criminal spree with romance, and it stars Samara Weaving, who’s recently been confirmed for Marvel’s new “X-Men” team. Or how about the latest Netflix original, led by an Oscar winner, that explores the darker side of Music City. Finally, there’s the movie of 2026, which might be primarily a horror, but still has plenty of thrilling moments.

All three of my picks this week are worthy of your attention, so without further teasing, let’s dive into the Netflix thriller movies to watch this week.

Watching “Carolina Caroline” feels quite appropriate this week as the entertainment world turns its focus to a little video game called Grand Theft Auto VI. You might be wondering how the two are related; after all, one is a game set in a fictional version of Miami, the other a movie set in the ‘90s American South. Well, both are clearly inspired by “Bonnie and Clyde,” with each exploring a romance between two criminals caught up in a dangerous spree.

Caroline Daniels (Samara Weaving) is a gas station attendant in rural Texas, dissatisfied with her life; she impulsively decides to skip town with Oliver Anderson (Kyle Gallner), a charismatic con man. The two begin a criminal spree across the country, ranging from small cons to daring heists, all while falling madly in love. But much like the infamous misadventure of Bonnie and Clyde, this doomed relationship can surely only end one way.

Sorry, Tyler Perry, “The Gospel of Christmas” looks heart-warming enough, but Netflix’s most buzzy original this week is “Heartland.” This new mystery-thriller combines the always popular genre with the world of country music, which has enjoyed a resurgence in recent years. All signs point to a Netflix original that will rocket straight to the No. 1 spot in the streaming service’s top 10 most-watched list. Here’s hoping it’s good enough to deserve it.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

“Heartland” stars Oscar-winner Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, once a country music megastar, now a reclusive figure who has stepped away from the Music City spotlight. However, when Misty’s niece, played by IRL country singer Carter Faith, goes missing, she returns to Nashville to investigate. This forces Misty to grapple with her own complicated past and also to delve into the city’s underbelly. Expect a twist or two to keep you hooked.

Watch "Heartland" on Netflix starting November 13

Okay, so “Obsession” is predominantly categorised as a horror flick, but I’m including it here because it’s an acclaimed movie that blends multiple genres. In this well-crafted mixture, you’ve got horror, comedy and thriller elements. A box-office juggernaut, made for less than $1 million and grossing more than $500m, it’s one of 2026’s biggest success stories, and with awards buzz growing, now is the time (re)watch it as it heads to Netflix on Nov. 16.

Written and directed by Curry Barker, now one of Hollywood’s hottest talents, “Obsession” focuses on a timid music store worker named Bear (Michael Johnston). Hopefully infatuated with his friend Nikki (Inde Navarrette), Bear makes a wish for his feelings to be returned, which actually comes true, and then spirals totally out of control. Anchored by Navarrette’s incredible performance, “Obsession’s” position as a modern classic is already secured.

Watch "Obsession" on Netflix starting November 16

#3206. HubSpot brings back co-founder Brian Halligan as CEO to ‘refound’ it

Brian Halligan told Bloomberg he does not want HubSpot “swallowed up by a private equity firm”. Its shares have halved this year, and Adobe’s Karen Burgess will become finance chief.

HubSpot co-founder Brian Halligan is back as chief executive, five years after he stepped down. He replaces Yamini Rangan, who also leaves the board, with immediate effect from 12 November, the company announced. HubSpot calls it a “refounding” of the company.

Halligan told Bloomberg’s Brody Ford that he plans to overhaul HubSpot’s product, culture and sales processes.

“I don’t want to see HubSpot swallowed up by a private equity firm or shrink,” Halligan told Bloomberg. “I want to rebuild it and reimagine it.”

HubSpot’s shares had lost half their value this year through Wednesday, on slowing growth and fear of disruption from AI-native tools, Bloomberg reported. The company may have focused too much on short-term financial targets rather than great products, Halligan said.

“I don’t know if you looked at the last earnings, but the numbers aren’t great,” he told Bloomberg.

Halligan co-founded HubSpot in 2005 with Dharmesh Shah, its chief technology officer, and ran it for 16 years. He led it through its stock market listing to a market value of more than $30bn in 2021, the company said. He has sat on the board since 2005.

He stepped down as CEO in 2021 after a snowmobile accident, Kevin McLaughlin noted for The Information. Since then he has spent time at Sequoia Capital, including hosting its podcast, according to Bloomberg.

“This is a refounding, and I can’t wait to start!” Halligan said in the announcement.

Under Rangan, who took over in September 2021, HubSpot grew from 135,000 customers to more than 311,000. Revenue rose from $1.3bn in 2021 to an expected $3.7bn in 2026, according to the company. Rangan will stay until 1 December to hand over.

“Brian knows this company better than anyone, and I have tremendous confidence in his leadership as HubSpot enters its next chapter,” Rangan said.

HubSpot is also changing its chief financial officer. Kate Bueker will retire on 11 February 2027, which the company called long planned. Karen Burgess will replace her.

Burgess is chief financial officer of Adobe’s Creativity and Productivity unit, a $20bn business, and has been at Adobe since 2002. She joins HubSpot on 30 November and takes over as CFO in February.

Many software companies face a crisis of confidence about the AI era, Bloomberg reported. Adobe named a new CEO in September, and Workday has also changed its leadership. ServiceNow’s shares had their record 25% drop last month.

HubSpot said in October it would cut 660 jobs as it pivots to AI. On Thursday, it reaffirmed the guidance for the fourth quarter and full year it gave on 4 November.

#3204. Nebius shares fall 16% as data centre delays cut its 2026 outlook

Revenue rose to $980.8m and beat estimates, but delayed third-party sites push some sales into 2027. Nebius now plans to spend up to $45bn next year.

Arkady Volozh, founder and CEO of Nebius.

Nebius shares fell 16% on Thursday after the Amsterdam-based AI cloud company cut its outlook for this year. It also raised its spending plans, CNBC’s Jordan Novet reported. The fall came despite third-quarter revenue that rose 571% from a year earlier, to $980.8m.

Analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected $907.5m, according to CNBC. Nebius posted adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $465.8m, against a loss of $5.2m a year earlier, its results show. Its net loss narrowed to $37.5m from $119.6m.

Nebius now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3bn to $3.4bn range. Founder and chief executive Arkady Volozh gave the outlook in his letter to shareholders. Analysts had expected $3.37bn, CNBC reported. For 2027, Nebius expects revenue of $12bn to $13bn.

The cut comes from delays at data centre sites that Nebius rents from other companies. Some capacity due this year has moved to the first half of 2027. The contracts behind it remain in place, Deborah Sophia reported for Reuters.

One of them is a 300MW site in Vineland, New Jersey, held up by delays in power, John Reynolds reported for Tech.eu. Microsoft is a major customer there.

“Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now. We are not immune,” Volozh said, according to Tech.eu. “Customers have been kept informed and none of that capacity is cancelled.”

All of Nebius’s own sites under construction are on track or ahead of schedule, Volozh said, according to Reuters. He added that most of the next gigawatt Nebius brings online will be on its own sites.

Nebius now expects to spend about $27bn this year, up from its earlier forecast of $20bn to $25bn, CNBC reported. For 2027, it plans $40bn to $45bn, well above the $28.77bn analysts expected, according to FactSet data cited by CNBC.

Customer prepayments and asset-backed financing will cover 75% to 85% of next year’s spending, the company said. That financing rests on existing contracts with large customers such as Microsoft and Meta, according to Reuters.

“We have no doubt that this capacity will be sold. Clients are looking for capacity already for 2028, and prices for 2027 are going up. We do not see any risk,” chief financial officer Dado Alonso said, according to Reuters.

Nebius expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the end of 2027. In October, it borrowed $3.5bn from Citi.

Thursday’s fall came on the day Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive. Nvidia held about $329m of Nebius shares at the end of June, CNBC reported, citing a filing.

Rival CoreWeave reported results that beat estimates on Tuesday, and ruled out new unsecured debt. Nebius had lost more than a third of its value in October, Reuters reported. Investors had questioned the cost of the AI build-out.

“The demand for AI is real and substantial. Everything else, like building the capacity and financing it, is just a task,” Volozh said on a call with analysts, according to CNBC.

Kicking things off with a good ol' dad movie, "Black Bag" is a cross between "Ocean’s Eleven" and "Mr. and Mrs. Smith" with some charming chemistry on display between co-leads Michael Fassbender and Cate Blanchett. Tightly crafted, smart, and with plenty of dark humor to spare, it stars the two as a married couple who are both spies for the British intelligence service.

He's a human lie detector, but when his wife is suspected of being a double agent, he’s forced to use his skills on the one person he thought he knew best. Clocking in at just 94 minutes, "Black Bag" checks all the boxes, nailing exactly the kind of ever-rising stakes that you're looking for in an action movie without overstaying its welcome. It's just the kind of thing to throw on in the background for a night on the couch.

My colleague plugged "Heart Eyes" in last week's column, but I have the wheel of your attention now, and I say it's worth a second shout-out. The premise is hokey but fun: Each year on Valentine's Day, a masked serial killer known as Heart Eyes hunts down couples — except this time, he messes with the wrong one. For starters, they're not even together. Not yet, anyway, though it won't be long given all the meet-cute romcom movie magic propelling them into each other's orbit with the subtlety of a sledgehammer.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Ally (Olivia Holt), a newly single ad designer, is stuck working with her hopeless romantic colleague Jay (Mason Gooding) on a big project when Heart Eyes mistakenly targets them as this year's victims. It's a fun watch with plenty of tongue-in-cheek humor and solid scares. The biggest jumpscare came at the end, though, when I saw Josh Ruben, a name any Dropout or College Humor fan will recognize, was in the director's chair. His love of romcoms and horror comes through loud and clear.

"The Secret Life of Walter Mitty" is one of my husband's comfort movies, and I include it on today's list for that fact alone. It's an epic about the whimsy in life we may always find if we look for it, with Ben Stiller at his peak as Walter Mitty — a lovable sap you can't help but root for. He's a lowly office drone toiling away for a decade and a half as a photo manager for Life magazine when he gets pushed into what becomes the sort of adventure he often daydreams about. It's "Forrest Gump" by way of "Cats," if you will.

"The Secret Life of Walter Mitty" is a bunch of short stories James Thurber wrote in 1939 cobbled together and given a 21st-century overhaul with Stiller at the helm. Kristen Wiig is also worth shouting out as Cheryl, his co-worker love interest he quietly pines for. Stiller brings an infectious sense of joy to this one that'll leave you feeling like you're walking on air.
