#3201. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3200. Adecoagro (AGRO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fertilizer gains offset sugar softness as debt climbed on the Caarap3 deal.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Adecoagro S.A. (AGRO -6.41%) achieved a record 9-month Adjusted EBITDA of $471.8 million, driven by the integration of its fertilizers business and operational improvements in its dairy operations. Management stated that the company successfully integrated the Caarap3 mill into its Mato Grosso do Sul cluster, expanding its total industrial capacity. The company reported that it is prioritizing ethanol sales to capture high domestic prices while maintaining a 100% hedge on its 2026 sugar production. CFO Emilio Gnecco indicated that the company is on track to reach its year-end net leverage target of 2.5x as seasonal working capital requirements reverse in the fourth quarter. Management indicated that the fertilizers segment reached new production records for urea and ammonia, supported by the completion of a scheduled maintenance turnaround in late 2025.

Operator: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you for waiting. At this time, we would like to welcome everyone to Adecoagro's 2026 Third Quarter Results Conference Call. Today with us, we have Mr. Mariano Bosch, CEO; Mr. Emilio Gnecco, CFO; Mr. Renato Junqueira Pereira, Sugar, Ethanol and Energy VP; and Mrs. Victoria Cabello, Investor Relations Officer. We would like to inform you that this event is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] Before proceeding, let me mention that forward-looking statements are based on the beliefs and assumptions of Adecoagro's management and on information currently available to the company.

They involve risks, uncertainties and assumptions because they relate to the future events and therefore, depend on circumstances that may or may not occur in the future. Investors should understand that general economic conditions, industry conditions and other operating factors could also affect the future results of Adecoagro and could cause results to differ materially from those expressed in such forward-looking statements. Now I will turn the conference over to Mr. Mariano Bosch, CEO. Mr. Bosch, you may begin your conference.

Mariano Bosch: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining Adecoagro's 9 Months 2026 Results Conference. Consolidated 9 months adjusted EBITDA reached an all-time high of $472 million. This is almost $100 million more than our previous record for this period. A year ago, we announced the acquisition of South America's largest urea plant. Today, it is fully integrated to our operations and continues to set production records. Consistent gains in efficiency, competitiveness and operational excellence, combined with our team's knowledge are generating these greater results. In Brazil, cane productivity continues to improve month-over-month. We are maximizing crushing across all our mills while capturing better sugar and ethanol prices.

With Caarapó mill now integrated into our cluster in Mato Grosso do Sul, we have additional industrial capacity and together with our continuous harvest model, it will enable us to crush excess cane and keep growing in volumes. By applying our know-how and best practices in the region, we are becoming the largest sugar and ethanol cluster in Brazil, and we believe the lowest cost producers, too. In Food and Agriculture, crop productivity reached a new quarterly record followed by an all-time high in October. Strong operational performance and better commercial results mainly from our dairy consumer goods drove the improvement in the earnings.

We are now in the middle of the planting season with very good conditions and favorable forecast pointing to good crop development. Following the strategic opportunity that we got with the Caarapó mill, we still remain committed to achieving our year-end target in terms of deleveraging the company. To conclude, I would like to thank everyone at Adecoagro. These achievements are the results of their daily commitment, hard work and constant drive to do better. Thanks also to our shareholders for their continued trust and support. Now I will let Emilio walk you through the numbers of this period.

Emilio Gnecco: Thank you, Mariano. Good afternoon, everyone. Let's turn to Slide 4, which presents a summary of our consolidated financial results. As a reminder, we are presenting our numbers on a pro forma basis, assuming our fertilizers business had been part of Adecoagro since the beginning of 2025. We believe this provides a more meaningful year-over-year comparison. Gross sales totaled $591 million in the third quarter and $1.5 billion year-to-date. The year-over-year increase during both periods was mainly driven by a stronger performance in our fertilizers operations, which more than offset the lower revenues in Sugar, Ethanol and Energy due to lower sugar prices and sales volumes.

While quarterly adjusted EBITDA remained in line with the prior year, the 9-month result reached a new all-time high, approaching the company's full year record. Strong urea sales drove the year-over-year growth in the fertilizers business, while improved domestic dairy performance supported a significant rebound in Food and Agriculture results. This performance, in turn, more than offset the softer results in Sugar, Ethanol and Energy, which I will discuss in a moment. Let's move to Slide 6 to review the financial and operational performance of the Sugar, Ethanol and Energy segment. First, I would like to remind you that we completed the acquisition of the Caarapó mill on September 1, 2026.

Since then, the mill has been fully integrated into our operations and consolidated into our results. Turning to our operational performance. We crushed 4.6 million tons of sugarcane during the quarter, slightly below the prior year as above-average rainfall in September reduced effective milling days. Cane productivity improved significantly with TRS per hectare increasing 31% during the quarter and 24% year-to-date, supported by favorable growing conditions. As a result, year-to-date crushing volumes reached 10.4 million tons, remaining above the prior year level and sustaining the growth trend observed since the beginning of 2026. Regarding our production mix, we continue to maximize crushing volumes while giving priority to the product offering the highest marginal contribution at any given time.

Year-to-date, our production mix was 35% sugar and 65% ethanol. Production costs were negatively affected by the appreciation of the Brazilian real. Excluding this foreign exchange impact, year-to-date production costs in local currency remained in line with the prior year. Sales declined both during the quarter and year-to-date, primarily reflecting lower sugar prices and volumes, which more than offset higher ethanol volumes. During the third quarter, we accelerated ethanol sales to capitalize on the significant recovery in prices. This improvement was supported by tighter domestic supply and demand conditions and government measures that strengthened ethanol's competitiveness relative to gasoline. This was consistent with the strategy we implemented during the first half of the year.

We sold ethanol inventories and daily production at peak prices ahead of the new harvest and subsequently rebuilt inventories to capture more favorable pricing opportunities later in the year. Overall, adjusted EBITDA totaled $101 million for the quarter and $120 million (sic) [ $195 million ] year-to-date. The year-over-year decline primarily reflected lower sales and the impact of lower Consecana prices on the mark-to-market valuation of our biological assets, particularly harvested sugarcane. Looking ahead, we continue to expect mid-teens growth in crushing volumes, supported by greater cane availability. Our continuous harvest model allows us to process any sugarcane left unharvested at year-end beginning in January.

This positions us to benefit from strong yields and potential increases in sugar and ethanol prices during Brazil's traditional interharvest period. Let's now turn to Slide 8 to discuss our fertilizers operations. We delivered another strong quarter, supported by solid operational execution and commercial performance. The plant continued to operate at high utilization rate, achieving a new monthly urea production record in August and new ammonia production records in both August and September. As a result, urea production increased 4% year-over-year during the quarter and 11% year-to-date, supporting further cost dilution. On the commercial front, urea demand strengthened ahead of the 2026/'27 planting season, supported by normal seasonality and lower prices following the peak recorded between March and May.

Despite the sequential price decline, our average realized price for the first 9 months reached $561 per ton, that is $81 per ton above the same period of last year. This performance generated adjusted EBITDA of $109 million for the quarter, up 7% year-over-year and $283 million year-to-date, 65% above the first 9 months of 2025. Higher production volumes and operating efficiencies also contributed to a meaningful expansion in margins. In 2026, we expect the business to outperform prior years, supported by higher production, including new monthly records for both urea and ammonia in October and the higher prices captured during the first half of the year.

Please turn to Slide 10 to review the performance of our Food and Agriculture segment. We completed the 2025/'26 harvest season with better-than-expected yields, producing more than 1.2 million tons of agricultural products. In dairy, productivity at our free-stalls reached a new quarterly record, while milk processing volumes also increased. On the commercial front, our consumer brands continue to perform strongly in the domestic market, particularly in UHT milk. We also accelerated white rice sales as prices gradually recovered, contributing to higher sales during the quarter. Together, these operational and commercial improvements drove a significant recovery in Food and Agriculture results. Turning to the 2026/'27 season, planting is progressing with 57% of the planted area already seeded.

We are increasing planted area by 3% year-over-year, mainly in rice and peanuts. We expect yields to be in line with or slightly above historical averages, supported by above-average rainfall during crop development and El Niño conditions expected to persist through the first quarter of 2027. In dairy, we expect milk processing volumes to continue growing, supported by new product launches across our consumer brands. Productivity at our free-stalls also continues to improve, reaching an all-time monthly record of 41 liters per cow per day in October. Let's move to Slide 12 to review our capital allocation strategy. During the quarter, we completed the acquisition of Caarapó mill for approximately $136 million paid in cash at closing.

Caarapó has been fully integrated into our Sugar, Ethanol and Energy cluster in Mato Grosso do Sul and is already proving accretive by processing surplus cane from Angelica and Ivinhema. This should enable the mill to operate above its historical crushing levels from its first year under our ownership. We are also applying our operational best practices and gradually introducing our continuous harvest model to improve efficiency. Because Caarapó is located in the same microregion as Angelica and Ivinhema, it benefits from the same competitive advantages. As we transition to this model, we expect to progressively increase effective milling hours. Including the acquisition, year-to-date, expansion CapEx totaled $602 million.

The final payment for Profertil completed in the first quarter of 2026 remains our largest capital deployment. We also continue to invest in attractive organic growth opportunities across our businesses, including biomethane production in Brazil. Now let's turn to Slide 13 to review our debt profile. Net debt totaled $1.8 billion at the end of the quarter, while our pro forma net leverage ratio stood at 3.2x. The quarter-over-quarter increase in net debt was entirely attributable to the Caarapó acquisition. Our debt levels also reflect seasonal working capital requirements and higher readily marketable inventories, consistent with the seasonality of our operations. Excluding these effects, net leverage would already be below the levels recorded in previous quarters.

We expect leverage to decline as EBITDA generation increases, enabling us to reach our year-end target of approximately 2.5x. During and after the third quarter, we completed several liability management initiatives, including the redemption of our 2027 global notes in late October, further strengthening our debt profile. Following these transactions, long-term debt represents 78% of total debt and average maturity has been extended to 4.2 years. The currency composition of our debt remains closely aligned with our cash generation profile, helping to mitigate foreign exchange risk. We remain focused on deleveraging while maintaining a balanced debt structure and extending maturities.

Finally, on November 19, we will pay the second $17.5 million installment of our annual cash dividend, equivalent to $0.12 per share. This payment will complete our 2026 shareholder distribution program. Thank you very much for your time. We will now open the call to questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Gustavo Troyano with Itaú BBA.

Gustavo Troyano: My first question is on Caarapó mill. And now that it's already part of your portfolio, just wanted to have a clear road map for the ramp-up of the asset. You have discussed the 4.5 million tons of crushing for 2027 and potentially higher volumes over time. I just wanted to understand a little bit more the ramp-up curve for this asset and how quickly could Caarapó converge towards the operational KPIs of your existing cluster? And also to understand a little bit more if the carryover impact of the crushing ramp-up throughout 2027 would automatically imply more volumes for 2028 onwards. That's my first question.

And on the second one, still in the sugar and ethanol space and with the above-average rainfall levels that we're seeing recently in the Brazilian Center-South that is likely to postpone industry sugar crushing towards next year. I just wanted to have an updated view on the commodity prices going forward for 2027, basically to understand if you understand that we are heading towards a more challenging year in terms of commodity prices.

Mariano Bosch: Gustavo, thank you for your question. Before passing the word to Renato that will answer in detail, I would like to point out this Caarapó mill. I think that the Caarapó mill acquisition was something very important for us. It was a very attractive opportunity. We acquired a mill very near within our own plantations being really part of the cluster. And this mill has the capacity to mill between 5 million to 7 million tons that is similar to what we already mill in Ivinhema. It even has more capacity on some parts of the system. So it is something really attractive for us.

So if we only assume that we acquire this mill where we can mill 5 million tons with no problem at all with the cane that we already have in the cluster, we have excess cane in the cluster because this excess of rains that we have, and we have a very high productivity this year. So we are having excess of cane that we couldn't have milled. So we acquired this mill, if we assume 5 million tons, is less than $30 per ton, this is something impressive in terms of the quality of the mill that we acquired for such a low price that includes everything. So we are really happy with this transaction.

We think this was a great opportunity, and we are very comfortable that we will start showing the results as soon as we continue to mill. So after making this quick clarification that I wanted to point out because it's something an extraordinary opportunity that presented in front of us this quarter, we couldn't have been so clear in our previous call. So that's why we wanted to point it out this time this great opportunity that we had by acquiring the Caarapó mill. So making this quick clarification, I will ask Renato to go in detail to your question.

Renato Pereira: Okay. So as Mariano mentioned, Caarapó is in the same microregion as Angelica and Ivinhema. So it's part of the same cluster. So we see Caarapó almost as an organic growth of the cluster. So we're going to adopt the same operational model that we have in Angelica and Ivinhema. The equipment of Caarapó have a lot of potential. The milling system is exactly the same as Ivinhema, which is crushing 6.5 million to 7 million tons. The sugar factory is the same size as Ivinhema and the distillery is even higher than -- bigger than Ivinhema. The steam generation is also bigger than Ivinhema. So we think that Caarapó has a lot of potential.

Also, we think that we can adopt the best practices that we are -- that we have in our cluster to improve some important KPIs of Caarapó. For example, the industrial efficiency, which is basically the sugar input and the sugar output transformed in either sugar or ethanol. We think that we can improve this KPI, which is very important. Also the use of time, we think that there is a lot of potential to improve the use of time. In other words, we think that we can have less mechanical problems in Caarapó and crush more hours during the year. Also the energy consumption in Caarapó is higher than in our cluster.

And we think that with small adjustments, we can put it in the same level. And finally, in the agriculture area, we think that we can improve the sugar or the TRS per hectare of Caarapó adopting the same way that we are doing in our cluster. Also, the Caarapó team is very good. I think the integration was very, very good. It seems that they are working with us for a longer period of time. So we are very, very happy overall. And regarding our second part of the question, I think it's important to talk about 2026 before to get into 2027. I think the scenario is very positive, especially for ethanol.

Today, the supply of ethanol is smaller than everybody was thinking as a consequence of the rains that the whole Center-South region is receiving. So the delay in crushing and also the lower TRS content decreased the ethanol output. On the other hand, the demand of ethanol is very high. Actually, the higher demand since 2019. The hydrous demand per month is more than 2 billion -- 2.3 billion liters of ethanol. The parity at the pump is still in São Paulo, 62% so favoring ethanol consumption. If you take the inventories now, it is 14% lower than the same period of last year.

So we think that the scenario is very tight, and prices should be high until -- at least until -- to finish the first quarter of next year. We are taking advantage of this scenario. The price is very good. And also, we are taking advantage of the subsidies that the government is giving. The subsidy is in the hydrous ethanol and is based in the sales of ethanol that we have during the period, and we are taking advantage of that. I think it's very important to mention that we don't have any commitment of anhydrous with contracts of anhydrous. So we are maximizing hydrous now to get all this benefit.

So we believe that the beginning of next year, the scenario for ethanol is going to be really good. Once the season starts, we think that the ethanol supply is going to increase. But although the amount of the sugarcane probably is going to be very high, that sugarcane first has to be crushed. I think Brazil has crushed 655 million just 1 year in the history in 2023. So it's not easy to crush all that cane. Also, we believe that the mix is going to be more sugar oriented. This year probably is going to finish around 46%. And next year, probably is going to be close to 50%.

So part of the ethanol is going to be transformed in sugar. But the corn ethanol is going to increase. But if you put all those variables into equation, we think that the ethanol supply is going to increase around 3% only. We think that 3% more ethanol can be easily absorbed by the flex-fuel cars. We could see this year how responsive the demand is to the parity of the rate -- the parity at the pump. So this ethanol, the excess of ethanol is going to be absorbed. In the case of sugar, we think that Brazil is the same situation of ethanol.

So the 40 million tons that everybody was talking at the beginning of the season today is difficult to reach 37 million, 38 million tons. So the amount of sugar that Brazil is going to produce is lower. Also, this El Niño effect is causing a dry weather in other producer countries, especially in India. So India probably is going to produce less than it consumes this year. And for the next year, probably India is not going to increase the production because of the planting period that was very dry. So we think that the scenario is good for sugar as well.

Operator: The next question comes from Matheus Enfeldt from UBS.

Matheus Enfeldt: My first question on Profertil -- rather my 2 questions on Profertil, but the first one on the potential expansion of the urea plant. So any updates around that on potential timeline for an FID? That's sort of the first point. But I also want to get your sense on how do you think that once your project potentially is running and then the other competitor is also producing urea in Argentina and Argentina becomes a net exporter of urea. I know that Brazil may be a target for sales, but price will need to absorb freight costs to Brazil.

So I'm just curious on how you think that the outlook for urea production expansion looks in Argentina and how that could negatively impact prices, particularly domestic even if you have to export to Brazil. That's my first question. And then the second one is on Profertil costs. It looks to us, if we're not seeing the wrong number here, that OpEx per ton for urea production is up 16% year-on-year. And then when I look into natural gas prices in Argentina, again, might be seeing the wrong reference here, but we see them up 5% in the same period. So the question is, what's driving this increase in urea production cost?

And if you could just help us sort of understand what's the outlook from here and normalization from here just because we're seeing about $270 per ton cash cost per ton of urea for this quarter. And at this level, it looks like the normalized EBITDA for Profertil will be slightly below what we were previously discussing once the acquisition was concluded. So just to get a sense of really how to think total cost for the urea plant there. Those are my 2 questions.

Mariano Bosch: Okay. Thank you, Matheus for your question. I'm going to address first your second question, just to clarify in terms of cost of production of urea that there were some misunderstandings here. Number 1, it is important to look at it on an annual basis or at least on the 9-month basis because when we talk about quarter-by-quarter, sometimes there are some small specifications. So going specifically for the 9 months, we have 9 months '25, $262 per ton, while in 9 months '26, we have $237. So this is a 10% decrease in terms of cost of production. So we are having a lower cost of production this year than in the pro forma of the previous year.

And this is around 10% lower cost of production. This also includes some additional expenses. So in reality, it's even lower than this number of $237 because we are including the sales of some other products on top of urea and that's the cost of production of all that when you make that type of calculation that includes ammonia, Proaire and N+. So that is a small change that has to be adjusted. And then we are also including in the $237 some growth and maintenance CapEx that are marginally contributing today to an increase in production. So -- and also some of the expenses that may be related to this potential expansion that is what you were also asking.

So all in this, we are around 15% lower costs comparing to the previous year. This means some improvements in terms of gas prices, some improvements on logistics. So there are several improvements that are being happening during this year that makes this improvement in terms of the total cost of production up to now. Then going to your first question related to the expansion of the plant or this possibility of more than duplicating today's Profertil plant and the other projects that are here.

What we believe and we believe since the very beginning when we analyzed this business and when we acquired this Profertil business, we were always thinking on this increase of the plant of this project or potentially more than duplicating because what we see is that we can be the lowest cost producers in terms of urea to export within the region. We are going to be very competitive to go to Paranaguá. Going to Paranaguá is even cheaper than going to Rosario ports within Argentina. So once Argentina completes its normalizations in terms of imports and exports, it's going to be equally cheaper or even cheaper going to Paranaguá port in Brazil than to Rosario port.

So for us, we are not looking at the plant in Argentina as only for the domestic market. Argentina has a possibility to sell within the region. The region still imports more than 8 million tons. And so it's 9 million tons what the region is importing today and the ability to make these 2 projects will only add 3.5 million tons. So they are still more than double to be a net importer in the region that is how we really look at this potential business. So we don't see any risk if the 2 projects are being completed. We think that we can continue to deliver the kind of results that we are delivering today.

That's why we are so optimistic. And we are working hard on developing all the engineering and all the necessary needs to reach the FID that we hope to reach to it within next year or some point of next year. But we are working hard on that to happen.

Matheus Enfeldt: Okay. And just 1 clarification on the urea cost. Back in December, I think we were discussing normalized mid-cycle EBITDA for Profertil of around $300 million per year. Do you think that's still reasonable compared to what you're seeing today? I know that prices can move, urea prices can move, but in general, that's the mid-cycle EBITDA that you can expect for Profertil.

Mariano Bosch: Yes. And as I was mentioning before, we are finding more and more opportunities to continue improving. So we can even have better numbers than that. We are certainly going to close this year on a higher number. This is affected by only 2 months of higher prices than normal because March, April and a portion of May were -- when the prices of urea were out of the historical numbers. Then the rest of the year -- then during the rest of the year, we had historical numbers when you look at the CFR urea price in Brazil.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from Guilherme Palhares from Santander.

Guilherme Palhares: Just a follow-up on Matheus' question. Of course, you have a great opportunity there on the fertilizer market in Brazil and the Argentina consumption. I just want to try to drill down a bit on the costs between natural gas and other costs. And if you could just explain a bit on a high level, you mentioned a bit the benefits that you guys are seeing because you are reaching the record production levels. So which of the lines and fixed costs are you being able to...

Guilherme Palhares: I just want to understand, you mentioned that you guys are putting out record production numbers for the fertilizer business. I'm just trying to understand a bit how much is fixed versus variable cost there and how we can model a bit the cost curve going forward as you guys continue to deliver those lower costs year-over-year? And what is the level that we should be looking at long term?

Mariano Bosch: Okay. In terms of fixed cost or variable cost, probably 70% to 75% are variable costs. But within the variable cost, you can also work on them. The gas is the #1 variable cost, and there are some opportunities to continue improving this gas pricing and especially gas pricing at the level of the plant, including all the transportation of that. So that is something that we do expect to continue to improve. And then on the logistics in general, have been improved and there is still some room for improvement while Argentina continues to normalize.

Guilherme Palhares: That makes sense. But just drilling down a bit on that, if you could just share with this such high level of production, how much of the gas today is coming from the fixed cost that you guys have and how much is variable? And have you already been able to manage a bit those spot prices of natural gas and how are they doing now?

Mariano Bosch: Yes, sure. Around 80% or 85% is a fixed price. And then there is still a 20% to 15% variable price that you can take opportunity of cheaper gas prices at these moments of the year.

Operator: The next question comes from Gabriel Barra from Citi.

Gabriel Coelho Barra: I have 2 from my end here. The first one, the discussion about ethanol is quite interesting at this point, right? You have the subsidy that should be renewed by next month. We are seeing the anhydrous ethanol in a really tight market today when you take a look at the inventory levels, demand is peaking on the hydrous. So my question is how do you operate this market, right, in terms of -- mainly in terms of the commercialization strategy here from now on until next crop season. I want to hear a little bit more about in terms of mix.

You mentioned that you don't have contracts on anhydrous, but on the other side, we are seeing a more tight market on this side. So you have oil price decreasing and crack spread normalizing. So it's an interesting moment to understand a little bit more on the commercialization side from you guys. The second one, back to Caarapó discussion in the end of this crop season, we still see some challenges here in order to crush the rest of the sugarcane. We understand that you have this continuity on the crushing process during the end of the year. And you have this spare capacity on Caarapó, right?

So given the fact that you have more sugarcane and you have, I would say, if you correct right here, you are reaching the maximum capacity of the legacy plants that you have, Caarapó could be one of the ways to debottleneck this higher productivity and high production of sugarcane. So if you could give us more color about that. And in terms of cost, if this should be a net positive or a net negative in a cost perspective for the average cost for the company, this could help us a lot here to understand the trend of the cost and the crushing dynamic.

Mariano Bosch: Thank you, Gabriel, for your color. In a quick answer, we are selling as much ethanol as possible. We are selling all our ethanol during this period of time. And also, the second question is a clear net positive. Then Renato can give you some more color on these 2 questions. Renato?

Renato Pereira: Okay. So regarding the ethanol question, we are producing hydrous ethanol now to take advantage of the subsidy. And we think that in the first quarter of next year that we're going to be crushing in our continuous harvest model, we're going to be producing anhydrous. We have the equipment to produce anhydrous in all our mills. So we are ready to change the mix to anhydrous and to capture this price. We think that the hydrous is going to increase also because the gasoline consumption is going to increase because hydrous ethanol is going to move towards the 7% (sic) parity.

Regarding the second part of your question, I think it's important to mention that Caarapó, we are going to have 2 months of interharvest because Caarapó is not ready to do the continuous harvest. So we are going to start crushing in Caarapó in March 1. And that's why we are considering that Caarapó is going to crush between 4 million and 5 million tons of sugarcane. In our continuous harvest model, we don't see those cane as a kind of cana bisada. So in this model, at some moments when the weather is wet and it's rainy and we are delayed in the crushing, we end up crushing that sugarcane with more months.

But in other moments, when the weather is drier, we anticipate the crushing of those sugarcane, sometimes with less than 12 months. So we expect at some time during the year, the weather is going to give a chance to put the sugarcane in the right age to be crushed.

Gabriel Coelho Barra: I’m going to follow up here. I don't know if you could comment on that, but what's your base case in terms of the subsidy? You guys are working with the subsidy being postponed for some months here? Or do you think that's going to end by December? How are you guys working with this base case at this point?

Renato Pereira: We also don't know. We are selling as much as we can. Today, the hydrous equivalent is $0.21 per pound in Mato Grosso do Sul. And we know that the subsidy is going to be in place until December 9. After this date, we don't know what's going to happen.

Operator: The next question comes from Thiago Duarte from BTG Pactual.

Thiago Duarte: Two questions on my side. First one, following up on Renato's previous comments on the market outlook and very detailed color that I appreciate very much. And so a follow-up on that, Renato, particularly with regards to ethanol market, right? So I get your optimism regarding prices for the coming months, especially towards the beginning of 2027. But as you mentioned, there is like a mounting supplies coming from -- especially from corn ethanol. So my question to you is really where you think the demand is going to have to come from?

Do you think it's just a matter of hydrous ethanol becoming more affordable and then gaining share against gasoline, so it will be a price mechanism and/or how optimistic or confident you are that other routes for ethanol will deploy such as SAF and bunker and other different sources of demand that might absorb this mounting supply of ethanol. So that would be the first question. And the second question, I appreciate the target leverage for the end of the year, 2.5x, as you put in the presentation.

So the question is how -- where do you expect or where do you want to see the net leverage ratio getting before you can start thinking about new uses of capital, either speeding up dividends or new M&A in the front that you have today? These are my questions.

Mariano Bosch: Okay. Thank you, Thiago, for your question. I will ask Renato to answer your first question and then Emilio, your second question. Renato?

Renato Pereira: Thiago, as I mentioned, we think that for next year, there are 2 variables that we don't know what's going to happen. First is the amount of the sugarcane that's going to be crushed. I think it's difficult to crush 650 million tons. And even if it's crushed, I think the mix is going to be more sugar oriented. So it's going to decrease the mix -- the ethanol mix in the sugarcane ethanol. And the excess of ethanol that we are going to have, even considering those variables that I mentioned, we think in the short term is going to be absorbed by the hydrous market share as we saw this year happening.

If you think in the mid-, long term, and then we think there are other sources of demand as the agricultural machines, bio-bunker, SAF. But in the short term, I think it's going to be the hydrous market share.

Mariano Bosch: Okay. Thank you, Renato. Then Emilio, can you take the question on the leverage?

Emilio Gnecco: Sure. First, and I will use this opportunity to reiterate that as we do from time to time, our businesses are best evaluated on an annual basis. Accordingly, the results of any single quarter are not necessarily representative of the full year performance of each business. As we showed in the presentation and you just mentioned, we are anticipating that we will be -- or we will fall to 2.5x our net debt-to-EBITDA ratio by December 31. But this is after doing certain liability management that allow us to extend the maturity of our debt for more than 4 years. And most importantly, with a cost below 7%.

Now specifically to your question, we always said that something between 2x and 2.5x where we would feel comfortable to be. And if you look at our history, we've been below that threshold. And that is when we took the opportunity of increasing our leverage when we saw very accretive opportunities such as Profertil. And to the extent we reach that level, which hopefully, we can be there by 2027, well, we are going to be in a position to rethink.

But as always, and what happened in the past, if there's an opportunity that meets our thresholds and the repayment is clear going forward, we might take that chance and always with the support of our shareholders that has been there in recent acquisitions.

Operator: The next question comes from Julia Rizzo from Morgan Stanley.

Julia Rizzo: I think I have 2 questions, maybe a third. I know you have already discussed a lot about the ethanol and commercialization. But if you could be a little bit more specific of how much we are already in November, how much was already sold and the price improvement that you're seeing in the fourth quarter versus the third? And I'm saying that the direction is important to us because it was quite confusing the third quarter analysis because of the subsidies, and that will be helpful to know a little bit of the direction here in the commercialization pace.

Also, if you could give us some clarity of how much cane do you expect to crush in 2026 and the leftovers, if any, for 2027? And the third and the final one is the running rate of Profertil EBITDA, the $110 million that you did on the third quarter. Is that a good running rate that we can assume in the next couple of quarters?

Mariano Bosch: Julia, I'm going to get your last question on the EBITDA Profertil. As I mentioned before, somewhere above the $300 million is okay. So $110 million is a little bit higher per quarter than what we would expect per quarter. This quarter, we sold some more urea from the previous quarter, as we explained before in our previous call. That's why you are seeing this. And again, it is important to see it on an annual basis as we were explaining before also. So we will always expect to sell almost 100% of what we produce.

And if we don't sell 100%, it's because we have a specific strategic view of putting a little bit more urea from 1 quarter to the other or from 1 year to the other. So all what we produce is being sold because it is a commodity. And as I explained before, the whole region imports a lot more than what is being produced here. So making that clarification, I will ask Renato to answer your questions on the ethanol specifics.

Renato Pereira: Julia, in the last quarter, we believe that we are going to sell 200,000 cubic meters more ethanol than in the third quarter with a price approximately 25% higher than in the third quarter, already including the subsidy. And regarding the crushing, we believe we are going to crush about 15% more than we crushed last year, including Caarapó crushing.

Julia Rizzo: Leftover for the next one, Renato, sorry to interrupt.

Renato Pereira: The leftover, as I mentioned, we have the continuous harvest model. So we don't consider that cana bisada. So it's a cane that is with age in months higher than usual. So we are going to be crushing in the first quarter. And at some point, when the weather gets drier, the age of the sugarcane is going to be more close to 12 to 13 months, which is the normal age of the sugarcane.

Operator: The next question comes from Lucas Ferreira from JPMorgan.

Lucas Ferreira: Two questions, 1 to Renato. Renato, what's your forecast for sort of the unitary cost of production this season? And how this number should compare like now in the second half of the season versus the first half? I would imagine that some of these effects of El Niño end up impacting a bit the pace of crushing and could have some issues there. But I wanted to ask if you see an increase in the unitary cost now in the end of the season versus the first half and how the full year looks like? And then on the farming and rice business, pretty much how do you guys are seeing productivity?

I think they have been much better and then boosting your results. But wondering if you have any views now into the summer season coming in, in terms of how to think about the productivity in each of the crops, so we better understand what's coming next in terms of margins and especially that prices have been a bit better for most of the products, right?

Mariano Bosch: Okay. Thank you, Lucas, for your question. Renato, do you want to answer the cost of production on the sugar and ethanol.

Renato Pereira: Okay. So Lucas, we think that the cost of production just makes sense to look at the annual basis. So if you take the annual base, we think that our cost of production is going to be similar to slightly lower than last year in reais terms. In dollar terms, even though the real has depreciated now, the average of the year, the real is stronger than last year. So the cost should be around 5% higher than last year. And I think the reason for this increase in cost is the cost dilution that is lower now.

We are going to crush less sugarcane than initially thought because of the rains and also the TRS content, which is lower also because of the rains.

Mariano Bosch: Thank you, Renato. And then answering your question on Food and Agriculture business, that is a business that we've been suffering in the last 1.5 years -- from now onwards, we are in a very good situation. All our production costs are doing very well because they were all adjusted accordingly. And also, we are having an excellent planting season. We are just finishing or in the end of the planting season. All our plantations are in excellent conditions. As was expressed before, the productivity is also getting records and all the sales in the domestic market is also doing great and the export market also doing great.

So we are in a very good situation going forward, especially because of the price recovery coming from the rice and the peanuts that are the 2 products that substantially changed prices, reaching the bottom of prices -- historical bottom of prices around 6 months ago. So we are well positioned, and we should continue to see this somewhere above 10% EBITDA sales, more than 10% of EBITDA over the sales. So that's what we should expect going forward.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer section. At this time, I would like to turn the floor back to Mr. Bosch for any closing remarks.

Mariano Bosch: Thank you all for participating in this conference, and we hope to see you in our upcoming call.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's presentation. You may disconnect at this time, and have a nice day.

#3199. AMD plans to invest in PsiQuantum as they team up on quantum computers

The two will co-design the computing systems that run large quantum computers, starting with drug discovery. Neither PsiQuantum nor AMD has said how much AMD will invest.

AMD plans to invest in PsiQuantum, as the two expand their partnership on quantum computing. The companies announced the deal on 12 November. Neither said how much AMD will invest.

PsiQuantum already uses AMD’s Versal FPGAs to develop its fault-tolerant quantum computer. These are chips that engineers can reprogram after manufacture. The new deal adds AMD’s Instinct GPUs, EPYC CPUs and ROCm software. PsiQuantum brings its silicon photonics, which uses light to compute.

The two will co-design the infrastructure that runs large quantum computers. They will also build hybrid software that mixes quantum, high-performance and AI computing. They expect the result to be the world’s most powerful hybrid computing fabric, the companies said.

“Quantum computing will enable solving problems in healthcare, materials, energy, finance, and other domains that are out of reach today, working in concert with AI and high-performance computing,” said Victor Peng, PsiQuantum’s chief executive.

Working with AMD, PsiQuantum researchers have tuned PRISM, a machine-learning decoder, to run fast on programmable chips. Its job is to correct errors in real time in large photonic quantum computers. The companies linked a research paper on the work.

The first focus will be drug discovery. PsiQuantum runs its chemistry methods on AMD GPUs. The companies say this has already produced breakthrough results in simulations of covalent inhibitors, molecules relevant to cancer drug research.

The work fits the US Department of Energy’s Quantum Genesis list of science problems for quantum computers, the companies said.

“We see that same opportunity with quantum computing, where leadership in classical computing is essential to building systems at scale,” said Mark Papermaster, AMD’s chief technology officer.

PsiQuantum is the anchor tenant of the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park in Chicago. The two companies will look at working together there too. They plan to share more at the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, from 15 to 20 November.

In October, the Pentagon offered PsiQuantum a conditional $150m loan. The same month, AMD agreed to invest $1bn in Meta. Last week, it reported a record quarter.

#3198. Opera One for iOS adds Data Saver feature, cutting browsing data usage by up to 80%

Opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active users. Here are the details.

In a press release published today, Opera celebrated a 20% year-over-year increase in monthly active users on iOS last month, “building on its established presence in Asia and Africa while expanding its reach in the US and Europe.”

In the US alone, growth was even stronger, with monthly active users increasing 46% year over year.

In both cases, that outpaced the 16% year-over-year growth Opera reported on PC just a few days ago, when the company also announced it had surpassed 100 million monthly active users for the first time.

Behind this growth across both desktop and mobile is a broader shift in consumer expectations – users are increasingly reconsidering the default as their understanding of what a browser can do evolves.

In today’s announcement, Opera also touted the arrival of Data Saver on Opera One for iOS, which the company says can reduce browsing data usage by up to 80% by compressing images and text on its servers before they reach the user’s device.

For users, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid plan or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

I won’t be putting up my Christmas tree just yet, but my home already looks festive thanks to my seasonal indoor plants. Aside from a pretty white cyclamen and bright red poinsettia, I also have a Christmas cactus.

Now that I have completed my winter houseplant collection, I’m wondering how I can help my Christmas cactus thrive and stay vibrant and healthy over the festive season and beyond.

It turns out there’s a natural fix, and it’s sitting in the compost caddy in my kitchen. Besides giving me a kick in the morning, coffee grounds are a natural fertilizer that can perk up your Christmas cactus.

But before you start adding all your spent coffee grounds to your Christmas cactus, take it easy. Although coffee grounds can be used as a mild fertilizer, there are other steps you can take to help your plant thrive.

What’s more, there are certain times of year when your Christmas cactus will appreciate a feed, and other times when it won’t.

The Christmas cactus grows in tropical rainforests of Brazil, and thrives in rich, organic compost, unlike the desert cacti that grow in arid, sandy ground. Coffee grounds can help mimic this rich environment, and their nitrogen content supports healthy new growth. They are also acidic, which this plant favors.

Beyond promoting lush growth, vibrant color and a strong root system, coffee grounds can enhance soil structure by improving aeration and water retention.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond promoting lush growth, vibrant color and a strong root system, coffee grounds can enhance soil structure by improving aeration and water retention.

Although I’m happiest when I have a daily fix of coffee grounds, your Christmas cactus won’t appreciate a daily sprinkle of grounds. In fact, it only needs a coffee fix every four to six weeks in the spring and summer.

If you add coffee grounds to your plant’s soil over the festive season, it can stress the plant during its flowering season. Instead of adding nutrients to the soil, the extra nitrogen can disrupt the plant’s cycle, preventing buds from forming or causing flowers to fall early.

It’s best to dry the coffee grounds first and mix them into the soil or another compost before adding them to your plant.

Wet coffee grounds sitting on top of the soil can develop white mold and attract fungus gnats; drying them first eliminates this risk. Wet grounds are also likely to clump together and form a dense layer on the surface, hindering aeration. While, fresh or uncomposted grounds break down more slowly and take longer to work.

This set of three ceramic planters features a reactive beige glaze and includes drainage holes and saucers. They are the ideal gift for the plant lover in your life. You can place them together or spread them across different rooms in your home. The largest pot measures 6.5 inches in diameter, the medium pot 5 inches and the smallest container 4 inches.

1. Coffee grounds and potting soilSpread used coffee grounds on a plate and let them dry completely. Once dry, mix 1 to 2 tablespoons of the grounds with 1 cup of potting soil. Spread the blend over the top of your plant’s soil, repeating every four to six weeks during the spring and summer.

2. Make a liquid feedMix 1 teaspoon of used coffee grounds into 1 cup of warm water and let the solution steep overnight. Strain out the grounds and use the coffee-infused water to feed your plant, repeating monthly during the spring and summer.

3. Create a coffee compostAdd used coffee grounds to your compost bin. Once the compost has fully broken down and is ready to use, add a fresh layer to the top of your plant’s soil. While it takes the longest to prepare, composting is the safest and most effective way to fertilize your Christmas cactus with coffee grounds.

While it's best not to fertilize your Christmas cactus during its flowering season, you can help it thrive by providing the best conditions.LightPlace your Christmas cactus in a bright spot, such as near a window, but keep it out of direct sunlight, as harsh rays can scorch, bleach or weaken the plant. Because these plants are native to tropical rainforests, they thrive best in dappled shade.

TemperatureAim to keep the room temperature around 65-75°F during the day, while a cooler nighttime temperature will help trigger blooming.

WaterBecause it’s not a desert cactus, it needs to be watered, but don’t go overboard. I use a simple tool, like this Hathdia Soil Moisture Meter, $5 at Amazon, to check when my plants need a drink.

#3196. Apple HomeView launches tomorrow, but its first security update is already here

While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that users who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to update it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Here’s the full security content of HomeView Software Version 27.2

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory

Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption

Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction

Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation.

Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined

Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code.

Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Earlier today, Apple also confirmed that a software update coming next month will add support for security accessories to HomeView’s Siri AI, which currently refuses to unlock doors or open garage doors via voice commands.

With Jensen Huang stepping down, a new leader is in

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's official: Jensen Huang is no longer the CEO of Nvidia. His personal affairs, including one with potential security risks, have caused the Nvidia board to push him out of the company he helped start.

Stepping into the role as interim CEO is Colette Kress, who previously held the role of executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia. She first joined the company in 2013, so she's no stranger to the massive chipmaker and how it operates.

She seems like a logical choice to run the company as it tries to navigate these tumultuous times. Between the AI boom (and possible bubble burst) and the company's stock dropping like a stone, it won't be an easy road to navigate for Kress.

Kress is very much finance-focused. Her most recent role is CFO (chief financial officer) at Nvidia, and she brings 25 years of finance experience at major technology companies.

During that time, she spent 13 years at Microsoft, serving as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She also worked for three years as senior vice president and chief financial officer at Cisco’s Business Technology and Operations Finance organization.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, the newly appointed chair of the Nvidia Board of Directors, who has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

As you might expect, Kress has a background in finance and business, holding a B.Sc. in finance from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University.

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA, in Nvidia's release . “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Interestingly, her title is listed as interim CEO and CFO, so it appears she'll retain her CFO position for some time, perhaps permanently if she doesn't become the permanent CEO.

“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," continued Jones.

There is also an internal memo from Jones making the rounds. In it, he offered Kress high praise: "As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you."

Perhaps most importantly, running her name through a Google search reveals no scandals. She seems to have a completely clean record, which could be exactly what Nvidia needs after the Huang situation.

#3194. Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings a fast, cheaper model to everyone

The model scores close to Google's flagship Argon, runs faster and costs less than half as much.

Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and is free in the Gemini app and Search.

Google has launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a fast, lower-cost model for coding and AI agents. It is available to everyone in the Gemini app and Search, and to developers at $1.50 per million input tokens. Google says it nearly matches its flagship Argon.

Google has launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster and cheaper model built for coding and AI agents, the company announced on Thursday. Unlike its more powerful Gemini 4 models, Hydrogen is open to everyone, including free users of the Gemini app and Google Search.

For developers, it costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. That is less than half the standard price of Google’s flagship Gemini 4 Argon. Hydrogen can handle up to 1 million tokens of input at once.

Google says Hydrogen finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than the older Gemini 3.8 Flash. On a ranking by independent tester Artificial Analysis, it scores one point higher than Argon at its default setting. Vals AI calls it the cheapest and fastest model in its top six.

Hydrogen is meant to do the everyday work while bigger models plan. Google also launched Orchestrator in its Antigravity coding tool, which switches between Hydrogen and its top model, Gemini 4 Carbon. Google says this gets close to Carbon’s results while using 24% less quota.

Google also says Hydrogen makes up facts five times less often than 3.8 Flash. In Search, it is meant to handle messy, multi-part questions and link to a wider range of websites.

Hydrogen still trails some rivals. Artificial Analysis puts its top setting one point behind Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, and OpenAI recently cut GPT-6 prices with cheaper models of its own.

#3193. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Star Equity Holdings, Inc. (STRR +11.98%) reported third quarter results that reflected the impact of its 2025 merger and subsequent transition into a diversified holding company. Management reported that headline revenue and gross profit grew due to the inclusion of new operating divisions, though underlying market conditions in construction and professional talent recruitment remained soft. The company is actively executing a capital allocation strategy that includes share repurchases, bolt-on acquisitions in the Energy Services and Business Services segments, and the monetization of non-operating real estate assets to generate gross proceeds exceeding $9 million. Strategic focus remains on realizing merger synergies, which have already exceeded initial expectations, and leveraging a significant $215 million tax asset to enhance future after-tax returns.

Jeffrey Eberwein: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. We greatly appreciate your interest in Star Equity, and we thank you for joining us today. And in Building Solutions, we continue to experience soft residential and multifamily construction markets. Going back to Business Services, gross profit declined 2% year-over-year due to those pressures in the professional talent market, and we're continuing to invest for growth.
