We repurchased almost 29,000 shares in the third quarter for $0.3 million under our share repurchase program, and we have $1.3 million remaining on this $3 million authorization that was approved last year. We continue to believe our stock is undervalued, so we view share repurchases as a very attractive allocation of capital. Before I turn the call over to Jake, just a word on corporate costs.

On a pro forma basis, corporate costs a year ago were $2.6 million, and so we did reduce corporate costs by $0.8 million year-over-year, which reflects the elimination of duplicative public company and corporate overhead following the Hudson Star merger.

These corporate costs do exclude nonrecurring expenses, which were $0.7 million in this year's third quarter and $1.3 million in last year's third quarter. Across the company, we remain focused on operational excellence, cost management and investing in growth initiatives, and we think this will enhance our competitive position and drive improved operating and financial performance going forward. I'll now turn the call over to Jake to discuss our Business Services division.

Jacob Zabkowicz: Thank you, Jeff, and good morning. Our Business Services division is building momentum through strong performance in the Americas, expanding our digital capabilities, and increased engagement with prospective clients. While the professional talent market remains challenging, we are investing selectively to strengthen our competitive position and support for future growth. Starting on Slide 11, third quarter revenue was $33.8 million, compared with $37 million in the prior year quarter, a decline of 9%. Gross profit was more resilient, declining just 2% to $18.2 million versus $18.6 million. Adjusted EBITDA was $1 million compared with $1.7 million a year ago.

The decline largely reflects deliberate investments in our digital solutions, Hudson Fusion (sic) [ TalentFusion ], and expanding into new geographies and related growth initiatives. These investments totaled $1.4 million in the quarter, compared with $1 million in the third quarter of 2025. Turning to Slide 12 now. Our rolling fourth quarter RPO new business total contract value was $121.3 million, including $12.9 million in new logo wins and $108.4 million in renewals and expansions with existing clients. The trailing 12-month gross profit of $71.5 million has remained relatively stable over the past 4 quarters. As shown on Slide 13, Asia Pac remained our largest region, accounting for 62% of the divisional revenue and 45% of the gross profit. The Americas contributed 40% of the gross profit, and EMEA contributed 15%. Across the business, we're combining growth investments as well as focus on operational efficiencies. We're expanding our use of agentic AI and automation to help recruiters work more productively, improve our candidate matching, and deliver greater value to our clients.

These initiatives help us sustain gross profit despite a mixed regional environment and are essential to our technology-enabled delivery strategy. We are encouraged by uptick in new customer conversations and new logo wins in recent months, supported by our broader geographical reach and enhanced digital offerings. In November, we added those capabilities with the acquisition of Cornerstone RPO, strengthening our U.S. presence and bringing established enterprise client relationships and experienced U.S. sales leadership to our platform. We've also advanced to #3 globally in HRO Today's 2026 Global RPO Baker's Dozen Customer Satisfaction Rankings, a significant improvement versus history.

We believe this recognition reaffirms our continued commitments to our clients and strengthens our position as we compete for new enterprise RPO relationships. Our focus now is converting that interest into new business and expanding existing client relationships. We continue to execute our land-and-expand strategy, including leveraging our presence in Japan and Latin America, while we maintain discipline in how we invest and operate. With our expanded capabilities, stronger customer recognition and growing geographical footprint, we believe we're positioning our Business Services to capture opportunities as market conditions improve. Richard Coleman: Thank you, Jake, and good morning, everyone. Starting on Slide 10. Our focus in Building Solutions is on growing orders and backlog and positioning the business for improved performance. These results compare with pro forma revenue of $21.4 million, gross profit of $5.3 million, and adjusted EBITDA of $2.6 million in the third quarter of 2025.

In the meantime, we're maintaining discipline in project selection, execution and margin management to strengthen the foundation for future growth. Turning to Energy Services on Slide 14. With these added capabilities and continued investment in our tool fleet, we see opportunities to deepen customer relationships and expand our presence across the markets and geographies we serve. I'll turn the call back over to Jeff now for closing remarks. Jeff?

Jeffrey Eberwein: Thank you, Rick. Our focus is on translating the broader platform that we've built into stronger earnings, cash flow and long-term shareholder value. We're making progress on several fronts: growing gross profit and adjusted EBITDA in Energy Services; sustaining resilient gross profit in Business Services; and growing orders and backlog in Building Solutions. We're encouraged by our progress as we manage through ongoing macroeconomic challenges and position the company for sustained growth and profitability. To that end, as we announced this morning, our KBS business signed a $2 million contract to manufacture a workforce housing project on Nantucket. Production has already commenced for this project and delivery is projected before year-end 2026.

Our recent bolt-on acquisitions in the Business Services and Energy Services divisions reflect our continued focus on growth opportunities and our disciplined approach to adding capabilities within our existing platforms. We continue to evaluate additional acquisition opportunities across all 3 divisions, as well as potential new verticals where we can apply our operating model. Looking towards 2027, we're focused on 3 priorities: first, driving organic growth by investing in the people, technology and processes that help our businesses compete, scale and serve customers; second, improving profitability and cash generation through operating efficiencies, shared services and continued realization of merger synergies.

Since completing the Hudson Star merger in August 2025, we made great progress in bringing our businesses together, strengthening collaboration and putting our more diversified structure to work; and third is disciplined capital allocation. Alongside our acquisition strategy, we've launched a process to monetize our noncash-generating real estate assets as part of our broader effort to unlock value. The one asset is a factory in Colfax, Wisconsin, and we've signed a purchase and sale agreement for that facility and that's filed as an 8-K earlier this week. As we enter this next phase with a strengthening Energy Services platform, a resilient Business Services franchise, growing Building Solutions backlog and additional contributions from our recent acquisitions, we have, we believe, multiple paths to improve profitability in 2027 while navigating near-term market conditions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Joe Gomes from NOBLE Capital.

Joseph Gomes: Jeff, I want to start out -- Jake, maybe you can help with this -- over at Hudson, what improvements have you seen so far with the automation, the agentic AI investments in terms of placements per recruiter, delivery costs, things of that nature?

Jacob Zabkowicz: Yes, Joe, great question. And one of the things that we talk about with a lot of our partners is, what's the ROI that we're seeing as we continue to invest in further automation, agentic AI. And we're seeing it on a couple of different fronts. First and foremost, with some of the agents that we've had deployed within our partnerships, we're seeing a greater intake and uptick of client satisfaction.

And what I mean by that is hiring manager satisfaction, candidate satisfaction, because our recruiters are allowed to be more consultative with both the hiring managers and candidates and spending more time on understanding their needs and wants versus sourcing and screening and going through the normal processes with the recruitment team. Where we're seeing another uptick in ROI is on the coordination side. And what I mean by coordination side, it's interview scheduling, Q&A with candidates, allowing candidates to understand what the hiring managers are looking for. And so we're seeing a broad range of productivity and it really depends on the client and their workflow, but also to the region that we're supporting and how we're supporting them.

It's hard to quantify in an exact percentage right now because the adoption is still undertaking and it's actually workflow-driven and not specific to a broad function. But we're expecting further automation, further consistencies and further ROI as adoption does happen. But when we think about AI and we think about the adoption of AI, we're really workflow-driven in that regards versus a broad spectrum. So more to come. But one of the things with Hudson Fusion (sic) [ TalentFusion ] and our agentic AI strategy is to not only create that further automation and see efficiencies and recruiter productivity, but also bring that higher level of customer and client satisfaction to the table as well.

Jeffrey Eberwein: And Joe, I would add to -- this is Jeff. I would add to that. We've had softer hiring conditions for 3 to 4 years now and that's coincided with increasing use and interest in AI. And so we felt it necessary, despite the market softness, to step up our investment in our technology, our digital offering, as well as sales and marketing. And we believe in our business, there's going to be more and more of a separation over time between those service providers who are facile with digital and AI and ones that are less so. And in the HRO Today rankings, which are all based on client surveys, we have risen in the rankings.

A few years ago, we ranked 9th globally and in the most recent rankings that came out, we've moved up to 3rd. And we think that's the clearest indication that we're on the right track and that there is a benefit to the investments we're making. And we think that improvement in reputational capital will ultimately translate into market share gains, improvements in revenue growth and profitability and so it'll ultimately translate into improved financial performance.

Joseph Gomes: And then kind of switching over to Building Services. If you look at some of the commentary coming out of the National Association of Home Builders, they're talking elevated financing, construction costs will continue to constrain housing production in 2027. So how is that factoring into your demand assumptions for your budgeting for Building Solutions for 2027?

Jeffrey Eberwein: Yes. It's a really good point, Joe, and we do follow kind of the nationwide trends as well as the trends that are in our particular geographies. And we would describe single-family as weak and commercial/multifamily as very weak. And what we have done in our businesses is a few different things: one is we've really made a focus on the theme of affordable housing, workforce housing, like the project we announced this morning and the areas of senior living, assisted living and we had a project along that theme earlier this year.

Those are markets that are -- where there's a strong need, we have a great solution and they're a little bit independent of things like interest rates and macroeconomic factors. It's more driven by need. And when I think about -- there's a lot of statistics out there showing that we're underbuilt as a country and it's unfortunate that construction costs are up and interest rates are higher because we need more units being built, not fewer, as a country.

And if there's one thing that would make an improvement, which is permitting reform, one of the reasons why this large project that we thought was going to happen in 2026 got shifted to 2027 is some permitting issues in an urban area. But we're -- I would say we're cautiously optimistic. We're focused on the things we can control. And our new orders have improved the last 2 quarters versus where they were earlier in the year, so that's somewhat encouraging. We would like new orders to be $20 million a quarter, if not higher, and get our book-to-bill ratio up above 1.

And we would like this business to be generating $20 million of revenue a quarter and it's not there yet. So another thing I would say is that our sales teams have been spending more time on the road, making new relationships, educating people about the benefits of building in a factory. The construction market is a big market and factory-built construction is a small share of the total and we do think that share will grow over time. And so we do think that's a secular growth theme in a cyclical business.

Joseph Gomes: Jeff, this is Joe. Can you hear me?

Joseph Gomes: We got lost for about 30 seconds, so I apologize. I don't know if it's my end or your end, but no, I did not hear your response to my last question.

Jeffrey Eberwein: Okay. Well, the short version is we're cautiously optimistic about things getting better. We'd like to see our new orders $20 million a quarter or higher and we're doing a lot of things to get there.

Joseph Gomes: So let me just ask one more question here. I don't know if you can provide us any update either on Harte Hanks or GEE Group.

Jeffrey Eberwein: On Harte Hanks, we filed our S-4 filing with the SEC. That's our preliminary filing. And if one goes back and looks at all the documents, the filings we made in August and then that S-4 filing, there are some things that we're waiting on. So in order to get to a closed deal, we need the SEC's clearance of the S-4. And then on GEE Group, they've publicly announced that they have hired a bank. They're running a process, a sale process, and we have been public with our proposal and we're waiting to see how that plays out.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from Michael Mathison with Sidoti & Company.

Michael Mathison: My first question is for Jake. You guys described Business Services kind of being soft globally. I wonder if you could just give us a regional breakdown about the 3 regions you operate in.

Jacob Zabkowicz: Michael, thank you for that. So as I mentioned in the earnings release, Asia Pac is still our largest region that we support, both from a revenue and from a gross profit standpoint. But we're seeing different results in specific regions or specific countries within the Asia Pac market, right? Australia is still one of our largest areas that we support. And some of the feedback that we're getting with our clients there is some hesitation on volumes on where they're going to invest and where they're going to grow in this year and into next year.

However, we're also seeing an uptick in newly acquired geographies in the Asia Pac region like Japan and we're seeing growth in our Japanese market, which we're excited about. A recent acquisition a couple of years ago, we bought a Singapore business and we're still seeing that grow steadily, but also there's some hesitations in that market. So Asia Pac will still be a cornerstone for us and we are going to continue to invest in that market, but it is softer than previous years.

If you look at the Americas, where I shared earlier that we are growing -- and it's part of both from our investment strategy in Latin America and our recent acquisition of Cornerstone RPO in November here -- but the Americas, we do expect to see further significant growth because not only of our investments, but also our land-and-expand strategy and growing some of our legacy clients from our APAC region into the Americas region. So really excited to see that growth this last quarter and hopefully into the next quarters. EMEA is still hit and miss.

EMEA, with the geopolitical issues, with the ongoing pressures in EMEA, we're seeing spotty results in certain areas, but we are tightening our strategy and our operational rigor in EMEA and it is still a pinnacle of our delivery excellence. But I do expect EMEA to be soft in the coming months, in the coming quarters. And obviously, focus our investments in the other regions. Mike, I hope that answers your questions there.

Michael Mathison: It does. Very informative, very thorough. Some other questions on the revenue side. You've spoken about Building Solutions and how you -- $17 million back-to-back quarters, that's great. But you're aiming for $20 million as kind of a target. Do you have a sense of how long the ramp to $20 million would take? Is that a year from now?

Jeffrey Eberwein: Yes. This is Jeff, Michael. It's really hard to predict because it's a mix of -- a decent amount of the business is residential and smaller projects, repair and remodel type of projects. And then the larger projects, the multifamily ones, like the one we announced this morning, are lumpier. So it's very difficult to predict. But if we continue to make progress in the areas of focus, so workforce housing, affordable housing, senior living, we're hopeful that the new orders will get above $20 million at some point next year, maybe in the spring of next year.

And that will be a good leading indicator for getting revenue back up to $20 million a quarter, which is what we view to be normal. There's been times that our revenue has been above that; times we've been below that. But when people say, "Gee, this is a cyclical business. What is mid-cycle? What should this business average over time?" We would answer that by saying, $20 million a quarter of revenue, 25% gross margin and EBITDA margins in the 10% to 15% range. That's what we view to be mid-cycle industry conditions and we're clearly below that right now. But we're hopeful we can get there next year, even without improvement in any macro conditions.

Michael Mathison: Very informative. Last one for me. For the transaction announced this morning, you sold the asset for $5.2 million, so that's $5.2 million of incoming cash. Is there anything you can say about the lease obligation that will be taken on, operating the asset going forward?

Jeffrey Eberwein: Sure. So not to get into too much complexity, but the real estate assets that we own are held in our Investments division. And so and the business does pay rent to our Investments division. In consolidated accounting, that gets consolidated out at the holding company level. But you're right, when we sell an asset, then the business that's used to paying rent pays it to a third-party instead of paying it to our Investments division. And what I would tell you is that the market for both of these properties, a typical cap rate is 8% to 9%.

And if you look at the 8-K that we filed earlier this week, I do think it has a rent figure in there. But if you just take the proceeds and multiply it times, call it, 8%, that will get you approximately what the annual rent payments are.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our last question comes from Theodore O'Neill with Hills Litchfield Research.

Theodore O'Neill: So let me start with the building side of the business. I have looked for sort of statistical correlations between the business and stuff that's going on in the rest of the world. And there isn't any good correlation, I think, because I really need New England -- sort of, Northern New England or Northern latitude construction metrics to bank off of. So if I look at your Slide 10 for historicals and try to find something here I can use as a forecast, because the numbers keep bouncing all over the place and it makes the difference between us, me having a sales number that you meet or don't.

It looks to me like whatever the ending backlog is in the previous quarter ought to be my revenue forecast for the next quarter. Do you have any thoughts on that?

Jeffrey Eberwein: I think that's directionally right, but it's not going to be a perfect correlation. A decent amount of business that we do is pretty short cycle. And so and it's in the backlog, but it's in the backlog for less than 1 quarter. So I think the better leading indicator is the new orders line. So I would encourage you to take, let's say, the new orders line, like the last 4 quarters, like the average of the last 4 quarters. And that's probably a better leading indicator than just the backlog number exactly.

But the backlog going down at the end of last year and in Q1, those were kind of leading indicators into the softness that we experienced really Q4 of last year and the first half of this year. But we do think our revenue has bottomed on a, say, like a trailing 4-quarter basis and is improving going forward. And I'll just remind people that because we're in the upper Midwest and the Northeast, Q1 is always a very weak quarter for us. So I would encourage people to look at like a rolling 4-quarter average.

Theodore O'Neill: That makes sense. Refresh my memory on the KBS $2 million business for workforce housing in Nantucket, the timing of that. Refresh my memory on this, you can't do the construction until the summer people leave and then you can bring the stuff in? Is that the way -- Is that the timing?

Jeffrey Eberwein: That's right. And then you have the winter to deal with. So there's basically no deliveries. Roughly Memorial Day to Labor Day is a good way to think about it. That's peak season for them, no deliveries. We are past that. And even though we just got the contract signed, we've already been producing the project, and it's similar to other projects we've done before and the current schedule has us delivering it on site before the end of the year.

Theodore O'Neill: Okay. And on the Business Services side of the business, the year-over-year decline, is that structural across sort of your business and it's not a market share issue for you? Or is there some idiosyncratic part of this by country or by the type of job you fill that's part of why it's down year-over-year?

Jeffrey Eberwein: Yes. I would note a couple of things there. So in our Hudson business, which makes up our Business Services, there's really 2 businesses in there: one is the true RPO and the way the accounting works is that there's no cost of sales there, cost of revenue. All the costs are down in SG&A. And then contracting, which is a service we do for existing RPO clients. Most of the time, it's only a service we do for existing RPO clients. We did lose a client that's solely on the contracting side. It never converted into a full RPO. And so that's about, I think, a 3% margin.

And so we did have a revenue loss, but much less of a gross profit loss because of that one contracting client. So that's kind of one thing. And then you're right, if you look at gross profit, which is, we think, a better metric to look at for like fee income, which is what a term that a lot of people in the industry use. We do have a different geographic mix than some of the peers. And our strongest area is, as Jake mentioned, is the Americas, and we are growing from scratch in Latin America and starting to get traction there.

So really good growth in our highest area of investment, which is the Americas and we think that will continue into next year. And as Jake mentioned, we're more international than some of the peer group and we did have some softness in areas of Asia Pac. And then in EMEA, the Middle East was much worse year-over-year, as you might expect. And Continental Europe and the U.K., we would describe as the weak side of neutral. So we really don't think we're losing share. If anything, we are gaining share. And if we're down in Q3 and a competitor happened to be up, I would say that's because of geographic mix, not because we're losing share.

Theodore O'Neill: And then Energy Services, sort of I understand the machine shop acquisition is to try to support your broader geographic mix of customers. And if that's the case, is there a limit to the number of machine shops you should be buying?

Jeffrey Eberwein: Yes, in any one geographic area. So the original location of this business is Evanston, Wyoming. They added 3 other locations over time, and I think that's in our materials and so happy to talk about those. The other 3 locations, let's just say, aren't as fully built out as the Evanston location in terms of the number of machines, in terms of the capability. And so in this instance, our existing shop in Vernal, Utah, would have to outsource that work to that machine shop in Vernal. So they were kind of like a subcontractor at times for us, in a way, a business we've known for a very long time, have done business with, know them very well.

They have their own clients as well, in addition to doing work for us. And the owners wanted to retire and so we ended up acquiring it, and it makes that Vernal, Utah location more capable. I'm not going to say quite as capable as Evanston, but more so. And so it just enables us to better serve clients in that region. And we'd like all 4 of our geographic locations to have improved capabilities over time and we'd also like to add more geographic locations.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, this was our last question. I would like now to turn the conference back over to the management for any closing remarks.

Jeffrey Eberwein: All right. Thank you, operator. So we thank you for joining us today and thank you for your interest in our company. We look forward to continuing to update you on our progress as we move forward. #3189. Apple TV just debuted three new originals, including a heist thriller series

Up first is “Being Heumann,” which tells the true story of how Judy Heumann led a 1977 protest that resulted in the longest occupation of a federal building in US history.

The movie is directed by Siân Heder, whose previous film, “CODA,” earned Apple its first Academy Award for Best Picture, in addition to winning Best Adapted Screenplay for Heder and Best Supporting Actor for Troy Kotsur.

The premiere of “Being Heumann” also marks the debut of Apple TV’s new sign language accessibility feature, which allows viewers to watch select titles with an American Sign Language (ASL) or British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter appearing in the corner of the screen.

In addition to “Being Heumann,” the feature is also available for “F1 The Movie,” with “Greyhound” and “Way of the Warrior Kid” gaining support later this year. The latter premieres November 25.

The first two episodes of Apple’s anticipated heist thriller series “12 12 12” are now available.

Starring Anthony Mackie (Captain America: Brave New World) and Jamie Dornan (Belfast), the series also features Patrick Fabian (Better Call Saul) and Kali Reis (True Detective: Night Country), among others.

Here’s Apple TV on the new show, which will release new episodes every Friday through December 25:

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

The first of two holiday specials coming to Apple TV this season, “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy” is now also available to stream, the other one being “Fraggle Rock: A Holiday Gift,” which arrives December 4.

The premiere marks the latest release under Apple’s ongoing partnership with Peanuts, and joins a growing collection of original Peanuts productions, alongside classics such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving,” and “It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown.”

In fact, “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving” is free to stream on the platform this weekend, meaning even those without an Apple TV subscription can watch it.

Back to “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy,” it follows Snoopy as he tries to get off Santa’s naughty list in the 12 days leading up to Christmas, learning along the way that “there’s more to Christmas than just getting gifts.”

Watch the trailer for “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy“:

Watch Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy on Apple TV

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

#3188. Top Wall Street analysts like these dividend stocks for steady income

The stock market has been volatile due to rising Treasury yields and high oil prices amid tensions in the Middle East. Amid this uncertainty, dividend stocks can help investors secure consistent portfolio income.

Top Wall Street analysts can inform investors on their search for attractive dividend stocks that have the ability to generate solid cash flows and pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Energy Transfer owns and operates a diversified portfolio of energy assets in the U.S., with about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated infrastructure. The company recently announced an increase in its quarterly cash distribution to roughly 34 cents per common unit. Energy Transfer offers a yield of 6.7%.

Recently, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer and slightly raised his price target to $23 from $22, saying, "We continue to see upside from underappreciated growth potential including underused assets in second-tier gas basins."

The five-star analyst highlighted that Energy Transfer raised its full-year earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, guidance, with the company capturing its full-year optimization target in the first quarter itself. The revised outlook reflects upside from higher volumes, rates, and spreads. Gabelman expects EBITDA to reach the high end of the outlook at current commodity pricing.

Furthermore, Gabelman expects ET to see a gain of $200 million in EBITDA from some new projects and 800 million cubic feet per day Haynesville volume growth this year, which is projected to add $100 million in EBITDA. Interestingly, the company expects to sanction multiple projects in 2026, which could contribute an additional $400 million in EBITDA.

Gabelman ranks No. 660 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.4%. See Energy Transfer Financials on TipRanks.

The next dividend-paying stock is oil-and-gas giant Chevron. The company recently announced its first-quarter results. It paid $6 billion of cash to shareholders in Q1 2026, including share repurchases of $2.5 billion and dividends of $3.5 billion. Chevron offers a current dividend yield of 3.7%.

After hosting investor meetings with Chevron management, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin reaffirmed a buy rating on CVX stock with a price target of $222. "The company is in a favorable operating posture with transparent capital allocation and asset momentum yielding positive FCF/leverage outcomes," said the analyst.

The five-star analyst noted Chevron's solid operating momentum, with key assets in the Permian, Kazakhstan, Australia LNG and Guyana running at full capacity or above their designed production levels. He added that CVX's downstream is gaining from stronger vertical integration and access to equity crude supplies in California and Asia, helping ease potential feedstock constraints.

Additionally, Margolin highlighted that Chevron plans to maintain a 1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day plateau in the Permian Basin, driven by operational efficiencies achieved under its current program. He added that advanced chemicals treatment in wells, including both proprietary and third-party, has delivered about 20% productivity benefits in the first 10 months.

The analyst also noted that CVX is advancing the first project under its power joint venture through an exclusivity agreement with Microsoft. Margolin believes that the company's advantage lies in being an early mover, with 5 gigawatts of turbines already on order, along with access to land and natural gas supply needed for power generation and data center development.

Margolin ranks No. 455 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.3%. See Chevron Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Williams runs interstate natural gas pipelines and gathering and processing operations throughout the U.S. The company recently announced a dividend of about 53 cents per share, payable on June 29. WMB offers a yield of 2.7%.

Recently, UBS analyst Manav Gupta reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock and increased his price target to $91 from $89. The analyst is optimistic about the company's Power Innovation business and noted the updates on two recent projects – NEO and Atlas. With the addition of these two projects, which WMB announced alongside its Q1 results, the company now has $9.65 billion in Power Innovation projects.

The five-star analyst noted that WMB continues to stand out by expanding its Power Innovation business at a faster pace than investors' and UBS' expectations. Based on projects already announced (Socrates, Atlas, Apollo, Aquila, Socrates the Younger and Neo), Gupta expects Williams' Power Innovation business to drive EBITDA upside of $1.93 billion by 2029.

Gupta believes that the addition of NEO further bolstered WMB's position, giving it an edge over rivals such as Chevron in showcasing integrated, end-to-end power solutions tailored to hyperscalers. The analyst emphasized that while Chevron has confirmed its partnership with Meta Platforms on a project, that deal has yet to reach a final investment decision, which limits near-term visibility.

"We remain constructive on WMB's Power Innovation platform and see potential upside to 2028–2030 consensus earnings estimates as additional projects achieve commercial operation and contribute to earnings growth," said Gupta.

Gupta ranks No. 168 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 70% of the time, delivering an average return of 21.9%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.
