#3179. Sandisk Stock Is Back Above the $900 Price I Set for Buying It. Here's Why I'm Holding Off.

Should a quick bounce change what I'm willing to pay for the same guided profits?

Last week, I put a number on what I'd be willing to pay for Sandisk (SNDK -4.12%) stock. My rule was that I wouldn't pay over four years' worth of earnings at the rate management guided for this quarter, which came to around $900 a share.

The stock didn't stay under that price long. Sandisk closed at about $806 on Nov. 5. Then shares soared on Wednesday, Nov. 11 -- the day after AI cloud provider CoreWeave lifted its 2026 revenue forecast.

At roughly $990 as of this writing, the flash memory company is up about 23% since that Nov. 5 close. Under my own rule, that means I'd hold off for now, and nothing else in the last week gives me a reason to bend it.

Sandisk's guidance for its fiscal second quarter of 2027, which is underway now, calls for non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share between $55 and $57 on a pre-split basis. The $56 midpoint comes to around $224 a share for a full year, and four years of that is where my $900 price came from.

At about $990, Sandisk trades at about 4.4 times those annualized guided earnings, so a buyer is paying for around 4.4 years of them rather than four. In other words, the stock is around 10% above my price.

The eight-for-one stock split doesn't change any of this.

Shareholders of record on Nov. 9 get seven more shares for every one they hold, issued after the close on Nov. 19. Trading on a split-adjusted basis should start the next morning, Nov. 20. After the split, my price works out to around $112 a share, while the current price comes to about $124.

Ten percent might not seem like much for a tech company whose stock has swung this hard. After all, Sandisk still trades around 58% under its late-June record close of $2,335.

But the point of setting a price beforehand is so a fast run-up doesn't talk me into paying more for the same earnings.

On paper, a price so low compared with earnings might make Sandisk look like a value stock. Still, I think four years is about as much as a memory maker's peak profits deserve. Sandisk's adjusted earnings per share hit $49.51 for its last quarter, up from $1.22 a year before. Profits that climbed that fast might drop fast, too, if flash prices turn.

Not that I can see. Sandisk hasn't updated its guidance since the Oct. 29 report, so the earnings behind my price are the same ones I used last week.

If anything, every new outlook has gone up by less than the one before. Management's fiscal Q4 2026 outlook called for adjusted profit of $30 to $33 per share, a $31.50 midpoint. The outlook for fiscal Q1 of 2027 (the quarter ended Oct. 2, 2026) lifted that midpoint around 43% to $45. And the current fiscal Q2 outlook raised it about 24% to $56.

In short, the boom is still adding profits, just at a slowing rate.

Of course, Sandisk has earned more than it guided recently. In fiscal Q4 of 2026, its adjusted earnings were $39.25 a share, beating the $30-to-$33 range, and fiscal Q1's $49.51 topped a range of $44 to $46. But the gap narrowed, from around 19% above the top of the range to about 8%.

My rule uses guidance on purpose -- so I'm not paying ahead of time for results that haven't happened yet.

The simplest one is the price. If the stock drops back below about $900 (or about $112 once split-adjusted trading starts) before I've bought, I'd look at it again as a buyer.

The other is a higher guided pace. When Sandisk reports its fiscal Q2 results, it will probably give an outlook for fiscal Q3. A midpoint near $62 a share would raise four years of guided earnings to about $990, close to where the stock trades as I write.

That would mean a step of about 11% from the latest midpoint, which is smaller than either of the past two, so it's arguably within reach.

But I'd rather see management give that number than assume it. Until one of those two things happens, I'm holding off. The company is still earning more every quarter. I just think a buyer at this price is paying for growth that Sandisk hasn't guided to yet.

#3178. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.

#3175. What to Learn About Meta’s Muse AI Before It Learns Too Much About You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta’s Muse AI agent quietly builds a profile on you the second you start using it, even if you explicitly tell it not to. That turns Jolly, its supposedly cute and cuddly mascot, into the friendly face of some serious security flaws.

On top of that, Muse asks for the keys to your digital life: passwords, full disk access, emails, calendar invites, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp chats. Meta also feeds your conversations into its AI training pipeline by default, leaving it on you to dig through the settings and opt out.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.

#3174. Reddit launches AI-powered Reviews feature – with 10,000 products to start

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Reddit is adding AI-generated product reviews that compile real user sentiment from across communities. Here's how they work.

If you regularly turn to Reddit for product advice, your experience is about to change.

Reddit announced a new feature on Tuesday called Reddit Reviews, which takes conversations from subreddits across the site and compiles them into AI-generated, in-depth product summaries. The feature works much like Google AI Overviews and is likely an attempt to better compete with them.

When you search for a product on Reddit, you’ll see an “easy-to-digest format” that has a “what people are saying” recap. A visual breakdown will show whether conversations are generally positive, mixed, or negative, as well as common sentiments among users. If you want to go deeper, Reddit says you can browse comments about a product, apply topic filters, read original user discussions, ask follow-up questions, or explore other commonly compared products.

In an example shared by Reddit, a user searches for “Best headphones 2026.” The search returns several results with tags like “Very positive,” “Positive,” and “Mixed.” Clicking on one expands to a review that says, “Reddit likes the XL224’s fantastic battery life, powerful bass, and strong sound quality, while the steep price and fit on smaller heads draws criticism.”

“A mix of generative AI and other in-house technology” is used to identify themes and summarize what people are saying, a representative explained, and added that “the technologies and models we use may evolve over time to best support the experience.”

Perhaps the most important part is that Reddit Reviews are shaped by users, and companies can’t pay to have product features. For a community sensitive to commercialization, this is a big deal.

My first concern was about bots or other fake reviews, but a Reddit representative said they’re taking that into consideration. “Platform-wide,” the representative said, “we are labeling apps and prompting accounts we detect to be running automations to either verify there’s a human behind the username or be labeled as an app.” In this context, an app is a registered API client that’s developed to interact with Reddit (including posting, commenting, upvoting, and scraping). In short, the system will label known bots.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep watch – even upstairsSpecifically for reviews, a “review conversation” will appear that describes a person’s experience with a product. Reddit also has “defined rules,” it says, “to help our LLMs identify these review conversations based on the surrounding conversation for context.”

You’ll start to see Reddit Reviews over the next few weeks in the US on iOS, Android, and browser versions of the site. Around 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel will be available to start.

I find myself frequently adding “reddit” to Google searches for everything from the best restaurants in a city to the best headphones for my kids, so these overviews are definitely intriguing. It’s not easy right now to wade through numerous threads, so if this does make it easier to get true user sentiment, it could be a big plus.

#3173. Who Will Replace Jensen Huang? Here's What Prediction Markets Think.

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia.

Throughout the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia (NVDA -4.34%). As the company's co-founder and longtime CEO, Huang helped transform Nvidia from a graphics chip manufacturer into a dominant supplier of AI computing infrastructure.

Recent reports concerning Huang's personal relationships and potential exposure to foreign intelligence have prompted an independent board investigation and raised questions about his future. Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12. As investors focus on leadership succession plans, prediction market platform Kalshi offers an interesting glimpse into who might lead Nvidia next.

According to Kalshi’s trading odds, Ian Buck is currently in the lead, with an implied probability of approximately 36% of becoming Nvidia's next CEO. Buck joined Nvidia in 2004 and helped develop CUDA, the software platform that allows developers to program GPUs for applications beyond graphics processing.

That's particularly relevant because hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Oracle account for most of the investments in AI infrastructure. During Nvidia's fiscal second quarter, hyperscalers accounted for $48.7 billion of the company's total data center revenue.

Nvidia's chief financial officer (CFO), Colette Kress, currently has a 19% chance to emerge as Nvidia's next CEO. For now, Kress has been named interim CEO.

Kalshi traders are also considering candidates from outside Nvidia. Rene Haas, CEO of semiconductor designer Arm Holdings, currently has 10% odds. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia, giving him familiarity with the company's operations and semiconductor strategy. His experience running Arm, whose chip processor designs are used across various devices, makes him a logical candidate.

Former Apple CEO Tim Cook is also among the possibilities, with recent odds around 4%. Of note, Cook's name may only be among the top ranks because President Trump floated the idea of Nvidia appointing him as its CEO.

While Cook's experience managing Apple's global supply chain and navigating international business relationships could be valuable, his candidacy seems speculative, as there's no confirmed indication Nvidia is pursuing him.

Prediction markets can offer useful insights into investor expectations, but they are hardly infallible. Kalshi's probabilities change in real time as they reflect trading activity rather than inside knowledge. Limited liquidity in niche markets can also cause outsize swings in the odds.

Nvidia's next CEO will inherit a business with enormous competitive advantages. The company's Blackwell and Vera Rubin computing platforms, proprietary networking technology, and CUDA software ecosystem have established robust barriers to competition.

These assets are not going to disappear because of a leadership change. Ultimately, investors should pay more attention to Nvidia's ability to execute its technology roadmap than to the latest fluctuations in prediction market odds or rumors.

#3172. Hasbro Is Using AI to Bring Characters to Life — With Limits

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

For the next time you need Cobra Commander to crash a Teams meeting.

Have you ever thought your day-to-day might be enhanced by a running commentary from Optimus Prime? Sixth Wall, the AI offshoot of Hasbro, has got great news for you.

Hold music replaced by chitchat with Mr. Monopoly, a digital personal assistant with the voice and personality of Megatron and maybe even the surreal experience of watching G.I. Joe episodes with Cobra Commander adding live, RiffTrax-style commentary could be coming soon.

It’s all part of a plan by Sixth Wall, an AI offshoot of Hasbro, to marry licensable characters with unlimited AI possibilities.

“We started just testing internally,” Sixth Wall CEO Bertie Thomson told me in an interview following a media event in Los Angeles last week. “What would it look like if you took a Peppa Pig doll and rigged her with a Raspberry Pi and ElevenLabs and chatted back and forth, and it turns out the answer is incredibly fun.”

Creating these lighthearted moments with licensed IP and characters isn’t an entirely new concept. Services like Character.AI (which just filed for bankruptcy amid legal controversy) and others have made it possible for people to take beloved fictional folks for a conversational ride for years.

What’s different about Sixth Wall and Hasbro’s work is not just the way in which they deploy the audio interactions with characters, but also how they’ve jumped into the development of those characters through upfront and ongoing compensation for voice actors and what they say are strict guardrails around the creation of their operating system, which they call Character.OS.

“Very quickly, our mission emerged for Sixth Wall as not just having a character speak and come to life but really preparing all of this iconic IP for the age of AI,” Thomson said. “And the way that we chose to do it was by building this platform that we call Character.OS, a character operating system that contains what we like to call a golden record for each of our characters.”

The team at Sixth Wall worked with voice actors to record bespoke performances for Character.OS, separate from those used in animated series and films. Sixth Wall also developed contracts that compensated those voice actors for both the studio recordings and the ongoing use of their rights.

Character.OS is like the repository for the governing rules and data that make each of Sixth Wall’s characters operate the way they’re meant to, so you don’t get Peppa Pig talking about eating bacon with her breakfast or have Optimus Prime go on a tangent about the merits of cheating on your final exams.

“It’s a set of metadata that encodes the lore and canon of the universe, the personality and emotional range of the character, and then crucially the guardrails that keep them safe, but also on brand,” Thomson said.

Read more: From Green Screen to Gray Box: AI Is Stepping Onto the Hollywood Sound Stage

These golden records essentially create a world within each character meant to create an interactive audio experience that mimics their essence and keeps them from advocating self-harm or delving into dangerous subjects beyond their scope of knowledge.

But the team is focused on more than just single voices.

“What would it look like to have an AI Ouija board where you could convene with the spirits and know you were going to get a response?” Thomson said. “We also experimented with things like Trivial Pursuit Infinite, where you can ask questions or receive questions about any topic that you like.”

Thomson said Sixth Wall hopes to build golden records for characters beyond Hasbro’s IP and has created a roster of more than a dozen characters currently out for licensing as AI conversationalists. It also has an eye on forging the path for the future of how “blue-checked” AI characters are created and deployed.

Sixth Wall is starting with audio-only, with hopes of integrating visual avatars as it solidifies its roster of voice actors. The interview for this piece included a quick, live conversation with Cobra Commander’s AI voice, in which he gave Thomson some advice about how to handle our back-and-forth.

“State your business at once, recruit!” Cobra Commander barked out of the Teams window. “The commander’s time is precious.”

“Hey, Cobra, I am on a very important call with a reporter right now,” Thomson said. “Do you have any tips for me on how I could make this a great conversation?”

“Tell them that you are the most powerful and brilliant genius in the world!” Cobra Commander said. “And if they dare to question your magnificence, have your troops launch a barrage of cream pies at their headquarters. Hail Cobra!”

#3171. Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next – 7 reasons why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

After using a Debian-based distribution, you may find yourself longing for something different. I know exactly what you should try next.

Back when I was constantly distro-hopping, I found it important to have a “what’s next” mentality. That way, I could plan accordingly, instead of jumping in blind. I could prepare myself for the installation, the package management system, the desktop, and other necessary bits and pieces.

Also: Fedora Everything let me build the Linux desktop I actually want

But more than anything, I always found it best to know which type of distribution should be next.

You wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to, say, Gentoo, as the leap in required skills is considerable. You also wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to Debian, since Ubuntu is based on Debian, making it a lateral move. From my experience, when coming from an Ubuntu-based distribution, the best next distro is one based on Fedora.

This statement wouldn’t hold water five years ago because Fedora often required work to get it running properly. Now, Fedora requires no work or effort to get it working out of the box. Hardware support is on par with Ubuntu, modern boot processes are supported, it has an excellent first-boot experience, Nvidia driver support is out of the box, the touchpad works out of the box, suspend and resume work flawlessly, it ships with a newer kernel, it includes built-in support for modern display stacks, and it’s clean and bloat-free.

Like many Linux distributions, Fedora lets you choose your desktop, but it does so better by offering dedicated spins for each. You’ll find Fedora spins for KDE Plasma, Xfce, Cinnamon, Mate-Compiz, i3, LXQT, LXDE, SOAS, Sway, Budgie, Miracle, Plasma Mobile, and COSMIC. Instead of manually installing your desktop of choice, just download the Fedora spin with your desired desktop.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way

Yes, there’s a Debian-based distribution for every desktop, but knowing you can just go to the Fedora Project Spins page and quickly find what you’re looking for makes the process easy. As well, Ubuntu has its own “flavors” (such as Kubuntu, Lubuntu, etc.), so coming from an Ubuntu flavor will make total sense.

When using a Debian-based distribution, if you install/manage software from the command line, you’re used to APT, such as sudo apt install quillmark. Did you know that Fedora’s DNF works in the same way? That’s right: sudo dnf install quillmark will get you the same results as sudo apt install quillmark (so long as the app is found in the Fedora repositories).

The same holds true for removing software. One difference, however, is that when system software is upgraded, you’ll have to reboot a Fedora-based distribution for the upgrades to take effect. The only time you have to reboot on a Debian-based distro upgrade is if the kernel is upgraded in the process.

If you’re using Ubuntu as your Debian-based distribution, you’ll find that it includes a universal package manager, just as Fedora does. On Debian, the package manager is Snap, while on Fedora it’s Flatpak. While these two are different, they do have some similarities, such as app installation.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

With Snap packages, the installation goes something like this: sudo snap install quillmark. On Fedora, that command would be flatpak install quillmark. You’ll notice that sudo is not used with Flatpak; the reason for this is that Flatpak apps are typically installed on a per-user basis. Yes, you can install them system-wide, but that defeats the purpose of sandboxing.

Both Fedora and Ubuntu are secure, even if they arrive at that security by different routes. For example, Ubuntu has AppArmor and Fedora has SELinux. However, both of these tools manage Mandatory Access Controls — just in different ways. The good news is that you’ll probably never have to touch either system.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: After years of testing both, here’s my verdict

Also, both Debian- and Fedora-based distributions tend to ship with a GUI frontend for the firewall. If you don’t find one installed, you can install one through your package manager. It is important to know that the Fedora firewall manager is considerably more powerful than Ubuntu’s, which also means it has a steeper learning curve. The good news is that, out of the box, you probably won’t have to make many changes to the firewall, other than ensuring it’s enabled.

Once upon a time, I would have debated such a statement, but Fedora is now on par with Ubuntu in terms of user-friendliness, especially if you choose one of the more user-friendly spins (such as KDE Fedora, Cinnamon, or MATE-Compiz). Fedora also has a System Settings app similar to Ubuntu’s; each one lets you manage nearly every aspect of the computer, so there’s no need to use the command line with Fedora (unless you want to).

With Debian, the release cycle is every 2 years, and support is 5 years. With Fedora, the release cycle is every 6 months, and support is 13 months. If you’re using an Ubuntu-based distribution (which is based on Debian), the release cycle is the same as Fedora, but there are two versions: LTS and interim. LTS support is considerably longer than interim releases: LTS releases receive 5 years of free support, while interim releases receive 9 months.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

In the end, the Fedora release/support cycle is faster and simpler.

Because both development teams focus on building a user-friendly distribution out of the box, migrating from a Debian-based to a Fedora-based distribution is seamless. When making such a transition, aside from a few minor differences, you’ll feel like you never left your Debian-based distro, especially if you choose a Fedora Spin that includes the same desktop you’ve been using.

#3170. Why This Anker Universal Charger Is the Only Power Accessory I Pack for Travel

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The slew of port and plug options is great, and the built-in display is just as useful.

I never realized the importance of having a universal charger until I traveled to Berlin a few months ago. It was a last-minute work trip, so I packed lightly, stashed my go-to portable charger — with its flip-out plug — and flew out not knowing what struggles lay ahead.

I had it all mapped out. I’d top up my phone, laptop, earbuds and cameras at the hotel each night, go out for a döner and be ready to tackle all my work the next day. But my lack of an international plug adapter — specifically, US to EU — meant that I’d have to deal with a series of physical, technical and safety obstacles first.

Had I discovered the Anker Universal Charger sooner, I wouldn’t have gone through the ordeal of finding an electronics store open late on a Sunday. That’s because the latest product from the mobile accessory brand takes a kitchen sink approach to charging — whether you need its more excessive features or not.

I’ve been testing the $80 Anker Universal Charger, both for general use in the States and abroad, and it’s more practical than I thought. Here’s why it’ll stay in my bag going into the holiday travel season.

The Anker Universal Charger is two things: an international plug adapter and a multiport charger. It has slide-out Type A, Type C and Type G prongs that lock each other whenever one is active. That covers most countries in the world, including the US, Canada, Japan, China, Europe and the UK. Notably, the charger doesn’t have a Type I prong (commonly used in Australia and New Zealand), so it’s not completely universal.

The charger can output up to 100W, either individually through one of the two USB-C ports (labeled USB-C1 and USB-C2) or shared across the third USB-C port, which caps at 15W, and the one USB-A port, which caps at 10W. So if you want the most optimal charging, stick with only one of the main USB-C ports.

In practice, the Anker is powerful enough to charge a modern-day iPhone or Android, smartwatch or laptop. My 14-inch MacBook Pro, for example, supports 100-watt charging, so the Anker is just enough to fast-charge it. It took 33 minutes to charge my MacBook from 0% to 50%, and about 50 more minutes to reach 100% as trickle charging kicked in.

The Anker wouldn’t be able to hit the 140-watt rating of a 16-inch MacBook Pro or a similarly specced laptop, though. I also noticed the charger would throttle its output — as shown on its smart display — after prolonged use at 100 watts. That meant when I charged devices back-to-back, the second device charged much more slowly because of the reduced output.

Generally speaking, make sure you’re using a proper, high-quality charging cable with the adapter, as Anker doesn’t include one in the box.

One of the key features of the new Anker Universal Charger is the 1.3-inch smart display on the front. It’s there to show live line voltage, internal thermal readings and real-time wattage draw per port, so you know exactly how effectively it’s charging your device(s).

You navigate the display with short and long taps on the capacitive button below it, which I’ve found less intuitive than just swiping on the display, but at least it reduces fingerprint smudges.

That said, I’ve still found the smart display quite useful, as I don’t have to second-guess whether the cable I’m using or the outlet I’m plugging into can charge my phone or laptop efficiently. There’s nothing worse than plugging a device in, only to come back to it barely charged because the wattage wasn’t as high as you expected.

I’m particularly fond of how the display indicates when an outlet is safe to charge, as it can detect the output (so long as it’s within 100-275V) and signal when there’s excess electrical pressure in the circuit.

This is important when you’re traveling abroad and/or plugging into a high-voltage outlet; if you’re using a charger that’s not rated for the higher capacity, you risk sparking and other dangerous thermal reactions.

The Anker Universal Charger is relatively compact for how much power it delivers. In the past, I’ve lugged around larger charging bricks — such as Apple’s proprietary one for MacBooks — that had fewer ports.

For reference, the Anker is about the size of a small computer mouse; it’s tiny enough to fit in a backpack pocket, with just enough weight (262 grams) to keep it from shifting when plugged into an outlet. Yet, I wouldn’t say this is a lightweight charger by any means, especially when compared to a conventional plug adapter.

The Anker Universal Charger is fairly priced at $80, though it’s still more expensive than generic international adapters that sell for around $20 to $50. Those don’t have a cool smart display, though.

While the price keeps the Anker out of “impulse purchase” territory, I’ve found it easier to justify than most other high-end chargers, given its functionality and safety features.

#3169. Your FitBit Versa and Sense smartwatches will lose some features this month – what to know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Time's running out for some Versa and Sense models. After Nov. 28, you can no longer install or update third-party apps or clockfaces on these Google smartwatches.

If you have a Fitbit Versa or Fitbit Sense smartwatch, you’ll soon be unable to update the third-party apps on these devices. Google announced on Monday an update to its older lineup of devices that may signify the beginning of obsolescence. Users can no longer install or update third-party apps or clocks on these Fitbit smartwatches, beginning on Nov. 28.

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously

The apps will continue to work after that date, but if users delete any of these apps, they will not be able to reinstall them. The changes affect the Fitbit Sense and Fitbit Sense 2, as well as the Fitbit Versa, Fitbit Versa Lite, Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Versa 3, and Fitbit Versa 4.

Google noted that users will still have access to Fitbit- and Google-developed apps and clocks, and that they should update to the latest app versions to keep those apps functioning properly.

The Nov. 28 support cut-off comes right on the heels of this season’s Black Friday sales. (Google’s Pixel Watch 5 just got a $100 discount at Amazon.)

So the smartwatches aren’t dead — they can still perform the same primary functions, like recording workouts or receiving or responding to messages and calls. Still, the news is a downer for Versa and Sense users who’ve been using their smartwatches and the many third-party apps on them for anywhere from two to eight years now.

All signs point to these devices being slowly phased out in favor of Google’s latest lineup of fitness trackers and smartwatches.

Also: Google’s new Fitbit Edge solves my biggest gripe with the Pixel Watch

Within the past few years, Google has unveiled an impressive new lineup of health trackers, including the screenless Fitbit Air, the screened Fitbit Edge, and the Pixel Watch 5. For those looking to ditch their Versa or Sense, a few affordable options exist in the ecosystem to take their place.

The earliest and most recent Fitbit Versa models were launched in 2018 and 2022, respectively, and the first and last Fitbit Sense models launched in 2020 and 2022, respectively — making the oldest of these devices eight years old.

I'm joined today by Peter Greenleaf, our Executive Chairman; John Gay, Chief Financial Officer; and Sai Rangarao, our Chief Commercial Officer. The third quarter of 2026 was a successful one for Pelthos with progress made in several key areas. We're excited about the impending launches of Xepi and Xeglyze as we expect they'll have a meaningful call overlap for our existing field force which we expect will provide the company with greater operational and financial leverage from our existing team and infrastructure.

Before we cover our commercial and financial results, I want to spend a few minutes on the exciting Castle Creek Biosciences transaction we announced on October 30. While I'm limited in what I can say given that the S-4 has not yet been filed, I believe it's important to comment on why we have such strong conviction in this acquisition and the long-term opportunity it creates for Pelthos and our shareholders. Since our formation in July of last year, our strategy has been focused on building a strong commercial organization in dermatology with the physician relationships, commercial infrastructure and manufacturing expertise necessary to succeed in bringing innovative therapies to market.

Having made substantial investments in establishing that foundation, we see great synergy and opportunity to leverage these capabilities across a broader portfolio, expanding our potential future revenue base and generating greater revenue on the investments we've already made. Castle Creek represents a particularly strong fit with that strategy. Its lead candidate is D-Fi, an investigational redosable gene-modified cell therapy being developed for dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa or DEB, a rare lifelong disease characterized by extremely fragile skin, chronic wounds and serious complications. D-Fi has been granted orphan drug designation. And once the transaction closes, we expect to continue development of its Phase III clinical trials.

Patients who suffer from DEB live with intense wound burden, frequently accompanied by serious complications, including a greatly increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma, which is the leading cause of death in DEB patients. The wound burden never goes away, creating sustained demand for multiple therapies that can close wounds and keep them closed. The market for DEB therapies has already proven its commercial potential. The first gene therapy approved for DEB, a weekly topical treatment launched in 2023, generated $127 million in global net revenue in the third quarter of this year, up 30% from a year ago and more than $1.1 billion since launch with over 760 U.S. reimbursement approvals to date.

The pace of this launch demonstrates that payers recognize the severity of this rare disease. Coverage has been broad. Revenue per patient is high and gross to net adjustments have been modest relative to many specialty markets. We also believe there remains significant unmet need in this disease state. And so far, our conversations with KOLs and health care providers who treat DEB have consistently highlighted the need for further treatment options. We believe D-Fi, upon approval, can leverage this need and capture a meaningful share of the market because it offers a differentiated approach. It uses the patient's own skin cells engineered to produce Type 7 collagen and delivered by intradermal injection directly into the wound.

It is designed to be redosed with treatment sessions every 8 weeks in the planned Phase III trial. We expect the treatment paradigm with DEB to increasingly evolve more than one therapy across different wounds and stages of the disease. And we see a clear role for D-Fi as a stand-alone first-line treatment as well as being used alongside existing treatment options. This opportunity is also not limited to the U.S. We believe that approximately 1/2 of the market for DEB treatments is outside the U.S. and our agreement with Castle Creek includes rest of the world rights to D-Fi as well.

This is exactly the kind of high-value specialist-driven market where we believe our commercial model provides a great deal of synergy. It is concentrated. It is served by dermatologists we already have relationships with, particularly in pediatric dermatology and the economics per patient support an efficient, focused launch. Beyond D-Fi, Castle Creek's proprietary fibroblast-based technology adds a cell and gene therapy capability to Pelthos' existing Nitricil manufacturing platform. Together with our 3 FDA-approved products, Zelsuvmi, Xepi and Xeglyze, the combined company will offer a more diversified portfolio spanning marketed, launch stage and late-stage assets across multiple therapeutic modalities. This combination of complementary capabilities is central to the strategic rationale of the transaction.

By leveraging our existing manufacturing expertise and commercial infrastructure, we believe we may be able to accelerate the development, and if approved, launch of this product candidate. If successful, we believe this program has the potential to expand our revenue base and create long-term value for our shareholders. But the potential of this transaction extends beyond the addition of a single development asset, no matter how great D-Fi potential. This transaction positions Pelthos to be a stronger, more diversified biotech company, poised to pursue additional pipeline opportunities, build a broader commercial portfolio and expand its long-term earnings potential. A disciplined capital allocation approach remains central to this strategy.

And we intend to focus on translating these opportunities into sustainable revenue while maintaining the financial discipline necessary to generate attractive long-term returns. In short, we are extremely enthusiastic about the potential of D-Fi and are confident that the Castle Creek transaction can be a foundational pillar of the next phase of Pelthos' growth. I'll now turn it over to Sai to provide more specifics on the results of our commercial performance. Sai?

We believe our Zelsuvmi YouTube commercial and patient testimonial videos continue to serve as highly educational resources, encouraging caregivers and patients to ask their HCPs about Zelsuvmi.
