These engagements translated into meaningful interest in both continued and new use of Zelsuvmi, reinforcing its utilization among HCPs. We continue to strengthen our differentiated commercial platform, leveraging a strong foundation and the outstanding execution capabilities of our sales team to drive continued growth of Zelsuvmi. Lastly, here in Q4, our commercial leadership team has begun planning for the March 2027 launch of Xepi.

Extensive strategic brand and tactical planning is underway to align our go-to-market strategy to meet our customers' needs and position us for a successful launch of Xepi for the treatment of impetigo. I am proud of the strong performance we have delivered to date, which reflects the passion, commitment and outstanding execution of our exceptional commercial team. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to John to walk us through our financials. John?

John Gay: Thank you, Sai. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on today's call. As Scott and Sai have already touched on, we continue to focus on driving growth for our lead product, Zelsuvmi, and look forward to launching Xepi in the first quarter of next year. With today's filing of our quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the period ending September 30, 2026, we have now completed and reported 5 fiscal quarters of commercialization efforts for Zelsuvmi. While these quarters straddle 2 fiscal years, we have reported in aggregate $57.5 million of net product revenue since the commercial launch of Zelsuvmi. Turning to the operating results of our business.

Please note that my comments will focus on our third quarter 2026 results as compared to the second quarter of 2026. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported $15.2 million of net product revenue as compared to $15.4 million in the second quarter of 2026. Our gross to net for the third quarter of 2026 was 31.5% as compared to 29.6% in the second quarter of 2026. As Scott and Sai mentioned, we signed a major PBM agreement to unlock access for patients seeking Zelsuvmi with no prior authorization. While overall gross revenue increased, the gross to net increase in Q3 reflects the formulary agreement, which we believe will contribute to future incremental revenue growth.

Cost of goods sold was $1.7 million for the third quarter of 2026 as compared to $3.6 million in the second quarter of 2026. As discussed in our last quarterly earnings call, cost of goods sold for the second quarter of 2026 also included a $900,000 write-off of commercial API inventory identified through the company's quality control process. We had no such write-offs of inventory during the third quarter of 2026. Absent the impact of inventory write-offs in the second quarter of 2026, the key driver of the quarter-over-quarter reduction in COGS was primarily due to an approximate 39% reduction in the U.S.

GAAP per unit cost of goods sold during the third quarter of 2026 as compared to the second quarter of 2026. As we have previously discussed, the component of our cost of goods sold includes fair value adjustments associated with the July 2025 merger. At the time of the merger, all finished goods and active pharmaceutical ingredient inventory on hand was fair valued as prescribed under U.S. GAAP. At the end of the second quarter of 2026, we had sold through all of the stepped-up finished goods inventory. And we expect to consume the remaining stepped-up ATI inventory within the next 12 to 15 months.

Once we have sold all inventory with a base of step-up, we expect to have a normalized per unit cost of goods of approximately a mid- to high single digit of our WAC price. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported $18.8 million of SG&A expenses, representing a 25% decrease from the second quarter of 2026 at $25 million. Excluding the $5.3 million of onetime nonrecurring sales-based milestones related to our Zelsuvmi license recorded in the second quarter of 2026, SG&A decreased 5% during the third quarter of 2026. One additional point I would like to call out with respect to SG&A.

Beginning this quarter, we have presented royalty expense associated with our licensing partners as a separate line item within operating expenses on our income statement. We made a slight change in presentation to provide a more disaggregated level of detail for OpEx on the face of our P&L. Please note that we provide a detailed breakdown of the components of SG&A within the MD&A section of our quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the period ending September 30, 2026, filed this morning. But in total, cash basis SG&A, defined as SG&A less milestones and stock-based compensation, was approximately $16.9 million for the third quarter of 2026 as compared to $17 million for the second quarter of 2026.

Net loss for the third quarter of 2026 was $7.9 million as compared to $23.4 million for the second quarter of 2026. Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 was a negative $5.6 million as compared to a negative $5.7 million for the second quarter of 2026. Turning now to our balance sheet. As of September 30, 2026, we had $17.7 million of cash and $13.4 million in accounts receivable. Our working capital at the end of the third quarter of 2026 was $24.6 million as compared to $31.4 million at the end of the second quarter of 2026.

As previously discussed, in January of this year, we entered into a $50 million senior secured term loan facility with Horizon, of which we drew $30 million at close. On October 30 of this year, we executed an amendment to this facility and borrowed an additional $10 million. In addition, this lending facility also provides for an additional $10 million in funding prior to December 31, 2027, subject to the lender's discretion and certain conditions, including the company achieving trailing 12-month net revenue of at least $70 million.

Based on our current projections, including forecasted cash flows related to net product sales of Zelsuvmi and Xepi and proceeds drawn from the Horizon facility to date, we believe we have the flexibility to advance our business plan. In summary, while we are pleased with our performance since the launch of Zelsuvmi in July of 2025, generating $57.5 million of net revenue, we look forward to continued growth. Furthermore, since launch, we have strengthened our balance sheet and believe we are well positioned to continue our commercial execution story, bringing a much needed treatment to molluscum patients. With that, I'll now turn it back over to Scott. Scott?

Scott Plesha: Thank you, John. In closing, while we are pleased with the success of Zelsuvmi, our financial results and commercial reach since we launched in July of last year, we continue to focus on accelerating the growth of Zelsuvmi, preparing Xepi for launch, and continuing to expand our reach to help patients. Before we move to our Q&A session, I did want to remind those on the call that while we are excited with the announcement of the Castle Creek Biosciences transaction, we are limited in what we can say or discuss at this time.

As you're aware, we are in the quiet period between the signing of our merger agreement and the expected close of the deal expected in the first quarter of next year. During this time, we must limit public commentary, forecast, promotional statements involving the transaction to only that information that is publicly available. That being said, we plan to be as transparent as we are able to be while abiding by the rules and regulations associated with the transaction such as this. However, we do expect to be able to provide more information once we file our S-4 in due course.

In the meantime, I'd like to direct you to our Form 8-K that was filed on October 30 for additional information until we are able to provide additional information. I want to thank you for joining us today to learn more about Pelthos story. We'll now turn the call over to the operator for any questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of David Amsellem with Piper Sandler.

David Amsellem: Just a couple for me. I know you can't say all that much just yet on the transaction, but nonetheless, wanted to get your thoughts on how you see D-Fi's points of differentiation versus VYJUVEK. So that's number one. Then, in terms of the base business on Zelsuvmi, can you talk through how you're thinking about the direction of the gross to net in 2027? And then a question on Xepi. This in terms of volumes, seems like a fairly large market, particularly with a lot of usage of Naprosyn ointments. I guess my question here is, with that in mind and bearing in mind that Naprosyn is fairly inexpensive, how do you see usage paradigms evolving here?

And how do you see the payer landscape for Xepi evolving?

Scott Plesha: Okay, David, I'll kick it off. I'll handle -- talk about Zelsuvmi first and Xepi and then maybe we can transition to the capsule-free transition. So first off, a little bit of a background here. But on the GTN side of things, we've always said that we would be strategic about our contracting going forward with the different plans. And we have the opportunity in the situation to unlock a PBM, remove PA process there. And if you look at the quarter, we would have been up modestly if we decided not to do that. But it's a long-term investment in the brand and long-term growth.

We still have very reasonable gross to net rate for a newly launched product at 31.5%, especially in the derm space. And the rebate that we were able to get this win at was very reasonable. It did not trip our best price with the government, really important. So for the quarter, we were up 4% on units. Prescribers were up 8%. So really -- and other underlying metrics, increase in prescribers, new prescribers coming in, we were strategic in being willing to kind of take this hit on GTNs, very modest hit. We would have had actually a positive revenue growth quarter-over-quarter if we hadn't done it.

But we believe it's going to accelerate growth going forward not only next quarter, but into 2027 and beyond. On the Xepi front, yes, we -- one of the things we really like about the market besides just the synergy with the call point there is that it is a large market, to your point, a little bit more skewed to pediatrician, just slightly more, maybe 60% versus 40% derm, p-derm. And to your point, there are products in the market like Naprosyn. So we are already having payer conversations. They're going quite well.

One of the things we keep hearing is that there's a need for this product in the market, mostly due to the resistance you're seeing with Naprosyn. It's been used at a very high level over many years. So as you know, with antibiotics, a lot of times, when you put that pressure on it, you end up with resistance. And in fact, that's been seen. We've actually pulled some data and done additional research and you're seeing multiple therapies being used a lot of times in impetigo because of that. Next, the question you had asked kind of transitioning to Castle Creek. You had mentioned about the differentiation between the products.

I think that's something right now that we're not really able to discuss what we will be doing. And I think once the S-4 is filed, we can start talking a little bit more about the profile of the products and how they compare in the marketplace. But we're -- just high level, we feel very comfortable based on the research we've done, diligence that it's going to fit very well in that treatment space and be sometimes complementary to VYJUVEK and maybe used in places it's not.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Jeff Jones with Oppenheimer.

Jeffrey Jones: Just if I could, a little more color -- ask for a little more color around the revenue trajectory on Zelsuvmi. We've talked in the past about the colder months and quarters trajectory being reduced prescriptions and diagnosis for molluscum. But revenues flattened somewhat noticeably over the spring as well. And just thinking about what you're seeing in the market with your sales force, what you're learning, how you're adapting your strategy? And then, in the context of SG&A spend, how that might change as you adapt your strategy to increase penetration there and also in preparation for the Xepi launch? And maybe just one quick follow-up on the Xepi question.

Do you have numbers around the resistance levels to Mupirocin at this point?

Scott Plesha: Okay. So a lot to unpack there. So first off, on the revenue trajectory, what -- we're just getting around like one year and going back and being able to see what we -- since launch, just through the fifth quarter and we're learning a lot about the market. We do know that during the summer months, we saw a lot of the physicians out of office. We have people obviously taking vacation. Patients are taking vacations. They were just weren't in the office as much. There was typically, if you look at claims, about a 7% to 10% decline in Q3 from Q2 as far as claims go.

But Jeff, we're really confident if we go forward in time that our base business is very strong here. And if we were next year in Q3, we look back, we'll have very meaningful growth revenue. We do anticipate acceleration as we go into 2027, Q1, Q2 just based on what we've learned this last year. And Sai, I don't know if you want to comment a little bit more on the dynamics with the HCPs?

Sai Rangarao: Sure. Thanks, Scott. This is Sai. Just in terms of the qualitative feedback we consistently hear the Zelsuvmi profile and the clinical profile amongst our data across efficacy and safety is still considered very, very high, very valuable to those respective practitioners. So even as we saw in our Q2 results and the overall growth that we had, which we were hitting our all-time highs, as expected, some of the fluctuations, as Scott mentioned, are tied to seasonality and some of the points that you made around colder months. But we still see a high level of utilization, a high level of adoption across several tiers of our prescribers, which again instills our belief going forward.

Scott Plesha: Yes. I'll just add. I think one of the important concepts and one of the things we're seeing, we just -- we're continually adding new prescribers. And I think that will serve us well as we go forward in the future. And really, we've seen -- that's been very strong, just the number of new prescribers from week-to-week, month-to-month basis. And then on the Xepi front regarding -- specifically around resistance. We've actually worked with thought leaders to try to identify that and some of the really the foremost leaders there. And the data is a little bit all over the board right now.

And the issue we have is a lot of hospitals and organizations are not really testing to actually draw real numbers there. So I do think there's an interest in the physician community to mine that and also to start sharing their thoughts on that in the literature. So I think you might see some of that here in the near future. Regarding SG&A and Xepi, I'll let John maybe chime in on that.

John Gay: Yes, as it relates to that, so if you look at our financials, we've been preparing for that, both from a manufacturing perspective and also from a commercialization. So if you kind of look at our run rate of SG&A, as I touched on in my prepared remarks, that includes preparing the market and preparing for launch for next quarter for Xepi. So I think it's fair to say that, that spend level is not going to change materially, specifically for Xepi going forward.

Scott Plesha: Yes, that's one of the powers of that launch, obviously, is that we can leverage our infrastructure there.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Thomas Flaten with Lake Street Capital.

Thomas Flaten: I'll gamble a little bit on the Castle Creek question. So Scott, I was curious if you could maybe peel back the curtains a little bit on the thinking that pushed you kind of to evolve from a traditional spec pharma model into more of a biotech model. Kind of what was the discussions that precipitated that?

Scott Plesha: Yes. So Thomas, I think we've been very open about being aggressive on acquisitions and we've seen that -- we formed the company back in July of 2025 and already acquired 2 other assets. And as we were looking out in the marketplace, what else would make sense, we wanted, first off, for it to fit in our current model. And when we started looking at D-Fi, it's just a perfect overlay with our thought leaders, especially in the pediatric derm space, a lot of synergy. We have this base business that we're building that can actually help fund this pivot also as well as we go forward. So 2 more launches next year supporting this.

But for us, it was also making the pivot to kind of a biotech company that kind of unleashes and uncaps the value of the company going forward. So just a whole different profile on the product. And I have Peter Greenleaf here also, who's our Executive Chairman and I'll let him weigh in as well on that.

Peter Greenleaf: Listen, I think Scott did a really nice job of sort of covering the strategic rationale, but just a few things to add. One, this pivot from sort of a classic specialty pharma company into more of a research and development-oriented diversification of a biotech was critically important. Castle Creek brought to us a late-stage asset, the diversification, the pipeline orientation, a rare disease asset, but completely aligned with our therapeutic area, solid data in the early stages of development, a large, still unmet medical need market. When I say large, this is a rare disease market.

But in terms of the potential opportunity of the company and the opportunity for the company to make an impact on the disease, there still is an unmet medical need. We think this is differentiated. And to go backwards a little bit into the question that was asked about how D-Fi potentially differentiates. The one thing we can say that's out there publicly is, one, that the current methods of treatment that are out there are more oriented around either skin graft or live virus orientation with somewhat of a burdened administration. What we do know from the early data is that we do not have a live virus orientation.

And two, that there could be potentially better benefits to dosing this product, but we have to complete the Phase III trial. So there are points of differentiation. And I guess I would say lastly, this gives us yet another shot on goal. And we think we did it for the right value to get a late-stage asset for the amount that we paid upfront and the milestones that we've seen, at least as we've benchmarked it through other deals. We actually believe we got a good value in terms of the acquisition and the merger. So I'll leave it there. Thomas, if you've got another question?

Thomas Flaten: Yes. And just a question for Sai. Any commercial realignment mostly in the sales footprint side that you need to undertake ahead of the Xepi launch? And then obviously, just 2 quarters later with Xeglyze. Are you pretty confident that the current alignment will allow you to launch both of those equally successfully?

Sai Rangarao: Yes. Thanks for the question, Thomas. I think what we've said previously is right now we feel like our alignment and our overall footprint is poised for growth amongst our Zelsuvmi targets and as we go into the Xepi model. However, what Scott and I have talked about extensively is we'll always take a closer look at specific territories where we might be able to get a little bit more breadth and also continue our depth strategy across our targets. So as we go into the Xepi launch, there might be the opportunity that we might add some territories and that might be more in the single-digit range there, Thomas.

And then the evaluation for Xeglyze will continue as we get closer to that launch probably within the spring, summer of next year. But again, we're always looking at the opportunities in front of us to ensure we have the optimal field force to cover our targets.

Scott Plesha: Yes. Thomas, this is Scott. I'll just weigh in a little bit more. So we always use the word optimization. And I think we've been thoughtful and kind of earned the right to expand previously. We did 14 in the beginning of the year and then another 3 kind of midyear. And each time we've done that, they've paid for themselves in a very short period of time, actually brought in incremental revenue. So Sai mentioned we could add more reps. We're always going to probably say we could add a handful of reps here or there to just to make sure we're maximizing our growth and opportunity. So we'll do analysis.

If we feel we can bring in incremental revenue above the cost of a rep that's meaningful, we'll consider it. But we want to make sure we pay for that very quickly if we do it.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Brandon Folkes with H.C. Wainwright.

Brandon Folkes: Congrats on the quarter. I stick to Zelsuvmi too. I think we've asked a few on the acquisition. So maybe just if we think about the current Zelsuvmi script trends. How do we think about growth in 2027? Is that just a continuation of the momentum we're seeing today? Or as you see these increased formulary coverage, do you expect any sort of step-wise function? And I'll ask my second because it sort of follows on to that, if I may. Any update on the pediatrician penetration? And does the core frequency to pediatricians change as you add these 2 additional products in 2027?

Scott Plesha: Yes. So maybe we'll let Sai talk to the ped space and then I can talk about trajectory quickly.

Sai Rangarao: Yes, sure. Thanks, Brandon, for the question. From a pediatric coverage perspective, I think as we've mentioned, we have almost equal coverage amongst the dermatology specialty, which is inclusive of pediatric dermatology, but specifically the general peds category, we have equal coverage and equal footing there. And we see the growth there continue. I mean, we have some regions across the country that are doing exceptionally well within that specialty category. And that continues again, because they're a big part of our coverage. They are also the first line of defense for all the disease states that we are going into market with even in the future. So that will continue as our focus.

As we get into the Xepi planning, that is a bigger part of our calibrated efforts of just kind of the hypertargeting efforts, which may potentially allow us to concentrate even further as again, they are the true first-line defense for these disease states. But as we do see ourselves today, the coverage, the overall approach, again, has been optimal for where we're going forward, and I think dovetails nicely into what we expect for growth even out of Zelsuvmi going forward.

Scott Plesha: Yes. And I'll comment on the growth concept. And really, what we expect is consistent growth going forward. To your point on the market access win, we really haven't seen the impact of that yet fully. Those take time. Those take multiple quarters to really recognize the benefit of that. We made an investment. That's why our gross to net, I would say, went up modestly. It was very minimal. And that was a PBM that we've cited a contract with that also has the opportunity to unlock additional lives in the future also. We have work to do there. We'll see if that happens, but at a very reasonable rate.

And to your point, as we add those additional plans, we could see additional uptake over time as well there. So -- but I think as said earlier, we're confident that we're going to see growth in this product going forward. If you look at October, it was our second highest month ever. It actually was up 4% from September, which is, I think, a good sign of the market recovering. We're seeing good early signs also in November here. We are coming up against some holidays, which people aren't in practice, people aren't being seen by doctors. But then we believe Q1, Q2, we'll see very strong growth again once we get through that holiday period.

Peter Greenleaf: Yes. I guess the one thing I would just add to Scott's comments. As we look at this at the Board level and for the company, there are very few companies out there that have complete strategic alignment towards the peds, peds derm targets. So we have a leveraged OpEx base and sales force. We have a current in-market product that's continuing to show robust growth. And we have 2 products that we're launching in a diversified pipeline down the road that's in late-stage development that will be a contributor to that.

So a base operation that can produce cash flows to be able to fund the pipeline into the long term, I think, is a message that at least in the early coverage of the Castle Creek deal that's been missed that there are very few comps out there that you can find of companies like ours that are trading at the level that we're currently trading with the level of revenue, future commercial diversification and now pipeline diversification.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of James Molloy with Alliance Global Partners.

James Molloy: I wanted to follow up on the Castle Creek. Again, noting there's not lot -- not too much you can talk about. But there is a public data out there, Castle Creek put out on their Phase I/II and their wound healing. I'd love to get your thoughts on what you saw in there that you liked, in particular, as it relates to what's out there with ozenoxacin and VYJUVEK. And could you talk a little bit about the relative positioning, again, should D-Fi ultimately get approved versus those other 2 assets that are already out there on the space? And I'll hold for a couple of follow-ups.

Peter Greenleaf: Yes. I'm happy to start. So listen, we've got to conduct a Phase III trial. So all of this is with the caveat that this is a super rare disease. The data even for VYJUVEK and as another company out there, Abeona has been a limited number of patients, but in a small rare disease, obviously, that limited number of patients have been what have drived -- has driven approvals. As I mentioned earlier, as we look at the comparable set of potential newly launched products, first, we don't see this as anywhere near comparable to Abeona's product. Abeona's product is a skin graft. It has more intensive in terms of its application, et cetera.

As we look at this, it's more akin to a VYJUVEK. It doesn't have the live virus orientation. It potentially has better dosing and administration benefits that we have to prove through the Phase III. And as you mentioned, you've seen the data that's out there in the earlier stages of development. We're encouraged by it. We think the patients that have seen impact with the drug have seen pretty solid wound closure and healing that we think is -- and was a big part of when we did diligence on the product, what we believe it will actually show through in the Phase III study. But obviously, there's more to come. We've got to do the study.

We'll have more disclosure in the upcoming S-4 and as we roll this out when we hope the deal closes in the near future.

Scott Plesha: Yes. The one thing I'll add here just quickly, Jim, is that we did a lot of diligence. We have the -- we're very fortunate to have very strong relationships with KOLs in the derm and p-derm space. A lot of them were involved with the development in these areas of the other products. They know it very well. They speak about it. And we got a lot of validation from them based on that data that you just referenced early on. So we spoke to the top-tier people around this. And ultimately, they kept coming back and saying, there's a need in the market.

This will be used first line and/or in combination because there's just such a wound burden here that the current products in the market are just not meeting all the needs. So we felt very good about these individuals, especially -- I mean, these are worldwide experts. I mean these are the top of the top-tier KOLs. So that gave us even more confidence as we looked at it.

James Molloy: Great. And a quick follow-up on Zelsuvmi. Obviously, as you said, it's the first year of launch, still a lot of learnings. What learnings do you guys think you'll take into next year's back-to-school from this year's to drive growth? And how is the -- what's the counter detail from why can't you guys talk about it or they talk about you? What anecdotal story are you guys hearing from the field, if any?

Sai Rangarao: Yes, Jim, I'll answer both those questions. This is Sai. So from a learnings approach and how we're going into next year, I think the back-to-school category at times, while we feel like that's, let's call it, "opportunistic" for disease manifestation or growth at the same time, as we've discussed here, a lot of the vacation scheduling, the HCPs in and out of office has that level of disruption. So a lot of what we believe we can control are still our educational methods via conferences, via digital mediums. We do intend on actually launching even more awareness campaigns next year. That will target maybe even the teens category and other categories that we know are affected by molluscum.

So those will actually truly help us grow more notoriety, more connection and ultimately conversion. And I think as you've seen throughout this first year, all those efforts have proven to be incredibly helpful and incredibly beneficial for our patients and ultimately the business as well. Just the other point on the counter detailing pieces. I think we have visited this question a few times in this forum. I'll repeat that, again, we never counter detail against any other product. We stay true to our clinical profile on efficacy and safety. At all times, our field force is trained to be compliant on those messages and to share them very formatively and confidently amongst our HCP customers across the board.

So we affirm to that. And we really stay true to our profile as the first and only at-home prescription treatment for molluscum for which we feel incredibly confident with, and again, affirms our confidence and our consistent approach to growth as we go forward into next year.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Olivia Brayer with Cantor Fitzgerald.

Olivia Brayer: I have a couple of follow-ups. First one on Zelsuvmi launch dynamics. Are you guys seeing an increase in prescriptions that are being written that maybe just aren't yet translating into filled prescriptions? Or has prescribing activity itself been relatively flat? And then among physicians who are already starting to use Zelsuvmi, are you seeing them prescribe it maybe more frequently over time or getting more patients on drug? And then I've got a follow-up on Castle Creek.

Sai Rangarao: This is Sai. I'll take those questions. From an overall prescription to fulfillment standpoint, we don't see much change from a granted approval rate to then pick up. I mean, those are typical dynamics in an acute market. And I think those have remained stable. And I think from what we've seen throughout the summer months and obviously, as we talked about the fluctuation as it pertains to MC claims, we still grew in the quarter. And we are seeing really promising growth here in October over September, as we've mentioned. The overall cohort of clinicians that have a strong level of adoption continues. We have several physicians that have reached these higher tiers of consistent prescribing.

Also, our refills quarter-over-quarter exceeded close to 22%, which really speaks to the consistency and continuity of therapy, which, again, is our message. It's what we really go out there educating the field force on, but really every day. So those measures have helped. And I think those are also elements that, again, affirm our confidence going forward.

Scott Plesha: Olivia, if I can add just a couple of things. There are some -- I'm trying to peel back your question a little bit here. But it sounds like you're trying to understand if there's some kind of prescription fulfillment issue. And honestly, what we're seeing, number one, is a higher approval rate over time and adding the plan we just did it will only help for that as well. And then also the time to fulfillment, so some of the metrics that are really important. So when a prescription gets submitted, those have increased. I'm sorry, the days to get it filled actually has improved. So it's gone down the amount of time.

So some of the dynamics, I think, that are important that we track monthly have actually gotten better. And Sai mentioned the refills. We're actually starting -- we have seen a little bit of a lift in the number of units per patient also slightly. So it's gone from like 1.2, just over 1.2 to just over 1.3 in the last couple of months. So we see that as a good sign as well.

Olivia Brayer: Okay. That's helpful. And then on Castle Creek, I'm sorry to ask another follow-up. But how are you guys thinking about value creation as an opportunity just relative to the level of dilution that does come with this deal? I think most people were surprised to see this deal, especially just given how early you are into Zelsuvmi's launch still. So anything that you can say about maybe how the transaction came about or why now is the right time, I think, would be helpful.

Peter Greenleaf: I guess just to go back to the strategic rationale. I think if you look at -- and at least at what I've seen printed so far, I haven't seen many pick up the benefits. I have seen some pushback on sort of behind what your question is here, Olivia. But let me kind of go into first benefit, then I'll get into where we see the near-term or future value creation. One, we took a very strong and growing strategically aligned commercial organization that's got a capability that's launched one product, is growing one product.

We have the benefit of being able to launch 2 new products in the next, call it, 12 months' time period to continue to grow our revenue base. And as we're doing that, we want to always continually think about how we're growing and diversifying. We had the opportunity come along both through relationship and through doing an external scan to bring in this potential late-stage asset that takes our commercial organization and capability, completely aligns with it, gives us the ability to work the cash flows that we will eventually generate from that commercial business and put them towards the development of a pipeline. So there's less dilution in that.

We could have gone out and done a deal, had it be a license or had it been a cash-based transaction where we would have had to raise money if we didn't have this commercial business. So we look at that as a potential huge benefit. It brings us into the rare disease space. It gets us out of just a value orientation and puts us into a growth biotech orientation and puts us into what is a very large market opportunity still with unmet medical need. All for the price of -- and again, I haven't seen many people do comps of what late-stage asset deals cost today, but for an upfront consideration of equity.

And if successful, milestone payments upon data and approval of the drug. And if you add those 3 up, the amount that we paid was, I believe, our Board believes a huge value to the organization.

Operator: And we have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back to Scott Plesha, Pelthos' CEO, for closing remarks.

Scott Plesha: Thank you, operator. I want to thank everyone for joining today's call. I would also like to thank the Pelthos' employees for their continued focus, execution, hard work, and dedication to supporting patients, caregivers and health care providers. Thank you again for joining our call. And we look forward to updating you on our progress in the future. Have a great day.

Operator: Thank you. And this concludes today's conference. And you may disconnect your lines at this time. We thank you for your participation.

Top Wall Street analysts can help pick stocks that pay regular dividends while having the ability to generate capital appreciation and boost total returns.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy is a subsidiary of Diamondback Energy and is focused on owning and acquiring mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. For Q1 2026, the company declared a base dividend of 38 cents per share and a variable dividend of 30 cents per share. VNOM offers a dividend yield of 5%.

Recently, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold initiated coverage of Viper Energy stock with a buy rating and a price target of $58. "The company is advantaged given its scale, core Permian focus, inventory duration, and aligned operating partner," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst highlighted that Viper's Permian-focused asset base and significant scale relative to peers position it as a best-in-class operator. Hanold added that VNOM's 75% liquids-weighted production mix offers meaningful leverage in a strong oil price environment.

Additionally, Hanold projects Viper's inventory life at 15 to 20 years, considering the current development pace of its operating partners, which is significantly higher than that of peers. Among the other advantages, the analyst highlighted VNOM's relationship with Diamondback Energy, which has about a 39% ownership in the company. #3165. Google’s new AI tool just proved Signal encryption really works – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With the aim of securing other vital systems, Google DeepMind plans to open-source its AlphaProof Code.

Researchers at Google DeepMind used AI to formally verify portions of Signal‘s underlying code — meaning they’ve mathematically proven that at least parts of the encrypted messaging app’s code do what they say, without errors. That’s reassuring given how many vulnerabilities AI systems have discovered in software lately, and how many people’s communications are protected by Signal’s cryptography. WhatsApp and Google Messages use the same encryption.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

DeepMind used AlphaProof Code, “a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents,” the researchers said. They added that formal verification “is the highest standard of security assurance,” but, without automation at scale like AI systems, difficult and time-consuming.

AI companies like OpenAI have been on a math-breakthrough tear as of late, in some cases solving nearly century-old math problems with AI. By computing at such vast scale, AI models can rapidly accelerate much of the manual work mathematicians do.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Using AlphaProof Code and building on earlier verification work by the Signal Foundation, DeepMind researchers divided the verification task into two camps. Humans worked with agents to identify what they needed to prove, and multiple agents running Gemini Carbon, the company’s latest model, then executed it. The agents also audited the proof and “highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human — just 1% of the codebase, a massive time savings,” the researchers wrote.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

For good measure, researchers tested AlphaProof Code’s ability to distinguish correct from flawed code by showing it two previously fixed Signal bugs, for which it produced correct proofs.

“Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth,” the researchers wrote. “It’s also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.”

Normally, researchers need to manually develop a proof to verify software, which takes much longer. That labor-intensive barrier has made formal verification a distant promised land, until now. The DeepMind team’s verification took a month to do what might normally take experts years.

DeepMind did not verify all of Signal’s code, but noted that this test is a step toward improved security infrastructure at a time when AI is disrupting the entire cybersecurity space.

Also: How to encrypt emails in Gmail, Outlook, and more

The breakthrough reiterates how deeply AI is both a massive risk for cybersecurity and an equally powerful fix. The year 2026 has been especially marked by AI-related security incidents, many of which involve agents. At the same time, companies like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI are developing models geared specifically toward cybersecurity, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos.

Also: How to easily encrypt your files on an Android phone

DeepMind did not share any plans to release its findings as a consumer product, though the researchers are open-sourcing their code to help others with formal verification efforts. “Verifying Signal’s core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software,” DeepMind added

#3164. Is Your Console Ready for Grand Theft Auto 6? Here’s What You Can Do to Make Room

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Deleting old games isn’t the only option you have to make space for GTA 6.

Grand Theft Auto 6 hits shelves on Nov. 19, 2026, and if you preordered the game, you can preload it on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S now. Preloading ensures you can quickly boot the game up when it’s released.

Rockstar Games revealed that GTA 6 is 212 GB, which will take up about half of my Xbox Series S’s storage space. The company announced that GTA 6 is available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming without downloading it to your console. However, cloud streaming GTA 6 might affect the game’s performance and relies heavily on a strong internet connection. To avoid those issues, I plan on downloading the game.

If you’re like me and are excited to play GTA 6 but don’t have much storage space, you have two options: delete games or upgrade your console’s hard drive. Here’s what you should know about both options.

The simplest and cheapest way to free up space on your console for Grand Theft Auto 6 is to delete files and other games, which is what I’ll be doing. Uninstalling games is a good choice for folks who plan on spending a lot of time with GTA 6 and don’t intend to juggle different games. Rob Nelson, who oversees Rockstar North with Aaron Garbut, told The New York Times that he had an 80-hour playthrough of the game in February, so you can easily stay immersed in Grand Theft Auto’s state of Leonida.

You may not need to delete much – uninstalling a game like Call of Duty alone could free up nearly 315 GB, giving you enough digital storage for GTA 6. Since deleting files is almost instantaneous, you can quickly reclaim hard drive space. Because you don’t need to buy additional storage, you’ll also save a lot of money – storage prices are through the roof at the moment.

Ultimately, deleting games is a great option if you don’t want to spend any additional money or you don’t mind redownloading games later.

If you plan on hopping between GTA 6 and other games, or you don’t want to delete many of your downloaded titles, you can upgrade your console’s storage. Buying storage is more expensive than deleting files from your console, but benefit from being able to seamlessly hop between Grand Theft Auto 6 and Call of Duty or Madden.

You can use internal or external storage for your console, but you might have to move files between your internal and external storage to launch games. An internal hard drive lets you seamlessly play games. Xbox consoles rely on proprietary expansion cards from Seagate or SanDisk that plug into your console for additional storage. The PlayStation 5 uses M.2 solid-state drives, which are installed alongside the PS5’s built-in storage, and CNET’s David Carnoy recommends the Lexar NM 790 as a fast SSD with a straightforward installation process.

There shouldn’t be any performance, quality or load-time differences between running games from installed storage expansion devices versus your console’s internal storage. Both expansion cards and SSDs can be expensive, especially when compared with deleting games.

You could also use an external hard drive to expand your storage, which can be cheaper than buying expansion cards and internal SSD upgrades – you may even have a compatible USB external drive sitting around that you can use. However, there are caveats around what games can and can’t be played directly from external HDDs.

For Xbox consoles, some older Xbox, Xbox 360 and Xbox One titles can be stored and played from external HDDs. But games optimized for Series X/S consoles can only be stored on HDDs and must be moved back to your internal drive to play. Similarly, the PlayStation 5 only lets you store PS5 games on external HDDs, while you can store and run PS4 games from external drives.

Therefore, using an external HDD requires playing digital musical chairs, moving current-gen games back and forth between your external hard drive and internal console storage in order to play them. The LaCie Rugged SSD4 earned a CNET Editors’ Choice Award and could be a good option. If its price tag scares you, the Western Digital P10 offers more storage at a more economical price point.

Rockstar announced that GTA 6 will be available to stream on the Xbox consoles – no download required – via Xbox Cloud Gaming, with some quality and time limitations. You’ll need to purchase either an Xbox Game Pass plan or Cloud Gaming hours. Folks who don’t want to delete games or upgrade their console storage can stream GTA 6, but you’ll need an Xbox One or Series X/S console, won’t get the highest visual quality and will have to pay for more playtime hours if they run out. Streaming GTA 6 could help budget-conscious gamers who don’t want to upgrade from Xbox One consoles or who don’t have the allotted storage space on their devices.

Normally, you can stream many games on PCs, mobile devices and TVs or streaming devices using Xbox Cloud Gaming or Game Pass, but Grand Theft Auto 6 is limited to the Xbox One, Series S and Series X. Additionally, GTA 6 streaming quality is capped at Series S graphical settings. So if you have a Series X, consider deleting games or upgrading your storage to run the game locally with better graphics.

While you’ll need to install the full game on your console first, remote play for Xbox and PlayStation consoles lets you stream GTA 6 to other devices, like your phone, tablet, streaming device or TV.

If you’re willing to pay a little more for the convenience of having multiple games ready to play at a moment’s notice, Xbox expansion cards or an internal SSD for a PS5 are your best options. If you want a cheaper option and don’t mind moving game files around, an external hard drive could be for you. If you have Xbox Game Pass or Xbox Cloud Gaming, you could stream the game to your console without needing more storage space. However, the cheapest option is to delete games from your internal storage and redownload them later, which can be time-consuming.

You only have a few days left until Rockstar releases GTA 6, so you’d better prepare your digital storage now, or you might not be immediately able to play. I plan on deleting old games to make room on my console. You won’t catch me slipping on Nov. 19.

#3163. You Can Get Google’s New Smart Glasses Next Month. I’ve Tried Them Out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Warby Parker's and Gentle Monster's Google and Samsung-created smart glasses have cameras like Meta's, but these have some subtle differences when it comes to AI.

In Gentle Monster’s hallucinatory showroom, I stared up at four robotic heads turning and talking inside floating spheres. I listened to them speak different languages. All of them were translated in my ears, on the fly, as I wore a pair of Gentle Monster smart glasses — “Intelligent Eyewear” codeveloped by Google and Samsung that will finally arrive Dec. 10.

Google’s return to smart glasses has been promised for nearly two years, but the first waves of actual prescription-ready eyewear are only now rolling in nearly at year’s end, an unusual time for a product launch. Really, it feels more like a kickoff for efforts that will continue next year, as Google also works on AI-enabled glasses that have displays built in.

I’d worn Google and Samsung’s smart glasses in multiple demos before, but this month for the first time I got to try on and test the final versions designed by Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. I also visited two immersive showrooms the companies are opening in New York City to demo how these glasses work. These showrooms will be open by appointment.

The showrooms were like playgrounds, full of installation art to try the glasses in. Warby’s space was a series of library-themed rooms, with travel themes and whimsical sculptures. Gentle Monster’s was a stark, surreal series of rooms, blending industrial design and realistic (sometimes robotic) horses, people, chickens, floating heads and… a big blue gentle monster.

The glasses I wore gave me a strong sense of deja vu after years of reviewing Meta smart glasses and lots of others, but there are also signs of how their deeper-connected Gemini smarts could be a big difference-maker — and likely a sign of how Apple might approach its own glasses expected in 2027.

The various models of smart glasses across Warby Parker and Gentle Monster designs, which start at $395 and $449 respectively, all work the same: The frames do not have displays, just standard glasses lenses that support a range of prescriptions and lens types that match what Warby and Gentle Monster already offer. They have speakers on the arms that project audio, along with four beamforming microphones that filter out background noise and focus on the direction you’re facing. They have a single camera on the left side, and an LED light indicator on the right.

I got to try on all the frame designs and then wore frames with my prescription lenses popped in so that I could actually use the glasses around the exhibits. The glasses feel reminiscent of what Meta’s made for years, with a similar frame size and arm length to recent Ray-Ban Gen 3 models. Most of the frames weigh around 40 grams, which felt pretty easy on my face, but I wear chunky glasses to begin with.

And the frame designs, while mostly clean and somewhat conservative, all looked really good. Warby Parker’s collection of designs came in several understated color shades (I liked the dark green pine the best), and familiar round and square frames.

All of the Intelligent Eyewear models across both brands have cameras, a feature that Google’s head of XR, Shahram Izadi, still sees as key to having a deep assistive experience, although he’s also open to the idea of future versions that could be camera-free like Meta’s recent Ray-Ban Audio model.

These glasses use the same type of indicator system as Meta’s glasses do, flashing an LED that also auto-adjusts brightness outdoors and playing a sound when taking photos and videos.

I was particularly impressed by how Gemini can just listen to any snippet of speech and translate it into the language you need, a trick that makes these glasses feel like a Swiss Army knife for travel. Several demos showcased this, including the surreal room of robotic heads that discussed Gentle Monster’s design philosophy in a handful of languages. I heard them all, sometimes with a short delay or hiccup, over 10 minutes or so.

The glasses can recognize written languages, too, in a much larger range than I’m used to: over 70. Live translation kicks in when you press and hold two fingers on the glasses’ temple, and the translated voices adjust to match different speakers in a room and varied intonation.

Pressing and holding the side temple turns on Gemini, and once it’s on, it stays on until a significant pause of about 15 seconds or so. That meant that I could keep chatting and asking questions without asking, “Hey Google,” (or, “Hey Gemini,” a new trigger phrase). I could end a session by swiping backward on the arm.

Any of the chats I have can also be turned into a note or summary instantly, hooking into Google Keep. The glasses connect with Google Maps, and Izadi promises that most of Gemini’s key features on phones will carry over to the glasses. On iPhones, the glasses will be able to triangulate across Google apps via the cloud to access Gmail, calendars and more.

I found a few clever demos that showed me some promise. In a pantry installation full of world foods in Gentle Monster’s showroom, I asked Gemini to compare brands of international mayo in front of me. I could point to things and casually ask, “What is this?” and Gemini knew what I was referring to. In another demo, Gemini knew the sheet music I was holding up and played back the matching song. In another demo, I sat down and gave myself a tarot card reading — Gemini could read the cards, regardless of whether the cards were right-side up or reversed.

Other times, Gemini said the text I asked it to read was too far away, even though I could read it on a wall. Sometimes it seemed to hallucinate an odd answer to a question. (It responded with “8 minutes” to a question on a wall about whether it was OK to wait 45 minutes for a restaurant table.)

Tapping the temple arm starts and stops music, swiping changes tracks and two-finger swipes change volume (which was a bit confusing). Meanwhile, a top button on the arm takes photos and videos just like Meta glasses do, but in some demo sessions, it seemed like photos got beamed over to a Pixel phone much faster than they do to Meta’s app.

The music playback sounded good based on some quick tries in a crowded room. The audio seemed particularly loud, maybe even a bit more so than Meta’s glasses, but I’ll know more about that when I review them.

The real test of Google’s Intelligent Eyewear is in how truly well connected those AI services feel and in the battery life. Meta promises up to eight hours of battery life on the Scriber Optics glasses I’ve been wearing the last few months, but the battery drains faster than that in heavy use. Will Google manage battery better, or similarly?

It’s the AI features and Google app hook-ins that could give Google a leg up. My several hours wearing pairs and wandering through two different immersive public installation spaces only showed me hints, and really, I’m most curious about how the glasses can tap into my entire Gemini history, my Gmail, my Google Docs, or my Google Maps history. How smart and connected can they be, and how good (or unsettling) will that feel?

Google’s also not enabling any livestreaming from these glasses, a move that leans careful compared to Meta’s livestreaming modes on its glasses. “We’ll always take the conservative path right now just to rebuild trust,” Payne said.

But it remains to be seen how much any of this will help make anyone in public feel comfortable with someone wearing a pair of these glasses with camera-enabled AI modes on. It’s already hard to convince people that smart glasses aren’t recording people all the time, and Google’s clearly trying to restore confidence in the idea of smart glasses in public situations.

The Warby Parker and Gentle Monster models are not the only new smart wearables Google has coming: A pair of tethered mixed reality glasses that come with a processor puck and work almost like a portable VR headset, called Xreal Aura, is arriving in the next few weeks. And Google’s also starting to test its display-enabled Intelligent Eyewear ahead of a possible launch next year.

Izadi also told me that more assistive features are coming to these camera-enabled glasses, including what Google calls Guided Vision, something of an extension to the Project Astra tech Google has been working on for years. “You’ll hear more about our plans in the coming months,” Izadi said.

But agentic AI is clearly the road going forward, something both Google and Meta are expanding on for glasses. “We’ll bring more and more agentic and core AI features so that people can depend more on the AI capabilities,” Izadi said. Google’s leaning on these glasses being true phone extensions, as well as watch-connected.

But there could be a lot of cascading hardware pieces in between. Google and Samsung have already promised multiple waves of tethered and wireless smart glasses, ones with displays and ones without, and these glasses are apparently just the start.

I’m curious to see how well Warby Parker and Gentle Monster approach support for the glasses and how easy it’ll be to understand how they work. Dec. 10 isn’t far away.

#3162. All your Apple devices need to be patched ASAP – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security updates for iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and Vision Pro just rolled out.

On Tuesday, Apple released security patches for iOS, iPadOS, MacOS, WatchOS, and VisionOS, which address wireless security flaws in Bluetooth pairing, AirPlay, and Messages.

According to Apple’s security notes, vulnerabilities can allow attackers to establish a Bluetooth connection without user interaction, bypass AirPlay connection rate limits, and join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Around half of these flaws were found internally by Apple, while the others were submitted by researchers.

You should update your devices now, as several generations are affected across device categories. The following software versions include patches:

Apple’s security notes list a fix for Messages to prevent attackers from remotely joining an iMessage group chat and reading its messages. According to Apple, “an authorization issue was addressed with improved validation” to fix the issue.

There was likely a flaw in Apple’s iMessage authorization logic that allowed an unauthorized user to inject themselves into a group chat roster without permission from an existing member.

Also: Your iPhone can spot scams for you with iOS 27

Another issue in Messages could allow an authorized added member to access messages within a group chat that were sent before they joined. According to Apple, the code that caused this issue has been removed.

One security fix across devices and software versions addresses an issue where a malicious actor could establish a Bluetooth connection to your device without user interaction.

Apple was not specific about which kind of Bluetooth attack this fix addresses; however, it’s reminiscent of Bluetooth Low Energy Re-Pairing vulnerabilities found earlier this year by French researchers.

This study explains how bad actors can exploit vulnerabilities in Bluetooth Low Energy pairing logic to execute one-click or zero-click impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks against unsuspecting devices, regardless of Bluetooth version or security level.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: Your favorite gadgets could expose you

The study was published in January of this year, and the researchers reported initial findings to Apple, which “[appeared] to have hardened the re-pairing logic in MacOS/iOS 26,” according to the study. It’s possible that Apple internally found another vulnerability in the same Bluetooth pairing logic, given how many devices across Bluetooth versions are affected.

According to Apple, this issue was fixed with “improved checks,” likely meaning strengthened verification steps during pairing.

Another vulnerability pertains to AirPlay, allowing an attacker within Bluetooth range or on the same network to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. This issue also affects iOS, iPadOS, MacOS, VisionOS, and WatchOS.

This vulnerability is similar to the AirBorne attack method. This report, published in 2025 by Oligo, describes how zero-click remote code execution, user-interaction bypass, denial-of-service, man-in-the-middle, and other techniques can be used to take control of a device that supports AirPlay.

However, the current security issue is likely less serious or far-reaching and was discovered internally.

For this issue, when you pair a device with an AirPlay receiver, such as an Apple TV, AirPlay-enabled TV, or Mac, it will prompt you for a security PIN to verify your device. You can only input an incorrect PIN a certain number of times before you’re denied pairing for a period of time.

Also: The new Apple TV 4K is always listening for ‘Hey Siri’

A vulnerability in this defense mechanism can allow an attacker within Bluetooth range of, or on the same network as, your device to use a brute-force attack, bypassing the mechanism that limits the number of incorrect PIN attempts, and eventually gain access to your device. There are only so many PIN combinations.

According to Apple, “a logic issue was addressed with improved state management” to fix this problem.
