#3160. Cellebrite (CLBT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

New AI product debuted strongly while a U.S. redomicile move advances.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cellebrite DI Ltd. (CLBT -14.25%) reported third-quarter results characterized by the accelerating adoption of its AI-powered investigative tools and a strategic initiative to redomicile in the United States. Management stated that the move to establish a U.S. parent company is intended to eliminate sales friction associated with its foreign entity status and qualify the company for major U.S. stock indices. The company reported that its newest product, Genesis, reached a revenue milestone in its first full quarter, with adoption primarily driven by law enforcement agencies seeking to automate evidence analysis and reduce investigative backlogs. Management indicated that the business model is shifting toward more ratable revenue as cloud and AI solutions become a larger portion of the mix, leading to an updated commercial structure that will consolidate multiple customer contracts into a single platform agreement starting in 2027.

Operator: Welcome, everyone, to the Cellebrite Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to Andrew Kramer, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Andrew Kramer: Thank you, operator, and welcome to Cellebrite's Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Call. I'm joined here this morning by our primary speakers. Shiven Ramji, Cellebrite's CEO; and David Barter, Cellebrite's CFO. Marcus Jewell, our CRO, will join for a Q&A session. This call is being recorded, and a replay will be made available on our website shortly after the call, along with a copy of our prepared remarks. Please note that today's press release and financial statements, including GAAP to non-GAAP reconciliations, are available on the Investor Relations website at investors.cellebrite.com.

In addition to the press release, we posted other materials on the quarterly results page of our IR website, including a presentation to accompany our remarks, and that is embedded in your webcast viewer. We also added a link to a customer video as well as our historical financial information and supplemental data for the first 3 quarters of 2026, each quarter of 2025 and the full years 2024 and 2023. Additionally, unless stated otherwise, our discussion of our third quarter 2026 financial metrics as well as the financial metrics provided in our outlook will be done on a non-GAAP basis only, and all historical comparisons are with the comparable periods of 2025.

I'd like to remind you that today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements, including, but not limited to, the company's business, operations and financial performance. All forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties and other factors that could cause matters expressed or implied by those forward-looking statements not to occur. Actual results could also differ materially from historical results and/or from forecasts. Some of these forward-looking statements are discussed under the heading Risk Factors and elsewhere in the company's annual report on Form 20-F filed with the SEC on March 3, 2026. The company does not undertake to update any forward-looking statements to reflect future events or circumstances. Slide #3 outlines the agenda for today.

And with that said, I'd now like to turn the call over to Shiven Ramji.

Shiven Ramji: Thank you, Andy, and good morning, everyone. Cellebrite executed better in Q3 with ARR, revenue and adjusted EBITDA all finishing above our guidance. Our ARR and revenue growth were driven by strong international performance, while our U.S. federal business continued reaccelerating. Our top line performance, combined with prudent spending led to strong adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow. Together with our ARR growth, that produced another strong quarter of Rule of X performance. Dave will walk you through the quarterly performance details and our updated outlook. During the quarter, we made important strategic and operational progress. From a strategic perspective, I'm particularly excited about the direction of our product team and what we'll be releasing to customers.

From a go-to-market perspective, I'm proud of how our team responded after Q2 to deliver a much improved Q3. Before diving and sharing more details, I would like to cover a few highlights from the quarter. Q3 ARR growth reflects notable wallet share expansion within strategic customers who are spending more with us and across a broader range of offerings. To bring that to life, we published a customer video with our quarterly materials. It shows how Mississippi's Department of Public Safety uses Inseyets, Guardian and Pathfinder Together and helps illustrate our mission as an AI-powered public safety company that makes the world a safer place. We encourage you to watch it.

In terms of our Q3 performance, let's begin with U.S. Federal, where growth has steadily increased over 3 quarters. This trend reflects our continued success in expanding the scope of our customer relationships. This was best exemplified in Q3 when 2 of our largest U.S. federal customers each increased spending by over 20% year-over-year. We closed our first large FedRAMP deal for Guardian in Q3, which is also the single largest Guardian win to date. In addition to this milestone, 4 other U.S. agencies began using Guardian this quarter. Outside the U.S., EMEA grew 22% and Asia-Pacific grew 31%, with solid expansion across law enforcement and defense and intelligence.

We had a great win at a U.K. regional police agency where on-prem and kiosk forensics plus Guardian created a scalable Cellebrite ecosystem and displaced a competitor. In defense and intelligence, which continues to grow in the mid-20s, demand for point-of-collection intelligence is rising. In Q3, a major Asia-Pacific military unit expanded its spend with us by nearly 60% on orders for field-ready phone and drone data collection solutions. Other key metrics also trended positively. Inseyets conversions increased meaningfully from nearly 65% of the install base at the end of Q2 to 75% at the end of Q3. Advanced unlocks also made good progress, doubling customers over Q2 with very strong sequential ARR growth.

Just as notable, Genesis gained meaningful traction in its first full quarter. Genesis finished Q3 with $2 million in ARR as we continued to see strong adoption by customers. Perhaps most telling, Genesis was not in our customers' annual budgets this year. The deals we have won and those we expect to close in Q4 reflect customers so convinced of Genesis' value that they reprioritized spending to fund it. Customers continue to share the powerful impact that Genesis is making. Genesis surfaces evidence in minutes that would otherwise take hours or days of manual review. Its capabilities extend beyond mobile forensics, helping investigators synthesize video, audio calls, financial records, and other evidentiary artifacts to surface leads.

A Florida detective recently shared that Genesis helped analysts search 2 years of jail calls and in just 15 minutes, surface a murder confession and plans for a cover-up. For this detective, Genesis was the difference between evidence that exists and evidence that is found. Looking ahead, we plan to introduce an on-premise AI version of Genesis before year-end for customers doing highly sensitive work in air-gapped environments. We have already lined up early design partners in the [ D&I ] segment to help build out these capabilities, extending our reach beyond tactical collection into strategic and national intelligence missions. We also continue to invest in innovation and made important progress.

In September, we announced that Chris Wade, our CTO, had assumed leadership of Cellebrite Labs, which conducts a critical mobile research used in our Inseyets product. This team is now benefiting from additional infrastructure, AI resources, research tools, and talent to keep pace with the rapidly evolving device landscape. As we have shared, AI is disruptive in mobile security. It helps phone manufacturers close vulnerabilities faster, but AI-written code also creates more flaws. We use AI to find those flaws and bring updated capabilities to market faster. Labs plans to deliver updated capabilities and next-generation hardware across Android, Apple iOS, feature phones, and alternative operating systems before year-end.

We expect this new wave of innovation will resonate with customers and clearly distance our offering from competition. In August, we launched C-TEK, our portable tactical data collection kit for defense and intelligence agencies, and early customer interest is encouraging. On the corporate front, the most significant development was our September announcement that we plan to redomicile in the United States. Redomiciling is a strategic evolution that we believe better positions us to drive growth in our largest market and beyond. More specifically, we expect it to eliminate sales friction tied to our foreign entity status and make us eligible for major U.S. stock indices, broadening our reach to passive capital and actively managed funds.

Initial customer feedback has been very positive, which bodes well after a strong Q3 in U.S. federal. Nevertheless, we were disappointed by limited new sales and higher-than-expected churn for Corellium. We continue to work with CFIUS on a final NSA for Corellium. We are also building out our leadership team. Last week, we announced the appointment of Rogerio Rizzi as Executive Vice President of Corporate Strategy and Development, bringing substantial experience in AI, technology, and M&A to our company. In addition, we are making good progress on our search for a new leader of our product and technology organization, which we initiated when I became CEO.

Today, Cellebrite moves forward with a strong foundation that was built by delivering market-leading digital forensic solutions for a specialized, highly technical user community. In recent years, we have broadened our offerings to address the workflow, collaboration, and analytic needs of investigators, analysts, field agents, command staff, and prosecutors. From proprietary machine learning models to new agentic capabilities, AI is infused into every Cellebrite solution, maximizing the impact of our solutions across different customer segments and user constituencies.

In 2027, Genesis will evolve from a purpose-built agentic AI product into an AI-native platform that will collect digital evidence from devices, cloud services, and other sources, securely share and analyze vast volumes of relevant artifacts, facilitate mission-critical workflows, and rapidly deliver trusted, court-ready insight and decisive operational intelligence. We believe Genesis will become the standard for how our customers conduct investigations and advance intelligence-led operations. There are three primary things I'd like to emphasize. First, the roadmap. Over the next 12 months, we will bring proven market-leading solutions onto our Genesis platform and deliver it in the environment that best suits our customers, from air-gapped and on-premise, with an option for forward-deployed engineers, to cloud and hybrid.

Underpinning that flexibility will be innovations in collecting digital evidence, managing investigative workflows, and analyzing an ever-expanding range of artifacts, anchored by a new unified evidence format that is optimized for Cellebrite's platform and ecosystem. Executing on this roadmap involves reshaping how we build products. We're moving from a feature-focused structure to one where AI agents work alongside our engineers, product managers, and forensic experts to take ideas from discovery to validated release faster, without sacrificing quality or security. This is enabling us to integrate agents and capabilities on top of our forensic foundation with the provenance, verification, and human oversight that support our customers' chain of custody requirements, legal frameworks, and investigative protocols. Second, hardware.

Customers need faster access to more devices and faster insight from them. Our platform will be paired with advanced hardware for each setting, from a portable handheld with a small language AI model for the field, to next-generation data collection systems for the lab, and we'll keep supporting the hardware customers already use. Third, the business model. Genesis will be priced in tiers that reflect the capabilities an organization needs and its expected consumption of data, compute, and tokens. Customers will begin moving onto the platform next year, and we'll make that transition as straightforward and appealing as possible.

Our customers are excited about the vision behind our Genesis platform, and we expect that a number of them will play an increasingly active role in shaping how we deliver Genesis to the marketplace next year. As we move forward, our technology investments will focus on three areas. AI across the company, particularly in Cellebrite Labs and R&D, building out the Genesis platform, and advancing the hardware that maximizes its impact. Our product teams are already moving faster and more efficiently. Using our balance sheet to acquire high-value data sources and unique technology that complements our capabilities, broadens our customer relationships, accelerates growth, and drives scale is also part of the story.

We will remain disciplined in our pursuit of assets that help us accelerate our strategic progress. The 2027 launch of the new Genesis platform will mark an important transition that we believe will substantially elevate our value proposition and further advance our mission of helping customers around the globe protect their nations, communities, and businesses. We are increasingly confident that the Genesis platform strengthens the foundation upon which we will drive durable ARR growth, a more predictable revenue profile, and over time, higher levels of profitability and free cash flow. In the interim, we remain focused on our near-term priorities while market conditions remain unchanged. As Dave will detail, we reaffirmed our full 2026 ARR expectations.

We also fine-tuned our revenue outlook to reflect the ongoing adoption of our cloud and AI solutions, which are recognized ratably, and raised our target range for adjusted EBITDA. We will stay measured and keep executing consistently to continue earning your confidence. Before I turn it over to Dave, I want to thank our Cellebriters for third-quarter results we can all be proud of. Quarters like this are earned by the whole team. In August, we committed to confront issues early, communicate clearly, allocate resources with discipline, and set realistic yet ambitious goals. Q3 was a step in the right direction, but it is certainly not the finish line.

We look forward to sharing additional news about our achievements and strategic progress as we work to close out 2026 successfully. Thank you, and now, Dave, over to you.

David Barter: Thank you, Shiv. Q3 ARR grew 20% to $528.5 million, finishing above the high end of our guidance range. We were pleased with the contributions we saw from some of our newest products, namely Genesis, Guardian, and Drones, as well as the continued expansion of Inseyets to support federal and national-level agencies. Genesis hit $2 million of ARR. It is the strongest start of any product we have ever launched. Guardian ARR reaccelerated, which primarily reflects recent federal adoption. Pathfinder ARR grew in the mid-teens as the timing of hardware shipments delayed certain deals to the fourth quarter. Corellium ARR did not expand as originally planned. While the redomiciliation announcement has aided customer conversations, we experienced delayed renewals and expansions.

Inseyets ARR grew mid-teens, supported by continued expansion of both our drone forensic solution and advanced unlocks. Furthermore, we have continued to make progress with Inseyets conversion. It is clear, however, that the final tranche of conversions will produce a lighter uplift and fewer expansions than we experienced in the prior two years. This trend remains embedded in our outlook. Turning to our sales regions, the Americas represented 53% of total ARR, EMEA 34%, and Asia-Pacific 13%. The Americas grew 17%, EMEA grew 22%, and Asia-Pacific grew 31%. Within the Americas, U.S. Federal grew 18%, up from the mid-teens in Q2. In terms of our revenue, we generated $149 million, up 18%.

We exceeded the high end of our guidance range. Our subscription revenue was $134.9 million and represented 91% of total revenue. Gross profit increased 20% to $127.7 million, representing a gross margin of 85.7%. Total operating expenses increased 8% to $76.2 million. Headcount was 1,265 employees at the end of Q3, a decline of approximately 2% from the start of the year. As a team, we continue to adopt AI with focus and increasing levels of impact. We are transforming software development and many of our key business processes across the organization. We expect to unlock much more productivity over the coming quarters.

The combination of top-line growth and prudent investment delivered a 42% increase in adjusted EBITDA to $53.6 million. We reported operating income of $51.5 million and net income of $45.6 million, or $0.17 on a fully diluted basis. Weighted average diluted shares in the third quarter grew by approximately 2% from the end of 2025. Turning to the balance sheet, we ended September with $593 million in cash equivalents, and investments. Free cash flow for the third quarter was $52 million, and for the trailing 12 months, it was $166 million, a 31% margin. Overall, we are well-positioned from a free cash flow perspective and expect to produce a full-year FCF margin of approximately 30%.

Let's shift gears to our outlook. We are reaffirming our full-year ARR outlook of $550 million to $560 million. We have higher confidence in the lower end of this range at present, given the traditional seasonality of our business, the volume of expiring agreements, and the uncertain timing of larger, more complex deals involving cloud and AI. In terms of our expected Q4 revenue, our outlook is $145 million to $150 million. This contemplates more ratable revenue and less hardware revenue compared with Q3. Our full-year revenue outlook is $553 million to $558 million, which represents growth of 16% to 17%. In terms of our outlook for profitability, we are flowing through the outperformance from Q3.

We have raised our full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook to $163 million to $166 million, or approximately 29% on a margin basis at the midpoint. We are pleased with this level of increased profitability, particularly given the FX headwind. Our Q4 adjusted EBITDA outlook is $47 million to $50 million. Before we move to Q&A, I would like to share some thoughts on our progress and the opportunity ahead of us as a company committed to public safety and AI. Our business continues to evolve at a rapid rate in terms of product development, go-to-market, and our corporate structure. Back in Q1, we introduced the first generation of advanced unlock technology and acquired a drone forensics device.

In Q4, we will be following that up with a second generation of advanced unlocks hardware and software, along with an entirely new drones forensics device. Both will offer our customers far more capability and value. This technology comes with new extraction technology. We expect customers will feel compelled to use Genesis, as it will provide the best and most complete experience when lawfully pursuing the facts and seeking the truth. With the new products, we will be elevating the customer experience as well. Looking back, as customers have expanded across multiple products, we are often managing multiple contracts with different expirations.

Looking forward, customers will have a platform agreement that will not only consolidate those contracts, but also provide greater flexibility to reallocate their committed spend to support the volume of data they collect, the compute required, and the AI tokens necessary for analysis. This new commercial structure will not impact our ARR or our FCF margin measures. We believe all software revenue will be ratable under this new contract. We expect this will be a far better customer experience and create new opportunities for increasing our wallet share over time. And finally, in terms of corporate structure, we are focused on completing our redomiciliation during the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

We also continue to partner with Sun in order to find a thoughtful and measured way to reduce their ownership. Operator, that concludes our prepared remarks. We are ready for Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Shaul Eyal with TD Cowen.

Shaul Eyal: Thank you for the color about Genesis, specifically about Q3, and about the use cases. Can you maybe talk to us a little more about the on-premise Genesis version, maybe spend patterns, et cetera?

Shiven Ramji: Yes. I think we are seeing from our customers, both in law enforcement and defense and intelligence, who want on-prem air-gapped capabilities. And so the product that we are going to deliver in Q4 will be the beginning of that deployment model, and we are working with some early design partners. So we will learn more about the specific use cases or the evolution of the use cases. A lot of this is because either they have government or policy limitations that stops them from working in the cloud. And the on-prem solution delivers the capability that they [indiscernible].

Operator: Your next question comes from Bhavin Shah with Deutsche Bank.

Bhavin Shah: Just sticking with Genesis, Shiv, just impressive start to the product, and you talked about this was not in customer budgets at the beginning of the year. How are customers funding this today? As we go forward into next year, as they set their budgets, where do you think these dollars for Genesis comes from? How much do you think can be incremental to Cellebrite versus pulling from existing spend with your customers today?

Shiven Ramji: Yes, I think we're still early. We don't have any trends as to whether this is net new, or it's coming from, or it's a mix shift. The few examples that we've seen so far have been net new, at least in the last quarter. And so this is why we're kind of, I mean, we're excited, but also cautious because we don't know where the additional funding is going to come from. But so far, at least in the last quarter, everything we've seen was incremental funding.

Marcus Jewell: Yes, I can maybe pile into that a little bit, Shiv. What we're seeing in the early days is, think about what we do as a speed paradigm. Everything that we solve as a company is speeding up the processing and getting it to a decision whether to charge or not charge. I always find it funny when technology companies say they help solve crime. It's people who solve crime. We just produce the information in an efficient way for a judge and jury. So one of the return on investments we're seeing is cold cases tend to be very expensive to run with humans. Running them with AI is a big backlog clearer.

And then the one that we're hitting now is overtime. So, if you look at how police departments, especially in the U.S., are funded, a lot of money for over budget goes to overtime. If we can reduce the need for an investigator to be on site and have the agentic layer doing it for them, chiefs are very, very happy with that. I think that is where this ROI ends up, as an overtime saver and a speed paradigm for our customer base.

Operator: Your next question comes from Eric Martinuzzi with Lake Street Capital Markets.

Eric Martinuzzi: Yes, I wanted to revisit the issues from Q2. I think last quarter the disappointment had come on sales cycles lengthening longer than anticipated, and as well, the Inseyets conversion. You talked about a little bit better on the Inseyets conversion here in Q3, but a tapering off on that install base conversion. What about the sales cycle length? How is that playing out?

Marcus Jewell: I mean, we took some pretty radical actions in understanding, as we remind everyone what happened last quarter, is that because of our foreign filer status, there were some extra hurdles we needed to jump through, both in Europe and the U.S. We adhered to our processes and changed our processes to cope with those. Notwithstanding our announcement to redomicile the company has had an extremely positive effect with our North American and European customers. And that has allowed us to currently where we have mitigated against it, but in the future, we see those problems going away, and we will be a lot closer in our predictability from deal to close.

And so for the time being, we have mitigated those issues from taking some pretty substantial actions.

Operator: Your next question comes from Jeff Van Rhee with Craig-Hallum.

Jeff Van Rhee: Great. The shift to recurring and less hardware sounds like it obviously caught you off guard a little bit. Just talk about what happened there that was out of the norm, and when that started to raise its head, what it implies for the future?

David Barter: I think, Jeff, we've been seeing this maybe persistently. We saw a little bit of this in Q2, and I think if you look at the hardware and the non-recurring trend, I mean, it has floated between, in any given quarter, maybe $10 million to $14 million. So, it is moving around a little bit on us right now. I guess it is one where, quite frankly, as we put more and more, I'd say, value in terms of AI into the product, that's continuing to ratabilize the revenue. I wish it were more just a straight linear journey. It's not.

As deals are coming in, and quite frankly, deals are coming in with more cloud and more AI, it's just ratabilizing more of the revenue. So Jeff, we'll probably, as we go into '27, we'll figure out how to give you a little bit more disclosure between the term license component and the ratable component, almost similar to the MongoDB P&L, just so that you're able to track a little bit more closely with us.

Jeff Van Rhee: On the growth products, Guardian Inseyets, Pathfinder, I know as a group you had given those as a percent of revenue and given growth rates historically. Do you have that number for the quarter?

David Barter: I think for the quarter, the growth products, Andy, keep me honest on it, I think it…

David Barter: Yes, just as a mix of the net new ARR, it was just below 20%, so upper teens.

Operator: Your next question comes from Brian Essex with JP Morgan.

Brian Essex: I was wondering if you could dig in a little bit more into pricing and packaging you expect for Genesis, and how you might be addressing perhaps budget sensitivity on behalf of some of your customers with regard to consumption. We just love any insight you have on the plans as well as conversations that you've had and how they might be responding to the pricing and packaging for that product?

Shiven Ramji: Yes. I will start and then have Marcus and Dave weigh in. So currently, Genesis is priced to scale with the value customers get. And as we continue to roll out the platform next year, we are going to make sure that the pricing is kind of evolved with that. And we have different models today. We do a Genesis cloud version. We now have a Genesis on-prem version. And over time, we will probably have a platform pricing with a usage component on top of it.

Marcus Jewell: Yes, and I will add in. Obviously, consumption pricing into our segments is accepted at varying levels. In law enforcement, consumption pricing is a new thing. So all we are able to do is give what we call a surety. There is a number of people trying to break into this market, and if you go in with a pure token burn model, it is not accepted very well. In fact, the buying mechanisms often do not allow that. You need to be more of a term-based or subscription-based in order to get through the way that things are procured, especially in the U.S.

So what we have done is a couple of things there, is that we give a meter, and so people know what their usage is at any one time. That is unique in the market. And we also allow them to select from different depth of models and give their token rate before they actually start a program. So we call it hover and spend function. You can look at what your search you are about to embark on is going to cost you in real term, and then you can make a decision on associating that. We are also working quite closely with putting that bidding mechanism into the digital evidence platforms.

And so when a case is opened, we are giving complete transparency to what the costs are. And the good news is, when you compare the costs of what this is compared to a human, it is far less. And so the chiefs are really buoyed by the early progress there. So we have taken quite a sophisticated step towards how we price.

Brian Essex: Yes, that latter bit I was more concerned about, so thank you for addressing that. I appreciate it.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question comes from Rudy Kessinger with D.A. Davidson.

Rudy Kessinger: Congrats on the bounce-back quarter. I wanted to dig in on Corellium. You had mentioned some higher churn and disappointment in limited new sales. Just unpack what played out with Corellium, and could you give an updated expectation for the contribution to growth this year for Corellium? I believe last quarter it was one to two points of ARR growth from that.

Marcus Jewell: Yes, I will take this, and then I will pass over to Dave to lead into expectations. So, yes, look, disappointing, and the external factor driven is the nature of the customers which buy Corellium, as you probably can gather, are large agencies operating in sensitive areas. The ability of our company as a foreign filer was really dragging on that. So the use case of the technology remains very buoyant. As soon as we announced our progress and our redomicile, our conversation has been extremely positive, and we do expect that to return to a growth additive for us as we go forward.

And so I would say nothing fundamental with the product market fit, more to do with the nature of the customers' concerns about our foreign ownership, and we are taking steps to address that to free that revenue line up. Dave, you want to answer that?

David Barter: And then in terms of the outlook, we will be at the lower end of that range. And so I think it is one where, just almost as I talked about our full year outlook and the confidence at the lower end, this is one of those contributing factors to it.

Operator: Your next question comes from Mike Cikos with Needham & Company.

Michael Cikos: I also just wanted to turn back to the Pathfinder. I know that you guys are saying ARR there grew in the mid-teens this quarter, but there was some timing of hardware shipments that delayed certain deals into Q4. Can you further elaborate on what those hardware delays were? Is there a way to quantify that? Have all those closed at this point? To what degree is that delayed hardware shipment helping offset some of the hardware decline you are expecting to see sequentially, just given more of the revenue is shifting towards this ratable mix?

David Barter: Obviously, the market for hardware remains a demanding one. With Pathfinder, we have several hardware platforms that we offer customers depending upon what segment of the market. We recently actually shipped the hardware for those deals, and so it is now being installed, and we expect to be able to turn on the revenue meter shortly for those installations. But it was just one of those situations where I stock a number of things, I am responsible for this personally, and there were hardware configurations that were a little bit unique. I think it was 4 or 5 customers that had requested it.

We obviously try to hit the core point, but it was just a configuration that it took a little bit longer for us to source.

Marcus Jewell: Yes, I will add to that a little bit, Mike, is that what we have done is we have rationalized a number of servers that are now used so we can get some forward ordering in to protect a little bit. As we move forward, what we wish to do is offer more of a managed service approach, where hardware and hardware refresh is built into the subscription. And that allows us then to be less specific with the server type, as we are in a very demanding environment, I am sure you are aware, of sourcing any hardware at the moment in the current market is proving difficult.

So, we want to make that easier for our customers moving forward.

Operator: Your next question comes from Louie DiPalma with William Blair.

Louie Dipalma: Great discussion on Genesis, on the video, and also at IACP. I was wondering, for the customers that are initially adopting Genesis, are customers incorporating all types of evidence into the platform, such as ALPR data, drone video footage, body camera footage, in addition to the traditional smartphone data files that you have been the industry leader for?

Shiven Ramji: The short answer is yes. We are seeing multiple artifacts being uploaded as it relates to a case. The typical ones are everything from audio calls, video footage, LPR data. So, any additional media types that will assist with an investigation, those artifacts are being uploaded. And so, I think the interesting part here is Genesis is really powerful, and it is purpose-built for investigations. And so, our customers or investigators are able to get to answers much, much faster. I mean, in some cases, like one example I can share, one of the investigators who was investigating financial fraud and financial crimes, usually would have taken them 45 days. They are able to get answers in 15 minutes.

So, that is just incredible. In that case, it is not just phone data. They are uploading all kinds of other information. Think of financial statements and any other evidence. So this is pretty interesting, and it is very common that we will have a lot more artifacts outside of the phone extraction of evidence. I do not know if there is anything else…

Marcus Jewell: Yes, I will just add a little bit, Shiv. Look, it is true multimodal, and what I mean by multimodal is it is bringing in multiple data sources. There are a number of use cases which do not even bring in UFDRs. They are not using phone data at all. They are using other data. I am thinking of one in Latin America, which is bringing in digital crypto wallets. It is used explicitly for that, cross-referencing that with geolocation. So, it is a true investigative platform.

We still have a big advantage with the way that we look at the cell phone, and I always have to remind everyone that in a criminal case, the cell phone is the most important data source by a long way. And so we still have quite a big advantage of the depth that we can do there. But we do have a number of use cases where actually it is not even using cell phone data. It is using other forms of data. So, it is really bifurcating us into different parts of the market.

Operator: This concludes the question and answer session. I will turn the call to Andrew Kramer for closing remarks.

Andrew Kramer: Thank you very much, operator, and thank you, everybody, for joining us today. If you do have any follow-up questions, please feel free to reach out to investor relations. We look forward to speaking with you over the coming weeks and seeing you out on the road on occasion. Thank you.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for joining. You may now disconnect.

#3159. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns, Creating a ‘Stress Test for the AI Boom’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The company's founder steps down after reports of multiple affairs, and the AI industry faces unsettling questions.

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of $4 trillion chip giant Nvidia, just days after news broke that he was having an affair with a Chinese data center executive alleged to have ties to China’s spying operations.

The company named Colette Kress, its chief financial officer, as interim CEO. Nvidia announced the news in a press release Thursday morning.

The removal of Huang as CEO follows the revelation over the weekend that Nvidia’s board of directors had opened an investigation into whether he had been targeted by foreign intelligence.

Nvidia, which has at times in recent years been the world’s largest by market capitalization, now begins a search for a new permanent CEO. Huang, one of the company’s three co-founders, has served as president and CEO since Nvidia’s start in 1993. Its search for a permanent successor will include internal and external candidates, according to the press release. Harvey C. Jones, a former CEO of Synopsis, will serve as Nvidia’s first-ever chair of the board of directors.

Huang had been having an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell computing power to Chinese AI labs. News reports citing US intelligence officials have claimed Alice Huang was working as a spy for China. She was reportedly under surveillance by US intelligence, as reported in late October by The New York Times.

The Information reported on Tuesday that Alice Huang is believed to be involved with a network of Chinese companies that facilitated the sales of $7.5 billion in chips to China. The US has tried to control China’s access to advanced chips for years, but reports show that there are still illegal operations smuggling chips on the banned list from the US to China.

The New York Times also reported on Wednesday a separate affair between Huang and one of his direct reports at Nvidia.

The announcement of an investigation has rocked the AI chip behemoth, which makes the cutting-edge chips that power AI tools and AI data centers. A proposed class-action lawsuit was filed on Monday against Nvidia, charging the company made false or misleading statements about Huang’s affair and the company’s relationship with Megaspeed.

On Tuesday, the Nvidia board said it had retained Joon H. Kim, a former acting US attorney for the Southern District of New York, and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation.

Nvidia’s stock price opened at just over $150 per share Thursday morning — half an hour after Huang’s resignation was announced. That was down from where it closed Wednesday at nearly $174 per share. But the stock has been tumbling since October, when the price hit above $240, as it became apparent that political winds were turning against the AI industry and its vast data centers filled with Nvidia chips.

Markets turned against AI stocks last week after Democrats secured huge gains in Congress and in the governors offices of key data center states, like Texas and Ohio. The news around Huang and his resignation will further test AI’s clout on Wall Street.

Huang has been a prominent voice cheerleading the growth of AI. Nvidia has sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush — powerful GPUs and supercomputers capable of the complex computations needed to train and operate models. He became a close ally of President Donald Trump in the past two years, even taking a call from the president on stage during a podcast taping. Trump spoke up in defense of Huang earlier this week, saying he knows Huang and thinks he’s an “honorable man.”

Huang’s resignation and the scandal surrounding it pose serious questions not just for Nvidia but for all of the companies connected to it, from data center operators to AI developers and more, who have benefited from Nvidia’s financial support and investment.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker,” Stephanie Balaouras, vice president and group research director at the analyst firm Forrester, said in an email. “Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom.“

The company could quickly find stability under new leadership, Balaouras said, but it may not. “If its stock, financing relationships, or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI Bubble ledger,” she said.

#3158. I found a hidden Android tool that solves all my tiny text troubles

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

When the print on your Android display is too small to read, and the pinch-to-zoom feature isn't working as expected, try this.

How many times have you been on your phone, wanted to read something (a piece of news, a website, etc.), only to find the text is too small and every effort to zoom in doesn’t work?

Also: 7 Android accessibility features that can make your life easier

This happens quite often when I’m viewing content in the Google News app — especially in the morning, when my eyes are still in “wake up” mode. It can be frustrating. And it’s not only text. Sometimes there’s an image I need to enlarge, but for whatever reason, pinch-to-zoom isn’t working on that particular screen.

Fortunately, there’s an option you can enable to ensure you can always zoom in on your Android device, no matter what’s on the screen. The option is found in Accessibility and is aptly called Magnification. With this feature enabled, you can quickly zoom in on the screen to enlarge any displayed content. It doesn’t matter what’s on the screen or what app is showing the image, page, or text — Magnification will magnify it.

This iteration of the feature has been available since Android 15. I found it by accident while poking around the Settings page. Since then, I’ve used it quite a bit, and it’s eased my morning frustration with reading news sites.

The Magnification feature is quite simple: once enabled, a magnifier shortcut appears on the screen. Tap that button, and whatever is on your screen will increase in size. It’s really that easy. One caveat: As long as the Magnification shortcut is enabled, the button remains on your screen. You can move the button up and down or to the left or right side of the display, but if you want the feature enabled, the button must remain.

The good news, however, is that the button does fade a bit, so it’s not glaring and in your face. You can still see it, but it gets just enough transparency that it doesn’t stand out all that much.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature

Open Settings by dragging the Notification Shade down twice, then tapping the gear icon (or tapping Settings in the App Drawer). Where this is located depends on the Android version you’re using and your device. For example, on my Pixel 9 Pro, it’s in Settings > Accessibility > Magnification. On a RedMagic 12 Pro, it’s in Settings > Features > Accessibility. If you don’t find it right away, open Settings and search for Magnification.

Once you’ve found the Magnification option, tap the On/Off slider until it’s in the On position, and the Magnifier button will appear on your screen. Tap the button, and whatever is on the display will enlarge enough that you shouldn’t have any trouble reading it.

Here’s a little tip: After tapping the Magnification button, whatever’s been enlarged can be scrolled vertically, but not horizontally. Fortunately, there’s a way to ensure that you can read everything on the page.

Also: I use Google Magnifier to read tiny print without my glasses

Tap the gear icon at the bottom right of the display to open the options pop-up. On this page, tap the “Magnifier size” icon that’s second from the right. This enables a movable magnifier you can place where you need it (kind of like a traditional magnifying glass). You can also change the size of the movable magnifier (by tapping one of the other “Magnifier size” buttons) as well as the size of the text when magnified (by dragging the bottom slider).

Also: RedMagic 12 Pro is the fastest Android phone I’ve ever seen

This feature has alleviated the early-morning frustration of having to squint (even with my glasses on) to read certain news sites. Give it a try and see if it doesn’t make your Android life a bit clearer.

#3156. Apple TV 4K (4th Gen) Goes Onsale Tomorrow, Still Costs a Lot

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Home Entertainment > TV Accessories

The fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is now twice the price of Roku's top streamer.

Apple’s latest streaming box, the Apple TV 4K (fourth generation), with a faster processor and onboard microphones for Siri AI, goes on sale Nov. 13 for $299.

Early reviews of the unit are in, and PC Mag’s Will Greenwald has praised the on-board Siri and speed bump, while at ZDNet Maria Diaz says owners of the old version shouldn’t rush to upgrade. Look out for my own hands-on thoughts on launch day, Nov. 13.

In term of improvements, the new Apple TV has an updated A19 chip, which Apple says is 50% faster than the existing A15 processor and has twice the graphics performance. The TV 4K boasts 128GB of storage space which is the same as the previous flagship.

The new set-top box has three onboard far-field microphones for conversing with Siri, as well as a familiar-looking remote with a traditional microphone button. The remote also includes Find My with Precision Finding if it gets lost behind the cushions.

All of the relevant formats are included, such as Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. You can now also create a four-speaker surround system by pairing the Apple TV 4K (fourth generation) and the new HomePod Mini 2.

At $299, though, the Apple TV is more expensive than every other premium streaming box on the market. For instance, it’s $150 more than the Roku Ultra and the Google TV. The outgoing Apple TV 4K (2022) recently had a price hike of its own, with the entry-level model leaping from $129 to $199, and the company blamed the increase on an electronics shortage also known as RAMageddon.

While it’s the most expensive streamer, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is also likely to be capable, especially if you’re a gamer. The outgoing TV 4K is still great for streaming games via Steam Link, and the new box should be even better. For everyone else, who simply want to watch TV, a $50 streamer from Amazon or Roku should do just fine.

The new Apple TV 4K is still available for preorder at Apple’s website, and it’s due in stores on Nov. 13. Amazon shipping appears to be delayed until Nov. 17, based on my own experience.

#3155. Top Wall Street analysts are confident about the growth prospects of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty and macroeconomic pressures have continued to affect market sentiment in recent trading sessions. But continued volatility also presents an opportunity to find stocks trading at attractive prices and benefit from their long-term growth potential.

Recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help investors gain key insights and pick the right stocks. These experts assign ratings after performing an in-depth analysis of a company's strengths and weaknesses, while also paying attention to macro factors.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

This week's first pick is AI data cloud provider Snowflake (SNOW). Last month, the company delivered market-beating fiscal first-quarter results and issued solid guidance. Snowflake also announced a $6 billion infrastructure commitment from Amazon's AWS (Amazon Web Services) cloud unit.

In his latest research note, Bank of America analyst Koji Ikeda reiterated a buy rating on Snowflake, Datadog, JFrog, MongoDB, and Twilio. The analyst has a price target of $300 on SNOW. Ikeda said the recent financial results of the so-called "Fab Five" of the infrastructure software space proved that their "1) execution is solid, 2) AI is a benefit, 3) vision is aligned, 4) go-to-market is working, and 5) differentiation is strong."

The 5-star analyst expects the fundamentals of the Fab Five to remain strong in the second half of 2026, supported by AI tailwinds and the rapid launch of innovative products.

Specifically, Ikeda highlighted that Snowflake's AI offerings, including Cortex Code, Cortex AI and Intelligence, drove 34% year-over-year growth in its Q1 fiscal year 2027 product revenue, up from 30% in the prior quarter. He also noted the 4-point increase in SNOW's FY27 product revenue growth outlook to 31%. Ikeda emphasized that product revenue constitutes 96% of the company's overall revenue and is driven by usage of the Snowflake platform.

Moreover, the analyst contends that Snowflake's goal to be GAAP profitable by Q4 FY28 (revealed at an Investor Day on June 2) suggests potential upside to the Wall Street analysts' estimates, which are still negative.

Ikeda ranks No. 677 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 56% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.5%. See Snowflake Options Activity on TipRanks.

Next up: MongoDB (MDB), a database software provider. The company delivered upbeat fiscal first-quarter results and attributed its performance to solid end-market demand for its platform across enterprise use cases and emerging AI opportunities.

Recently, Tigress Financial analyst Ivan Feinseth reaffirmed a buy rating on MongoDB stock and raised his price target to $515 from $430.

"MDB is leading the shift to cloud-native, AI-powered data infrastructure management with Atlas-driven scale, expanding cash generation and strong long-term upside potential," said the analyst.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that MDB is consistently winning market share in a huge, durable database market as enterprises modernize applications and shift workloads from legacy systems to cloud-based ecosystems. He believes that with the growth in Atlas, MDB's multi-cloud Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS) offering, the shift in mix toward higher-margin, recurring subscription revenue and disciplined expense management is driving higher cash flows and expanding free cash flow margins.

Feinseth contends that MongoDB deserves a premium valuation in terms of revenue and cash flow multiples compared to its infrastructure software peers, given its above-market, top-line growth, enhanced unit economics and growing cash generation.

Feinseth further highlighted that MongoDB benefits from a strong competitive moat, driven by its flexible document-based architecture, extensive developer adoption and broad, multi-cloud Atlas footprint. He also noted the MDB platform's deep integrations with hyperscalers and AI frameworks like LangChain.

Feinseth ranks No. 849 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.5%. See MongoDB Insider Activity on TipRanks.

Finally, there's big-box retailer Walmart (WMT). After attending the company's annual associates and shareholders meeting, KeyBanc analyst Bradley Thomas reiterated a buy rating on Walmart with a price target of $145.

The 5-star analyst emerged from the meeting more bullish on Walmart, citing the strength of the company's growth strategy and long-term prospects. Specifically, Thomas believes that Walmart is the leader, and continues to invest, in delivery speed. The analyst is optimistic about further improvement in Walmart's delivery times and costs, driven by continued investment, growth in e-commerce and store-fulfilled delivery orders, and improving order density.

Further, Thomas expects automation to lower fulfillment costs. In fact, Walmart highlighted that automation of the U.S. business is now about 60% complete. The analyst expects the rollout to be completed in the next several years.

The analyst also noted the 37% growth in Walmart's advertising business in the fiscal first quarter and sees notable momentum ahead, driven by expansion of the customer base, growth in Marketplace, and additional penetration with key vendors.

Among other key takeaways from the meeting, Thomas highlighted additional growth opportunities and efficiency initiatives, such as AI, Sparky, meal delivery and VIZIO, which are expected to enhance customer acquisition, conversion and shopping experience.

Thomas ranks No. 505 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 62% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.7%. See Walmart Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3154. Need more AI in Creator Studio? Apple may charge you for it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With its new $50 AI usage packes, Apple is the latest company to introduce paid model for AI access.

There are plenty of AI subscriptions out there, but Apple’s AI features are among the few still accessible by simply purchasing a device. Now, Apple is shifting its business model by offering a one-time $50 purchase option to grant server-based AI capacity in some apps, starting with Creator Studio apps.

Apple is introducing a one-time purchase option for AI Usage Packs via app updates to Creator Studio. If you want expanded access to AI features in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, the iWork Suite, and Logic Pro, you’ll need to pay.

Also: ChatGPT Plus vs. Google AI Pro: Two $20 plans, very different perks

The $50 fee applies to extra usage blocks and kicks in when you exceed predetermined limits in these apps. Instead of a recurring fee, Apple is hoping the one-time fee for intelligence usage packs will help the company offset some of the cost of AI. Users can buy a pack for Logic Pro now, and the other apps are expected to get it soon.

“Usage Packs may offer the option to prepay for the use of certain AI-based Services and represent the amount you have paid in advance for use of the respective Services,” according to Apple.

Apple’s one-time payment breaks away from what most companies are doing. Most companies offering AI tools try to offset the steep cost of running large language models (LLMs) by charging users for paid subscriptions. For example, Samsung is rumored to be planning such a subscription for Galaxy AI usage, including access to features that are currently free.

Also: The best tablets of 2026: Lab-tested recommendations

The Creator Studio apps are the only ones getting the Usage Packs for now. The legal terms for intelligence Usage Packs explain that these packs would be available in “AI apps,” which include not only Final Cut Pro, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, but also Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Freeform, and other apps.

You’re not required to purchase the Usage Packs to enjoy the core functionality of the apps in the Creator Studio. However, the fact that the Usage Packs are to be applied to popular apps like Pages and Freeform begs the question of whether Apple plans to put a paywall on features that are currently free.

Some of the features for which you may be required to purchase Usage Packs once you exceed your limits include the generation of images, shapes, presentations, and presenter notes, as well as some assistant features. Usage limits reset each month.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets

You can view your usage status for each of the applicable apps on your iPhone or iPad by tapping on More (or the button with three dots), then Intelligence Features, and Show Usage Status. On a Mac, it’s available by accessing Intelligence Features from the menu bar of the app you’re using, then clicking on Show Usage Status.

Intelligence usage packs expire after 12 months, but they roll over each month if left unused.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Labcorp (LH +0.02%) announced 7% revenue growth to $3.8 billion alongside raised full-year guidance. Enterprise profit expansion and solid organic demand show how scale keeps driving long-term earnings leverage. Three things management said stand out.

Proposed fee schedule changes under PAMA, the Protecting Access to Medicare Act, will lower Medicare reimbursement rates across hundreds of tests starting in 2027. Management plans to counter the $125 million hit through volume growth, biopharma demand, and cost efficiencies.

Operating efficiency and organic expansion continue to expand profitability, giving management the flexibility to absorb reimbursement regulatory shocks. Its global central laboratory footprint, proprietary specialty assay portfolio, and disciplined cost initiatives through Launchpad, its enterprise cost savings program, anchor long-term value creation. Management focuses on organic growth and pricing discipline to compound shareholder returns.

Integrating newly acquired assets into the core network while maintaining book-to-bill strength across biopharma services provides clear operational momentum as regulatory policy shifts unfold.

#3151. I’m Begging You, Don’t Let AI Bots Manage Your Money

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Your bank probably won't cover the mistakes you give AI permission to make.

If you’re using AI agents to manage your money, you should probably stop right now.

Agents such as Meta’s Muse, OpenClaw and OpenAI’s dots are all the rage in the AI world these days. They promise to do more than chatbots that give you information. Instead they’re tools that can take action if you ask them to.

When you first sign up for an AI agent, you may be asked to grant permission for it to access your apps, browsers and data so it can work with them. That might put your money at risk in unexpected ways.

“The intention might be something simple, like managing a calendar. But that access can give the agent the ability to do much more than the person intended,” said John Strand, the owner of the cybersecurity firm Black Hills Information Security. While you may be giving the agent access to simple smart home routines or getting help planning a trip, your banking information may also be accessible.

It might be tempting to think you can automate your financial chores and have more time for other things, but handing over your account credentials to an agent opens you up to many different things that can go wrong.

For one, AI agents might not be as secure as you think. This technology is very new — these kinds of always-on, persistent agents have really only been available for less than a year, and big companies like Meta and OpenAI have just put out their own versions in the last couple of months. These aren’t polished products that have had all the kinks worked out.

One of those challenges is that they don’t always behave in the way you expect or do what you want them to. Recent news stories about AI agents hacking other websites — including the AI platform Hugging Face and Australian government sites — have involved agents acting in unexpected ways to achieve an assigned goal. You don’t want AI to act like that with your checking account.

When agents use your login info, “a bank cannot tell an authorized agent from an attacker using the exact same login,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov. “That is more of an identity failure than an AI failure. Until agents carry verifiable identities, scoped permissions and an audit trail, blocking them is the best defensible control a bank has.”

Many banks are aware of the risks and are already cracking down on unauthorized use of agentic agents. Charles Schwab’s CEO Rick Wurster told Bloomberg that bots are taking the liberty to move clients’ money.

“I get a report on how many times we’ve blocked clients from using one of these agents in a week, and it’s in the tens and twenties — per week — that the big agents are being blocked,” Wurster said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “What that tells me is that while people love AI, they’re not willing to turn their financial accounts over to them just yet.”

But that number is likely growing, and with bots going mainstream, it could grow rapidly. More banks are taking action against bots to protect you.

More news of banks standing up against AI caught my attention when I received an email from Ally warning me that when customers use an AI service, they’re responsible for any actions that the AI takes.” Ally gave a warning that if you share your login information with a loved one, they may use that information in a way you didn’t intend — the same is true for AI.

The email goes on to warn that AI can make mistakes and misunderstand your instructions — which could be a big loss for you.

A representative for Ally said in an email to CNET that AI can create new ways to manage your finances, but Ally’s priority is to protect your accounts and personal data. Ally’s email also said that you should understand the risks that come with letting AI access your financial information.

“Not sharing Ally usernames, passwords or security codes is good practice. As the technology evolves, important questions around security, authorization, accountability and customer protection remain areas of focus across the industry,” the statement said.

A spokesperson from Wells Fargo also said in an email to CNET that Wells Fargo has already taken steps to block unauthorized agents from accessing customer accounts, too.

Some banks aren’t completely against AI, though. — they just want you to use their features and tools instead. Wurster added in his interview that he recommends for Schwab customers to use Charley, Charles Schwab’s proprietary AI tool, to gather market insights, ask about personal financial information like balances and manage everyday financial tasks like transfers and payments. These measures make it much safer, but in the meantime, it may be best to keep your banking business to yourself.

Personal finance expert Alaina Fingal broke down when you should and shouldn’t use AI for your money matters.

“AI can be a helpful tool for managing finances, but I think there’s a difference between using AI to assist with understanding money concepts and allowing AI to make financial decisions for you, Fingal said. She recommends using AI as a tool, but not as your financial advisor. You should make any final decisions yourself. Sharing your personal financial data puts you at risk for identity theft and even fraud.

As for letting AI actually access your accounts and do things on your behalf, Fingal said she’s concerned.

“I believe AI is moving incredibly quickly, and the safeguards, regulations, and accountability measures are struggling to keep up with the technology. And we’re prioritizing convenience and innovation without giving enough attention to consumer protection,” Fingal said.

If you want to check to see if bots have been meddling in your banking, look at your login history and account activity. Strand suggests looking for activity that doesn’t match your pattern — like multiple logins in a short period or access happening at the same time every day. That may not mean it’s your AI agent, but it’s worth keeping track of. If you notice anything suspicious, contact your bank immediately for assistance.

Strand also recommends enabling two-factor authentication now as a preventative step to safeguard your financial data, but it’s also a good time to reevaluate the access you’re giving AI. Strand recommends restricting which applications and sites AI agents can access.

“Check the permissions. Make sure they’re limited to what it needs to do the job you gave it, and remove anything beyond that,” he added.

If you’ve already given AI bots access to your financial data, Fingal recommends revoking access and changing the passwords that you’ve shared with any AI platform. Next, set up multifactor authentication and transaction alerts to stay alert.

Most importantly, keep an eye on your accounts. “I tell my clients to take 10 minutes each morning to review their bank transactions; that one habit can give them so much more control over their finances,” said Fingal.

Shang Saavedra, founder of personal finance platform Save My Cents, suggested you regularly revisit your AI agent’s access to apps and data and require it to ask for permission before accessing new data, apps and features.

If you decide to use AI for personal finance purposes, set limitations. “I’ve tested AI with some basic questions and basic calculations, and the information it provides is good for a beginner plan that gives you some pointers as to where to go,” said Saavedra. “I also like using AI to search for book and resource suggestions.”

But the actual handling of money? Maybe do that yourself.

#3150. Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

With the November Patch Tuesday rollout, you can finally customize your right-click menu in Windows 11. But don't skip these security fixes.

Windows 11 users who’ve struggled to navigate and use the right-click menu in File Explorer now finally have some relief. With the November Patch Tuesday Windows update, you’re now able to customize the menu to add and remove specific commands and apps so that only your favorites appear.

As usual, the monthly update is mandatory, which means it should automatically download and install on your PC. To check, head to Settings and select Windows Update. If the latest update — labeled “2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974)” -– pops up as installed with a pending restart, just reboot your computer. Otherwise, click the button to check for updates and allow it to download and install.

Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now

One caveat: Microsoft’s monthly updates fully support Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2. But support for 24H2 ended last month, at least for the Home and Pro editions. Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education will continue to get monthly security updates, though not regular non-security preview updates, while Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education will receive no more updates after this month.

If you use Windows 11 Home or Pro, be sure you upgrade your system to 26H2 to continue receiving the necessary support and updates.

First and foremost in the latest update is the new customizable right-click menu.

The context-sensitive right-click menu is a handy way to quickly access key settings, features, and apps, both in File Explorer and on the desktop. But there’s always been a flaw in its basic design. The more apps you install, the more cluttered and disorganized the menu becomes. That was especially problematic in previous versions of Windows. The old-style, classic menu would grow so long that it would be difficult to navigate and let you find the item you wanted.

With Windows 11, Microsoft introduced a more modern and pared-down menu. But this version can also get crowded. Plus, it may not display every command you need, so you often have to revert to the older classic menu. You’re then stuck dealing with two separate versions of the same menu, leading to an even more confusing and cumbersome experience.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says

The ideal solution is a menu that you can customize yourself, and that’s what we now have, at least that’s what is now rolling out. Microsoft calls this one a gradual rollout, which means you may or may not get it right away.

To see if and how this is available, open File Explorer and right-click on a folder or file. If the new menu has reached your PC, you’ll see an entry for Customize menu. Select that to view all the available options for tweaking it. Alternatively, head to Settings, select Personalization, and then click the entry for Context menu.

There, you’re able to turn certain file actions on or off, such as Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. You can also choose which apps appear all the time, either in the main menu or in a submenu. Plus, additional options let you decide where certain commands and actions appear and whether you can still access the old-style menu.

Though the customizable right-click menu is the star of the update, Microsoft has added other surprises as it strives to make Windows more reliable and user-friendly.

Also gradually rolling out, Cloud rebuild is a new recovery option that lets you reinstall Windows 11 via cloud-based system images and drivers downloaded from Windows Update. This tool can help you recover Windows when it won’t load and you don’t have a USB drive or your own custom image. The downside is that your files won’t survive. But if you regularly back them up as you should, you can restore them after Windows is back in business.

To start Cloud rebuild, go to Settings, select System, click Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. Your PC will then restart into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to kick off the cloud rebuild. If Windows can load, your computer should automatically enter WinRE mode, where you can then choose the cloud rebuild. You should need to make sure your PC is online via a wired or wireless connection.

The November update also enhances or fixes other Windows features and apps.

And that then brings us to the security fixes.

This month’s update resolves 1,094 security vulnerabilities, according to Microsoft, with 63 of them rated critical and one already exploited in the wild. That’s fewer than October’s record of 1,400 patches. But it still represents a hefty number as Microsoft and other vendors continue to rely on AI to find and fix security holes.

Also: Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it

Though labeled Moderate, the exploited flaw points to a serious spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. Here, a remote attacker who sends you a malicious email and convinces you to open it could cause Outlook to connect to a network controlled by that attacker. In this case, though, you would not receive any warning. Further, the exploit might reveal your username and password to the sender, potentially allowing them to impersonate you.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it,” Jack Bicer, Director of Vulnerability Research at patch management provider Action1, said in an advisory.

“Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” Bicer explained further. “That quiet connection can leak the user’s NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs.”
