#3109. Should You Buy Alphabet Stock Now That Google Will Let Customers Run Its AI Chips in Their Own Data Centers?

The search giant's turning its AI chips into hardware it sells. Is the stock a buy around 28% below its peak?

Alphabet (GOOGL +1.79%)(GOOG +1.62%) just gave its custom artificial intelligence (AI) chips another way to reach customers. On Monday, Nov. 9, Google Cloud announced two new versions of its tensor processing units (TPUs) -- chips Google designs to train and run AI models. And Google Cloud vice president Mark Lohmeyer told reporters that select customers will be able to install one of them, the TPU 8tx, in their own data centers.

For most of their history, the only way to use a TPU was to rent one in Google's cloud. This changed in the second quarter, when Alphabet started booking revenue on TPU systems it sold to customers running their own data centers. Google now says almost 100 customers use the chips.

Meanwhile, Alphabet shares trade near $292 as I write. Its record close was on May 13, at $402.62, which puts the stock about 28% under that peak.

Most of the revenue from those chip sales won't arrive until 2027, and Alphabet pays for the hardware first. But I think the move makes the long-term case for the stock a bit stronger.

The TPU 8tx is made for confidential work. Google says it's designed for regulated firms and governments running AI alongside their most sensitive data, and it protects that data even as the chip is processing it. (Usually, data needs to be unlocked in memory as a computer works on it.)

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian described the appeal on Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call in late October.

"For some industries, they have data in their premise that they cannot move to a cloud, and it allows us to bring accelerated compute to where the data sits," Kurian said.

Put another way, on-site TPUs can reach customers Google's cloud can't fully serve. Some TPU customers Kurian named on the call seem to match that description, such as capital markets firms Citadel Securities and Jump Trading.

The market these chips compete in is huge. Nvidia posted data center revenue of $89.0 billion in its fiscal second quarter alone (the period ended July 26, 2026). Even a small slice of that kind of spending could matter to Alphabet.

Showing how quickly Google's own AI business is moving, Google Cloud's third-quarter revenue more than doubled year over year to $30.7 billion, and management said TPU system sales were a meaningful contributor. The growth rate has climbed every quarter this year -- 63% in the first quarter, then 82% in the second. Cloud's backlog (contracted revenue not yet recognized, including the TPU sales deals) hit $561 billion, up from $462 billion at the end of March. And the segment's operating margin widened to 36.2% from 23.7% a year before.

Still, the chip sales themselves are early. Alphabet's quarterly filings say it's signed a limited number of agreements to supply TPU systems to customers who run their own infrastructure. The company expects the significant majority of the revenue from these deals to be recognized in 2027.

Of course, selling hardware also changes how cash flows through Alphabet. It buys parts after a contract is signed but before the customer pays, so the money goes out first.

Alphabet's inventory, which consists mainly of TPU systems and Pixel devices, jumped to $13.3 billion at the end of September from $2.4 billion at the end of 2025. With that build and $51.4 billion in capital spending, free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter.

On the upside, Kurian said putting TPU systems in customer data centers "offsets the need for us to have to prebuild facilities to host these TPU systems." But Alphabet still expects capital spending of $195 billion to $205 billion this year, and it expects that number to grow significantly in 2027.

Does this change the case for Alphabet stock? Not overnight. But it gives Google a second way to make money on chips it already designs for itself, from business its cloud couldn't reach alone.

Alphabet stock costs around 19 times expected 2027 earnings. That's a fair price, I think, for a company whose cloud revenue just more than doubled. Free cash flow will probably stay weak for a few more quarters. Still, at this price, I'd consider buying shares.

#3107. After Jensen Huang, Big Tech Has a Chance to Learn From Nvidia’s Mistakes

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech insiders and commentators say Nvidia will survive Huang's departure, but it's time for more accountability among CEOs.

What now for Nvidia? This was the question on everyone’s lips at the illustrious Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon on Thursday in the hours after CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation.

Huang’s departure followed a series of allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an Nvidia employee and one with a woman who has been identified as a possible Chinese spy. The company, whose computer chips are at the core of generative AI’s disruptive powers, is valued at around $4 trillion, making it one of the most valuable in the world. A co-founder, Huang has been with Nvidia since its earliest days three decades ago, making it hard to imagine the company without him at the helm.

There’s nothing quite like a salacious, market-moving scandal to create a buzz at a tech event. The Web Summit organizers leaned into the news, quickly assembling a panel of tech experts to discuss whether Nvidia was bigger than its CEO.

Nothing in the allegations changes the fact that Huang is probably the godfather of the AI revolution, said investor and financial writer Adam Kobeissi. “He was the central figure,” Kobeissi said, even if he wasn’t the only person responsible for Nvidia’s success.

“This company is going to survive and thrive with or without him,” he added. “I don’t think this is some sort of bubble-popping moment where everything comes crumbling down.”

Sweeping financial investments and expectations across the AI industry have driven stock prices and company valuations to dizzying heights, with many critics warning of a bubble just waiting to burst with destabilizing effects. As powerful as Nvidia has become, it could be caught in the center of such a maelstrom.

While such a concentration of power is not the way to create resilient companies, said Ryan LaSalle, CEO of cybersecurity company Nisos, like Kobeissi he thinks Nvidia will weather the storm.

Interim Nvidia CEO Collette Kress, who has been with the company since 2013, is known for having a ton of loyalty within Nvidia, he said. “In a company of that much brainpower, there will be some natural leaders who can help shepherd them to the next chapter.”

One big question put to panel participants was whether Nvidia’s board made a mistake allowing one person to have so much power.

It wasn’t just a mistake of corporate culture, said Carissa Veliz, associate professor of philosophy at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. It was also a mistake in terms of democracy.

For one person to wield so much power over decisions affecting the economy and national security means something has gone wrong and has revealed how vulnerable we are, Veliz said. If we look at the history of corporations, she said, there used to be a tradition of proving to the government that you were doing good for your country to earn your right to exist and get certain tax breaks.

“At the moment, we have shifted from that kind of framework to a framework in which a corporation is allowed to be essentially a kind of psychopath that only cares about its own profits, that only has duties to shareholders and which can be structured in any way, including a very powerful CEO with very little oversight,” she said.

Gil Duran, author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, said that he thought Nvidia’s errors in the lead-up to this moment would be studied in business and public relations crisis management classes.

“The board was completely missing out on most of the truth and the facts,” he said, referencing news reports that said Huang a year ago hired a law firm known for covering up sex scandals and President Donald Trump in May had been told about the CEO’s affair with the alleged Chinese spy.

“I don’t think there’s any other way to look at it but a catastrophe,” he said.

Duran and Veliz agreed that it was time to ensure tech CEOs face real oversight.

“These guys face no accountability and no supervision, and that’s part of the problem,” said Veliz. “These kind of small kings have their own small kingdoms… and they get away with almost anything.”

CEOs like Elon Musk at SpaceX and Sam Altman at OpenAI have enormous influence not only in their own companies but also across the national economy.

What we’re seeing in Huang’s downfall is the shattering of a myth about genius founders, said Duran. He questioned whether it would spark actual change, however, given that the market’s addiction to the narrative of great, powerful founders.

“The fact that they can just tumble markets with their personal lives that become geopolitical crises – this is an insane amount of power to outsource,” he said.

If we can tone down the myth, this moment provides a chance to look at where we’ve gone wrong and do better, Veliz said. There’s opportunity here, she added – to raise up companies that can build the kinds of technology we need, support democracies rather than erode them, aren’t based on surveillance and prediction, and can behave transparently.

For every other tech behemoth out there, there is plenty to be learned from Huang’s downfall. The concentration of power in one individual is not, as LaSalle pointed out, a safe long-term strategy.

What’s needed is more oversight and accountability from a company’s board of directors. In announcing Huang’s resignation, Nvidia also said it was appointing its first chairman for its board.

Huang’s entanglement with a potential honeypot is also an opportunity for tech companies to think about security, said LaSalle. No matter how sophisticated cybersecurity threats are becoming in the age of AI, he added, “people are still the simplest way in.”

Duran warned about the potential damage ahead if we fail to seize this as a moment to change. “If you look at the AI CEO vision of the future, it’s massive economic destruction so that a handful of people can become trillionaires,” he said. “No one voted for that. Nobody wants that, and we have a short window of time to collapse it before they collapse us.”

Disclosure: Katie Collins traveled to Lisbon as a guest of Web Summit to serve as a panel moderator. Her reporting from the event was independent of that role.

#3105. What Is T-Mix? Navigating T-Mobile’s All-New Phone Plans and Perk Scheme

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With a new system of "Picks," T-Mobile lets customers mix and match mobile add-ons.

T-Mobile is remixing its unlimited phone plans and introducing a structure where customers choose which services, like streaming video subscriptions or phone financing, apply to their accounts. Called T-Mix, the lineup is available now and includes four core plans that include “Picks” that can be mixed and matched every 90 days.

“T-Mobile and [other carriers] have really built a ‘good/better/best’ world” where customers choose prepackaged plans, Allan Samson, T-Mobile chief marketing officer, said during a call with CNET. “We’re going to blow that whole thing up, and you get to individually curate every experience you want.”

Much like with Verizon’s current plans, T-Mobile’s new offerings let customers pick and choose the perks they want rather than reserving some perks for certain plan tiers, as it had with its former Experience plan options. If you wanted a perk such as Hulu streaming, you had to pay up for the pricier Experience Beyond 2.0 plan. Conversely, even if you picked the Beyond plan for another reason, like unlimited mobile hotspot data, you still got Hulu whether you watched it or not.

Each of the new T-Mix plans includes a core set of high-speed data, hotspot data, video streaming speeds and international options. On top of that – and the feature that gives T-Mix its name – is a selection of Picks, which work like a type of currency to choose perks like streaming services, game passes, and services like DoorDash or T-Satellite. Picks can also go toward financing a new phone.

T-Mix replaces the existing Experience 2.0 plans for new customers, though existing customers can stay on their plans.

Despite the modular nature of Picks, T-Mobile is still sticking with its one-plan-fits-all policy for accounts with multiple lines. Unlike Verizon and AT&T, where each family member can have their own plan, everyone needs to agree on which T-Mix base to start from: Standard, More, Loaded and T-Mix Saver. The number of Picks you get depends on the plan and the number of lines on the account.

The Standard plan includes 50GB of high-speed 5G data, unlimited hotspot data at 3G speeds, unlimited international data while traveling in Canada and Mexico at 2G speeds, unlimited texting in more than 215 countries and up to 480p (SD) streaming resolution. A single line includes one Pick.

The More plan includes unlimited high-speed data, up to 60GB of high-speed hotspot data (which drops down to an unlimited amount at 3G speeds), 15GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico (then unlimited at 256Kbps), up to 5GB of high-speed data when traveling internationally (then unlimited at 256Kbps) and up to 4K (UHD) streaming resolution. A single line on More includes two picks.

The Loaded plan also includes unlimited high-speed data, up to 250GB of hotspot data (then unlimited at 3G speeds), 30GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico (then unlimited at 256Kbps), up to 15GB high-speed data when traveling (and down to 256Kbps unlimited after reaching that cap) and up to 4K (UHD) streaming resolution. On the Loaded plan, you can also connect a cellular-enabled device, such as a smartwatch or tablet, for $5 an item. A single line includes three Picks.

For those who want just basic phone service, the T-Mix Saver plan includes the same features as the Standard plan, but does not include Picks and is limited to two lines.

All plans include unlimited texting when traveling in more than 215 countries, long-distance calling at $0.50 a minute and T-Mobile’s Basic Scam Shield service.

For each plan, you can choose to finance a new phone using T-Mobile’s Standard 36-month term or the recently introduced Flex 36-month commitment that rolls in all of the upfront costs.

Pricing (with AutoPay and not including taxes and fees) for the Standard plan starts at $55 for a single line, jumps to $85 for two lines (or $42.50 a line) and then increases to $100 for three lines (or $33.33 a line). Additional lines cost $15 more apiece.

The More plan starts at $75 for one line, then goes to $130 for two lines and $155 for three lines. Additional lines add $25 each to the monthly cost.

The Loaded plan is $95 for a single line, $160 for two lines and $200 for three lines. Adding more Loaded lines costs $40 each.

The Saver plan costs $45 for a single line and $80 for two lines (the maximum number allowed). T-Mobile is currently running a promotion that brings those prices down to $30 and $65 if you switch from another provider and bring along your phone number.

An account on the first three plans can have up to 12 lines.

One advantage of T-Mobile’s now-old Experience plans was the simplicity of knowing that if you moved up to a higher tier such as Experience Beyond, you’d get a specific set of additional perks.

Picks gives you the flexibility to only activate perks you’ll actually use, but working out which to opt for is a bit complex. With Picks, there are two components at play: How many Picks you get on your account, and when you can change them. It sounds low-key chaotic on the surface, but it will start to make more sense, I promise.

T-Mobile assigns a Pick value to the perks it’s offering. For example, one Pick could get you Netflix Standard with ads or the DashPass service by DoorDash. If you want an Apple Music Individual or Google AI Pro subscription, that would use two Picks.

Higher-tier offerings such as Netflix Standard and Xbox Game Pass Ultimate are three Picks each, while Netflix Premium and ESPN Unlimited are four Picks.

Those are all services offered by T-Mobile partners, and can change over time (more on this in a moment).

T-Mobile also has its own Picks services. T-Satellite can be activated with one Pick, and so can the company’s new Optimized Video Calling service, which gives video calls a higher data priority for better quality.

If you’re looking to buy a new phone, you could get one for between one and three Picks depending on the device — in other words, you can forgo fancy add-on perks to get discounts on a new handset. Phone picks automatically inherit the Flex 36-month financing term.

To give Picks a real-world analogy, picture a restaurant buffet. You’re given a plate that’s sized based on how many Picks are available to your account. A Standard plan with one line would have the smallest plate (one Pick), while a Loaded plan with four lines would have a much larger plate (11 Picks).

The Picks on an account can be pooled depending on the group’s needs. A family of four on the Loaded plan, for example, might decide to get Netflix Premium to watch movies without ads (4 Picks), DashPass to save money on food deliveries (1 Pick), Xbox Game Pass Premium (2 Picks) and Pandora Plus (1 Pick) for entertainment and then a new phone for Mom (3 Picks).

The number of Picks you get depends on the plan and how many lines it includes. Not using a Pick doesn’t lower the plan price, and you’re not able to pay more for extra Picks (like adding a Verizon perk, for example) aside from moving to a more expensive plan.

Also, Picks are separate from the company’s perks such as T-Mobile Tuesdays promotions, discounts on hotels and rental cars, Delta premium in-flight drinks and MLB TV.

The next Picks component is timing. Every 90 calendar days, you can switch your Picks. Did you burn through all the shows you wanted to watch on Hulu? At the next Picks window, you can switch it for another option, or dump some 1- and 2-value Picks and pool them to get a new phone.

If you’re in the middle of the schedule and want to pick up Netflix to see what everyone is talking about in season four of The Diplomat, you can do that by canceling an existing Pick service and adding the streaming service for a fee, which Samson said would be in the $10 to $15 range. Or, at any time you can move up to a plan with more Picks (such as from More to Loaded).

The exceptions to that timing are T-Mobile’s Picks; you could turn on T-Satellite if you know you’re going remote backpacking, as long as a Pick is available in your plan.

#3104. History Says This Investing Strategy Has Never Failed After a Midterm Election

The midterm elections are over. Starting in January, Democrats will take control of Congress from the Republicans. As usual, political change creates a backdrop for heightened stock market volatility. And this year was no different.

The biggest question mark is what impact, if any, the new political regime will have on the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. Investors generally believe that the entire industry will be under more scrutiny. Moreover, data center construction could slow, a development that the hyperscalers, which are spending huge sums of capital, depend on so heavily.

Uncertainty is the key theme. And investors are trying to figure out how to best position their portfolios. History shows there's an investment strategy that has never failed after a midterm election.

Elections naturally get all of the attention. And media outlets never hesitate to draw connections between the political arena and your financial situation. This can drive a sense of urgency. You may feel like you need to take deliberate action immediately. That's not the right thing to do.

This might come off as the most boring piece of advice ever. But the best move that investors can make is absolutely none. A smart investing strategy is to avoid making portfolio moves strictly based on election outcomes.

History proves that this is the optimal course of action from a purely financial standpoint. Since 1980, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.35%) produced a positive total return over the 12 months right after a midterm election 100% of the time, with an average gain of 13.7%. It's impossible to argue with this track record. It doesn't matter whether Congress is blue or red.

You might start to think that this time will be different. After all, valuations are high. There's geopolitical tension. Inflationary pressure is persisting. And the AI boom, which is sucking up so much capital, is sparking fears of a bubble.

To be clear, there are always reasons to worry. Seasoned market participants know that this is true. Uncertainty is nothing new. In fact, it's par for the course.

History shows that staying invested in the stock market is the winning strategy. Over the long term, it pays off. On the other hand, panicking and backing out will prove to be a costly mistake.

Investors are to do nothing after a midterm election. This leads to the next point: Investors' specific portfolio management strategies don't need to be altered. Everything should generally be viewed as noise, no matter how many headlines a particular topic grabs.

The recipe for long-term success in the stock market is still the same. It depends on identifying high-quality businesses that come with wide economic moats. These companies sell differentiated products and services. They have durable growth potential. From a financial perspective, they operate with solid balance sheets and generate consistent profits.

This is a good list of characteristics investors should look for. Once you've narrowed down a group of businesses, valuation comes into focus. It's not ideal to buy stocks when they're expensive. All else equal, purchasing shares at a margin of safety is optimal.

If picking stocks isn't on your radar, then consider buying an S&P 500 tracker, like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.34%). At an extremely low expense ratio of 0.03%, this exchange-traded fund (ETF) offers instant exposure to the biggest businesses powering the U.S. economy. You'll own about 80% of the entire country's stock market capitalization in a hassle-free manner that requires no active portfolio management.

The midterm elections are over. While your investing playbook won't change, events like these should reset your perspective, which can be an invaluable exercise.

#3103. Fastly vs. UiPath: Which Artificial Intelligence Stock Is a Better Buy Going into 2027?

Fastly grew revenue 14.8% but still lost money, while UiPath swung to a $282 million profit and trades at a lower forward P/E.

Modern digital experiences require speed and intelligent automation to remain competitive. If you are choosing between Fastly (FSLY -0.41%) and UiPath (PATH -0.30%), you are weighing two distinct ways to bet on software infrastructure.

Fastly focuses on moving data closer to the user to reduce lag for websites and apps while managing the massive growth in artificial intelligence bot traffic. UiPath uses artificial intelligence to automate repetitive office tasks across entire organizations. While both are high-growth businesses among tech stocks, they operate in very different corners of the technology landscape.

Fastly operates an edge cloud platform that serves as a vital component for high-traffic websites. The company moves processing power closer to the end user to improve speed and security for global brands. Key customers include TikTok, though relying on a few major accounts adds a layer of risk to the business. Fastly also maintains strategic partnerships with providers like Comcast (CMCSA -0.88%) to expand its reach.

According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached $624.0 million. This represents a growth rate of 14.8% compared with the prior year. While the business is not yet profitable, it reported a net loss of $121.7 million, which is an improvement over the previous year.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.5x. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity to show how much a company relies on borrowed money. The current ratio, which divides current assets by current liabilities, is 2.6x. Free cash flow reached $65.8 million, representing the cash remaining after the company pays for its operations and capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 124.2% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

UiPath provides a business orchestration and automation platform that coordinates artificial intelligence agents and human workers for complex workflows. The company focuses on enterprise-scale use cases, helping large organizations manage repetitive tasks across their systems. Its customer base has grown to include over 10,000 clients, with a strong emphasis on those contributing $100,000 or more in recurring revenue. UiPath has also expanded its capabilities through strategic partnerships with data leaders like Snowflake (SNOW -0.84%).

According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached $1.6 billion. This indicates a year-over-year growth rate of 12.7%. The company achieved a net income of $282.3 million for the period, marking a significant transition into profitability compared with the net loss reported in the prior fiscal year.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was zero, indicating a very low reliance on borrowed funds. The current ratio is 2.5x. Free cash flow for the period was $352.2 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 78.3% of operating cash flow.

Fastly faces operational risks, including the potential for platform outages and performance degradation that could drive customers away. The company also deals with significant revenue concentration, as its top ten accounts comprise roughly 32% of its total revenue. Intense competition from public cloud giants like Amazon (AMZN +0.48%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.36%) also pressures its market share and pricing power.

UiPath is heavily dependent on its top 10% of customers, making its results sensitive to their specific purchasing patterns. The market for automation is highly competitive, with pressure coming from established platform vendors like Microsoft and Salesforce (CRM -0.20%). Furthermore, the rapid development of agentic AI creates execution risks as the company must constantly evolve its technology to avoid being replaced by newer alternatives.

While Fastly trades at a lower P/S ratio, UiPath appears more attractively priced based on its Forward P/E and established profitability. The P/S ratio measures company value relative to sales over the past twelve months, while the Forward P/E compares the share price to future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Fastly and UiPath are a pair of mid-cap tech players trying to prove their relevance in an AI-heavy landscape. Between them, I would invest in Fastly.

Fastly is an underappreciated AI stock. Its focus on managing website traffic does not make it an obvious player in the artificial intelligence space. However, AI bots have scaled up tremendously in recent years, as they crawl the internet scraping content off websites.

This has made Fastly's solutions critical to ensuring human traffic is prioritized, so users can quickly reach online destinations. As a result, its business is growing. In the third quarter, the company achieved record revenue of $190.2 million, representing 20% year-over-year growth.

Although UiPath is profitable, and its stock sports a better valuation, its business depends on its artificial intelligence bots helping organizations automate complex enterprise workflows. However, its core mechanics could become obsolete if it cannot stay ahead of newer autonomous agentic AI systems that its customers could switch to, potentially making UiPath's offerings obsolete.

This may already be the case. UiPath's fiscal Q2 revenue of $410.3 million was a 13% year-over-year increase compared to 17% growth in Q1. For fiscal Q3, the company forecasted sales of at least $440 million, which is about a 7% increase over 2025's $411 million, suggesting its sales are slowing down.

#3102. Is Nvidia Undervalued?

Nvidia stock is down 30% from its all-time high.

It's been a brutal few weeks for Nvidia (NVDA -4.34%) investors. After reaching an all-time high of roughly $243 per share in early October, the artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker has experienced an epic sell-off.

On Nov. 12, Nvidia stock crashed as low as $148.80 following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang. Huang's departure follows revelations concerning two extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's board of directors has been investigating the allegations, which have not established that Huang compromised company secrets.

Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress is now serving as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent replacement. The uncertainty has rattled investors. However, the resulting sell-off has created an interesting valuation opportunity.

Nvidia stock is trading at one of its cheapest valuations in more than a decade. Here's why I think the recent decline could represent a compelling buy-the-dip opportunity.

One useful valuation metric for evaluating a growth stock is the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. This tool compares a company's current share price with analysts' expectations for its earnings over the next 12 months. Simply put, a lower ratio means investors are paying less for each dollar of anticipated profits.

As of this writing (Nov. 12), Nvidia's forward P/E hovers around 11, according to data from Yahoo! Finance. This is the lowest reading dating back to May 2016, according to data compiled by TradingView.

For perspective, Nvidia traded near 90 times forward earnings in late 2021. Nvidia has become a much larger and more profitable business since then, and yet investors are now assigning it a fraction of its former earnings multiple.

Of course, a lower multiple does not necessarily mean a stock is undervalued. If Nvidia's future earnings disappoint, today's seemingly attractive valuation could prove misleading. Nevertheless, the historical comparison suggests investors are pricing in considerable uncertainty about the company's future.

Despite Nvidia's cratering stock price, its latest financial results show little evidence of deteriorating demand. During its fiscal second quarter of 2027, Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, representing a 106% increase year over year. The data center business contributed $89 billion, growing 117% annually. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share surged 120% to $2.22.

These results reflect the enormous spending on AI infrastructure from Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Oracle, Anthropic, and OpenAI. Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs are central to many hyperscale projects, while its new Vera Rubin architecture is entering production. The company is also expanding into Vera CPUs, high-speed networking equipment, and specialized AI inference accelerators.

Importantly, Nvidia expects its momentum to continue. Management's guidance for the fiscal third quarter calls for $108 billion in revenue, plus or minus 2%. That would represent roughly 89% growth compared with the same quarter last year.

Nvidia is scheduled to report those results on Nov. 17. If the company delivers another strong quarter and maintains an encouraging outlook, investors may begin reassessing whether its valuation profile accurately reflects its growth trajectory.

There's an important distinction between an undervalued stock and a risk-free investment. Huang was instrumental in developing Nvidia's technology roadmap, forging customer relationships, and building its competitive advantages.

Competitors such as Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom are working to capture more AI infrastructure spending. Furthermore, many of Nvidia's largest customers are developing custom silicon, potentially reducing their dependence on the company's GPUs over time.

Nevertheless, Nvidia's moat isn't going to crack just because of a leadership transition. The company's CUDA software ecosystem, advanced chip designs, networking technology, and customer relationships help form strong barriers to competition.

At roughly 11 times forward earnings, I think Nvidia's recent decline has created a unique opportunity for long-term investors. To me, Nvidia offers an unusually compelling combination of growth and valuation.

While Nvidia stock will almost certainly experience additional volatility as investors assess the company's next CEO, investors willing to tolerate that uncertainty by investing in Nvidia at a substantial discount to its historical valuation could witness lucrative gains as AI infrastructure build-outs continue accelerating.

#3101. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for steady income

The ongoing earnings season, investor concerns about the durability of AI demand and spending, and geopolitical risks are key factors that have been contributing to stock market volatility in recent trading sessions.

In this scenario, investors seeking steady income can consider adding dividend stocks to their portfolios. Recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help them pick attractive dividend stocks that are backed by solid cash flows to support consistent payments.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Oil and gas exploration and production company ConocoPhillips is this week's first dividend pick. With a dividend of 84 cents per share (annualized dividend of $3.36 per share), COP offers a dividend yield of 3%. The company is scheduled to announce its second-quarter results on Aug. 6.

Ahead of second-quarter results, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin reiterated a buy rating on COP stock with a price target of $183. Despite the pressure on oil prices from an increase in OPEC production quota, the analyst finds ConocoPhillips and Shell stocks appealing as the earnings season approaches. He cited their operational visibility and resilience as factors backing their appeal.

The 5-star analyst expects ConocoPhillips to meet its production guidance of 2.2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day at the mid-point. He expects lower Waha natural gas prices in the Permian Basin to be offset by stronger Brent crude premiums. Margolin expects capital expenditure to remain within COP's prior guided range of $12.2 billion annualized, with no significant impact on spending on the Northfield East project in Qatar despite the Strait of Hormuz disruption.

Overall, Margolin expects COP to generate about $3.5 billion in free cash flow (before working capital) and earnings per share of $2.94. He expects continued strength in COP's free cash flow and regular dividend growth through the completion of the Willow project in 2028/2029. Prior to the Willow project coming online, the analyst expects free cash flow to grow by about $2 billion in 2027 and 2028, assuming Brent crude averages around $60 per barrel.

"COP's track record of capital efficiency and strong Permian well productivity underpins its ability to pursue long-cycle developments," said Margolin.

Margolin ranks No. 457 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 70% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.3%. See ConocoPhillips Financials on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer is a limited partnership that operates 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. With a quarterly cash distribution of 33.75 cents per common unit ($1.35 per unit on an annualized basis), ET offers a yield of 6.8%.

Heading into Energy Transfer's Q2 earnings on Aug. 4, Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith reaffirmed a buy rating on ET stock with a price target of $23. The analyst noted that his adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization estimate of $4.46 billion is 1% below the Street's consensus of $4.49 billion.

The 5-star analyst noted that Energy Transfer has slightly outperformed Enterprise Products Partners recently. However, it still trades at a relative discount of 19% compared to EPD, which is below its historical discount range of 17%-20%. Smith believes that ET stock could be re-rated higher if the company provides a clearer long-term strategy for natural gas growth.

Furthermore, Smith expects the current energy market to support a stronger outlook for natural gas liquids and crude oil. "The current energy macro backdrop positions ET to benefit in all three commodities," said the analyst.

He expects Energy Transfer's adjusted EBITDA to grow at a 4.8% compound annual growth rate in 2027-2030, which is 1%-3% above Wall Street's expectations. In fact, Smith sees the possibility of additional upside if ET announces more natural gas projects. He added that investors will await details on final investment decisions on new natural gas projects and any clues about additional projects in the pipeline. The analyst noted that ET has announced new gas projects consistently in recent quarters.

Smith ranks No. 550 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.4%. See Energy Transfer Statistics on TipRanks.

Finally, let's look at energy giant Chevron, which is scheduled to announce its second-quarter results on July 31. Last month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12, CVX offers a dividend yield of 3.92%.

Ahead of Q2 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on Chevron stock and lowered his price target to $216 from $236. Byrne expects the company to report adjusted EPS of about $5.86 per share, nearly 9% above the Street's expectations.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the challenges seen in Chevron's upstream business in the first quarter due to the disruption at the Tengizchevroil joint venture in Kazakhstan, Storm Fern downtime, and the Middle East conflict have largely been resolved. Consequently, Byrne expects production to recover in the second quarter to about 4,033 mboepd. He expects the upstream business to generate adjusted earnings of about $8.1 billion in Q2 2026.

Meanwhile, Byrne expects Chevron to generate downstream adjusted earnings of about $4.4 billion in Q2, with strength in both domestic and international markets. The downstream business benefited from higher crack spreads and strong refining performance.

Additionally, the analyst expects Chevron to generate $18.2 billion in cash flow from operations (before working capital changes), driven by stronger earnings and about $2.2 billion in dividends from affiliated companies. Unlike the first quarter, Chevron is not expected to make a TCO loan repayment in Q2, providing an additional boost to cash flow.

#3099. 3 Warren Buffett Stocks Just Closed at Record Highs. Here's the One I'd Still Buy Now.

Three stocks linked to the Oracle of Omaha hit records on the same day. Which one still deserves fresh money?

On Wednesday, Nov. 11, three stocks closely tied to Warren Buffett set records on the same day. Apple (AAPL -0.14%) closed at $355.63, Coca-Cola (KO -0.13%) at $97.57 and the Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.09%)(BRKB +0.27%) at $588.24.

Berkshire is the link. In its latest 13F filing, covering the end of June, Apple was its largest stock holding, and Coca-Cola its fourth-largest. Both stakes were built during Buffett's decades running the company, and he remains a director after becoming chairman emeritus in September.

Of the three, Berkshire is the one I'd still buy at its record. It's the cheapest against what it earns, and every Berkshire share comes with a piece of the other two.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

Apple stock is up around 31% this year, and Wednesday's close was its 28th record in 2026. The iPhone maker's fiscal 2026 (the year ended Sept. 26) was strong, with earnings per share up 20% to $8.98.

But growth cooled as the year ended. Apple's revenue rose 12% year over year in fiscal Q4, down from 16% in fiscal Q3 and 17% in fiscal Q2. Earnings per share climbed 14% in fiscal Q4, after a 29% jump in fiscal Q3. And the latest number included a $0.05 boost from tariff refunds, so the underlying rise was closer to 11%.

At Wednesday's close, Apple traded at around 40 times its fiscal 2026 earnings and about 38 times analysts' consensus earnings estimate for fiscal 2027. I'd say that's a hefty price for a business whose profit growth just slowed to the low double digits.

Berkshire cut its Apple holding by around 19% in the second half of 2025, to about 228 million shares, and still owned that many at the end of June. These shares would be worth about $81 billion at Wednesday's price.

I'd hold on to Apple. But at around 40 times earnings, it isn't the one I'd add to at a record.

Coca-Cola's close on Wednesday was its 29th record this year, and the stock is up around 40% in 2026.

Coca-Cola's comparable earnings per share (its non-GAAP, or adjusted, profit measure) gained 11% in the third quarter. Management now guides for at least 11% growth this year, which would raise adjusted earnings from $3.00 per share in 2025 to at least $3.33. Sure, around 3 points of that growth come from currency.

At $97.57, though, the stock costs around 29 times the earnings Coca-Cola expects for 2026. That might be too high for a beverage business benefiting from exchange rates. I'd be more interested in a price near $80, or about 24 times 2026 earnings.

Berkshire completed its purchase of 400 million Coca-Cola shares in 1994 and still owned them all at the end of June. The holding would be worth around $39 billion at Wednesday's close.

"When you find a truly wonderful business, stick with it," Buffett wrote to Berkshire shareholders in early 2024, using Coca-Cola and American Express as his examples.

Berkshire's Class B shares are up around 17% this year, well behind Apple and Coca-Cola. Wednesday's close was just its eighth record in 2026, and the stock didn't hit one between May 2025 and Oct. 20.

The stock costs less against its earnings, too. Berkshire's operating earnings (which strip out changes in the value of its stock portfolio) were around $47.2 billion during its last four quarters. That works out to around 27 times operating earnings, and about 1.6 times its Sept. 30 book value (assets minus liabilities).

Yes, third-quarter operating earnings slid around 6% year over year, as insurance underwriting earnings shrank about 43%. But even with that drop, the stock asks less of a buyer than either of the other two.

And Berkshire shareholders own the other two indirectly. Using the June 30 share counts, the Apple and Coca-Cola stakes combined would be worth around $120 billion at Wednesday's prices, or almost 10% of Berkshire's market value.

In the end, these are three great businesses, and I don't see any of the records as a reason to sell.

Apple's growth would probably have to pick up again to justify a multiple of around 40 times earnings, and Coca-Cola is still far above the $80 or so I'd like to pay. Berkshire has the lowest price of the three.

So, Berkshire is the one I'd buy today, but I'd likely add shares gradually. As recently as Sept. 30, the stock traded slightly below its 2025 closing price, and it's climbed about 18% since.

#3098. High Agency Matters More

Erdem Erkul, Founder and Chairman of Cerebrum Tech.

Today’s challenge isn’t accessing information, but taking ownership and acting on it. AI can complete tasks, but humans still need to direct and oversee these systems and, ultimately, take responsibility for the results. That’s where agency comes in.​

“High agency” is a popular term in tech. But what does it actually mean? The word “agent” comes from the Latin “agere,” which means “to do.” In other words, human beings who act have agency.

According to George Mack, it is a skill that can be learned from small practices. People with high agency may start with a small step, but they do something. They don’t just wait. They take responsibility. They think clearly, are ready to act and do not give up at the first “no.”

In the digital era, high agency matters even more. Why? Because AI agents are becoming increasingly common. These agents can take actions and finish tasks. Sometimes they work with people, sometimes they ask questions before they finish a task and sometimes they work alone. Is taking initiative more important than intelligence now?

According to AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, agency is more powerful than intelligence. It is also harder to find. High-agency people are the “I’ll figure it out” type. They keep going when problems arise. They verify results, exercise judgment and take ownership of outcomes. While AI can do the work, much of the responsibility for decision-making still belongs to humans.​

AI helps us do more work in less time. But is more work always better? A recent MIT study looked at this question by carrying out an experiment with more than 2,200 people who were asked to create several online ads. Some people worked with other people, while others worked using AI. The people who used AI made 50% more ads, and their ad scripts were also better. But the people who worked together created better pictures. Those who used AI altered their texts less, and their ads looked more alike.

AI can help us work faster, but we must not rely on it too heavily. To create truly unique results, we should start with our own ideas and use AI as a source of inspiration. AI can do a lot, but people must retain ownership of important decisions and take responsibility for the outcomes.

AI tools are becoming more powerful, making human contribution increasingly important. While these tools can help us get the work done, responsibility for the outcomes remains with us.

I’ve found that this is one of the most important qualities that drives progress. During times when resources are limited and uncertainty is high, taking responsibility, bringing the right people together and taking that first concrete step can make a world of difference.

When I encounter a problem, the question I ask myself is: “How can I solve this problem as soon as possible?”

Sometimes it’s a phone call, sometimes research, sometimes a small experiment and sometimes simply saying, “I don’t know this, and I need to learn it,” which marks the beginning of the solution. Then comes following up, getting feedback and adjusting the approach when necessary.

This is also why human skills are so essential. Leaders need to ask good questions, listen to different views and help people work together. AI can give us many answers, but it cannot decide what is best for every company or every person. Leaders must understand the needs of their teams, see problems early and make clear choices. They must also create an environment where people feel free to ask questions and share new ideas. This way, AI can support coming up with better solutions, while people keep the power to lead and take responsibility for the results.

This is why I do not see better AI tools as the real advantage. Every company can buy the same tools. The real advantage lies in the people who use these tools, recognize problems, take ownership and turn what is possible into measurable results.

This raises a question for every board and CEO: As AI gets better at execution, what should leaders get better at? I believe the answer has three parts. First, leaders must focus on the right problems. Investing in technology is not enough. Second, they must question how reliable AI outputs are, especially when the stakes are high. Third, they must protect accountability. A decision made with AI is still a human decision, and someone must answer for it.

Below are four simple steps to develop a higher level of agency. They are most useful when resources are limited and the future is not clear.

1. Define the problem. Ask yourself: “What can I do here?” Even in a hard situation, there is usually one thing you can control.

2. Take the first step. Do not wait for perfect conditions. It can be a phone call, an internet search or a small test. Choose a step that is small and easy.

3. Follow ideas. Many good ideas die after the first meeting, so follow up. Check the results, ask for feedback and change your method if it does not work.

4. Own the results. Good or bad, the result is part of your work. Take responsibility for both success and failure, and learn from the results.

As AI agents get better at doing tasks, human agency will matter even more. Our value will not be in doing every task ourselves; it will be in knowing what matters, making the hard calls and standing behind the results. AI gives us more power. High agency decides how we use it.

#3097. If an AI Bubble Triggers a Bear Market, History Says This Is the Best Move Investors Can Make

Don't assume your portfolio is diversified.

Several major AI stocks have now entered correction territory. Nvidia shares, for example, are down more than 25% over the past month, shedding more than $1 trillion in market value.

A bear market, however, has hardly arrived. Many AI stocks have continued to gain value during the rout, including BigBear.ai, Amazon, and C3.ai.

From a demand perspective, there's very little to worry about regarding the long-term promise of artificial intelligence.

"AI demand remains strong," stresses new research from Barclays. "What the market is questioning is funding, as hyperscalers keep lifting capex while free cash flow evaporates."

The issue, therefore, is a matter of logistics and timing, not a matter of demand prospects. "AI fundamentals remain very strong in absolute terms," Barclays' research affirms.

Still, the potential impact of a bear market in the AI sector is difficult to ignore. After all, overly optimistic valuations may shrink even as demand remains strong. It won't be difficult for a downturn in AI stocks to impact the rest of the market. Nearly half of the S&P 500's value is now tied to AI companies, whether that is AI developers themselves or suppliers to the industry.

How should investors respond to the popping of the AI bubble? The history of the dot-com crash offers clear advice.

From a market-value perspective, technology companies suffered significantly during the dot-com bubble. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.39%) fell nearly 80% over a 31-month bear market.

But here's the thing: Internet adoption continued to grow unabated. According to data from the U.S. Federal Reserve, 36% of Americans were active internet users in 1999. In 2000, that figure grew to 43%, reaching 49% by 2001. By 2002, nearly 60% of all Americans were regular internet users.

So while market valuations plummeted, the actual underlying technology -- the internet -- continued to experience sustained success. Nearly every business on Earth, not just technology companies, ultimately benefited from the internet's rise. So, to truly bet on the internet, it wasn't necessary to buy only dot-com companies. In fact, in the long term, the wisest decision may have been the simplest: maintain exposure to broad market indexes, ensuring your portfolio will benefit no matter how the internet's success is distributed.

The same should prove true for the current AI craze. AI companies are soaring in valuation, accounting for massive chunks of broader market indexes. But it's still far too early to know who the ultimate winners will be. Will it be GPU producers selling to AI software developers, or will it be the end users of that software development? As the dot-com bubble proved, predicting the future of a game-changing technology is more difficult than many suppose.

What's the main takeaway? There are two potential paths.

First, don't overthink the current environment. Throughout history, there has never been a bad time to buy an index fund tracking the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.35%). Bought in at the height of the dot-com bubble, then doubled down just before the financial crisis hit? No problem. If you maintained a long enough time horizon, your portfolio would still be in the black.

The second takeaway is to understand just how exposed you are to an AI bear market. Historically, owning a diversified index fund exposed you to a wide variety of industries. But due to rapidly rising valuations in the AI sector, nearly half of the components in many popular indexes are businesses tied to the AI economy. If that segment of the market struggles, it could disproportionately impact your entire portfolio.

If you're concerned about AI valuations, you don't necessarily have to sell your existing positions for something else. But it may be wise to look at small-cap or international index funds, as these segments of the market are far less dominated by U.S. mega-cap AI companies. Many international and small-cap funds also trade at lower valuations, given their relatively lower exposure to pricey AI stocks.

#3093. FirstEnergy: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

The utility is allocating infrastructure costs to data center operators, protecting existing customers from financial strain as grid expansion accelerates.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, FirstEnergy (FE -0.06%) announced that contracted and pipelined data center power demand jumped nearly 60% since year-end. Heavy power users are knocking on the door, giving the electric utility a long runway to build regulated poles and wires. When grid expansion accelerates, investors get durable growth in rate base, which represents the total value of property on which the utility earns an approved financial return.

Three takeaways from the call explain how this demand shapes the business.

Data centers need massive amounts of reliable electricity, and tech companies are securing grid capacity years in advance. West Virginia pipeline demand expanded sixfold to nearly 6 gigawatts, which represents 6 billion watts of electrical power capacity.

To handle exploding load requirements, the utility must expand its physical infrastructure. PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission organization operating the power grid across parts of 13 states, requires major capital upgrades to keep power flowing safely.

Building power infrastructure for massive commercial customers creates capital risk if projects stall or demand shifts. Management is structuring contracts so large power users cover project costs rather than shifting financial risks onto home energy customers.

Electricity demand across the service territory is accelerating past multiyear baselines, and capital execution is delivering target earnings. Management is watching regulatory decisions, pricing discipline, and project timing in key states.

The utility holds a strategic position at the geographic center of the regional power grid, creating a structural advantage as power demand expands. Disciplined risk allocation ensures new projects build shareholder value without overextending the balance sheet.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This morning the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) dropped the October Consumer Price Index, which shows that inflation rose another 0.4% last month. This outpaced expectations: Economists had forecasted an increase of 0.3%. Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, and futures traders are banking on a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Central bankers raised the federal funds rate in September, but it hasn’t been enough to pull inflation closer to the Fed’s target of 2%. Investors aren’t sure that one more hike in December will do the trick, either. According to CME FedWatch, further rate hikes may be in store for January.

#3088. Better U.S. Bank ETF: State Street's KBE vs. First Trust's FTXO

KBE carries a lower fee and higher yield, yet FTXO's concentrated 50-stock portfolio tells a different story about risk and reward.

The State Street SPDR S&P Bank ETF (KBE -0.68%) offers a more diversified, lower-cost entry into the banking sector compared to the concentrated and higher-fee First Trust Nasdaq Bank ETF (FTXO -0.43%).

Both ETFs target the U.S. financial landscape, yet they take different structural paths for investors seeking exposure to domestic banks. While FTXO focuses on "smart" indexing with fewer positions selected by factor criteria, KBE provides broader exposure across the industry, including regional players and diversified financial services.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-year return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

Investors may find the State Street fund more affordable, as its 0.35% expense ratio is lower than the 0.6% charged by the First Trust fund. Additionally, State Street SPDR S&P Bank ETF offers a higher payout for income-seeking portfolios.

The State Street SPDR S&P Bank ETF focuses 100% on financial services, providing exposure to large, mid, and small-cap companies across the banking landscape. Its largest positions include Central Bancompany (CBC -0.73%) at 1.14%, Customers Bancorp (CUBI -0.06%) at 1.03%, and First Citizens BancShares (FCNCA +0.10%) at 1.03%. The fund uses a modified equal-weighted approach to ensure the portfolio is not overly concentrated in a few giants. It launched in 2005, and has paid $1.47 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$66.8 share price works out to a 2.2% yield.

First Trust Nasdaq Bank ETF is also 100% concentrated in financial services but maintains a tighter portfolio of 50 positions based on liquidity and fundamental factors. Its largest positions include Wells Fargo (WFC -0.05%) at 8.07%, U.S. Bancorp (USB -0.38%) at 8.02%, and JPMorgan Chase (JPM -0.17%) at 7.81%. This structure creates a more top-heavy profile compared to the State Street fund. It launched in 2016, and has paid $0.77 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$40.2 share price works out to a 1.9% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

Investors looking for exposure to the U.S. banking sector have two distinct choices in the State Street SPDR S&P Bank ETF (KBE) and the First Trust Nasdaq Bank ETF (FTXO). Choosing between them depends on whether you want to target a handful of the largest U.S. banks through FTXO or prefer KBE's broader, more regional bank-focused holdings.

Over a five-year time horizon, both funds deliver about the same return. For cost-conscious investors, however, KBE's lower expense ratio and higher dividend yield can be compelling factors.

That said, a key consideration is the current interest rate environment. Major Wall Street banks and economists increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to continue raising interest rates into early 2027.

If that happens, KBE is more likely to outperform in a controlled, moderate rate-hike cycle where overall U.S. economic growth stays steady. That's because of the fund's focus on regional banks, which rely heavily on traditional lending and deposit-taking versus the big banks' greater fee-based businesses. When rates rise, regional banks can reprice loans quickly, and expand their net interest margin.

However, if the Fed is more aggressive with rate hikes, regional banks could suffer as loan volume declines, making FXTO the fund more likely to outperform in this scenario.

#3086. Cisco (CSCO) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Hyperscaler deployments are accelerating, and management lifted its full-year outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cisco Systems, Inc. (CSCO +1.24%) reported record first-quarter performance for fiscal year 2027, highlighting what management described as the early stages of a multiyear networking supercycle driven by agentic AI. The company reported its strongest top-line and bottom-line growth rates in over 15 years, prompting an increase in full-year guidance for both revenue and earnings. Management stated that hyperscalers are actively deploying Cisco architectures across production environments to extend AI workloads. The company is also seeing accelerated demand from neocloud, sovereign, and enterprise customers for AI infrastructure, with significant growth in Nexus data center switches. Operationally, the company is driving higher efficiency, expecting revenue per employee to grow 19% as it maintains disciplined expense management while scaling for AI demand.

Operator: Welcome to Cisco's First Quarter Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results Conference Call. At the request of Cisco, today's conference is being recorded. If you have any objections, you may disconnect. Now I would like to introduce Sami Badri, Head of Investor Relations. Sir, you may begin.

Ahmed Sami Badri: Good afternoon, everyone. This is Sami Badri, Cisco's Head of Investor Relations, and I'm joined by Chuck Robbins, our Chair and CEO; and Mark Patterson, our CFO. Cisco's earnings press release and supplemental information, including GAAP to non-GAAP reconciliations are available on our Investor Relations website. Today's call is also being live streamed on YouTube, LinkedIn and X. Following this call, we will also make the recorded webcast and slides available on the website. Throughout today's call, we'll be referencing both GAAP and non-GAAP financial results. We will discuss product results in terms of revenue and geographic and customer results in terms of product orders, unless stated otherwise. All comparisons will be made on a year-on-year basis, unless stated otherwise.

Please note that our discussion today will include forward-looking statements, including our guidance for the second quarter and fiscal year 2027. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties detailed in our SEC filings, particularly our most recent 10-K report, which identify important risk factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in our forward-looking statements. With respect to guidance, please also see the slides and press release that accompany this call for further details. Cisco will not comment on its financial guidance during the quarter unless it is done through an explicit public disclosure. Now I'll turn it over to Chuck.

Charles Robbins: Thanks, Sami, and thank you all for joining us today. I'm pleased to report that Cisco delivered an impressive start to fiscal '27. We're executing against our strategy, and seeing growing demand as customers invest in the infrastructure they need for the AI or SI era. What gives me the greatest confidence is not just the results we're seeing today but also the opportunities we see ahead. In Q1, we delivered record quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24% year-over-year and record non-GAAP earnings per share of $1.40, up 40% year-over-year. These are our strongest top and bottom line growth rates in over 15 years.

We are demonstrating strong operating leverage and enhanced earnings power with earnings growing faster than revenue. As a result of this strong performance, we are significantly increasing our fiscal year '27 guidance, which Mark will cover shortly. Our profitable growth generates robust cash flows and fuels consistent capital returns to our shareholders. In Q1, we returned $3.7 billion in value through dividends and share repurchases, representing 95% of free cash flow. Our strong start to fiscal year '27 demonstrates the criticality of networking and security together as agentic AI accelerates. As customers look to manage increasing traffic costs and threats, they are turning to Cisco for our networking expertise, security and observability solutions and services.

They trust us to help scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era ahead. The depth and breadth of our portfolio enables us to support our customers however they choose to deploy AI, whether in the public cloud, through neoclouds or sovereign clouds, on-premise, or at the edge. We believe we are still early in the networking super cycle driven by AI deployments with enterprise adoption just beginning. In Q1, we saw strong demand with total product orders growing 21% year-over-year on top of 13% growth a year ago. We saw strong demand excluding hyperscalers with product orders up 14% year-over-year on top of 9% growth a year ago.

We also saw double-digit growth across all geographies and customer markets. Enterprise product orders in Q1 were up 15% year-over-year on top of 4% growth a year ago with double-digit growth across all geographies and in networking and security. Public sector orders were up 13% year-over-year on top of 12% growth a year ago. We saw double-digit public sector growth in the Americas and APJC as well as in networking, security and collaboration. Product orders from service provider and cloud customers continue to be broad-based, growing 47% year-over-year. This is on top of 44% growth a year ago with triple-digit growth in APJC and double-digit growth in the Americas and EMEA.

We continue to see healthy demand from telcos with orders up approximately 20% year-over-year in Q1 on top of 24% growth a year ago. Turning to demand across our product categories. Networking product orders grew 28% in Q1, delivering our 9th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. In fact, we saw double-digit growth across every product family, service provider routing, compute, enterprise routing, wireless, data center switching and campus switching. These broad-based results support our view that we are in the early stages of a multiyear, multibillion-dollar networking super cycle, as I referenced earlier, and we are executing with focus and urgency to capture this incremental opportunity.

Overall, our hyperscaler business continues to show strong momentum with AI infrastructure revenue projected to grow to $9 billion in fiscal year '27, more than double fiscal year '26 levels. Hyperscalers are now deploying our scale across networking architecture and production environments as they extend coordinated AI workloads across data centers. This architecture combines our Silicon One P200 deep-buffered systems, market-leading Acacia coherent optics and open line systems with multi-rail optical systems coming soon. Together, these products provide a single unified compute fabric with deep programmability and embedded security. In Q1, we secured 3 new AI design wins, 2 were for our P200 powered systems and data center interconnect and scale across use cases.

The third was for 1.6 Terabit Optics for scale-out use case. In addition to hyperscaler demand, we saw accelerated growth in AI infrastructure orders from neocloud, sovereign and enterprise customers in Q1, with Nexus data center switches tagged for AI deployments up 47% year-over-year. During the quarter, we announced a new partnership with Supermicro, which expands our Secure AI factory with NVIDIA. By integrating Supermicro's high-density, liquid and air cooled compute into an NVIDIA cloud partner-compliant full stack architecture, we're delivering more efficient end-to-end infrastructure for massive AI workloads. As agentic AI expands, security threats have become more complex and conversations around sovereignty are intensifying.

Our focus is delivering trusted sovereign solutions to help customers scale their data center build-outs with confidence. During the quarter, together with AMD and HUMAIN, we announced that AMD GPU-based AI infrastructure built on Silicon One based systems is now in production in Saudi Arabia. This enables HUMAIN to offer GPU as a service across training and inference use cases. To meet our customers' evolving needs, we also introduced our Sovereign Critical Infrastructure portfolio in Europe a year ago. This portfolio spans networking, security, compute, collaboration and observability and can be configured for on-premise, air-gapped environments. In Q1, we expanded to Canada with additional countries to follow, giving government agencies and critical infrastructure providers more control, choice, security and resilience.

Customers are also focused on modernizing their workplaces for humans and agents. We continue to see robust demand for our campus networking solutions in Q1 with 14% year-over-year growth in product orders. Our next-generation portfolio continues to ramp faster than prior product launches and we believe we are still very early in this refresh cycle. Orders for our industrial IoT portfolio grew approximately 50% year-over-year in Q1 and have now grown at double-digit rates for 10 consecutive quarters. Now shifting to security. Orders excluding Splunk were up in the mid-teens. Within our security platform, orders for firewalls grew over 30% for the third consecutive quarter.

Cisco AI Defense is helping customers guard against unmanaged AI use across the enterprise and is protecting more than 2 trillion tokens per month. Our work with Workday Agent Passport, ServiceNow and DefenseClaw with NVIDIA OpenShell demonstrates how we're expanding our ecosystem and building trust into the use of agents in daily operations. Earlier this week, we announced that we are integrating Anthropic's Claude Mythos cybersecurity model into Cisco AI Defense for adaptive AI red teaming. This provides automated, continuous testing across enterprise systems, empowering defenders to stress test AI systems with frontier adversary reasoning. Turning to Splunk. The platform is helping solve some of the most pressing challenge organizations face in the AI era.

A Splunk study found that urgency to deploy agents is outpacing enterprise's ability to monitor and secure them. With Splunk, we deliver a common data platform that enables customers to monitor and enforce guardrails on agent behavior while also helping them understand and manage tokenomics. This gives them greater confidence and predictability as they look to optimize both the business value and the cost of AI. In collaboration with a leading hyperscaler, Splunk is exploring how AI agents can help security teams investigate threats and coordinate responses more efficiently while keeping analysts in control. This builds on our strategy to strengthen secure operations as threats grow more complex. We'll have more to share later this month.

Now on to our innovation. We are focused on 4 often overlapping objectives: number one, simplifying network operations; number two, scaling infrastructure for agentic AI; number three, reimagining security and trust for agentic AI; and four, delivering intelligent workplace experiences. Last quarter, we highlighted Cisco Cloud Control as a breakthrough in simplifying operations. Since launch, more than 6,000 customers have signed up and can increase productivity by accessing multiple Cisco and partner products through a single user interface. We are building integrations within the platform, including AI Canvas, Cisco IQ and the recently launched Cisco Model Foundry.

Cisco IQ now has more than 17,000 customers, nearly doubling quarter-over-quarter and visibility into 23 million devices, accelerating vulnerability tracking from days to minutes. To scale infrastructure and improve the efficiency of AI factories, we recently announced plans with NVIDIA to develop the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable or USFP optical module. We expect USFP to deliver 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of current models. We also plan to create an open industry USFP specification to drive adoption. Our advances in security and trust are ongoing as we continue to introduce resilient and quantum-safe innovations.

We've expanded support for Live Protect across more of our campus networking portfolio, extended quantum readiness to WiFi 7 access points and plan to provide quantum-safe communications across most of our core portfolio by the end of this calendar year. We continue to develop intelligent workplace experiences recently launching Claude Managed Agents and Dialog, an agentic harness in Webex. Our teams continue to drive this work forward through innovation, productivity and commitment to leveraging AI tools. At the start of fiscal '27, we provided an AI agent for every employee. We expect to continue accelerating AI adoption, helping our employees execute. Now I'll turn it over to Mark for more detail on the quarter and our outlook.

Mark Patterson: Thanks, Chuck. I'm proud to report that we delivered another record quarter, exceeding the high end of our guidance across revenue, operating margin and EPS, while also delivering strong operating cash flow. For the quarter, total revenue of $18.5 billion was an all-time high, up 24% year-on-year. Non-GAAP operating margin rose to 37.8% and non-GAAP earnings per share was $1.40, up 40% year-over-year, demonstrating continued operating leverage. Total product revenue was $14.7 billion, up 32% year-over-year, and services revenue was $3.9 billion, up 1% year-over-year. Product revenue growth was led by networking accelerating to 43% year-over-year growth with broad strength across the portfolio led by triple-digit growth in AI infrastructure and double-digit growth in data center switching and campus networking.

Security delivered a strong quarter, up 7%, reflecting growth in Splunk, network security and SASE. Collaboration was up 8% with double-digit growth in devices and growth in Contact Center. Turning to our recurring metrics. Total RPO was $46.2 billion, up 8%, with product RPO up 7%. Total ARR ended the quarter at $32.7 billion, an increase of 4%, with product ARR also up 4%. Total non-GAAP gross margin came in at 65.6%, slightly above the midpoint of our guide and down 250 basis points year-over-year as hardware revenue growth significantly outpaced software and services revenue growth. Non-GAAP product gross margin was 63.7%, down 350 basis points, primarily driven by higher hardware mix and elevated memory costs, partially offset by productivity improvements and price increases. Non-GAAP services gross margin was 72.9%, up 220 basis points.

As hardware continues to increase as a percentage of our overall revenue mix and with hyperscaler revenue expected to more than double year-over-year in FY '27, we are driving record scale and profitability in our business. In FY '27, we expect AI hyperscale revenue to represent 12% of total revenue, up from 6% in FY '26. Our non-GAAP tax rate was 18.5% for the quarter. Shifting to the balance sheet. We ended Q1 with total cash, cash equivalents and investments of $15.8 billion. From a capital allocation perspective, we returned $3.7 billion to our shareholders during the quarter, comprised of $1.7 billion for our quarterly cash dividend and $2 billion through share repurchases.
