Charles Robbins: He was asking, he said gross margins are holding up better than perhaps what we expected. What are the contributors to staying or...

Mark Patterson: Yes. I think -- so we still have the same headwinds in terms of component prices and mix is the big thing in terms of hardware growth just in general, really outpacing the software growth that you're seeing. I think that for the year, most of the expectations were for a gross margin number at just under -- just shy of the 65%, and we're comfortable with that for the full year.

Operator: Simon Leopold with Raymond James.

Simon Leopold: First one, I wanted to ask was you guys have shown some real progress with the AI back-end success. Within the systems value, can you give us a rough idea of the mix between top of rack, switching in the spine versus the routing used for scale across? Rough order of magnitude split is all I'm looking for. And then as a follow-up, I'm just wondering if you could update us on how much of your growth has come from price changes versus unit growth? I know it's not precise, but also rough idea of that would be appreciated.

Charles Robbins: Yes, I'll take the first one, and then Mark, you can take the second one. We don't -- I don't have the breakdown exactly between those technologies. I think the way I would think about it is in the last 5 quarters, we've had 18 design wins and we've had them across scale-out architectures, both systems and then scale across and systems as well as optics. We talked about in the prepared remarks, 2 wins with the P200 for scale-across and then a 1.6 Terabit scale-out optics win. And so we just -- we're actually active in all the places that you mentioned. We just haven't given those numbers at that level of detail.

So Mark, do you want to talk about gross margin?

Mark Patterson: And maybe just to reiterate, we've talked about just the split between optics and systems being roughly 50-50. That will vary in any given quarter, but that continues to be sort of what we're seeing. In terms of the price versus unit and Simon, I appreciate that you mentioned it, it's certainly an imperfect science. But I think that the estimate that we gave you a quarter ago was that we expected revenue to be impacted about 5 points for the full year. I think that's probably a pretty good estimate still for the year.

David Vogt: So maybe, Chuck, the first question. I know you don't want to be on this AI order treadmill. But just by doing some really quick math, it looks like we had a little bit of a sequential downtick in AI orders taken from hyperscalers in the quarter. I know the industry is somewhat lumpy and not linear. Can you maybe talk to kind of how you're seeing that develop as the year progress and characterize kind of like the effect of your conversation? Because I think later in the deck, you talked about potential wins for not only P200, but G200, G300 and other programs.

So I'd just love to kind of get your thoughts on how those conversations are progressing? And I'll give Mark my follow-up quickly. Maybe just a follow-up to Simon's question. I just kind of think your AI revenue guide. It looks like incremental growth coming from AI revenue today is about 2 points faster than we thought 90 days ago and pricing is relatively the same. Is it sort of the assumption that campus is kind of that incremental driver that kind of rounds out the upside to the outlook versus 90 days? Is that the right way to think about kind of the moving parts in the revenue guide?

Charles Robbins: Yes, David, on the AI order front, I'd say, on a year-over-year basis, we saw really nice growth. And I think if you look back at last year, I don't remember the exact number, but it was $1 billion and some change in year 1 -- in first quarter, and then we ended up $9.3 billion as it escalated during the year. So while I don't expect there's normal linearity in this business at all. I think you're right, it's going to be lumpy, and there's going to be some quarters that are going to be big, others that are going to be smaller.

And that's why we made the decision just to go to the revenue side so that it's just cleaner. And we don't get into these gyrations about what -- how many orders did you take in week 7 of Q1. Some color around the different technologies. Obviously, the P200 is being very successful. We've had lots of wins with the G200 in the scale-out space, as we talked about. I will say that we've begun to ship the G300 now, and it's now in labs, which is a really good sign for us, and we feel really good about that. And obviously, we continue to have more wins in the optics space.

The design win we had this quarter at the 1.6 Terabit optic was a client side win. And it was our first client side optics win at this particular hyperscaler. So we feel good about the continued progress that we make in that space.

Mark Patterson: Yes. David, just coming back to you on the numbers. So we've taken our guide up to 19% on the top line. About 8 points of that growth is attributable to hyperscale and 11 points then would be attributable to our ex hyperscale or more sort of our core business. So if you break down the overall guide, we raised by $2.5 billion. $1.5 billion of that was hyperscale and $1 billion was our core sort of ex hyperscale business. And in terms of what's driving it, you mentioned campus, but it's much broader than that. It's not just campus.

I think if you look at really all of the product families within networking, for example, every one of them grew double digits this past quarter. So we also saw double-digit growth across every region and double-digit growth across every market -- customer market as well. So it's broad-based and the core continues to do quite well.

Operator: Karl Ackerman with BNP Paribas.

Samuel Feldman: This is Sam Feldman on for Karl Ackerman. So we believe that Silicon One is primarily integrated into your AI products, while enterprise products rely on external silicon. First, has there been any change in thinking to the fiscal '29 integration time line? And then second, what does the $9 billion of AI sales imply with respect to your mix of internal silicon?

Charles Robbins: Okay. I would -- let me answer the first one, and I'm not sure I know the answer to the second one. So on the first one, we do have now Silicon One that has begun to be implemented in portions of our enterprise networking portfolio, in the fiscal year '29 target of having all of it converted is still on track. So we feel good about where we're headed with that. On the second question. You asked the split between Silicon One revenue and non-Silicon One revenue. Obviously, in the hyperscaler space, in the $9 billion, that's other than optics, it's 100% Silicon One-based platforms.

Operator: Gianni Conti with Deutsche Bank.

Gianmarco Conti: Congrats on the quarter. Perhaps one on P200 and scale-across. You won 3 P200 scale-across design wins with several hyperscalers. My question is, what's the catalyst to Silicon One winning those sockets? And how big could scale-across become as the model gets larger?

Charles Robbins: Thank you, Johnny. I think that it's about performance, it's about power consumption, and it's -- and I think that's it. I mean it's really about performance and power . And the -- and also there's just this whole focus on diversity of silicon inside the space. And I'd say if you want to talk about the size of this market, we did a study, and we think that bandwidth requirements are going to increase 14x in this space. So the TAM is quite large and continues to grow. So we see this as a great opportunity and we're really optimistic and pleased with the number of wins that we're getting with the P200.

Mark Patterson: Yes. And the other thing I'd just add is I think as you look at our offering, it's probably the most complete offering in the industry with silicon, the Acacia optics, optical, multi-rail to come in calendar '27. So I think we do a really -- we really measure up quite well here.

Adrienne Colby: It's Adrienne Colby for Atif Malik. I wanted to ask about the optics side of the business. I know in the past, you've talked about Acacia at about $1 billion or a little bit above that order run rate, didn't know if you could talk to if that's expanding. And then hoping to get a little bit of an update on the timing of Cisco's newer multi-rail line system? And also timing around the USFP product.

Mark Patterson: Yes. So thanks, Adrienne, for the question. I think on the optics side, yes, we see this as a really sizable opportunity for us and seeing a ton of growth there. We actually had a $1 billion quarter, just last quarter on the optic side. So it's growing substantially. Q1 was a record Q1 for us as well and really see the demand increasing there as we move forward.

Charles Robbins: And the USPF (sic) [ USFP ] platform is still a couple of years out, probably a few years out. And the multi-rail system, as I think Mark mentioned earlier, is the first few months of calendar '27.

Operator: Ben Bollin with Cleveland Research.

Benjamin Bollin: Could you talk about what we should expect from services. It's kind of come off its lows, but really not intensifying or accelerating. Any thoughts on when and how that gets better. And then as a follow-up, a little bit of a bigger picture question. It does seem like there's some high-level thoughts that raw material capacity adds are happening in the kind of picks and shovels raw material side of things, but maybe the volume of data center shells that come online into 2027, I guess, 2028 and beyond. Maybe there's more questions there.

Curious how you think about the potential imbalance where maybe we are in an oversupply situation from a raw material perspective and don't have anywhere to put that stuff in 2028 and beyond.

Mark Patterson: Yes, I'll take the first one. Ben, thanks for the question. So on the services piece, we've seen a significant uptick in hardware revenue. Hardware revenue actually grew over 50% for Q1. And the thing with services is it's ratable. And our hyperscalers don't attach a lot of services as well. So -- but what you're going to see is that business is going to continue to improve. We broke into the positive territory this quarter. I'd look for that to have some continued improvement as we move through the year.

Charles Robbins: And on the demand side, from a data center perspective and especially as we get out to '28 and beyond, I actually don't foresee. I think the geopolitical side of it is going to get worked out. And I think that -- I think given the demand that we see today, these data centers are going to get built. And so I don't think we don't feel like there's much risk on the resources side and anything that would surprise us relative to the data center build out over the next 2 years.

Michael Ng: First, for Mark, I was just wondering if you could -- just provide a little bit more color around the margin outlook for the second quarter and for the full year. I think it was better than expectations despite the growing hardware and hyperscale mix. So what's been coming in better? And then, Chuck, just as a follow-up, I was just wondering if you were seeing any early signs of demand shifting outside of the United States for data center AI networking, just given the results of the midterms and the risk of capacity becoming harder to originate in the U.S.

Mark Patterson: Michael, so I'll take the first one. Yes. I think that the 2 big factors, obviously, impacting gross margin are the component cost increases that we've been seeing. There's a lot of efforts to combat that, including some of the price increases that you've seen, but also these long-term agreements that we're entering into to get supply and in some cases, prices as well, and then there's the mix. But offsetting that is really a number of productivity improvements that we've had around memory as well as just the scale and efficiency that we're able to drive at this much higher revenue level than we've seen in the past.

I actually think that gross margins are pretty much right on target. We were just slightly above the midpoint of our guide for Q1. And I think that most have expectations of full year gross margin of just shy of 65%. And I think that's a reasonable expectation. I think that we should be right on there.

Charles Robbins: And then Michael, on the data center question that you have, we have not seen a shift of demand that we expected in the United States to go outside the country as of yet. And I candidly don't expect that to be the case. I think you've got a combination of -- you still have plenty of states that have not declared moratoriums, you have -- obviously, you've got to have the energy right in those states.

But we've also seen some of the -- at least one of the governors has come out and said that they're open to data center builds, they just need to be done in the right way with concern and commitments to the community, concerns and commitment to maintaining energy costs and things of that nature. I think this is too important to our country, and it's too important to the industry. It will get resolved. And I think that the last thing we want is for data centers to end up being built outside the United States. And I think that's how this will end up. But obviously, there's a lot of political dynamics in it right now.

Ahmed Sami Badri: Thank you, Mike. I'm going to hand it over to Chuck for some closing remarks.

Charles Robbins: Yes, I just want to thank everyone for joining us today. And I want to reinforce just how confident I am in Cisco's future and candidly the sustainability of the performance that we've seen. We're executing really well against our strategy. The teams are doing a great job. We're delivering strong results. And we're seeing the investments that we've made over the past several years, in some cases, a decade, they're translating into real momentum. The other thing I would point out is that this business is more efficient and has greater scale than anything I've seen.

If you just look at our revenue based on the guide we put up today and you go back 2 years, we're going to generate $19 billion in incremental revenue, and we're going to do that with less headcount than we had at the beginning, 2 years ago. And so the efficiency that we're seeing is just unprecedented and the teams are doing an incredible job of scaling the business and also driving productivity. I also gained a lot of confidence from what I'm hearing from our customers and our partners. We're truly in the very early stages of a multiyear networking super cycle, and we're confident in our ability to continue capturing the opportunity that it represents for Cisco.

I believe we have the right strategy, we have the innovation, the right team, and we're focused on translating that into sustained profitable growth. I want to thank our teams for their continued execution and thank our customers, partners and shareholders for their trust. And Sami, I'll turn it back over to you.

Ahmed Sami Badri: Thank you, Chuck. Cisco's next quarterly call, which will outline our second quarter fiscal year 2027 results, will be on Wednesday, February 10, 2027, at 1:30 p.m. Pacific Time, 4:30 PM Eastern time. This concludes today's call. If you have any further questions, please feel free to contact the Cisco Investor Relations department. And we thank you very much for joining the call today.

#3084. Car Insurance Soars for Drivers With Poor Credit; Here’s What to Do

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

While building your credit, shop around for auto insurance quotes. Some insurers are more lenient than others.

Lead Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

Your driving record may be spotless, but if you have poor credit, car insurance companies view you as a risk — and they’re significantly raising your rates.

Over the past three years, drivers with poor credit have seen auto insurance premiums surge 37.7%, according to NerdWallet’s 2026 Auto Insurance Rates Report. These price hikes were even steeper than those faced by drivers with good credit who caused a crash or got a DUI.

In January 2023, someone with poor credit and a clean driving record would pay a median of $2,864 per year for full-coverage car insurance, NerdWallet’s analysis found. By January 2026, premiums for this driver had risen to $3,944 — an increase of $1,081 per year. By comparison, the same driver with good credit saw an increase of only $576.

“Credit scores are one of the most harmful things that results in you paying higher auto insurance premiums,” says Michael DeLong, a research and advocacy associate with the Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. “The penalties are extremely severe.”

While higher premiums after a wreck or DUI may not be a surprise, DeLong says many drivers aren’t aware their credit scores will affect their car insurance rates. To further complicate things, building credit can take months.

But there are ways to get relief more quickly. DeLong suggests comparing car insurance quotes from multiple companies, because some insurers penalize poor credit less than others. Raising your deductible, evaluating your coverage and avoiding small claims can also help.

NerdWallet’s analysis found that insurers raised rates more sharply from 2023 to 2026 for drivers with poor credit than for those with good credit — even if the poor-credit driver had a flawless record while the good-credit driver had a DUI, speeding ticket or at-fault crash.

When our sample driver with poor credit also had a recent DUI or speeding ticket, rate increases were even greater. Prices for a full-coverage policy went up by more than 40% for drivers with poor credit and a recent DUI, the biggest increase of any profile we analyzed.

Drivers often think it’s unfair for credit to affect car insurance prices, DeLong says, since it isn’t directly linked to driving behavior. Some states agree; California, Hawaii and Massachusetts don’t allow credit as a factor in setting auto insurance rates.

However, insurers say credit scores can indicate the likelihood that a driver will file a claim.[1]National Association of Insurance Commissioners. Credit-Based Insurance Scores. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources They use what’s called a credit-based insurance score — similar to the typical credit scores used by lenders but weighted differently.

“It helps in predicting expected claims activity and loss costs more accurately,” said Norman Niami, a member of the American Academy of Actuaries' Automobile Insurance Committee, in an email.

The practice has been controversial, with critics arguing it disproportionately hurts low-income and minority drivers. But a Federal Trade Commission report to Congress in July 2007 concluded that credit-based insurance scores were strong predictors of risk even when controlled for income, race and ethnicity.[2]A Report to Congress by the Federal Trade Commission. Credit-Based Insurance Scores: Impacts on Consumers of Automobile Insurance. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources

The explanation may be that some people simply tend to take risks, according to a statistical analysis published in the North American Actuarial Journal in 2016.[3]North American Actuarial Journal. Empirical Evidence on the Use of Credit Scoring for Predicting Insurance Losses with Psycho-social and Biochemical Explanations. Accessed Nov 2, 2026. View all sources Researchers concluded that risk-taking behavior can affect credit scores as well as insurance claims. Their analysis found that average losses per policy were 64.6% higher for drivers with the lowest credit scores than for those with the best credit.

Working to build your credit over time may help lower your car insurance premiums, but it’s not a sure thing. A credit-based insurance score is just one of many factors (along with things like location, age and driving history) that insurers use to rate a person’s risk.

Building credit “can produce a noticeable premium decrease in some cases, while producing little or no change in others,” Niami said, depending on whether the new score causes an insurer to move you into a better rating tier. Each insurer sets its own score thresholds, so a score viewed as “poor” by one insurer might be considered “fair” by another.

At the same time, consumer advocates argue it’s difficult for many people to take the steps needed to strengthen their credit scores.

“Most people probably have some idea that you can improve your credit score by trying to pay your bills regularly and reliably, and using different kinds of financial resources and credit cards,” DeLong says.

“But again, that’s easier said than done," he says. "If you’re struggling at a low-wage job and trying to juggle bills, or if you don’t easily have access to a credit card, that advice may not be especially helpful."

Drivers with poor credit or no credit may be able to take other steps to lower their premiums.

Comparing car insurance quotes from different companies is one of the best ways to ensure you have the cheapest rate possible. Insurers set their own pricing formulas, and some are more forgiving of poor credit than others. A NerdWallet analysis of October 2026 rates found that in about half (49.3%) of U.S. ZIP codes in states that allow credit scoring, the cheapest insurer for a driver with poor credit was a different company than the cheapest for a driver with good credit.

Although you can’t improve your risk profile overnight, “there’s a bunch of small things you can do that over a two- to three-year span make you look a lot better” to insurers, says Bradley Flowers, founder of Portal Insurance agency in Mobile, Alabama.

Consider a higher deductible. Raising your car insurance deductible — the amount of a future claim that you agree to cover yourself — lowers your premium and signals to insurers that you’re less likely to file a claim. But be sure you can afford to pay the higher deductible if you have to make a claim.

Adjust how you’re billed by insurers. By signing up for automatic payments and ensuring you don’t miss insurance payments each month, you’ll get a small discount while improving your risk profile for insurers.

Avoid minor claims if you can. Flowers recommends thinking twice about filing minor claims, such as windshield cracks. “When you’re in one of these situations, let’s save our insurance for the really bad stuff,” he suggests.

Lastly, be sure your coverage fits your vehicle. If you could afford to replace your car on your own, consider dropping collision and comprehensive coverage to bring your premiums down. Your trimmed-down policy would still provide you with liability coverage after a crash, while leaving you to cover damage to your vehicle.

NerdWallet's 2026 Auto Insurance Rates Report is based on an analysis of more than 1.4 billion rate estimates provided by Quadrant Information Services for all 50 states and Washington, D.C., from January 2023 to January 2026.

Quadrant derives its rate data from modeled estimates based on carrier rating algorithms; figures do not reflect every available carrier or every consumer's individual rate. Liberty Mutual does not participate in Quadrant's rate data and is not represented in this analysis.

Quadrant’s figures are modeled rate estimates produced by running a fixed driver profile through carrier rating algorithms. They represent both new business and renewal rate estimates, and they are not a record of what actual drivers paid.

NerdWallet anchored its analysis to a 3-year old Toyota Camry LE, ensuring each analysis period reflected rates for the same-aged car.

The primary rate analysis is based on a 35-year-old single driver with good credit, no recent at-fault accidents or driving violations, and a full-coverage policy with $1,000 deductibles for collision and comprehensive coverage. Rates are pooled across male and female drivers.

In states where drivers must carry other types of insurance not included in our full coverage profile specifications, we added the minimum amount of coverage required by those states. Some policies include additional coverage at the insurer’s discretion.

In addition to our base profile driver with good credit and a spotless driving history, we analyzed rates for the following driver profiles:

Drivers with an at-fault crash. We added a single at-fault crash causing $10,000 in property damage.

Drivers with a speeding ticket. We added a single speeding ticket for driving 16 mph over the speed limit.

Drivers with a DUI. We added a single drunken-driving violation.

Drivers with poor credit. This is the same as our regular base profile, except the driver has poor credit instead of good credit. We also analyzed rates for drivers with poor credit and each of the three incidents above.

NerdWallet applied a strict comparability filter before calculating year-over-year figures. Only coverage variants and carrier/state combinations present in all four years of data were included in median calculations. This ensures reported changes reflect genuine pricing shifts among stable carriers, rather than differences caused by insurers entering markets, exiting, or going insolvent during the analysis period.

#3081. Arrowhead (ARWR) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Plozasiran launch prep and a multibillion sHTG opportunity come into focus.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (ARWR -4.48%) management indicated that the company is transitioning toward a commercial-stage organization as it builds a global cardiometabolic franchise. Management stated that the company is preparing for a potential U.S. launch of plozasiran in severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG) during the second quarter of 2027, following a recent supplemental application submission. The company reported a net loss for the fiscal year driven by onetime expenses and increased R&D investment, while maintaining a significant cash position. Strategic priorities include advancing a diverse pipeline of RNAi therapeutics targeting the liver, lungs, muscle, and central nervous system. Management indicated that commercial progress in the initial rare disease market is critical for establishing the infrastructure needed to address larger patient populations.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference call over to Vince Anzalone, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations for Arrowhead. Please go ahead, Vince.

Vincent Anzalone: Good afternoon. Thank you for joining us today to discuss Arrowhead's results for its 2026 fiscal year ended September 30, 2026. With us today from management are President and CEO, Dr. Chris Anzalone, who will provide an overview; Andy Davis, Senior Vice President and Head of the Global Cardiometabolic Franchise, who will provide an update on commercialization activities; Dr. James Hamilton, Chief Medical Officer and Head of R&D, who will discuss our development programs; and Dan Apel, Chief Financial Officer, who will give a review of the financials. Following management's prepared remarks, we will open the call to questions.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that comments made during today's call contain certain forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. All statements other than statements of historical fact are forward-looking statements and are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed in any forward-looking statements. For further details concerning these risks and uncertainties, please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent annual report on Form 10-K and our quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. I'd now like to turn the call over to Chris.

Dr. Christopher Anzalone: Thanks, Vince. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Arrowhead has fundamentally changed over the past 12 months. Where there was once a company that relied solely on great scientific promise, there is now a company that is beginning to translate promise into real patient outcomes and the potential for durable shareholder value growth. We are building a commercial business around REDEMPLO. We have delivered the pivotal data we believe is needed to pursue a much larger market in severe hypertriglyceridemia or sHTG. And we have demonstrated new capabilities that substantially expand what our RNAi platform can do. I believe we approach 2027 with the strongest combination of near-term commercial opportunity and scientific capability in our history.

For the long term, we intend Arrowhead to become a substantial pharmaceutical company that introduces important new medicines into the market virtually every year. We believe we've demonstrated that we have the platforms and development capabilities to do this, and the result could be an engine that improves innumerable patient lives and creates substantial value. But first things first, we need to build a commercial presence that matches the excellence we've built in discovery and development, and we need to demonstrate that we are capable of building out a new market, finding the patients who could benefit from our medicines and growing a profitable business. Simply put, commercial progress with REDEMPLO is critical.

We are focused on continued success serving the FCS market, planning a rapid launch into sHTG and positioning Arrowhead to maximize the sHTG market opportunity. Of course, revenue levels, growth and profitability will ultimately be the only metrics that matter when assessing how we are doing with REDEMPLO. However, that will not tell the full story until after the first several quarters of our planned sHTG launch as payer policies are being worked out, coverage is being secured and provider outreach is initiated. So during this period, we will regularly refer to 3 metrics that we believe capture the breadth and depth of early market penetration.

They are: one, total number of new-to-brand patient prescriptions; two, number of distinct prescribers writing prescriptions; and three, number of lives covered on payer formularies. We believe there are large pools of patients who can benefit from REDEMPLO, and these 3 metrics are intended to reflect how well we are building pipes to reach them. We launched into the narrow FCS market about 11 months ago and are still in the pipe building phase. This work has progressed well. As of September 30, we had 950 new-to-brand patient prescriptions, representing a 63% increase over the prior quarter end. This growth rate continues to increase rapidly as we have added another 300 since then.

At September 30, over 640 distinct individual prescribers wrote first-time prescriptions, and that number has grown to over 860 since then. There are now over 160 million lives covered in payer formularies in the U.S. We are seeing strong demand for REDEMPLO and continue to work with payers to increase the rate at which prescriptions are converted to paid shipments. This is still a choke point, and there is substantial work to do, but we are off to a good start. The pipes we are laying are also -- the pipes we are laying are critical for the FCS market and importantly, directly applicable to the next stage of our business in sHTG.

We intend to enter sHTG with an organization that already understands the medicine, its prescribers and the practical work needed to get patients on treatment. Let's now look forward. We are preparing aggressively for a potential U.S. launch in sHTG in the second quarter of 2027, subject to successful FDA review and approval. The FDA granted plozasiran entry into the Split Real-time Application Review, or STAR pilot program for our planned sHTG supplement. STAR provides a 6-month priority review framework and the possibility of action earlier than the formal goal date. We submitted our sNDA on November 2, so we expect to receive our PDUFA date over the next 50 days or so.

We are very optimistic about the potential for this launch. We believe the clinical profile, the unmet need and the capabilities we are building position REDEMPLO to become the leading treatment in this market. That conviction begins with data. In July, we announced that SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 met their primary endpoint and every prespecified secondary endpoint. The detailed results presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in August and at the American Heart Association just last weekend reinforced the consistency of plozasiran's activity. Median triglyceride reductions from baseline were 79% and 81% at month 12.

In the pooled analysis, cumulative acute pancreatitis events were reduced by 78% versus placebo across the broad sHTG population study with an impressive 100% reduction in patients at the highest risk of acute pancreatitis. These are results that we believe can change treatment expectations. Physicians see patients whose triglycerides remain dangerously elevated despite existing approaches. Our goal is to deliver those physicians a medicine that can produce deep sustained reductions with a simple quarterly injection, supported by evidence of fewer acute pancreatitis events in the SHASTA-3 and 4 studies. We believe that is a powerful proposition for patients and payers alike. We continue to describe the profile we are pursuing as safe, simple and strong.

Safe reflects the favorable tolerability observed in all of our studies, no increase in liver fat, no hypersensitivity and no notable changes in liver values. Simple reflects a fixed 25-milligram dose administered once every 3 months. We don't expect to need to monitor liver enzymes and there will be no need to titrate the dose up. Strong reflects the depth of triglyceride lowering and the pancreatitis results. The FDA will determine the final sHTG label, but we have a high degree of confidence in this medicine. We continue to see the potential for REDEMPLO to generate $3 billion to $4 billion in annual U.S. sales over time in sHTG.

These are large numbers, but we see many ways to get there. While there are thought to be 3 million to 3.5 million people in the U.S. with TGs greater than 500 milligrams per deciliter, we believe the early adopters will be the population at highest risk within this group. This is comprised of those patients with TGs greater than 880 without a history of pancreatitis and those with TGs greater than 500 that have a history of acute pancreatitis. Together, we believe this population totals almost 1 million people in the U.S. and their enhanced risk of acute pancreatitis would suggest that they are in real need of treatment.

In SHASTA-3 and 4, the number of patients needed to treat in order to prevent a single acute pancreatitis event was 9 in patients with TGs greater than 880 without history of pancreatitis and those with TGs greater than 500 and history of pancreatitis. Within that latter group alone, the NNT was only 3. These are very compelling numbers, and keep in mind that this is just after 1 year. We would expect those NNTs to decrease further over longer treatment periods. Our data suggests that this patient population could benefit from REDEMPLO, but a valid question is how long it will take to educate patients and providers about the need to treat.

There is clearly already some appreciation for this. For instance, we believe that around 1 million people with TGs greater than 500 are on prescription fish oils. This suggests to us that providers already have an urgency to treat TG levels for at least these patients. Remember that these fish oils only reduced TGs by 20% to 30%, while REDEMPLO reduced TGs by around 80% from baseline in SHASTA-3 and 4. Outside the U.S., our business is advancing as well. REDEMPLO became available for prescription, dispensing and reimbursement in Germany in August, following the European Commission's June authorization. In addition, in October, the U.K.

Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency, or MHRA, authorized REDEMPLO in the United Kingdom for adults with FCS and the U.K. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, or NICE, issued guidance recommending funding in England and Wales. These milestones expand the foundation of our global cardiometabolic business. Besides our commercial build-out, our discovery engine has delivered 2 important clinical advances. In September, ARO-DIMER-PA demonstrated that one RNAi molecule can silence both PCSK9 and APOC3 in people with mixed hyperlipidemia. That opens an important new approach to ASCVD due to mixed hyperlipidemia and gives us a basis for developing additional medicines that address more than one disease driver at a time.

Then in October, ARO-MAPT produced substantial and sustained reductions in tau measured in the cerebrospinal fluid after subcutaneous administration. We view this as early clinical validation of our ability to deliver RNAi across the blood-brain barrier. The opportunity to address CNS targets with an injection under the skin could dramatically expand the diseases we can pursue. I do not think this breakthrough can be overstated. We intend to move decisively to build on these results. This is the model we have been building for years, establish delivery to a cell type, learn how to do it reliably and then apply that capability to additional targets.

Our clinical work now spans the liver, lung, muscle, adipose tissue and CNS with additional tissue types we can study preclinically. Every successful expansion gives us the potential to create multiple new medicines and additional opportunities for partnerships. Our cardiometabolic franchise illustrates how that can translate into an efficient commercial business. REDEMPLO, zodasiran, ARO-DIMER-PA and our obesity and NASH programs could serve related physician audiences. We intend to build an organization that can support several products through much of the same infrastructure. That is an important part of how we think about growth and long-term returns on the capital we invest.

We have also announced an agreement with Sixth Street to retire our existing debt at a discount to the minimum multiple on invested capital provided for in the existing agreement and to establish a new facility at a lower cost of capital. The refinancing is designed to extend our debt maturity and provide financing terms more consistent with Arrowhead's current stage. We have a great deal to execute, and we are approaching it with urgency. The potential sHTG launch is our most important near-term commercial priority. We believe it can change the scale of Arrowhead's business, while the rest of our pipeline creates opportunities well beyond REDEMPLO.

I'm more optimistic than ever about the patients we can help and the value we can build. With that overview, I'd now like to turn the call over to Andy Davis. Andy?

Andy Davis: Thank you, Chris, and good afternoon, everyone. We are approaching 1 year since REDEMPLO's initial FDA approval and the FCS launch continues to progress. I'll cover 3 measures of this progress: number one, growth in prescriptions; number two, expansion of the prescriber base; and number three, advancements in market access. Then I'll connect them to our planned sHTG launch anticipated in the second calendar quarter of 2027. First, growth in prescriptions. Total new-to-brand prescriptions grew 63% in the fiscal fourth quarter, and that momentum has carried into this quarter, taking us well past 1,250 cumulative new-to-brand prescriptions. On prior calls, I cited a run rate of 20 to 30 new prescriptions per week.

Recent trends support approximately 50 to 60 per week. We are encouraged by the sustained increase in demand. Since expanding our field team this summer, we are reaching substantially more health care professionals, and we are seeing strong interest in REDEMPLO from prescribers across specialties. It's important to note, however, that these are written prescriptions, not paid claims. Moving from prescription to treatment requires patient engagement, benefit verification, physician office support and prior authorization submission and approval. Our dedicated REDEMPLO reimbursement navigator team is heavily focused on educating offices on the reimbursement process to convert this demand into treatment starts and durable access. Second, expansion of the prescriber base. Unique prescribers grew over 50% in the fiscal fourth quarter.

Since then, in the last 5 weeks alone, we added as many prescribers as in the entire fourth quarter, bringing the total as of the first week of November to over 860. We view this as an important indicator of future growth and a productive field engagement with the right providers. The specialty mix is led by cardiology and endocrinology with internal medicine of growing share. These are the same specialties we expect to engage for sHTG should REDEMPLO be approved for that use next year. Repeat prescribing is also building with approximately 27% of prescribers having written for more than one patient.

In recent market tracking research, prescribing physicians report strong satisfaction and high and increasing likelihood to recommend REDEMPLO since launch. Third, advancements in market access. Payers representing the vast majority of U.S. covered lives have published utilization management policies for REDEMPLO and FCS. These policies describe the criteria by which a payer will evaluate a reimbursement request. Additionally, more than 160 million U.S. lives now have coverage for REDEMPLO, with coverage defined as those eligible patients with a reimbursement pathway under the applicable policy criteria. Both of these metrics have grown steadily since launch. Our objective is to expand access for appropriate patients with genetically confirmed or clinically diagnosed FCS and to help practices navigate requirements efficiently.

We are working with payers, specialty pharmacies and physician offices to move prescriptions through the process and reserve points -- and resolve points of friction. Broadening access and improving the patient journey are central priorities as we prepare for a much larger opportunity. Turning to sHTG. Our enthusiasm is high. We are preparing for a potential launch in the second calendar quarter of 2027, subject to FDA approval. Our initial focus is on patients at high risk of acute pancreatitis, including those with triglycerides at or above 880 milligrams per deciliter or above 500 milligrams per deciliter with a prior history of pancreatitis. We have described this as approximately 1 million people in the U.S. within the broader sHTG market.

We have identified more than 20,000 health care professionals across relevant specialties as likely sHTG treaters, and we are well advanced in building our HCP engagement, patient services, distribution and market access capabilities. Our expanded sales team is now largely in place, building relationships and mapping priority accounts in preparation for a potential sHTG launch. What we are learning now will help us execute as the addressable population expands. Our One-REDEMPLO pricing approach supports this transition. The current U.S. wholesale acquisition cost is $45,000 per patient per year, and we intend to hold a consistent U.S. price across FCS and sHTG if the broader indication is approved. We believe that simplicity supports productive payer discussions and a clear value proposition.

Outside the U.S., Germany and the U.K. are now active commercial markets. In the U.K., the reimbursement authority recently issued final guidance recommending REDEMPLO for genetically confirmed FCS, supporting reimbursement in England and Wales, and we are working to serve eligible patients there now. To recap, the FCS launch is showing increased prescription demand, a broadening prescriber base and important advancements in access. This is the progress we intend to carry into sHTG. We believe the opportunity ahead is significant, and our team is preparing accordingly. With that, I'll turn the call over to James.

James Hamilton: Thank you, Andy. The fourth quarter and subsequent period included important progress in our late-stage cardiometabolic programs and clinical validation of 2 new applications of Arrowhead's TRiM platform. I'll begin with plozasiran and then discuss zodasiran, ARO-DIMER-PA, our CNS efforts as well as obesity and NASH. For plozasiran, the SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 results give us a strong basis for the sHTG sNDA, which, as Chris mentioned, has been submitted. Both trials evaluated 25 milligrams every 3 months and both met their primary and all prespecified secondary endpoints.

In addition to the triglyceride reductions Chris described, more than 90% of treated patients achieved triglycerides below 500 milligrams per deciliter at month 12 and more than half achieved triglycerides below 150 milligrams per deciliter. In the pooled acute pancreatitis analysis, the overall reduction in cumulative events was 78% versus placebo. Among patients with a prior history of acute pancreatitis, the event rate reduction was 91% with an estimated number needed to treat of 3 over 1 year to prevent one event. In the highest risk group with triglycerides above 880 and the prior history of pancreatitis, there were no events observed in the plozasiran group. These subgroup findings support our focus on patients with substantial ongoing risk.

Safety remained favorable overall and consistent with our previous experience. Treatment-emergent adverse event rates were similar in the pooled placebo and pooled active groups. There were no cases of anaphylaxis or systemic hypersensitivity, no clinically meaningful platelet changes and no meaningful liver enzyme elevations relative to placebo. The MRI sub-study showed no statistically significant change in hepatic fat fraction. Worsening glycemic control was reported more frequently with plozasiran at 14.3% versus 8.7% in placebo, with mean changes in hemoglobin A1C consistent with previous experience and importantly, the progressive worsening of A1C over time. Our regulatory package draws on SHASTA-3, SHASTA-4 and the MiR-3 safety database, working within STAR, which includes priority review, we continue to anticipate an efficient review process.

Entry into STAR reflects the FDA's assessment that the application meets the program's criteria for a potentially meaningful improvement over available therapy on clinically relevant endpoints. Approval and the ultimate label remains subject to regulatory review. Now turning to zodasiran. In July, we completed enrollment in the global Phase III YOSEMITE study in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. We enrolled 70 patients above the original target of 60, reflecting strong interest in this population. The trial evaluates quarterly dosing and the change in LDL cholesterol at month 12 as the primary endpoint. We anticipate study completion in mid-2027 and data in the second half of next year with a potential regulatory filing thereafter if the results are supportive.

Our previously stated goal has been an NDA filing by year-end 2027. Next, ARO-DIMER-PA. The interim single-dose results announced in September showed mean maximal reductions of 89% in PCSK9 and 95% in APOC3. The corresponding mean maximum lipid reductions were 65% for LDL cholesterol, 78% for triglycerides, 73% for remnant cholesterol and 66% for ApoB. These are early dose escalation results, with the ability to affect both pathways with one molecule, leading to large reductions in atherogenic lipoproteins is highly encouraging. No drug-related serious adverse events were reported in that interim analysis. Injection site events and headache were the most commonly reported treatment-emergent events and multiple dose assessment continues, and we expect additional clinical data around mid-2027.

We are evaluating a development strategy that could first seek approval based on LDL cholesterol lowering, subject to regulatory agreement. Turning to the CNS. Our October 14 presentation included the first interim healthy volunteer results for subcutaneous ARO-MAPT. At the 12.8 milligram per kilogram regimen administered on day 1 and 15, mean CSF total tau fell 73% by day 105 with a maximum individual reduction of 85%. Day 105 was 90 days after the last dose, and these findings support the potential for maintenance dosing every 3 months or less frequently. ARO-MAPT was generally well tolerated in the interim analysis, and there were no serious treatment-emergent adverse events or adverse events leading to discontinuation.

No persistent anemia or neurobehavioral adverse events were reported. These results provide evidence of target engagement in healthy volunteers. Multi-dose healthy volunteer cohorts are fully enrolled and enrollment in early Alzheimer's, patient cohorts is ongoing. We expect additional healthy volunteer data and Alzheimer's patient data in 2027. We've also begun regulatory discussions around clinical studies in MAPT-associated frontotemporal dementia and progressive supranuclear palsy. We have multiple additional CNS programs in development. As discussed at our October webinar, we are targeting CTAs for 2 wholly-owned candidates around end of 2026 or early '27 and additional CNS clinical entries by the end of 2027. The objective is to apply the CNS delivery capability across a broad set of diseases.

Lastly, we remain on track to share updates from our obesity programs, specifically focused on ALK7 nondiabetic monotherapy cohorts as well as the type 2 diabetic tirzepatide combo cohorts before the end of the year. I will now turn the call over to Dan Apel.

Daniel Apel: Thank you, James, and good afternoon, everyone. As we reported today, net loss attributable to Arrowhead for fiscal year 2026 was $724.2 million or a loss of $5.11 per share based on 141.6 million fully diluted weighted-average shares outstanding in the year. This compares to a net loss of $1.6 million or a loss of $0.01 per share based on 133.8 million fully diluted weighted-average shares in fiscal year 2025. First, fiscal year 2025 benefited from $829 million in collaboration revenue, largely from the initial recognition of the Sarepta and Sanofi arrangement. Second, fiscal year 2026 included a onetime $215 million expense for the priority review voucher we acquired in September. Excluding that expense, net loss would have been approximately $509 million. Turning to revenue. Revenue for fiscal year 2026 totaled $450.8 million compared to $829.4 million in fiscal 2025. Revenue in fiscal 2026 was driven by our license and collaboration agreements with Sarepta, Novartis, Madrigal and Sanofi, together with our first year of commercial sales of REDEMPLO. Of that total, $317 million related to our Sarepta collaboration.

This includes $181 million recognized for the second DM1 milestone, the ongoing recognition of initial Sarepta consideration, reimbursement of incurred collaboration program costs, and revenue under the clinical supply agreement, the $317 million compares to $697 million from the prior year with the year-over-year decrease related to the onetime recognition in 2025 of the transfer of the initial Sarepta licenses. For our Novartis collaboration, we recognized $89 million during the year, nearly all of which relates to the $200 million upfront payment we received in October. During the year, we also recognized a $25 million upfront payment from Madrigal for ARO-PNPLA3 following completion of that license and technology transfer. And we recognized $13.3 million related to Sanofi in Greater China compared to $130 million in the prior year, which related to the upfront consideration received when that agreement closed. While we have consistently stated that FCS revenue will have an immaterial impact to our 2026 financial statements, we continue to invest in supporting this FCS launch and preparing for the potential blockbuster opportunity in sHTG. R&D for the expense -- year was $739 million compared to $607 million in the prior year.

Candidate costs accounted for $96 million or the majority of that increase. Taken as a whole, these R&D investments supported the positive pivotal sHTG results reported this summer, the advancement of our broader pipeline and our efforts toward commercial manufacturing readiness in Verona. As a reminder, the Verona plant provides us accelerated and enhanced ability to prioritize and make new clinical GMP oligonucleotide drug substance and will be used to support future commercial products, the first one planned being zodasiran. SG&A expense for the year was $202 million compared to $124 million in the prior year. The increase was driven primarily by our investment in the commercialization of REDEMPLO.

As we have discussed, these capabilities more than support the current FCS launch and were built with the intention of being fully leverageable for the potential sHTG launch and ultimately for zodasiran in HoFH. As of today, our commercial organization is largely in place, and we expect only incremental additions as we approach a potential U.S. sHTG launch. Turning now to the balance sheet. Cash and investments totaled nearly $1.2 billion as of September 30, 2026, compared to $0.9 billion a year earlier. Cash used in operating activities was approximately $272 million for the fiscal year. Importantly, that year-end balance is after funding both our operating activities and the $215 million purchase of the priority review voucher.

Common shares outstanding at year-end were approximately 141.3 million. As to the voucher, following the FDA's acceptance of plozasiran into the STAR pilot program in October, it is no longer needed for our planned sHTG supplemental application and is eligible to be sold to a third party. Publicly announced PRV transactions over the last 12 months have ranged from approximately $180 million to $220 million. Purely illustratively, if we were to sell our PRV at prevailing market rates, our cash and investments would be approximately $1.4 billion on a rounded pro forma basis. To be clear, though, we have not entered into a sale agreement and no PRV sale proceeds are included in our reported statements.

Finally, I'd like to highlight the refinancing we recently completed with Sixth Street on November 2. We replaced the prior facility with a new $400 million senior secured term loan and 3-month SOFR-plus 5.5% compared to the prior facility's 15% annual rate. We also negotiated significantly a $68 million discount to the minimum amount required to retire the old facility in 2028. The new loan matures on November 2, 2031, has no scheduled principal amortization before maturity and importantly, eliminates any and all required cash sweeps to Sixth Street tied to product sales, royalty, milestones or any existing or new licensing and partnership proceeds.

To put our debt position in context, our funded debt now consists principally of the $400 million term loan due in November 2031 and $700 million of 0% convertible notes due in January 2032. In other words, no principal payments are required before late 2031. Compared with the retired structure, this materially lowers our borrowing costs, extends maturity and improves our near-term liquidity and flexibility. Taken together, we believe our strong balance sheet with approximately $1.2 billion of reported cash and investments, a transferable PRV with demonstrated market value and a meaningfully lower cost, longer-dated debt structure provides a substantial financial flexibility to support our current clinical and preclinical priorities, current and future commercialization activities and our long-term strategic priorities.

Lastly, and unrelated to our financial position, we announced today our decision to change our fiscal year-end to December to align with the calendar year. The calendar quarter ranging from October to December 2026 will be what is called a transitional quarter period with fiscal quarter 1, 2027 now referring to January through March 2027. We believe this change will ease a number of administrative burdens associated with the September year-end and ahead of a potential sHTG launch will improve company and investor communication. With that brief overview, I will now turn the call back to Chris.

And so we see a lot of demand out there waiting for REDEMPLO to be available for sHTG individuals. And then just on the discovery side, we have a number of things that are characterized by grade scarcity and our ability to deliver oligonucleotides to the brain via simple subcutaneous injection. We have really interesting clinical proof of concept there.

There's a lot of good CNS targets that we will go after ourselves as wholly-owned drug candidates, but there's room there to do partnerships with other folks as we have with Novartis so far. I think, same thing with other delivery, say, into the adipose, into lung, those are also scarce. So there's a number of ways we can go. We'll just have to look at opportunities and decide how those opportunities could fit in with our strategy going forward with the cardiometabolic franchise that we are building and with CNS franchise that we're building.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of June Lee with UBS.

Joon Lee: Congrats on the progress. Going back to REDEMPLO, what's the depth of conversations with payers you can have prior to the FDA approval without a label? How are you taking advantage of this time between now and approval to ensure maximum access and conversion of script to reimbursement upon approval?

Andy Davis: Thanks, Joon. This is Andy. Good question. So we are able to interact with payers using a pre-approval information exchange deck, which essentially articulates the value proposition of REDEMPLO, both clinically and economically. And so we are able to engage with both the clinical and negotiating teams of the large payers in a pre-approval context, and we're presently doing that now, and we'll continue to do that up until the approval of REDEMPLO expected in the second quarter of next year. Yes. Look, that was -- we were confident that we could do that, which is why we bought Priority Voucher. We're happy to report that we don't need that any longer and we can sell it.

But we saw a big opportunity to have those discussions early, particularly if we could have accelerated approval or the possibility for accelerated approval. But also, let's look at what this says about our data. If our data were ambiguous, if there were clear warts on this -- on REDEMPLO, it would be much more difficult to have these early conversations with payers. We don't see that as the case. And so the fact that there are payers talking to us right now before we have a label, I think is indicative of the power of this medicine and the unambiguous value proposition that we've got.

Operator: And that will come from the line of Edward Tenthoff with Piper Sandler.

Edward Tenthoff: Great. And I apologize if someone asked this, I don't think anyone has. But the pelacarsen miss and the data at AHA, any read-through or do you guys have any thoughts on Amgen partner, olpasiran with the OCEAN trial, I think maybe next year? And again, I apologize if someone asked this, I'm trying to listen to everything you guys are saying.

Dr. Christopher Anzalone: Ted, it's great to hear you. So as you know, we are largely out of olpasiran. We monetize those royalties. We still have milestone payments, of course, but we monetize those royalties. And we don't have good visibility on when Amgen may finish this or have data. We have no more visibility than anybody else. But from just my perspective, I don't know that the book is closed on Lp(a). My recollection is this -- that Novartis showed something like 77% reduction in Lp(a). Olpasiran is much better than that. I think that Amgen was seeing better than 90%, 95% reduction in Lp(a). That could make a difference. Of course, the baseline characteristics also could make a difference.

I believe that the Amgen studies have a bit of a higher baseline Lp(a) numbers than Novartis. So that can make a difference as well. So we'll see where that goes. The data were unfortunate with [ pelacarsen ], but I don't think the book is closed.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Eric Joseph with Citi.

Unknown Analyst: This is Charles on for Eric. Congrats on the quarter and the year. Maybe one from us on ARO-DIMER-PA sort of registration strategy. Do you mind spending on why you're seeking approval first on the LDL-C lowering versus perhaps a composite-based endpoint? More clarity would be great.

James Hamilton: Yes, sure, Charles. I can take that. Of course, this is all subject to agreement with regulators. But the LDL cholesterol is probably one of the most validated surrogate endpoints out there, and that's our thought is that if we could get -- we get approval and get on the market with an LDL endpoint in the mixed hyperlipidemia population, that would be great. The triglyceride component of mixed hyperlipidemia, that is more of a surrogate for the sHTG population, less so and less widely accepted for the less severe mixed hyperlipidemia population. So that's why we're focusing on LDL at least for now.

And if we can -- we're able to do that, that's a relatively quick time to approval to a fairly large market. We look forward to continuing to see data with ARO-DIMER-PA and to start to have discussions with regulators.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Prakhar Agrawal with Cantor.

Prakhar Agrawal: Maybe firstly, on REDEMPLO and sHTG. On the payer side, do you think you're at the right pricing range given some of the initial friction that's happening with the Tryngolza launch? You obviously have the flexibility of seeing what's happening on the market and change accordingly. So I just wanted to see the latest thoughts on pricing to get broad access. And secondly, if I can sneak in one more. On the ARO-DIMER data at AHA, efficacy is obviously great. But if you can talk about some of the detailed safety data in the fat portion. I think there were some injection reactions in pyrexia. So wanted to understand how long these events lasted?

Are these going to be single dose effect and implications for the MAD dosing?

Andy Davis: Thanks, Prakhar, for the question. This is Andy. We do believe we have the right pricing range here for REDEMPLO, and there are 2 kind of leading indicators that give us confidence. The first would be the currently published policies related to Tryngolza and sHTG, which do appear to have policy criteria consistent with label. We are optimistic that we will see in the future similar policy criteria to label for REDEMPLO. And then second, we are engaging with payers, as we mentioned, through the pre-approval information exchange process. And we haven't received pushback through those conversations with payers about the pricing range for sHTG. So we think we're in a great spot.

And look, and you mentioned the friction related to price. I don't know that we have seen that. There is always friction early between writing a prescription and working with payers to get that paid. It just takes a little bit of time to establish those processes. We're doing that now. I don't know that, that is price related. James, do you want to talk about?

James Hamilton: Yes, I can cover the question on the dimer safety. Like you said, what was presented in the SAD component of the study at some of the higher dose levels, 200, particularly 200 and 400 milligrams, we saw some immune-related AEs, specifically pyrexia, headaches, some ISRs. In terms of the ISRs, I mean they're generally consistent with what we've seen and what others have reported with siRNA therapeutics in terms of duration of activity. I'd say when it comes to dose selection, we still don't have all the data.

We need to get the PD and the safety data for all of the MAD cohorts through their second dose and then pick what looks the cleanest and what gives us the best combination of knockdown and safety.

Dr. Christopher Anzalone: Yes, I think that's critical that the data that you've seen so far is just single-dose data. We would expect for at least some doses, a further step down upon second dosing. So we will see what the right doses are. I think there's a reasonable chance that it's going to be less than 200 milligrams.

Operator: And one moment for our next question, and that will come from the line of Luca Issi with RBC.

Jiayi Yuan: Congrats on the quarter. This is Cassie for Luca. And coming back to the APOC3 launch and REDEMPLO, both you and Ionis have described having another competitor in the market as a tailwind. Recently we've learned that the Quick Start program that Ionis has adopted is essentially a bridge program before patients get covered. So wanted to get your thoughts on if REDEMPLO follows a similar playbook here for FCS, given that many of the patients may be first-to-therapy and not yet approved.

And related to it, is there a version of the world where maybe you don't see as many of your patients having to go through such a program, because one, going back to the point of having a competitor in the market, it would be a tailwind providers are already pretty comfortable with the APOC3 class by the time REDEMPLO arrives; and two, for REDEMPLO, perhaps you're getting some switch patients who already qualified coverage. Any color on how we should think about your new-to-class versus same-class switch patients, both in FCS and the upcoming SHTG launch, would be super helpful.

Andy Davis: Yes, thanks, Cassie, I can take the first part of that question. So like any rare disease launch, we do have a quick start bridge program ourselves and a patient assistance program so patients can start therapy while coverage is being established. And so we would expect a quick start program to be in place for SHTG as well, should we be -- should we indicated for that next year. What matters to us is that patients in the end convert to paid therapy as payer policies are put in place, and what matters is that persistence is high once these patients are on therapy.

So we will be heavily focused on ensuring that appropriate patients can get on REDEMPLO, whether that's through a paid claim or through a quick start program as their coverage is being determined, and helping support them with our patient access program so they can remain on therapy.

Operator: One moment for our next question, and that will come from the line of Andrea Newkirk with Goldman Sachs.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Bernan ]. At the recent Liver Meeting, Regeneron reported some proof-of-concept data for its CIDEB targeted siRNA in an all-comer MASLD population, and I'm just curious in light of this how you view the mechanistic positioning of ARO-PNPLA3, which you are partnered with Madrigal on, recognizing that, that may have efficacy only in a smaller subset of patients. And then in parallel to that, as others have stepped back from HSD to prioritize these other targets, I'm curious what your scientific conviction is in ARO-HSD to drive that clinically meaningful antifibrotic effect that may be independent of steatosis reduction.

James Hamilton: I can take both of those. So the first question about PNPLA3, you'd have to ask Madrigal what their plan is with that in terms of how they plan the development of populations to look at. I would highlight one other presentation that was interesting at AASLD that implied even on GLPs that patients that were homozygous for the I148M PNPLA3 variant seemed to have less of a reduction in liver fat. So there might be an opportunity there for combination therapy. But again, this is all up to Madrigal. And the same is true for HSD really.

That asset, of course, has been licensed to GSK, and so any development plans around where that one would go are up to GSK exclusively.

Operator: One moment for our next question, and that will come from the line of James Condulis with Stifel.

James Condulis: Maybe one going back to trigs here. Just curious what your latest thinking is around how many patients in the U.S. have had a prior pancreatitis event, and just in general, I guess kind of what you think the timeline and path is to really getting broad uptake outside those patients and kind of more of the primary prevention setting.

Andy Davis: Yes. Thanks, James. We estimate there are around 200,000 patients in the U.S. who have a prior history of AP due to high triglycerides. And that range -- there are various estimates on that, but we think that's a fairly good range for your modeling. Clearly, that is the population of highest unmet medical need. It was clearly determined through the data that was reported at AHA this past week, and that of the 2 variables of importance here -- high TGs and prior history of AP, prior history of AP pancreatitis is a very, very key determinant of recurrent AP, and the number needed to treat in those population, that secondary prevention population was incredibly high.

And so clearly that will be a heavy focus for us as we head into the SHTG launch. It's also a high willingness to prescribe from providers and a high willingness to pay from payers. Clearly, it will take some more time over the years to continue to expand into the broader SHTG population. As you would be aware, that high-risk segment we think is about 1/3 of the broader SHTG population, so about 1 million out of 3 to 3.5 million.

So it will take a little bit more time to penetrate that broader SHTG population, and that will largely depend on favorable payer policies, and we do anticipate that those payer policies will allow for penetration of that segment over time.

Dr. Christopher Anzalone: And look, that primary prevention is critical. We know that if you let a patient have a bout of acute pancreatitis, it's more likely that, that person will have another bout of pancreatitis and that it could be even more severe. So it is critical to get these patients on treatment before they're in trouble.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Joseph Thome with TD Cowen.

Joseph Thome: Maybe on the obesity ALK7 program, I guess how clear is the FDA guidance on what you would need to do next if the data are supportive? Is there a clear registrational path for a combination approach? And do you see a path forward to study the agent as a monotherapy, or commercially do you not think that's going to be the way to go here, basically, future obesity treatments are going to be some form of combination?

James Hamilton: Well, we've said all along that we think that either one of these, if we study them as a fat-loss or weight-loss drug, would be a combination that would be on top of a GLP-1 or in combination with a GLP-1, and that's still our strategy. In terms of what that development pathway looks like, I mean, the guidance for obesity drugs is a little bit old. I think the 5% weight loss, that may still be relevant, but of course there's a lot of combination products out there. So I would imagine we're not the only company that's having these combination-type questions and discussions with the FDA.

I don't have the definitive answer for you in terms of what this would look like from a development and regulatory pathway for the combination product. That's our plan largely, to continue to look at both of these in combination with the GLPs.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Madison El-Saadi with B. Riley.

Madison Wynne El-Saadi: Maybe with focusing on ARO-DIMER, on a patient-by-patient basis, did the biomarker knockdown move together? For example, did anyone achieve deep APOC3 lowering but weak PCSK9 lowering, or the reverse? And then secondly, across the cohorts, is there a responder profile emerging based on triglyceride level?

James Hamilton: Yes, I think in general they move together. Maybe you get a little slightly better APOC3 knockdown at lower doses, but we're able to get plenty of PCSK9 knockdown. So they move pretty much in lockstep as we dose escalate. And so far the response, like we've seen with plozasiran, has been pretty homogeneous. I mean, there's not really patients who we've called non-responders or hyper-responders. So I don't think we can pinpoint any population that's more likely to respond than others, at least not at this point.

Operator: One moment for our next question. And that will come from the line of Patrick Trucchio with H.C. Wainwright.

Patrick Trucchio: Just a follow-up on ARO-MAPT. I'm wondering what the next patient data set is that can connect the CSF total tau lowering to an effect on disease biology, and what result would justify advancing toward a registrational program? And what will determine the sequencing of Alzheimer's disease, MAPT-associated frontotemporal dementia, and progressive supranuclear palsy development?

James Hamilton: So, we're looking at the latter right now, meaning MAPT, FTD and PSP, and we've got study designs for Phase IIs or things that could be adaptive and progress potentially even into Phase III, and having some of those regulatory discussions now. Based on the knockdown data we have from healthy volunteers, we think that showing the knockdown and the safety is sufficient to at least get Phase II studies up and running in those indications. And eventually we'll look more at Phase IIs in Alzheimer's, but we have the Alzheimer's cohorts in the current study up and running, and I'd like to get some data from those cohorts first.

In terms of bridging data, I think the next data points from this program are still going to be in the healthy volunteers, probably the multi-dose healthy-volunteer safety and MAPT reduction data will come out first. Then beyond that, we'll have Alzheimer's patient data, of course, safety and then total tau knockdown, but also starting to look at some of the phospho-tau, the p-tau181, p-tau217, those are probably somewhat bridging biomarkers, indicating that we're influencing, sort of, more disease-relevant biomarkers downstream. And then of course, PET data, the PET tau data will probably come more towards the end of the year.

But those are the next few bridging biomarkers that we anticipate to help us make a call if we want to take something forward into later-stage Alzheimer's development.

Dr. Christopher Anzalone: Yes, I think qualitatively, I think it's fair to say that we are moving quickly in PSP and FTD and slowly in Alzheimer's.

Operator: I'm showing no further questions in the queue at this time. I would now like to turn the call over to Mr. Chris Anzalone for any closing remarks.

Dr. Christopher Anzalone: Thanks, everyone, for joining us today, and I wish you all a nice Thanksgiving holiday in the next couple of weeks.

Operator: This concludes today's program. Thank you all for participating. You may now disconnect.
