#3079. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on these 3 dividend stocks for passive income

The uncertainty in the Middle East and concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom and high spending continue to weigh on investor sentiment. Investors can consider strengthening their portfolios by adding dividend stocks.

Tracking top Wall Street analysts can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts provide useful insights after thorough analysis of a company's financials and growth prospects.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

This week's first dividend pick is natural gas producer Expand Energy, which recently announced the $1.25 billion acquisition of Twin Eagle Holdings, a private asset-backed natural gas marketing and optimization business. The deal is expected to accelerate EXE's marketing and commercial goals.

Meanwhile, Expand Energy impressed investors with solid second-quarter results. It repurchased shares worth $530 million in Q2 2026 and announced an additional $1 billion of buyback authorization. Expand declared a dividend of nearly 58 cents per share, payable on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend per share of $2.30, EXE stock offers a dividend yield of 2.5%.

Following the Q2 print, Wolfe Research analyst Doug Leggate reiterated a buy rating on EXE stock and raised his price target to $114 from $110. The five-star analyst noted that Expand delivered market-beating adjusted earnings per share and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, driven by better gas realizations and lower gathering, processing, and transportation expenses.

"Solid 2Q26 with in-line guidance keeps our focus on what it can control, walking the line between options to return value to s/holders," said Leggate.

As Expand Energy continues to weigh options to enhance shareholder returns, Leggate believes that net debt reduction is the best choice. He highlighted that the company repaid $1.3 billion of gross debt in April, supported by seasonally higher cash flows in the first quarter. EXE ended Q2 2026 with $3.1 billion in net debt. Leggate views buybacks as the second-best option and mergers and acquisitions as the third, with the Twin Eagle deal expected to lower Expand's breakeven by about 7 cents from about $2.80/Mcf.

Leggate ranks No. 807 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.1%. See Expand Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to SM Energy, an operator of oil and gas assets across four leading U.S. shale basins: the Permian Basin, DJ Basin, South Texas, and Uinta Basin. SM offers a quarterly dividend of 22 cents per share, or an annualized dividend of 88 cents per share, representing a yield of about 2.7%.

Following a preliminary update on Q2 metrics, Roth analyst Leo Mariani reaffirmed a buy rating on SM Energy stock and raised his price target to $34 from $32. The analyst cited higher oil prices and his optimism about a strong second-quarter report as the reasons for the upgraded price target.

Commenting on the key insights from the Q2 preliminary update, Mariani noted strong oil and gas price realizations in the quarter. However, the update reflected a slightly larger cash hedging loss of $220 million from derivatives, compared to Roth's estimate of about $211 million.

Meanwhile, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow per share estimate by 3%, citing a strong Q2 2026 pricing update. Mariani added that he expects SM Energy to report strong Q2 2026 results on Aug. 5, with oil production of 237,650 barrels of oil per day, which is around 1.5% above the Street's estimate. He expects capital expenditure of $820 million, in line with consensus.

"We rate SM Energy a Buy based on its reasonable returns of capital to shareholders, its discounted valuation vs. peers, and its upside potential in the Austin Chalk and Uinta plays," said Mariani.

Mariani ranks No. 65 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 27%. See SM Energy Financials on TipRanks.

Oilfield services provider SLB, formerly known as Schlumberger, reported better-than-expected Q2 earnings. The company attributed its Q2 performance to sequential growth across international markets, mainly led by offshore activity in Latin America, Europe and Africa, as well as Asia, helping offset disruptions in the Middle East due to the U.S.-Iran conflict.

SLB announced a quarterly cash dividend of almost 30 cents per share, payable on Oct. 8. At an annualized dividend per share of $1.18, SLB's yield stands at 2.4%.

Reacting to the Q2 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on SLB stock with a price target of $62. "Given SLB's position within international OFS, we reiterate our Buy rating and see forward activity expectations as a driver of earnings," said the analyst.

Within Goldman's oilfield services coverage, Mehta is optimistic about SLB as he expects the company to benefit from a recovery in international activity. The five-star analyst projects international revenue growth of about 10% between 2026 and 2027, driven by SLB's exposure to incremental intervention activity and a recovery in Middle East activity. He also expects international revenue to gain from higher offshore activity and a potential ramp-up of exploration activity across several geographies.

Furthermore, Mehta's bullish stance is backed by long-term growth prospects of SLB's data center business. He noted that the company expects the annual run-rate revenue of this business to exceed $2 billion by the end of 2027, with the potential to grow the customer base and products. Mehta also expects SLB to deliver strong free cash flow and shareholder returns this year, driven by higher activity and unique business lines.

Mehta ranks No. 666 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.4%. See SLB Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3078. 19 Ways To Rethink Network Design For Distributed Workloads

As workloads spread across cloud, edge and on-premises environments, network designs built around centralized infrastructure may no longer deliver the performance, security or flexibility businesses need. Longstanding assumptions about predictable traffic patterns and trusted internal networks can create bottlenecks, security gaps and other challenges.

Technology teams must determine which established network-design practices still make sense and which need to change to support more distributed operations. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council share longstanding network-design assumptions worth reconsidering and explain how businesses can adapt their approaches.

The assumption I’d revisit is that your network still has one front door. Workloads now run across cloud, edge and on-prem, so security needs to follow identity and applications, not a physical location. - Victor Cardona, SecureX

I think we need to stop treating broad network reachability as the starting point. We spend a lot of effort connecting campuses, clouds and data centers, only to add layers of policy to restrict communication afterward. Instead, we should design connectivity around what each user, device or workload actually needs to reach, with those boundaries enforced by the network from day one. This would greatly reduce exposure and operational complexity. - Jaswanth Kongara, Nile

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Businesses should revisit the assumption that they know where their network begins and ends. As application traffic moves between cloud, edge and on-premises environments, it crosses boundaries traditional monitoring tools weren’t designed to see. Network design must account for this movement, with end-to-end visibility into how these environments work together to deliver services. - Pavel Bykov, IP Fabric

Businesses should rethink the assumption that applications can always rely on a centralized data infrastructure. As workloads span regions and environments, networks must be designed for inevitable disruptions, not perfect connectivity. That means distributing data closer to applications while maintaining consistency, low latency and availability even when connections or entire regions fail. - Karthik Ranganathan, Yugabyte

Stop assuming that everything needs to route through a central cloud or data center. As workloads spread, the network must support decisions and actions where data is created and consumed. My test is simple: If connectivity to the cloud disappears, what stops working? That answer reveals whether you’ve designed a distributed architecture or simply stretched a centralized one across more locations. - Emma McGrattan, Actian

The design should be requirement-driven, starting with the application’s business criticality, expected throughput, latency tolerance and availability requirements. Those factors, not simply where the workload runs, should determine the connectivity, bandwidth and resilience an application needs. - Devendra Rajput, Accenture

Drop the misguided and outdated belief that being inside the network, or on the same cluster, means being trusted. With modern virtualization technology, workload location and network segmentation between them say very little about risk. Apps on the same infrastructure often share more than a network link, so the blast radius isn’t defined solely by the network. Draw the boundary around each workload, block everything by default, and allow only what is needed. - Claude Mandy, Edera

There is a broad assumption that achieving zero trust means routing every user, application and data flow through the cloud. But if our hybrid workforces have proven anything, it’s that this assumption is false. Rather than forcing every flow through the cloud and accepting the higher costs that come with it, enterprises must apply data security where work actually happens across offices, remote users, private applications, SaaS, cloud and AI environments. - Thyaga Vasudevan, Skyhigh Security

Retire the assumption that connectivity equals resilience. A network can be connected yet fragile when critical applications depend on distant services, congested routes or a single point of failure. Design around business-critical transactions, verified access and recoverability. The board does not buy connectivity. It buys confidence that the enterprise can keep operating when something breaks. - Kelvin Cheema

Revisit the idea that one central region can serve everybody. It can’t. Serve Latin America from North American or European infrastructure, and latency kills you—and voice fails first. Then regulation hits, and the first thing a new AI rule asks is where the data sits. So, place inference where your customers are. Latency and residency: Design for both, up front. - Merlin Bise, Inbenta

The concept of an enterprise WAN/LAN is outdated. The apps, services and computing required by a corporation are no longer hosted within a closed enterprise network. Security is now established at the application layer, not the physical network layer. But I still see enterprises managing private networks, spending millions on border protection and routers. The assumption that you need a corporate network needs to be revisited. - Siddhartha Rao, Oracle

Don’t assume two carriers give you two independent network paths. Both connections may still run through the same conduit or building entry point. For critical cloud and edge workloads, trace the physical routes, look for shared failure points, and test failover. One construction accident could otherwise take out both the primary and backup links. - Nicholas Domnisch, EE Solutions

Reconsider the assumption that healthy connections mean a healthy business workflow. For example, agentic AI can send a single task across models, tools and data in cloud, edge and on-premises environments. Each connection may work well individually, yet the overall task becomes slow, costly or unreliable. Network design must account for the entire environment, including how those interactions combine to deliver a business outcome. - Casey Kindiger, Droma (formerly Grokstream)

Revisit the assumption that more bandwidth fixes slow applications. A workflow making repeated, sequential calls between cloud and on-premises systems can spend most of its time waiting. Trace one complete transaction and count the round trips. Put tightly coupled work near its data before buying a bigger connection. - Nikhil Jathar, AvanSaber Technologies

I would challenge the assumption that moving data is always easier than moving computation. As workloads spread across cloud and edge environments, repeatedly transferring large datasets can increase latency, cost and exposure. I believe network architecture should consider where processing happens, not just how systems connect. Sometimes the better design is to bring computation closer to the data. - Prajkta Waditwar, Box Inc.

One assumption is that networks only transport data. With edge and generative AI increasing, networks are connecting complex intelligence models. Design must consider where decisions happen, how fast action must follow, industry type and cybersecurity protocols. Applications like autonomous driving need real-time decisions close to the sensor, whereas chatbot decisions can reside in the cloud. - Sachin Khanna, IQSIGHT

Stop sizing networks around average traffic. AI inference, replication, backups and edge synchronization create short, extreme bursts that can overwhelm links even when monthly utilization looks healthy. Engineer for burst envelopes and priority classes so critical exchanges are protected when background traffic spikes. - Akhilesh Sharma, A3Logics Inc.

Revisit the assumption that every workload needs to run close to the user. A chat reply feels slow with an extra 100 milliseconds; a video generation job that takes a minute or two to render won’t be noticed. I’d sort AI workloads by how much delay users will tolerate and send the ones users are patient about wherever GPU capacity is available and cheapest. - Jerry Tang, Atlas Cloud

Businesses should revisit the assumption that a workload has one permanent home. Cost, performance, data and resilience may move workloads between the cloud, edge and on-premises environments. The network should make that movement seamless, with connectivity, access and security policies following the workload wherever it runs. - Alex Spokoiny, Check Point Software

TMC the metals company Inc. (TMC -6.31%) reported a strategic transition toward a capital-light offshore production model designed to reduce upfront capital requirements by $500 million. Management stated that the company will initially deploy an upgraded version of its proven pilot collection system to target 1 million tonnes of annual production, rather than starting with a full-scale 3 million tonne system. This phased approach is intended to protect the production schedule while reducing engineering and integration complexity. Onshore, the company is pursuing a dual-track strategy by utilizing a tolling arrangement with PAMCO in Japan as a bridge to a permanent U.S. processing facility at the Port of Brownsville, Texas. Management indicated that this approach allows for positive EBITDA potential during the first two years of operations while deferring significant capital expenditures until higher production scales are reached.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to The Metals Company Third Quarter 2026 Corporate Update Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Craig Shesky. Please go ahead.

Craig Shesky: Thank you, Kevin. And I'd now like to turn the call over to our Chairman and CEO, Gerard Barron. Gerard, please go ahead.

Gerard Barron: Yes. Thank you, Craig, and thanks to all of you for joining us today. Before we dive in, I'd like to take the time to welcome our new Board member, Liam Mallon. Liam is a former President of ExxonMobil Upstream, and he joins us at a very exciting time as we prepare to move from exploration into commercial operations. And Liam brings more than 40 years of global energy and offshore operating experience, having led ExxonMobil's worldwide upstream business, overseeing $20 billion to $30 billion in annual capital investment, and he played a central role in some of the energy industry's most significant developments, from ExxonMobil's landmark offshore project in Guyana to a $60 billion acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources.

And since taking up his seat in September, we've benefited greatly from his expertise in moving complex and novel offshore operations into production. And Liam will chair our Sustainability and Innovation Committee, and he will be tasked in helping our project and environmental teams to improve project economics and manage environmental impacts. And my team and I look forward to his contributions moving forward. So to the agenda, we'll start with U.S. permitting, where our USA-A consolidated application stands with NOAA and the milestones ahead. Offshore, we'll walk through an updated plan we've built with Allseas that protects our schedule and cuts nearly $500 million from the capital needed to reach first production.

And onshore, we'll update you on Brownsville, where Mariana Minerals is leading feasibility-level engineering and U.S. government funding agencies are now working together on our Nodule City plan. We'll also cover a capital-light option to start by toll processing our nodules in Japan. And on the environment, we'll share our new peer-reviewed papers from our deep-sea data set published ahead of the environmental impact statement and how the research community is putting that open data to use. We'll then cover our partnerships and close with financial highlights and liquidity. So let's begin with permitting, specifically on our consolidated application over the USA-A area.

Following the application's publication to the Federal Register as reported last quarter, NOAA opened the first of several public comment periods to get the public's view on our application. The comment period closed on October 19, and NOAA is now reviewing those comments as part of its application review. Many of you were watching for certification in October. And as I shared earlier this week, NOAA has told us in a letter that it now expects to decide on certification by mid-December. This is taking longer than we had hoped, but ours is the first consolidated application done under DSHMRA and NOAA's new review process. And the regulator is rightly following the statute step by step.

Importantly, NOAA has not identified any issues or deficiency with our application. So what is certification? Well, it's NOAA's formal finding that TMC has the requisite finances and access to the technologies needed to commercially collect nodules and a rigorous plan to conduct such activities as required under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act. It also locks in the size and location of our area of activity and signals the transition into the final environmental review stage prior to the issuance of the commercial recovery permit.

Assuming a positive certification decision in mid-December, the application will then proceed into environmental review phase with NOAA publishing a notice of intent for this process publication of a draft environmental impact statement and the draft terms, conditions and restrictions and the required public comment periods before NOAA makes its final determination. This slide shows the remaining path for USA-A consolidated application. Since we last reported in August, NOAA has published the consolidated application in the Federal Register and as mentioned, has completed the first of several 60-day public comment periods and online webinars. The rigor of this review is ultimately helpful to the permit's legal defensibility in the coming decades.

It also helps ensure that there are no rubber stamps available for newer applicants that have not completed anywhere near the same level of work as TMC, its subsidiaries and our world-class partners. We've got some exciting developments with our offshore system to share. We've been working closely with Allseas on an updated offshore development plan with a clear purpose, protect our time line, derisk the system and move quickly into first production upon issuance of our commercial recovery permit. Instead of starting with the full 3 million tonne per annum system, we'll begin at 1 million tonnes per annum using an upgraded version of our proven pilot system.

That cuts engineering, procurement and integration complexity, lowers the upfront capital for both TMC and Allseas and means we can start commercial production as soon as possible after our permit is granted during the current administration. We'll then stage the major investments alongside the production ramp-up. So less capital is at risk in the early stages, running the system in sustained production builds operating experience demonstrates reliability and derisks the move to full scale. The result is a faster, leaner start and that stays close to our original 5-year ramp-up and gets the system out on the water sooner. This is good for TMC and Allseas and ultimately good for our shareholders.

The foundation of this plan is a simplified operating configuration with lower logistic costs, which builds upon the systems successfully demonstrated during our 6-month offshore pilot in 2022. The vast majority of the direct CapEx reduction comes from simplifying and upgrading the existing pilot production system and eliminating the transfer vessel. And this also allows us to eliminate the vast majority of long-lead-time items, which helps derisk the time line to first production in addition to a reduction of upfront CapEx.

Collectively, changes to the scope of the system reduced the estimated upfront capital required to reach first production from roughly $800 million under our prior schedule, of which TMC's share was approximately $500 million to roughly $300 million shared between the parties. Much of the remaining investment will be deferred to subsequent development phases. The simplified operating configuration and lower logistic costs also improved the economics of the initial operations, providing the potential to reach positive EBITDA even at the lower production volumes targeted during the first 2 years. So what does this mean in practice?

Well, by upgrading and scaling up the production system proven during our offshore pilot, we can reuse existing equipment and operate this upgraded system during the first 2 years of commercial production, deferring the full capacity equipment packages and more complex transfer interfaces until they are needed while maintaining our original production ramp-up targets. We plan on upgrading the existing 6-meter-wide pilot collector to 9 meters, deferring the new collectors until the point we are comfortable we can sustain production over long periods of time. And at the lower production rates anticipated during the early years, we can eliminate the need for a dedicated transfer vessel instead use -- instead load our nodules directly onto bulk carriers.

And by transshipping on U.S. West Coast before onward shipment to Japan, we can also combine nodule transport with regular offshore logistics, reducing the number of dedicated supply vessels required. Keep in mind, this is technology that both Allseas and TMC know very well, and it will undergo further optimization and testing during Allseas' upcoming Japan pilot program. So in short, the perfect proven foundation for the start of commercial operations. And rather than deploying the full 3 million tonne system from the outset, this upgraded pilot collection system will target approximately 1 million tonnes annually with the potential to increase up to 1.5 million in year 2.

And this fits with our existing production ramp-up strategy with the objective of maintaining the planned annual production profile as we progress towards 12 million tonnes across 4 production vessels. Building on our successful 2022 pilot with further optimization and testing planned by Allseas during the upcoming Japan pilot program, we intend to upgrade the existing collector, limit initial modifications to the Hidden Gem and simplify offshore transport and logistics. And these changes reduce complexity and both capital and operating costs. I'd like to now turn over to Craig to walk through our onshore partnerships as well as our latest environmental work and our financials.

Craig Shesky: Thanks, Gerard. So onshore, again, our primary objective remains, build a greenfield processing and refining facility in Brownsville, Texas. But having it up and running in time to receive the first nodules from our offshore operations may be a challenge given our anticipated permitting time line. And that's where we may lean on, as we noted, our 5-year partnership with PAMCO and their existing processing facility in Hachinohe, Japan, where they've been processing nickel laterites for many decades and where we successfully conducted an industrial-scale pilot in 2024 to 2025.

PAMCO will need to make some modifications to its plant to prepare for the arrival of first nodules, and our team and external engineering consultants have been in Hachinohe this week working through those plans just to make sure those schedules align. So taking a step back, PAMCO's history of smelting nickel laterite ores goes all the way back to the 1960s. And over the years, they built up significant processing infrastructure with 3 furnaces spread across the existing site.

Our history of working together is a bit shorter, but we have accomplished a remarkable amount over the past 5 years, including industrial-scale pilot processing, demonstrating technical feasibility of the process using existing architecture and a feasibility study demonstrating economic viability using their 80-megawatt furnace. So we know what needs to be done to bring the facility on-spec in preparation for nodules. And suffice it to say that our discussions with the U.S. government do include the potential of this attractive option at the start of production. And certainly, members of the U.S. government are in Japan as we speak, discussing the burgeoning seafloor minerals industry.

And you may have seen just moments ago, the U.S. and Japanese governments published a joint statement, which puts seabed minerals front and center of their plans to diversify mineral supply and support their industrial bases. And 2 particular lines from the State Department's release stand out: foster trusted commercial partnerships and secure processing capacity among trusted partners. PAMCO fits that bill perfectly. But again, we remain laser-focused on ultimately bringing nodule processing to the U.S.A. As a reminder, TMC USA holds an exclusive right of negotiation over a lease option for land at the Port of Brownsville.

The location provides direct access to the Brownsville shipping channel and sufficient land to evaluate an integrated processing and refining ecosystem serving TMC USA and potentially over time, other American operators. No investment decision has been made. And as we've said a few times before, any future capital commitment will remain contingent on U.S. government support. But we have started laying this groundwork to prepare for when bulk carriers with full nodule holds can begin arriving on U.S. shores. Site-specific feasibility work is a prerequisite for any potential U.S. government support, and we're happy to report that work is now well advanced.

And the Brownsville area under consideration covers nearly 1,500 acres across 2 parcels: 735 acres on the Shipping Channel and adjacent 731 acres. Prefeasibility level engineering is nearly complete and feasibility level engineering for the first smelting stage, as we mentioned previously, is underway, along with Mariana Minerals' leadership as part of TMC's ownership -- excuse me, owner's team. The engineering team is also testing the interfaces among the berth, ship unloaders, conveyors, stockpiles, processing facilities, utilities and supporting infrastructure, along with material flows, constructability and opportunities to phase future development.

And in late October, our TMC USA project team as well as our executive team spent 4 days in San Francisco with our partners at Mariana Minerals hosted at their San Francisco Bridge facility. Since we signed an MOU in April last year, the partnership has moved fast, and we signed a strategic partnership in March and a master service agreement in July. Mariana is a core part of our owner's team for Nodule City, which is, again, our proposed industrial park at the Port of Brownsville in Texas.

And in San Francisco, the teams reviewed the engineering completed to date and focused on 3 things: one, refining the plant's process flows, including the controls needed to meet stringent U.S. environmental requirements; two, identifying ways to bring down CapEx and OpEx; and three, aligning on a permitting strategy for this Brownsville site. And that work feeds directly into the next phase of development. We also want to take a moment to highlight some of the exciting developments with our royalty holder, TMCR, where The Metals Company holds a 20% equity interest in their stock.

And on September 28, Mesabi Metallics announced plans at the White House for a $15 billion steel complex in Iowa, described as the largest in U.S. history. Alongside its 2% royalty on our NORI area, TMCR holds a 2% gross production royalty on Mesabi's Minnesota mine, although they do not have interest in the Iowa complex. So we would like to commend the teams at both Mesabi and The Metals Royalty Company on the significant step forward in rebuilding America's domestic steel supply chain. And of course, as we know, steel requires manganese as well as iron ore and America's reindustrialization will depend on secure supplies of all 4 metals found in nodules, including manganese, nickel, copper and cobalt.

So on to some developments in our environmental program. Our vast deep-sea environmental data set, by far the industry's largest, continues to bear fruit as more of the data contained is published in peer-reviewed journals. And I'd like to highlight a few recent papers today. The first, published this week in the Journal of Marine Science and Engineering, presents the first commercial-scale sediment plume modeling showing that the vast majority of mobilized sediment settles within 10 meters of collector tracks with plumes dissipating within 2 to 5 days of operation ceasing.

The second paper, in press and soon to be published in that same journal, documents TMC's world-first environmental monitoring of an integrated collection system trial in near real-time and the technical expertise and choreography required to gather the empirical data that is essential to inform commercial-scale modeling. These new papers bring total peer-reviewed studies based on our data set to 46 with almost 220 citations by other researchers. But this is just scratching the surface. Our data set is 1 petabyte, among the largest single-project data sets ever compiled, larger than the Hubble Space Telescope archive, 1000 Genomes database and Sloan Digital Sky Survey combined.

And this will continue to deliver new insights with hundreds of papers expected in the coming months and years, particularly as we advance towards intensely monitored commercial operations. The size and scale of our decade-plus research effort and the resulting data set was on full display at the Underwater Minerals Conference in Japan this week, which we were pleased to attend and many of our team members were there for the first time, along with many members of others in the industry and many people who have been publishing work based on TMC data.

In fact, roughly half of all environmental research, whether delivered in presentation or poster format, was based on data collected during our offshore campaigns, reaffirming the immense value of our extensive investment in scientific research, and that investment has eclipsed $250 million to date. Members of our team as well as our research partners shared insights on a broad array of topics, including assessments of benthic impacts and recovery following test mining, sediment plume dynamics and monitoring, and the spatial distribution of dissolved metals. And our onshore team also presented on the development of our near-zero solid waste flow sheet. The conference is wrapping up this week.

And from where we sit, it was incredibly satisfying to see firsthand how our findings are shaping this new industry. So hopping to the financials, liquidity and valuation. As I'm sure you're all aware, the industry valuation metrics have moved down sharply since August. And while nickel and copper developers were valued at about 58% of NAV just 3 months ago, that same metric is now down to 34%. For producers, it's moved down from about 100% of NAV to 80%. And unfortunately, for TMC, we're valued at just 4% of the underlying net asset value for our SEC-compliant technical reports.

Bottom line, these valuations are swinging in our view, based on short-term technical and political factors rather than long-term realities for these metals that continue to be critical for the global economy. So rest assured, Gerard and I will be busy on the road in the coming months talking to new and existing investors about this very undervalued opportunity. Moving to liquidity. TMC liquidity, defined as cash plus borrowing capacity, stood at $123 million as of September 30, 2026, including $44 million available from our undrawn credit facility.

In the third quarter of 2026, TMC reported a net loss of approximately $28.4 million or $0.06 per share compared to a net loss of $185 million or $0.46 per share for the same period in 2025. The net loss for the third quarter of 2026 included exploration and evaluation expenses of $23.5 million versus $9.6 million in Q3 2025; G&A of $9.5 million, versus $45.7 million in Q3 2025; and other non-operating items totaling a gain of $4.6 million, versus the $125 million loss a quarter -- excuse me, a year ago in third quarter 2025.

Exploration and evaluation increased by $13.9 million in the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, mainly due to higher costs to recognize the full charge of ongoing development, operating and vessel costs. The increase also reflects higher share-based compensation, increase in feasibility and pre-feasibility study costs and increase in legal and professional costs related to the project. G&A expenses decreased by $36 million in Q3 2026 as compared to the same period due to $33 million lower share-based compensation expense and a decrease in legal fees.

Other non-operating items in Q3 2026 include the following: a decrease in the NORI royalty liability of $5 million, driven by an increase in the risk-free rate used to value the liability, which compares to an increase in the royalty liability of $131 million in the comparable quarter. There was also an increase of $4.4 million in equity-accounted investments resulting from TMCR's higher share-based compensation and changes in the fair value of derivative instruments and other financing costs. Net cash used in operating activities in Q3 2026 amounted to $19.4 million in comparison to $11.5 million in Q3 2025.

The increase in the outflow in Q3 2026 is mainly due to increased costs for the scaling of the nodule collection system, including $7.7 million in cash payments, fees, payroll, pre-feasibility, stakeholder engagement costs and legal and consulting fees. Free cash outflow for Q3 2026 was negative $19.4 million compared to negative $11.5 million in Q3 2025. And free cash flow is a non-GAAP measure, and I would point you to the non-GAAP reconciliation table included at the end of the slide deck. We do believe that our cash on hand is sufficient to meet working capital and CapEx commitments for at least the next 12 months from today.

And investments increased by $18 million, primarily due to $26.9 million in dilution gains on investment, partially offset by $9.2 million for our share of the loss in our TMCR investment. The warranty -- excuse me, the warrant liability decreased due to the expiration of all outstanding private warrants in Q3 and the royalty liability decreased by $5 million, driven by an increase, as said before, in the risk-free rate used to value the liability. With that, operator, we would like to take a moment to open it up to any questions from the audience.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Heiko with H.C. Wainwright.

Heiko Ihle: Let's talk a bit about the recent election results in the U.S. Can you give a bit of color on if there's been any strategic changes following the recent midterms? Gerard Barron: Well, on the election front, I think it's important to remember that our permitting pathway is through DSHMRA. And DSHMRA, of course, is in statute. And so it is a reliable framework upon which we are applying. And of course, critical minerals are a bipartisan issue, and we believe the timing couldn't be better on one hand. I just -- I'm in Japan at the moment. And this week, I've attended the flagship conference for the underwater minerals sector, where our team highlighted the enormous amount of environmental data that is now becoming available, which really highlights just the concerns that some people have previously had on what are the environmental impacts.

And I think our very heavy investment in first-class environmental research with the help of leading institutions around the world comes together now with all of these -- I think we have 47 papers being published at the moment, peer-reviewed papers, either published or about to be. And what that highlights is that the environmental impacts are all very manageable, that they're a fraction of what people ever thought they were. They are largely contained to the area of extraction. And of course, I think this helps make it a bipartisan issue because critical minerals are essential to the functioning and to the security of the U.S. economy.

And the only time ever -- anyone ever gave a pause was really on the environmental front that we've always maintained that the environment is actually the biggest positive for the development of this resource because of the lower environmental impacts and the lower impacts on humans. So I feel very confident that we'll be spending a lot of time in D.C. There's a lot of new representatives and senators that we need to, I guess, highlight the importance of this resource. And so we're feeling pretty good about it.

Craig Shesky: Yes. And just to add a bit of color on that as well. Again, as we know, what Gerard said at the beginning, NOAA is under the Commerce Department. This is an executive branch agency. And we have been going step by step through the process based on implementing regulations on DSHMRA, where NOAA was given the power to be the regulator for this industry back in the 1980s. So this is in the hands of the executive branch.

But also when we look at the funding side of it, I think a lot of other people, we've seen, Heiko, a lot of names, not just TMC, but others in your coverage, where [ pendulum ] swings back and forth based on the political winds. But the money that's available here and much of it not yet being deployed is generally devoted to certain cabinet departments and agencies based on a reconciliation process and budgeting that has already been approved. So those funds are earmarked and how they want to be spent by the various cabinet departments, many of which now are working together. We're happy to report on the Nodule City potential.

That's all really already devoted to them, and it's not something where we could necessarily see those funds at risk or taken away. Now over time, might there be impacts on future years in terms of appropriations in the reconciliation process, what's available to deploy? Sure. But the money that's already been allocated. And in fact, there's a good article from MINING.COM this week where they interviewed Clark Street Associates about this very point. So both on the money front as well as the permitting front, we feel we're in a very good position despite some of the narrative that's out there in the market. But again, this is not about an executive order.

This is about a clear regulatory statute that we're following step by step.

Heiko Ihle: Yes. That's a very fair and very comprehensive answer. And I think it probably soothes some of the concerns that I've gotten on the phone, and I appreciate the color. And then just a quick one. You were talking about the lower CapEx Hidden Gem and how you're planning on converting it in year 3 while it's being in production. And I'm just trying to figure out how exactly that's supposed to work. How do you anticipate having the assets stay operational while you like increase capacity on there?

Gerard Barron: No, that would be a swap out. So essentially, we -- as custodians of your capital, we're very mindful of restoring value to the equity. And of course, we are confident that as we can show that we can -- as we show how we move into commercial production, the most important thing is to get started because then it's widely acknowledged that the size and the quality of this resource. I mean, we've defined 1.6 billion tonnes. We think we have another 300 million to 400 million tonnes in the area that we've applied for. So now talk about 2 billion tonnes of high-grade nickel, copper, cobalt, manganese.

And if you put the copper and the copper equivalents, it's around 7-plus percent. So 2 billion tonnes of 7-plus percent copper and copper equivalents. I mean, there's no other resource on the planet that compares. So we took the view that keeping the schedule was of utmost importance, and we just need to get into production. And then, of course, we know that capital will be more widely available. We already have people coming to us with great capital ideas around financing new vessels and operators who want to put vessels to work, providers who would provide finance to enable us to get more boats on the water.

And so we can -- it means that we can defer that investment until what we believe to be more proper and appropriate value is restored to the equity. And so that would be -- we keep the first boat in production until the time is right, but then we would move the second boat on to the area and the third and the fourth.

Craig Shesky: Yes. So Heiko, think of it as really kind of a very short-term miss of production, let's say, when we then expand the Hidden Gem capacity of 3 million tonnes. But doing that expansion, which, by the way, requires the ordering of long-lead-time items, and frankly, would add a bit more risk, not only in terms of money, capital spent, but just what happens if a few items are delayed several months, that's not something you want to deal with if you're waiting to start first production.

But if it's something you can do after production has begun and then the second vessel has come on the water, that's a much better time for us to be able to do those modifications with Allseas, but then also do it at a time when our cost of capital would be much lower.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tate Sullivan with Maxim Group.

Tate Sullivan: Does the updated capital-light plan require meaningful changes to the NOAA application process?

Tate Sullivan: Nothing at all? Okay. And then for PAMCO, the PAMCO and, Craig, you went into the description about making some modifications to a plant in Japan to prepare for nodules. Can you remind us on the terms of the partnership? Would that be sharing those costs on the facility similar to what you're doing with Allseas as well?

Gerard Barron: Yes. Good question. And the Japanese government have already put in place a financing plan to cover up to half of that cost. And we are -- the arrangement with PAMCO is a tolling type arrangement, and we're having that sit down with them currently to see how we might support them to cover the remaining half. But while nothing has been agreed at this stage, it would seem fair that we would make some contribution alongside the PAMCO themselves.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dmitry Silversteyn with Water Tower Research.

Dmitry Silversteyn: Just wondering sort of what drove the revision in how you plan to ramp up production with Hidden Gem going from 3 million tonnes to 1 million tonnes. I mean, I understand the rationale behind it, but I'm just wondering why there was an approach from the beginning and what has changed that you now think this is the right approach?

Gerard Barron: Well, I think the -- keeping the schedule was of paramount importance. And I guess what we've seen are we were perhaps a little bit optimistic on when we might have seen permit in our hands, also optimistic about when we thought a government financing arrangement for Brownsville would be put into place. And so when you combine those 2 things and also combine the fact that the offshore oil and gas sector is quite vibrant at the moment. And so all of those point to tension in the supply chain, and so keeping the schedule was always of paramount importance. And so I guess it became just an obvious decision that we should not jeopardize first production.

As I said earlier, I think it's such a big valuable resource that if we can show the world just that it can be extracted and processed and we can produce these critical minerals, then all of a sudden, we can be valued against that resource as opposed to the first production vessel. As far as the -- I mean, it's a perfect scenario to have the boat moving to Japan to do some work with the Japanese government on some trials and then to be moving on to our license area once the permit is in our hands. And it means that there'll be learnings all the way along that.

And then it's just a methodical way of identifying the next vessel and vessels and taking those learnings and turning them into optimized production systems.

Operator: And I'm not showing any further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to Gerard for any further remarks.

Gerard Barron: Yes. Thank you. And thanks to all our shareholders who have tuned in and who continue to support. I think -- and thank you to all of our -- the team who are working exceptionally hard and our supply chain. And I celebrate the tremendous results we've had this week up in Japan as our team have showcased important environmental papers and results over the last decade or more of environmental research. So yes, so stay tuned. We think it's going to be a very exciting lead into the end of the year, and I look forward to giving you those updates as they become available. Thank you.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but not enough to bust your homebuying budget.

Yes, mortgage interest rates are higher today, but only by a little.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.09% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is nine basis points higher than yesterday and 13 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) dropped the October Consumer Price Index on Tuesday, which shows that inflation rose another 0.4% last month. This outpaced expectations: Economists had forecasted an increase of 0.3%. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, and futures traders are banking on a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Central bankers raised the federal funds rate in September, but it hasn’t been enough to pull inflation closer to the Fed’s target of 2%. Investors aren’t sure that one more hike in December will do the trick, either. According to CME FedWatch, further rate hikes may be in store for January.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.59% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3073. HeartBeam (BEAT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Operating costs fell sharply as its handheld heart monitor advanced through FDA review.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

HeartBeam, Inc. (BEAT -1.78%) reported that heart attack detection is its primary strategic priority, supported by the confirmation of a 510(k) regulatory pathway with the FDA. The company stated that its Breakthrough Device Designation and enrollment in the TAP program have facilitated frequent communication with regulators and payers regarding pivotal study design and reimbursement pathways. Financial results showed a reduction in operating expenses following the completion of primary product development for the HeartBeam cardiac platform and the ALIGN-ACS pilot study. Management indicated that clinical data from the ALIGN-ACS study demonstrated that the handheld 3D ECG device has diagnostic accuracy comparable to a standard 12-lead ECG. The company is currently finalizing its U.S. pivotal study design and expects to commence patient enrollment by the first quarter of 2027.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the HeartBeam Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. Before we begin the formal presentation, I would like to remind everyone that statements made on the call today and webcast may include predictions, estimates, and other information that may be considered forward-looking. While these forward-looking statements represent our current judgment on what the future holds, they are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause results to differ materially. You are cautioned not to place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements, which reflect our opinions only as of the date of this presentation.

Please keep in mind that we are not obligating ourselves to revise or publicly release the results of any revision of these forward-looking statements in light of new information or future events. Throughout today's discussion, we will attempt to present some important factors relating to our business that may affect our predictions. You should also review our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q for a more complete discussion of these factors and other risks, particularly under the heading Risk Factors. A press release detailing these results crossed the wire this afternoon and is available in the Investor Relations section of our company's website, heartbeam.com.

Your hosts today, Richard Ferrari, Executive Chairman; Branislav Vajdic, Founder and President; and Tim Cruickshank, Chief Financial Officer, will present results of operations for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Richard Ferrari.

Richard Ferrari: Thank you, and thanks to all of you that have dialed into the conference call. Let me just walk you through the agenda very briefly. We're going to give you the progress on our key strategic initiatives. We'll bring you updates regarding our cardiac platform and our heart attack detection, which is an incredible milestone that we've achieved this particular quarter. And then finally, we'll close out with the financials. Next slide. The progress on the key strategic priorities.

I think many of you that have been following the company will remember that in July of this year, we outlined our plan going forward, and we organized the focus on our core strategic priorities, which are shown on this particular slide. That was MI detection, working closely with the FDA, working on reimbursement, enhancing the long-term value of the company through AI and the other technological initiatives, and then on the financial side, cost efficiency and tight controls with respect to running the company.

Now, when you look at heart attack detection, I have to say that in the last 90 days, Q3 was a fabulous quarter for achievement, and I think that's a testament we have, and the shift to the priorities that I have already mentioned. When you look at those achievements, these milestones are, for a small company, quite significant. Getting Breakthrough Device Designation, something we were really going after, really wanted to count on. And just to give you sort of a reference point, the FDA, on an average over the last 5, 6, 7 years, only hands out about 164 of these designations.

So it's proof statement that the technology and the opportunity to enhance patients' lives is significant with respect to HeartBeam. That also enabled us to get enrolled, if you will, into their TAP program. Now, the TAP program is also quite significant because it enables us to have faster turnaround with our communications with the FDA. It also opens up CMS and payers so that we can have discussions with them regarding reimbursement and what are the needs that they need to see in our clinical trial to establish reimbursement.

And then I think many of you may know that we had our publication, our presentation at the TCT meeting at the end of October, which again, in our perspective, is the first study, it was 132 patients, first study to really look at, in an emergency room setting, a comparison between the gold standard of the last 50 years, 12-lead EKG, and our handheld device for MI detection. And those results, Branislav will touch on a little bit later in this presentation, which were significant. I don't know that we've said this before.

We did tell you that we were working hard with the FDA with respect to whether or not we would have a 510(k) or a De Novo path. We have a 510(k) path. That's significant because it streamlines our time lines with respect to ultimately getting approval to launch our MI initiatives. And then lastly, again, because of the path and the designation, Breakthrough Device Designation, we're in constant communications actually with the FDA on our pivotal study. We've had a number of interactions with them.

We are very confident in how we've structured that pivotal trial, and we're also very confident that we will getting approval with FDA very shortly on launching that trial and starting it, potentially this year, but certainly in Q1 of 2027. Now on the reimbursement path, we have a reimbursement consultant we're working with, and as I mentioned to you, we will be in discussions with CMS payers, seeing what it is that they need to have from us with respect to the clinical trial results or secondary endpoints that we might put in there that would enable them to go ahead and issue a DRG code for the HeartBeam technology. So we're pleased with the progress we're making there.

On the long-term value and the AI side, we're going to touch on this in a minute, the market opportunity here, which you'll hear me speak about more, is just gigantic actually. And the beauty to what HeartBeam's technology is that, we can embed this technology in several different form factors, which I'll also review. And the real benefit of HeartBeam is on its 3D technology. And you've heard me mention this before, that is the technology we have is simply the best signal capturing and interrogation product that exists. Now that's important because we're moving into utilizing AI to help further streamline the information to physicians, and the richer data one has, the more valuable the information is.

So we're really excited, and Branislav will touch on this, about our AI initiatives. And as Tim will touch on later as well, is what we've been doing in controlling the cost and managing our cash appropriately. Next slide. So I'm going to walk in -- walk us through the HeartBeam cardiac platform for you. So next slide. This slide really depicts, I think, the essence of what it is HeartBeam is dedicated to do.

Patient delay in terms of getting to the hospital from the time that they have the symptom is the #1 cause of death, and there is simply no device that a patient can have with them at their home, on vacation, traveling, that would enable them to determine whether or not they're having a heart attack. And if you look at the data on the left-hand side of that page, it's very, very revealing as to the damage that delay causes. Every 30-minute delay, 8.7% heart failure risk. This is a -- obviously, a big problem for the health care system.

People that have congestive heart failure, they are repeat flyers in and out of the hospital at huge costs in terms of care, and a 7.5% 1-year mortality. And again, at the bottom, very costly approach to delays. So we're very, very excited about, "our initial results," as you'll see from the ALIGN study and what that means, and the fact that we're really just improving how rapidly a patient has a symptom and can get to the hospital. And again, I'll just reinforce this. Currently, there is no home ECG tool that reliably detects heart attacks. So the importance of getting to the hospital is paramount. Next slide.

When you look at the core technology platform, I've said this a few times this morning, but I'll say it again, the size of the TAM, the cardiac platform opportunity that we have is simply one of the largest in the entire health care industry, a $40 billion opportunity affecting 50 million plus patients. And when you squeeze down on the specifics to heart attack detection, those patients that would be at risk, that's 20-plus million people.

So once again, you could see the importance of having a device that was with you at all times, specifically if you had already had balloon angioplasty, cardiac surgery, atrial fibrillation procedure, coronary stents, any predetermined risks related to your genetics in terms of heart health. So our goal is to close that gap between symptom onset and care by giving patients something that they can have with them and get an immediate response. It's a first-of-a-kind portable cable-free EKG device. And it provides a clinical-grade report to a bank of cardiologists that read that information and then provide notification to the patient. On top of that, we have 25 issued patents worldwide incorporating our proprietary technology.

And once again, the signal capturing and the ability to integrate the signal for us, the EKG signal, just opens up tremendous opportunities for us going forward to further and further enhance types of information we're providing to the physicians, the cardiologists, as well as to the patient themselves. Next slide. I think you've also heard us talk about the fact that the technology is already proven. We've already built this technology. We have utilized it in a number of clinical trials. There's nothing more for us to build with respect to the signal capturing and the hardware. All we're doing now is enhancing through AI initiatives.

And because of that, we're capable of taking that technology and putting it into different form factors depending upon the application. So in this particular slide, you see the HeartBeam card, and that will be an item that someone carries with them. As you know, it's just roughly the size of a credit card. It will allow them to determine whether or not they have AFib or whether or not they're having a heart attack. The patch is a different form factor and addresses a different aspect of the market. It's targeted more for the inpatient step-down units where the nurses are circulating and you may have an at-risk cardiac patient staying overnight or 2.

It'd be great if you had a patch on there where they said, "Gee, listen, why don't you put 2 fingers up and let's take a reading and see how you're doing?" But of course, when they're discharged, we want them to go away either with the card or the patch, again, depending upon the specifics of that particular patient.

And then we have what we call the HeartBeam remote unit, and this is, again, same technology, but it's something that we're looking at in terms of outside the United States in more remote locations where towns or villages or what have you, who don't have tremendous access to the new and greatest technology, would in fact be able to offer something to the people of that particular area that would provide, again, the type of information that's so critically important to their cardiac health. So next slide, please. So the heart attack detection and the milestones that we've achieved, now we've touched on this, but this is the road map going forward.

So when you think about HeartBeam, this is the way that you really should value the company, is these next series of steps. And we're really proud of the team that we've got because they execute flawlessly in Q3, and they will execute flawlessly, in my opinion, on these next series of milestones. So we already know positive pilot study data, and Branislav is going to touch on that. So we have agreement with the FDA on 510(k), and we indicated to you previously that we thought that's the way it would go. We are in constant communication with them regarding the pivotal study, mostly regarding the statistical model required, which drives the number of patients.

We're, again, very confident in getting that approval with a study design and a number of patients that we can manage exceedingly well. I mentioned that, and I don't want to be overly optimistic, but it's possible we may enroll the first patient before year-end. But if not, we're very confident in Q1 2027. And again, based on the conversations we're having and the size of the trial that I think we'll be doing, we would expect the pivotal trial to likely be finished mid-2027. And then after that, it's just simply compiling the data and providing that information to the FDA for clearance.

And I can't give too much more information on the time line-related to clearance because a lot of that is dependent upon, "the start of the trial and the number of patients." But when you look at this, the singular word that should come to your mind is execution. We know how to execute, and we know what's exactly required to deliver a green check in every single one of those boxes. And we have a great relationship with the FDA. The Breakthrough Device Designation and the TAP have really enhanced our ability to move through in a really expeditious manner. Next slide, and I'm going to turn it over to Branislav.

Branislav Vajdic: Thank you, Rich. Actually, I would like to emphasize 2 points. The first one is on the alignment with the FDA on our 510(k) pathway, which is a super important step. It clarifies the regulatory path for heart attack assessment, and we believe it shortens that path as well. Secondly, Breakthrough Device Designation and the TAP give us a prioritized interaction and dedicated FDA advisors as we finalize the pivotal study design. We expect to complete pivotal study design in the fourth quarter of this year. So far, the interaction with the FDA, and I have been part of all these interactions, through the Breakthrough and TAP programs have been outstanding.

The level of engagement and availability are providing opportunities for us to iterate faster and provide us with an increased level of confidence. Now, let me walk you through the data behind this progress. Next slide, please. Earlier this month, at TCT 2026 in San Diego, Dr. Graham Nichol of the University of Washington presented the results of our ALIGN-ACS pivotal study. The study enrolled 132 adults at the emergency department of 2 major cardiology centers in Belgrade, Serbia. It evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of the HeartBeam System compared with a standard 12-lead ECG in assessing acute coronary syndrome, which includes heart attack as well.

Eight cardiologists, blinded to each patient's diagnosis, independently interpreted both HeartBeam and standard 12-lead ECG recordings, with HeartBeam recordings read with the support of a clinical decision support system. Their interpretations were compared with each patient's final diagnosis for gold standard. At the top level, we can say that the results showed that the patient-recorded HeartBeam 3D ECG was as accurate as the standard 12-lead ECG. HeartBeam showed higher specificity at 81.8% compared with 71.4% for the standard 12-lead ECG, with comparable sensitivity of 60.2% compared with 63.0%. Very similar, which points to its potential as a rule-in diagnostic aid.

On the right-hand side, I would like to draw your attention to additional results of this study that are very encouraging indeed. The area under curve, so-called AUC, is a measure of overall diagnostic accuracy. Actually, you can view it as a measure of information content found in our 3D 3-lead and standard 12-lead signal as well. The 3D 3-lead and the 12-lead showed the same area under curve, same AUC. This is a super important finding, and we'll be using it in finalizing our U.S. pivotal study design. Also, every patient in the study was able to successfully obtain HeartBeam recording, which is a very encouraging sign for ease of use.

For STEMI heart attack, the most time-sensitive for all heart attacks, sensitivity was 82.9% for HeartBeam compared with 83.8% for standard 12-lead ECG. Again, very similar indeed. The cardiologists also agreed with one another more often when reading the HeartBeam recordings, with a reader agreement score known as Fleiss' kappa of 0.73 compared with 0.54 for the standard 12-lead ECG. As Rich mentioned, the results of this pivotal study will inform the design of our U.S. pivotal study, which is planned to commence in the first quarter of 2027, or possibly a little bit earlier, if everything gets accelerated. As Dr.

Nichol noted, these early findings demonstrate the potential of this technology to help shorten time to care for patients experiencing a heart attack. We want to say thank you to Dr. Nichol, all of our investigators, the patients, and all of the individuals that helped support this important study. Next slide, please. ALIGN-ACS is one of our growing body of clinical evidence. In October, we completed enrollment ahead of schedule in our HEADSTART-ACS, the largest heart attack assessment study to date using HeartBeam technology. The study was conducted in Indonesia, a country of 288 million people, spread across thousands of inhabited islands, where many patients are unable to readily access a 12-lead ECG when symptoms occur.

The study enrolled 486 patients presenting to the emergency department with chest pain at the National Cardiovascular Center Harapan Kita in Jakarta, Indonesia. The data analysis is underway, and we anticipate presenting the results at the cardiology conference in 2027. Together with ALIGN-ACS, we now have clinical experience with more than 600 patients in heart attack assessment. Next in line is our U.S. pivotal study planned, again, for beginning of 2027. It will support our FDA submission for the heart attack assessment. In October, we also joined the EU, actually, co-funded EXIT-CVD Research Consortium as a contributing partner alongside Philips, Medtronic, GE HealthCare, and other global health care organizations.

HeartBeam will lead the HEART-CHECK study, one of the project's 22 clinical studies examining high-risk patients. These studies are expanding our body of clinical evidence in heart attack assessment and are integral part, actually, of our heart attack detection commercialization plan. Next slide, please. Alongside the clinical and regulatory work, we are building the path to payment for our heart assessment product. It will highlight 3 areas. First, our acceptance into the FDA TAP program provides us with early connection with CMS, payers, patients, and provider organizations as we build real-world evidence and assess coding, coverage, and payment pathways. Breakthrough Device Designation is also a prerequisite for certain expedited Medicare coverage pathways.

Under the proposed RAPID pathway, CMS would issue a proposed national coverage determination on the same day an eligible Breakthrough Device receives FDA clearance. RAPID is proposed and not final yet, and we are actively evaluating how it may apply to HeartBeam. Second, the new CPT codes are emerging, including a recent Category III CPT code for algorithm-assisted ECG analysis to identify heart attack. This is an encouraging development, and of course, the coverage and payment decisions by CMS and payers are separate and still ahead. Third, we are building supporting evidence of our impact on reducing the time from symptoms onset to first medical contact.

We are working to determine endpoints related to reimbursement for a heart attack assessment study, informed by our early engagement with CMS and payer through TAP program. Next slide, please. I will finish with our AI program update, which builds on the same 3D ECG platform. Our data set includes more than 168 ECGs for heart attack training and more than 2,100 HeartBeam device recordings for testing. We finished development of our arrhythmia AI model, and our full attention and focus are now on heart attack assessment AI model. In early internal analysis of HeartBeam recordings, the AI identified more heart attacks than physicians reading the same recordings.

Sensitivity for our AI was about 12 percentage points higher across all heart attacks and 19 percentage points higher for non-ST elevation heart attacks, at actually similar specificity. These results are very encouraging, yet they are early, they are internal and not yet peer-reviewed, and HeartBeam AI remains investigational and is not FDA cleared at this time. Our initial atrial flutter algorithm, developed in collaboration with University Hospital Basel, Switzerland, showed 97% accuracy compared with electrophysiology study in 600 recordings using standard 12-lead ECGs. That work was presented as an abstract at EHRA 2026 European Conference and published in Europace, and the full manuscript has been accepted by Canadian Journal of Cardiology.

We are also collaborating on AI applications with Mount Sinai Hospital in New York and University Hospital Basel, Switzerland. Let me conclude by emphasizing our overarching goal: to shorten the time between the first symptoms and the decision to seek medical care. We aim to achieve this by providing patients and their physicians with clinical-grade cardiac information when every minute matters. We believe HeartBeam can help close the gap to the millions of people at risk. With that, I would like to hand it back to Rich.

Richard Ferrari: Yes. Thank you, Branislav. So, in fact, the next slide actually tees up Tim on the financials.

Timothy Cruickshank: Great. Thank you, Rich. Thanks, Branislav. Those were great updates. Taking a look at the Q3 2026 financials, and we'll focus in on cash flow first. Another $0.3 million from completing the ALIGN-ACS pilot study, and a further $0.1 million from lower employee costs. The takeaway here on cash flow, the focus on our heart attack detection programs providing an opportunity for enhanced capital efficiency. We keep a very low employee base, and we rely heavily on seasoned consultants focused on specific projects and objectives.

And so, when we determined it was time to go all in on accelerating our efforts towards heart attack detection, we're able to, not only quickly shift our capital allocation, but also reduce our overall spending significantly. And we're seeing evidence of that almost a quarter ahead of schedule. On the balance sheet, cash and cash equivalents totaled $6.1 million at September 30, 2026. And for the full year 2026, we now expect net operating cash outflow between $12 million and $12.5 million, which is a further reduction from prior guidance earlier in the year of staying below $14 million. R&D was $2.1 million compared to $3.3 million last year, and $2.3 million in Q2. Total operating expenses, $3.5 million compared to $5.3 million last year, and $5.1 million in Q2.

And net loss for the quarter, $3 million compared to the $5.3 million in the prior third quarter of 2025, and then $5 million in Q2. So across the board, SG&A, R&D, you're seeing evidence of the measures we put in place to enhance our capital efficiency, both in cash flow, but ongoing in the P&L as well. So for the 9 months of the year, operating expenses coming in at $13.3 million versus $15.8 million. That's a 16% decrease in the 9-month period. Net loss, $12.7 million versus $15.7 million in the prior 9 months, and cash used in operating activities, $9.5 million versus $11.1 million, a decrease of 14%. So as we look at that 9-month number of $9.5 million in net cash used in operating activities, you can quickly see the range of $12 million to $12.5 million for the full year and how that comes about with our anticipated spend of $2.5 million, and we've just buffered that for any acceleration we see in the pivotal study.

In summary, the purposefully variable nature of our cost base really allowed us to pivot quickly. We're laser-focused on accelerating the path to FDA clearance for heart attack assessment, and you're also seeing evidence of those efforts in our milestones, but amazingly in our cash reductions as well as we stay laser-focused. We're managing dilution to shareholders in one of the most controllable ways. We're reducing our noncore spend and really limiting our cash outflows. Richard Ferrari: Yes. Thank you. Our last slide is the summary and the key takeaways. We know exactly what needs to be done. We have great communications with the FDA. We're working on the really critical, important elements to really drive shareholder value. And between now and the end of 2027, I would tell you very little risk in our path going forward.
